The Moving World

Physics from the falling stone to the stars. Sixteen chapters on how things move, push, shine and spin, and how we know.

Written for Kym

Start reading

A letter to Kym

Dear Kym,

I should tell you something first: I am not a physicist. I don’t know much physics at all. What I have tried to do is make the book I would have loved to read when I was your age: one that tells you who found each idea and how, that lets you try things in the kitchen, and that never just hands you a formula to learn by heart. Much of what is in here was new to me too. I also had help: I made this book with the help of AI, which searched out the research, wrote the chapters to my design, and then checked them. The explanations draw on the free courses and books that MIT and OpenStax share with the world, and on what researchers have learned about the ideas students most often get wrong. Every fact, date and number was checked against reliable sources, more than once, by checkers whose only job was to find mistakes, and every number was worked out again from scratch. Even so, a few mistakes may have slipped through. If something here doesn’t match what you find somewhere else, or what your teacher says, or an experiment you do with your own hands, don’t simply trust the book: tell me, and we will find out together which is right. And where the people who really know physics still argue about something, the book says so.

Sit still for a moment. Really still: feet on the floor, hands in your lap. Now here is the strange part. You are moving at about 1,600 kilometres an hour. The ground under Mumbai is carried round by the turning Earth at that speed, faster than a passenger jet, and you are going with it. At the same time the whole Earth is racing round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second. Since you started reading this letter you have travelled further than the length of the Western line, and you have not felt a thing.

Why not? Fifteen hundred years ago, in Kusumapura, near today’s Patna, an astronomer named Aryabhata gave a beautiful answer. When you sit in a boat sliding smoothly downstream, he said, it is the trees on the bank that seem to move backwards. The stars seem to wheel across the sky for the same reason: it is we who are turning. It took the rest of the world more than a thousand years to agree with him, and it took Galileo and Newton to explain why steady motion cannot be felt. That explanation is the first big idea in this book, and you already half know it from every local train that has started so smoothly you only noticed when the platform began to slide away.

Physics is the study of how things move, push, pull, shine, warm up, cool down and hum. It explains why a cricket ball and a coin dropped together land together, why the steel thali feels colder than the wooden board when they sit in the same room, why the sky is blue and the Marine Drive sunset is orange, why the causeway to Haji Ali disappears under the sea twice a day, and how a magnet spinning inside a coil sends electricity to the fan above your head. It also explains the Moon, and how a spacecraft from Sriharikota could land gently near its south pole in 2023.

A lot of physics feels wrong at first. That is not because physics is weird. It is because your everyday experience is full of friction and air, and they hide the simple rules underneath. So almost every section of this book starts with an idea that seems obviously true: that a moving thing slowly runs out of push, that heavy things fall faster, that summer comes when the Earth is closer to the Sun, that something comes out of your eyes when you look. Clever people believed each of these for centuries. Then someone did an experiment that showed what really happens. You will do many of those experiments too, with things from the kitchen, your phone and a torch.

Before each answer the book will ask you to predict first. Please really do it: pick an answer before you read on. A prediction that turns out wrong is not a failure. It is the most useful moment in learning, because it shows you exactly where your picture of the world needs to change. Nobody is grading you here.

The book tries to explain everything in the simplest way that is still true. The physicist Richard Feynman, who was famous for making hard things clear, liked to say that knowing the name of something is not the same as knowing something about it. So you will see the thing first and learn its name afterwards. When a word sounds like an explanation but is only a label, like “energy makes it go”, the book tries to show you the spring and the gears instead. If something still doesn’t make sense, that is the book’s fault, not yours. Tell me, and we will find a better way to explain it together.

The heroes are real people: a Dutch engineer who dropped two lead balls from a church tower and heard a single thud, a doctor on a ship who noticed that sailors’ blood was the wrong colour, a man in Calcutta who rang a bell with invisible waves through the walls of a building, a physicist on a ship to Bombay who wondered why the sea is blue, and a nineteen-year-old on another ship from Bombay who worked out how stars die. When you see a word with a little book beside it, tap it, and you will get the whole story.

With love,

Amar

P.S. This is the second book. The first, The Invisible World, is about what things are made of. Whenever the two books meet, at atoms, at heat, at electrons, there is a link across.

How this book works

This book is one long adventure. It follows people across two and a half thousand years, from a Greek philosopher who was sure that a moving thing needs a mover, to an engineer dropping lead balls from a church tower in Delft, to a man in a shed in London weighing the whole Earth, to scientists in Calcutta, Bombay and Bengaluru working out what light is and how stars die. Each of them was trying to answer a question you will ask too: why do things move the way they do, and how do we know?

There are four volumes and sixteen chapters, numbered from 0 because Chapter 0 is the warm-up. Each chapter opens with a puzzle, follows the people who cracked it, and then explains the idea plainly, one numbered section at a time. You can read straight through, or jump to anything that makes you curious.

As you read, you will meet a few kinds of boxes. Each one has one job.

Story links
Some words in the text are marked like this. Each one opens a longer story beside the page: the full adventure of how that idea was found, with the idea explained slowly, step by step. They are all collected in Stories behind the ideas, and The adventure in time puts them in the order they happened.
The cast
Physics was made by people: a ship’s doctor, a bookbinder’s apprentice, a woman who found a measuring tape to the stars on glass photographs, a teacher in Dacca who wrote to Einstein. Their names are story links too. The cast, near the front, introduces them all.
Scenes
A small pin and a place and date, like Delft, 1586, means the story is taking you somewhere real. Every scene is on the adventure map.
Margin notes
When a new word matters, it is marked like this in the text and explained in the margin beside it (or just below, on a narrow screen). All of them are collected in Words worth knowing at the back.
Predict first
A question with a few possible answers. Choose one before you read on; the book remembers what you picked, and sometimes reminds you later.
Careful
A tempting idea that is wrong, and why it is wrong. Most of these are ideas that many clever people have had, so if you have had them too, you are in good company.
Understand it
Knowing the name of something is not the same as understanding it. Every major idea gets unpacked into five plain questions (what it is, why it is called that, what problem it solved, why it works, and how it helps), plus folded go-deeper notes and a space to explain it back in your own words.
Try it
Something to predict, sketch or work out.
Try it at home
A real experiment with things from the kitchen, a torch or your phone. Everything in these boxes is safe to do, but ask an adult first, and never use mains electricity.
Watch and play
Many pictures come alive: a button under them starts an animation, a sound, or a 3D model you can turn with your finger. Some can use your phone’s microphone or motion sensor, but only if you say yes, and nothing you record ever leaves your phone. They only move when you ask.
At school
A sentence on how your school book or exam might say the same thing in different words.
Check yourself
One question at the end of a section. The answers, with the reasoning, are at the back of the book.
Back from Chapter N
An old wrong idea, returning in a new place. Wrong ideas have a habit of creeping back, so the book checks on them.
Case file
A mystery at the end of each chapter. You get the clues; you work out what is going on. The solution is hidden until you ask for it.

Four explorers sit at the front of the book, for things you will want to come back to: Powers of Ten (from a proton to a galaxy), The Sky (the Sun, Earth and Moon, seen from space or from a Mumbai rooftop), The Ladder of Light (every kind of light, from radio to X-rays) and the adventure map.

Numbers in this book are real measured values unless the text says they are made up for a model. A few reading habits help: 10⁶ means a million (1 followed by six zeros), and 10⁻⁶ means one millionth. m/s means metres per second. m/s² means metres per second, every second. A newton (N) is about the weight of a small apple.

Five ideas that run through everything

Physics can look like a long list of separate laws and formulas. It is not. Almost everything in this book comes from five connected ideas, used again and again in different places. When something puzzles you, ask which of the five is at work.

  1. Forces change motion; they do not keep it going.A moving thing keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line unless something pushes or pulls on it. A sliding book slows down because the table rubs against it, not because the book runs out of push. A force is what makes something speed up, slow down or turn. And a force is never alone: whenever one object pushes another, the second pushes back on the first just as hard, in the opposite direction.
  2. Energy is never used up; it only changes form and spreads out.You can store energy by lifting a stone, stretching a spring, warming a pot of water or speeding up a ball. When anything happens, energy moves from one store to another, and the total amount stays exactly the same. What changes is how spread out that energy is. Once a bouncing ball has shared its energy with the floor and the air around it as tiny random jiggles of atoms, the energy is all still there, as warmth, but it is too scattered to gather back and lift the ball again.
  3. Everything is made of restless particles.Even a cold iron bar is made of atoms jiggling in place, and the air in a quiet room is made of molecules racing about faster than a rifle bullet, colliding billions of times a second. Temperature is simply how fast those particles jiggle on average. Pressure is the steady drumbeat of trillions of them bouncing off a wall. Melt, boil, cool or squeeze something, and you are just changing how its particles move and how closely they pack.
  4. Waves and fields carry energy across a gap without carrying matter across.Drop a pebble into a pond: the ripples travel across the water to the far bank, while a floating leaf only bobs up and down in place. Speak across a room: a pattern of squeezed and stretched air travels to your friend’s ear, while the air in front of your mouth stays near your mouth. A magnet pulls an iron pin across empty space, and sunlight crosses 150 million kilometres of vacuum to warm your face, carried by electric and magnetic fields.
  5. One set of rules governs both Earth and sky.For thousands of years people assumed that the heavens followed one set of rules and the Earth another. They do not. The gravity that pulls a dropped stone to the floor is the very same pull that holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth and the Earth in orbit around the Sun. The glowing gases in a streetlamp emit and absorb the very same colours of light as the gases in a distant star, which is how we know what the stars are made of without ever visiting them.

And underneath all five is a single habit of mind: keep what you observe separate from the model you use to explain it, and test every model by predicting what will happen next. What you see or measure is the observation. The story of forces, particles or waves that explains it is the model, and a good experiment can always sharpen it or prove it wrong.

Chapter 0

The physicist’s way of seeing

The big questionHow can one man, with a stick, a shadow and a traveller’s story about a well, measure the whole Earth?

  1. 0.1What we see and what we think
  2. 0.2Measuring anything
  3. 0.3Powers of ten
  4. 0.4Guess like a physicist

Nobody standing on the ground has ever seen the whole Earth. From Marine Drive the sea looks flat to the horizon. From a plane the horizon is a gentle curve, and that is all you get. Yet about 2,200 years ago, a Greek scholar living in Alexandria worked out how far it is all the way round the Earth, and his answer was good. He never left Egypt. His equipment was an upright stick, the shadow it cast at noon, and a story a traveller had brought from a town far to the south.

This chapter is about how he could do that, and it contains no law of physics at all. Its subject is a way of looking at the world that every later chapter depends on: keeping what you see separate from what you think it means; measuring carefully, and saying how sure you are; being at ease with enormous and tiny numbers; and knowing how to make a good guess before you make a careful measurement. The Invisible World used this way of seeing to find atoms. Here we use it to size up a planet, and then to start on the real subject of this book: things that move.

0.1What we see and what we think

Alexandria, around 200 BCE

Eratosthenes was told a curious thing. At Syene, a town far up the Nile to the south, there was a deep vertical well, and at noon on the longest day of the year the sunlight reached all the way to the bottom of it. That could only happen if the Sun stood exactly overhead. In Alexandria, on that same day at that same noon, an upright column cast a short but definite shadow. The Sun was not quite overhead there.

Two observations, from two cities. On their own they are just facts. What made Eratosthenes a physicist was what he did next: he asked what picture of the world would make both facts true at once, and then he asked what else that picture would let him work out. Hold on to his two facts. The chapter ends with his answer.

Observation

Something seen or measured that another careful person could check. Observations are where every investigation starts.

Model

A picture or description of how something works, built from observations, used to explain them and to predict new ones. Models are always simpler than the real thing and usually right only within limits.

Everything in science starts with an observation: something a careful person can see, hear or measure, and that another careful person could check. “The well is lit to the bottom at noon on the longest day” is an observation. “The Sun is directly over Syene” is already a small step beyond it, and “the Earth is round” is a much bigger step. Those bigger steps are a model: a picture of how things are, built to explain the observations. The observation is what anyone would see. The model is our best explanation so far.

Take the roundness of the Earth. Educated Greeks already knew it two thousand years before Columbus, and they knew it for good reasons. Aristotle collected them. When the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, the edge of that shadow is always a circle. Travellers heading south see new stars appear above the southern horizon, while the North Star sinks lower behind them. And a ship sailing away does not simply shrink to a dot. Its hull disappears first, while the mast and sail are still in view. Each of these is an observation. The model that explains all three is a ball. A flat disc can cast a round shadow only when it faces the light squarely; turned edge-on, it casts a line. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.

Predict first

On a clear day you watch a ship sail straight away from Marine Drive, through binoculars. As it gets further away, what do you expect to see?

  1. The whole ship shrinks evenly until it is a dot
  2. The bottom of the ship disappears first; the mast is the last thing you see
  3. The top of the mast disappears first; the hull is the last thing you see

What happens

The hull goes first and the mast last, as sailors have always reported. On a flat sea the whole ship would simply shrink. The bulge of water between you and the ship hides the lowest part first, which is exactly what a round Earth predicts.

Here is the part that matters most. Pythagoras, two centuries before Aristotle, also said the Earth was a sphere. His reason was that spheres were the most perfect shape, so the Earth ought to be one. He reached the right answer with no evidence at all. Aristotle reached the same answer by asking what shape would explain the shadow, the stars and the ships. Only the second way is science. A model earns its place by explaining what we see, and by predicting something we have not looked at yet.

Even a good model can be defended too long. The Greeks knew that if the Earth travelled round the Sun, the nearer stars should seem to shift against the farther ones during the year, the way a lamp post seems to shift against the buildings behind it as you walk past. They looked for that shift and could not find one. Most of them concluded that the Earth stays still. The other possibility, that the stars are so unimaginably far away that the shift is too small to see, seemed absurd. It was true. The shift was finally measured, with telescopes, about two thousand years later, and we will meet it again when we measure the distance to the stars.

Law

A short statement of a pattern that has held in every case tested, often a single equation.

Theory

A well-tested explanation, checked many times by many people. To a scientist, “it’s only a theory” makes no sense: a theory is as good as explanations get.

So a physicist keeps two columns in her head. In one column go the observations, which stay true whatever anyone thinks. In the other go the models, which are our best explanations so far and can always be improved. A law is a short statement of a pattern that has held in every case anyone has tested. A theory is a well-tested explanation of why the pattern holds. Neither is ever proved beyond all doubt, because nobody can test every possible case. What we can say is: every test so far agrees, and one good test that disagreed would sink it.

Careful

“The Greeks thought the Earth was flat, and Columbus proved it was round.”

Educated people around the Mediterranean knew the Earth was round at least two thousand years before Columbus sailed. Eratosthenes did not set out to prove it was round. He assumed it, because Aristotle’s evidence was already convincing, and used that model to do something new: measure how big the round Earth is.

Understand itModel

What is it?

A simplified picture or description of how part of the world works, built from observations and used to explain them and to predict new ones.

Why is it called this?

From the Italian modello, an architect’s small scale figure of a building, from Latin modulus, a small measure. A scientific model is a small mental working copy of something too big, too small or too hidden to take in all at once.

What problem did it solve?

Observations on their own are a heap of separate facts: a curved shadow on the Moon, a well lit at noon, a ship’s hull vanishing before its mast. A model ties the heap together into one picture so you can ask what else must be true.

Why does it work?

Because it leaves out the details that do not matter for the question in hand, such as mountains and waves when you are sizing up the whole Earth, and keeps the geometry or mechanism that does.

How does it help?

Once you have a model, you can calculate things nobody has directly measured yet, just as Eratosthenes used the round-Earth model and two shadows to work out the distance all the way round the planet.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

A model earns our trust when it predicts a new observation before anyone looks, and fails the moment a careful test disagrees with what it predicts.

What it isn’t

It is not the real thing itself, and it is not a guess made up without evidence. Pythagoras calling the Earth a sphere because spheres seemed perfect was a wish, not a scientific model.

Where does it stop working?

Every model has edges where its simplifications start to matter: a perfect sphere is fine for Eratosthenes, while satellite navigation has to allow for the real Earth bulging by about 21 km at the equator.

Your turn

Explain Model to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

At school

IB MYP science names models and evidence among the ideas every science shares. Cambridge IGCSE physics does not have a topic on this at all; its first topic is measuring. The habit is taken for granted, which is why we practise it here.

Check yourself

A friend says: “The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so the Sun goes round the Earth.” Which part of that sentence is an observation, and which is a model? Can you think of a second model that fits the same observation?

Answer at the back of the book

0.2Measuring anything

Sèvres, near Paris, 1879

In 1879 a metalworker named George Matthey made a small cylinder: 39 millimetres tall and 39 millimetres across, nine parts platinum to one part iridium. It went to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sèvres, just outside Paris, and sat under three glass bell jars, one inside the other, with six official copies kept alongside it. For the next 130 years, when anyone anywhere said “one kilogram”, that is what they meant: exactly as much stuff as that cylinder, no more and no less. Every kitchen scale in Mumbai traced back, through a chain of copies, to a lump of metal in a French vault.

It had a flaw. Over the decades, tiny amounts of whatever floated in the air stuck to its surface, and its mass slowly changed. The changes were far too small to feel. They were not too small to measure, and a kilogram that drifts is a kilogram nobody can fully trust. So on 20 May 2019 the cylinder was retired. The kilogram is now defined by fixing a constant of nature called the Planck constant at exactly 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, together with the already-fixed metre and second. The sentence is a mouthful, but the idea is simple. We stopped trusting a lump of metal and tied the kilogram to a number of nature that never changes, anywhere, ever.

The story behind this

The kilogram that changedFor 130 years the whole world’s kilogram was a small metal cylinder in a vault near Paris; when it began, slowly and inexplicably, to disagree with its own copies, the kilogram was rebuilt on a number of nature instead.
Unit

An agreed amount of something, such as one metre or one second, that everyone measures against. A measurement is a number of units: 20 metres, 3.5 seconds.

Why go to that trouble? Because a measurement is a number and a unit, and the unit has to mean the same thing to everyone. “The pitch is 20” tells you nothing. “The pitch is 20 metres” does. A unit is an agreed amount that everyone measures against, and a measurement is how many of those amounts you have. The world has agreed on a set called SI units. There are seven basic ones; for this book you need three: the metre for length, the kilogram for mass and the second for time. Everything else is built from them. Speed is metres per second, m/s. Later you will meet the newton and the joule, which are also just combinations of metres, kilograms and seconds with a short name.

The three basic units have each made the same journey, from an object to a number of nature. The metre began in 1791 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole, became a platinum–iridium bar in 1889, then a certain number of wavelengths of light from krypton in 1960, and since 1983 it has been the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The second was one 86,400th of an average day until 1967; now it is a count of 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a caesium atom. The kilogram was the last to leave its lump of metal behind. Since 20 May 2019 all seven base units rest on seven fixed constants, and a laboratory anywhere can build a kilogram, a metre or a second from scratch without asking Paris.

Now the part that trips people up. Suppose you measure a stick with a ruler marked in millimetres, and it comes to 36.5 mm. That last digit, the 5, is a guess. The end of the stick fell somewhere between the 36 and the 37 marks, and you estimated how far between. With a ruler marked only in centimetres you would have written 3.6 cm, or perhaps 3.7, and the 6 or 7 would be the guess. The finer the marks, the more digits you can honestly write down, and the last one is always uncertain.

Uncertainty

The range within which a measurement’s true value probably lies. Every measurement has one. As a percentage: uncertainty ÷ value × 100.

Every measurement carries an uncertainty: the range within which the true value probably lies. That range is honesty about what the instrument can tell you, and a careful measurement always states it. Physicists often write it as a percentage. If a kitchen scale reads 150 g for a katori of rice, and repeated weighings scatter by about 2 g either way, the uncertainty is 2 in 150, about 1.3%. (Those numbers are invented to show the method; your scale and your katori will give you real ones.)

Predict first

You weigh the same katori of rice five times on a kitchen scale, lifting it off and putting it back between weighings. What do you expect the five readings to look like?

  1. Exactly the same number every time
  2. Numbers that differ by a gram or two
  3. Numbers all over the place

What happens

Usually the second. The scale rounds to the nearest gram, the katori lands in slightly different spots, the air moves. The spread of your five readings is a direct measure of your uncertainty, and it is worth doing: it turns a vague “about 150 g” into “150 g, give or take 2”.

Two more words, which people mix up. A measurement is accurate if it is close to the true value. It is precise if repeating it gives nearly the same answer each time. They are not the same. A scale that reads 20 g with nothing on it will give you five very similar readings, all 20 g too high: precise and wrong. The cure is to check your instrument against something you trust, which is exactly why the world keeps standards like the old kilogram and its replacement.

Careful

“My scale gave the same reading five times, so it must be right.”

Agreeing with itself is precision. Being right is accuracy. A scale can be beautifully precise and still read 20 g too high every single time. Check it: weigh something whose mass you know, such as a sealed 1 kg packet, and see what it says.

At school

Cambridge IGCSE defines mass as “a measure of the quantity of matter in an object”. When the kitchen scale says 1 kg, that is the mass it means. Weight is something different, a force, and it arrives in Chapter 3.

Check yourself

A friend measures a pencil with an ordinary school ruler and writes down 17.3482 cm. What has gone wrong?

Answer at the back of the book

0.3Powers of ten

In the store cupboard there is a 25 kg sack of rice. How many grains are in it? Nobody is going to count them. And yet, with a teaspoon and a kitchen scale, you can know the answer well enough to be sure of it.

Predict first

How many grains of rice are in a 25 kg sack?

  1. About ten thousand
  2. About a million
  3. About a hundred million
  4. About ten billion

What happens

About a million, and the next section of text shows how you can find that out for yourself in ten minutes. Most people guess far too high or far too low, because big numbers all feel the same. The point of this section is to make them feel different.

Here is the chain. Count the grains in one level teaspoon. Suppose you get about 200 (your own count will replace that number). Weigh ten level teaspoons together, because a kitchen scale cannot weigh one grain or even one teaspoon honestly; suppose ten teaspoons come to 50 g, so one teaspoon is 5 g. Then 200 grains weigh 5 g, so there are 40 grains in a gram, 40,000 in a kilogram, and 40,000 × 25 = 1,000,000 in the sack. A million. If your teaspoon count is 20% different from mine, your answer will be 20% different too, and that is fine. The question was “how many, roughly?”, and for that kind of question an answer within a factor of ten either way counts as close enough.

A teaspoon of rice

Tip a level teaspoon of rice onto a plate and push the grains into groups of ten with a finger; count the groups. Do it three times with three fresh teaspoons: the counts will not agree exactly, and the spread between them is your uncertainty from Section 0.2. Then weigh ten level teaspoons on the kitchen scale, divide by ten for one teaspoon, and work out grains per gram, grains per kilogram packet, and grains per 25 kg sack. Write the sack’s number in the form “something × 10 to a power”. Everything goes back in the rice tin afterwards.

Power of ten

The small raised number in 10⁶ or 10⁻³. It counts how many times ten has been multiplied (or, when negative, divided). 10⁶ is a million; 10⁻³ is a thousandth.

Order of magnitude

The power of ten of a quantity when it is written as a number times a power of ten. Two things of the same order of magnitude are within about a factor of ten of each other.

A million is written 1,000,000, and physicists prefer to write it 10⁶: a one followed by six zeros, or ten multiplied by itself six times. A thousand is 10³. A thousandth, 0.001, is 10⁻³. The little number is the power of ten, and it is the single most useful number about any quantity, because it tells you the scale you are on. Numbers with the same power of ten are said to have the same order of magnitude: 800 and 450 are both around 10², both “a few hundred”, and for a rough question they count as the same size.

Look at where things sit on the ladder in Figure 0.3. A grain of sand is three steps below you: a thousand times smaller. A hydrogen atom is ten steps below you, and the Sun is nine steps above you, so from an atom to the Sun is nineteen steps of ten, which is a one followed by nineteen zeros. Each step multiplies. Ten times bigger, and then ten times bigger again, is not twenty times bigger; it is a hundred times bigger. People’s intuition treats the steps as if they were additions, and that is why a million and a billion feel like neighbours when one is a thousand times the other. This is also why “too small to see” is not one size. A bacterium and an electron are both invisible, and in mass they are fifteen steps of ten apart, far more steps than separate you from the Sun.

The prefixes you already use are steps on this ladder: kilo means ×1,000 (10³), centi means ÷100 (10⁻²), milli means ÷1,000 (10⁻³), micro ÷1,000,000 (10⁻⁶) and nano ÷1,000,000,000 (10⁻⁹). Converting between them is just moving the decimal point. Figure 0.3 itself is drawn with each step the same width, which is called a logarithmic scale. Such a scale never reaches zero, because there is always another step down: a tenth, a hundredth, a thousandth, for ever.

The Powers of Ten explorer at the front of this book lets you climb this ladder with your thumb, from a proton out to the Milky Way, with a readout of how many times bigger each thing is than the last. Spend a few minutes there now. The feel for scale you get from it will be used in every chapter after this one.

Investigation 0.3

In the Powers of Ten explorer, start at yourself and zoom out until the Earth fills the view, counting the ×10 steps. Then zoom in from yourself to a hydrogen atom and count again. Which journey has more steps? Check your counts against Figure 0.3.

Careful

“Ten times bigger, and then ten times bigger again, is twenty times bigger.”

It is a hundred times bigger. Each step on the ladder multiplies by ten; it does not add ten. Three steps is a thousand times, six steps a million times. The steps on Figure 0.3 are drawn equal in width, but each one is ten times the jump of the one before.

Understand itOrder of magnitude

What does it measure?

The rough scale of a number, given by the nearest power of ten: whether something is measured in tens, thousands, millions or millionths.

Why is it called this?

Magnitude comes from the Latin magnitudo, size, and order means rank or step on a ladder. Astronomers first ranked stars by brightness into first, second and third magnitude; physicists borrowed the phrase for steps of ten in size.

What problem did it solve?

Human intuition treats big numbers as one blurry crowd, so a million and a billion feel like neighbours when one is a thousand times the other. Counting powers of ten turns impossible-looking comparisons into small steps you can count on your fingers.

Why does it work?

Because when two quantities are multiplied or divided, their powers of ten simply add or subtract, letting you check the scale of an answer before touching a calculator.

How does it help?

It lets you estimate how many grains of rice sit in a 25 kg sack or how many tonnes of rain fall on Mumbai in a day, and catch a thousand-fold mistake in a calculation at a glance.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

When Fermi estimated ~100 piano tuners in Chicago by multiplying rough factors of ten, directory counts confirmed the real number was within the same order of magnitude.

What it isn’t

It is not a licence to be sloppy when precision is available; it is the first check that tells you which ballpark your careful measurement must land in.

Where does it stop working?

When two competing effects nearly cancel out, such as comparing two masses that differ by one part in a million, rough powers of ten cannot tell which one wins.

Your turn

Explain Order of magnitude to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

How many seconds are there in a day? Write the answer in the form “a number times a power of ten”, and say how many steps up the ladder a year is from a day.

Answer at the back of the book

0.4Guess like a physicist

It is a monsoon afternoon in July, the lanes are rivers, and the news says 100 mm of rain has fallen on the city since morning. A hundred millimetres is ten centimetres: it would barely cover your ankle. How much water is that, over the whole of Mumbai?

Predict first

How much rain falls on the whole of Mumbai on a day with 100 mm of rainfall?

  1. A few swimming pools’ worth
  2. A few thousand tonnes
  3. Tens of millions of tonnes
  4. More than the whole Arabian Sea

What happens

Tens of millions of tonnes. Hardly anyone guesses this right first time, because it needs two steps of reasoning rather than a feeling. By the end of this section you will be able to work it out on the back of a bus ticket.

Physicists make rough estimates like this all the time, and they have a name for them: Fermi problems, after Enrico Fermi, who was famous for working out surprising numbers on the back of an envelope. The method has two steps. First, find quantities you can estimate or look up. Second, find the relationship that joins them to the thing you want. Then check that the units come out right.

The story behind this

Guess like a physicistHow to get a number you can defend for something nobody has counted, from the grains in a rice sack to the rain on a whole city.

For the rain, the relationship is simple: the volume of water is the area it fell on multiplied by how deep it lies. Look at a map. Mumbai is a long, thin strip running north–south. Call it about 40 km long and about 15 km wide. That gives an area of about 600 km², which is 6 × 10⁸ m². The depth is 100 mm, or 0.1 m. So the volume is 6 × 10⁸ m² × 0.1 m = 6 × 10⁷ m³. A cubic metre of water has a mass of 1,000 kg, a tonne, so the rain weighs about 6 × 10¹⁰ kg: sixty million tonnes, in one day, on one city. Written as bottles, it is 6 × 10¹⁰ one-litre bottles: sixty billion of them.

Check the units before you believe it. Kilometres had to become metres before they met the depth in metres, and then m² × m = m³, a volume; volume × kg/m³ = kg, a mass. The units agreeing does not make an estimate right, but units that disagree always mean a mistake somewhere.

Now the honest question: how good is this number? Only as good as its weakest input. The city’s area you can read off a map to within perhaps 20%. The rainfall is much shakier. The 100 mm was one gauge’s reading, and rain over a city is patchy; Colaba and Borivali can have quite different days. If the real average depth was 50 mm, the answer halves. If it was 200 mm, it doubles. So the depth is the input worth improving, and you can improve it yourself.

A rain gauge on the balcony

Ask an adult before you set anything up on a balcony or windowsill. Find a tall glass or jar with straight vertical sides: a bottle with a narrow neck will not do, because then the depth of water inside no longer equals the depth of rain. Stand it in the open, away from the overhang of the roof, inside a bucket or weighed down so the wind cannot take it. After a day of rain, measure the depth of water with a ruler, in millimetres. That is your rainfall, in the same units the weather office uses. Compare it with the figure in the news for your part of the city, and then redo the whole-city sum with your own number.

The classic example is Fermi’s own: how many piano tuners are there in Chicago? Nobody knows the inputs exactly, and it does not matter. Chicago had about 3 million people, perhaps 5 to a home, perhaps one home in ten with a piano, so about 60,000 pianos. If a tuner can tune about 750 pianos a year, the city needs about 80 tuners. Fermi rounded that to “about a hundred”, and about a hundred is right. A blind guess might have been 10 or 100,000. An estimate like this is a chain of reasonable links, and anyone can check each link and tighten it; a wild guess offers nothing to check.

Notice how the answers are written: “about 100”, “about 60 million tonnes”. Never “60,300,000 tonnes”. An estimate whose inputs are good to 20% cannot have an answer good to the nearest tonne, and writing extra digits pretends otherwise. One significant figure, sometimes two, is all an estimate has earned. This habit, of guessing first and only then measuring, runs through every chapter of this book. Before any experiment, ask what you expect, roughly. If the measurement comes out a thousand times off your estimate, one of them is wrong, and you will want to know which.

Careful

“An estimate is just a wild guess with a number on the end.”

A guess is a feeling. An estimate is a chain: a few inputs you can defend, a relationship you can state, and units that check out. Anyone can look at the chain, point at the weakest link and replace it with a better number. That is why “about a hundred piano tuners” is worth far more than “lots”.

Check yourself

A new tower near your school has 40 storeys. Estimate its height, and say which input you trust least.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 0

The shadow at Syene

Back to Alexandria. Here is everything Eratosthenes had.

  1. At noon on the longest day of the year, sunlight reached the bottom of a vertical well at Syene, far to the south. So at that moment the Sun stood exactly overhead at Syene.
  2. In Alexandria, to the north, at that same noon, an upright column cast a shadow. From the lengths of the column and its shadow, the sunlight was arriving at an angle of 1/50 of a full circle away from straight down: about 7°, or exactly 7.2°.
  3. The distance from Alexandria to Syene was known: 5,000 stadia, a stadion being the length of a Greek running track.
  4. The Sun is enormously far away, about 150 million kilometres, so its rays reach the whole Earth travelling almost exactly parallel to one another. If everyone on Earth pointed at the Sun at the same instant, all their arms would be parallel.

Use Figure 0.5. What two things did Eratosthenes have to assume, beyond his observations? How far is it all the way round the Earth, in stadia? And why, more than two thousand years later, can nobody say exactly how close he came?

Show the solution

He assumed two things. The Earth is a sphere, which Aristotle’s evidence had made reasonable. And sunlight arrives in parallel rays, which is true because the Sun is so far away.

Then the reasoning runs like this. “Straight up” at Syene points at the Sun. “Straight up” at Alexandria points 7.2° away from the Sun. Since the sunlight is parallel at both places, “straight up” at the two cities must differ by 7.2°, and on a sphere that can only mean the two cities are 7.2° apart around its curve, which is 1/50 of the way round. So the whole way round is 50 times the distance between them: 50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia.

How good was that? The modern figure is 40,000 km. For Eratosthenes’ number to equal it, a stadion would have to be 160 m. The trouble is that nobody knows which stadion he used; several lengths were in use. With the common Olympic stadion his answer comes out about 20% too big, roughly 48,000 km. With another stadion of about a sixth of a kilometre it comes out at about 41,700 km, about 4% too big. (Some books say “within 1%” for that stadion; redo the multiplication and you will find they are wrong.) So the honest statement is: the method was brilliant, the answer was somewhere between a few percent and about a fifth too large, and we cannot say exactly, because a measurement is a number and a unit, and the unit was never written down precisely enough.

There is a lovely echo. In 1791 the metre itself was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the pole. That made the circumference of the Earth 40,000 km by definition: Eratosthenes’ question, answered by turning it into a unit.

One more thing. Mumbai lies south of the Tropic of Cancer, so twice a year, once in May and once in July, the noon Sun stands straight overhead and an upright stick casts no shadow at all. On those days Mumbai is Syene. A friend with a stick in a city far to the north could be Alexandria, and the two of you could measure the Earth with a phone call and a ruler.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You can now separate what you see from what you think, measure something and say how sure you are, place any quantity on the ladder of tens, and make a guess that is worth something. What you cannot yet do is describe the simplest event in the world: a ball tossed into the air. Where is it, how fast is it going, which way, and how is that changing from one instant to the next? Those words, position, velocity and acceleration, took people two thousand years to get right. Chapter 1 gets them right in a train and a bathroom.

Where this chapter comes from

1

Chapter 1

Describing motion

The big questionAt the very top of a throw, the ball stops for an instant. Is anything happening to it then?

  1. 1.1Where and when
  2. 1.2How fast, and which way
  3. 1.3Speeding up, slowing down and turning
  4. 1.4Galileo’s ramps
  5. 1.5The top of a throw

Eratosthenes measured the Earth by keeping two things apart: what he saw, and what he thought it meant. This chapter turns that same habit on the most ordinary thing in the world, something moving. Before anyone could ask why a ball flies, falls and stops, they had to learn to say exactly how it moves: where it is, when, how fast, in which direction, and how fast that is changing. Getting those words right took about two thousand years. Physicists call this part of the subject kinematics, the describing of motion, and it is the grammar of everything that follows.

Here is the puzzle to carry through the chapter. Toss a ball straight up. It rises, slows, and for one instant at the very top it is not moving at all. Then it falls. Is anything happening to the ball at that instant? Most people say no: it has stopped, so nothing is going on. In one study, 44% of students said the ball’s acceleration at the top is zero. By the end of this chapter you will film your own toss in slow motion and read the answer off the bathroom tiles.

1.1Where and when

Churchgate station, Mumbai, a weekday morning

The local pulls out so gently that for a moment it is the platform that seems to slide backwards, with its pillars and its tea stall and the people on it. Then your body catches up with what your eyes are saying and the world rights itself: the train is moving, the platform is still. But stop and ask how you know. If the windows were painted over and the ride were perfectly smooth, could anything inside the carriage tell you whether it was moving or standing at the platform? You could drop a coin, pour water, toss a ball, bounce it. Every one of those would happen exactly as it does in your kitchen.

Galileo made this point with a ship. Shut yourself in a windowless cabin on a ship moving steadily over calm water, and nothing you can do in the cabin will tell you whether the ship is moving or tied up at the quay. Steady motion cannot be felt. The word steady is doing all the work in that sentence; a braking train is felt by everybody, and that is the subject of Section 1.3 and of Chapter 2. But as long as the motion is steady, “is it moving?” turns out to be a question about what you are comparing the train with, and about nothing else.

Reference frame

The thing you choose to measure positions from, with a set of directions: the ground, a train, a boat. All steadily moving frames are equally good; motion only means something relative to a stated frame.

Position

Where something is, measured from a chosen point in a chosen frame: “3 m from the back of the carriage”, “200 m north of the station”.

That comparison is called a reference frame: the thing you choose to measure positions from, together with the directions you measure along. Standing on the platform you use the station as your frame, and the train moves. Sitting in the train you use the carriage as your frame, and the platform moves. Neither frame is the true one. The frame is the viewpoint you have chosen, not a backdrop that comes with the world, and once you have chosen it, every position is a location measured within it: three metres down the carriage, or two hundred metres north of the station.

Predict first

Your friend walks steadily along a corridor, bouncing a ball as she goes. To her the ball goes straight up and down beside her hand. You stand still at the end of the corridor and watch. What path do you see the ball trace?

  1. Straight up and down, the same as she sees
  2. A series of curved arcs: up and forward, down and forward
  3. It depends how fast she walks: a zigzag if she hurries, straight up and down if she strolls

What happens

A series of curved arcs, however slowly she walks, because between one bounce and the next the ball has moved along the corridor with her. For her the ball goes straight up and down. Neither of you is wrong. You are describing the same motion in two different frames, and each description is exactly right in its own frame.

Try it in a corridor at home or at school, taking turns to be the walker and the watcher. Then try it in your head on the train. You walk towards the front of a carriage at an easy 5 km/h while the train does 80 km/h along the track. Relative to the carriage you are moving at 5 km/h. Relative to the track you are moving at 85 km/h, and if you turn round and walk towards the back, at 75 km/h. All three numbers are true at the same time; each belongs to its frame. To change frames you simply add the frame’s own velocity, which is the whole secret of this chapter’s closing case. (The train’s 80 km/h here is a round number for the sum, not a timetable figure.)

Distance and displacement

Distance is the length of the path travelled, a scalar. Displacement is the change in position, from start to finish, with its direction: a vector.

Vector and scalar

A vector has a size and a direction (displacement, velocity, force). A scalar has a size only (distance, speed, mass, time).

Two more words have to be separated, because everyday speech blurs them. A cyclist rides 3 km west, turns round and rides 2 km east. The distance she has travelled is 5 km: the length of the whole path, the number her bicycle’s odometer would show. Her displacement is 1 km west: where she ended up compared with where she began, with the direction. If she had ridden back to her starting point her distance would be 6 km and her displacement zero. Displacement is a vector, a quantity with a size and a direction. Distance is a scalar, a size alone. The difference seems like hair-splitting until Section 1.2, where it makes two quantities that sound alike come out completely different.

Careful

“The platform is really still and the train is really moving. The ground is the true frame; the train’s view is an illusion.”

For steady motion there is no experiment, inside or outside the train, that can crown one frame the true one. The ground is the handy frame, because we live on it, and that is all. Keep the word steady, though. The moment the train brakes you can tell, with your eyes shut, that something has changed. Steady velocity cannot be felt; a change of velocity can. That difference is the hinge of Chapter 2.

At school

Cambridge IGCSE sorts quantities into scalars, which have size only, like mass, and vectors, which have size and direction, like weight. Distance is a scalar and displacement a vector in exactly that sense.

Check yourself

You walk from your front door to the shop at the corner, 300 m away, and come back. What distance did you cover, and what was your displacement?

Answer at the back of the book

1.2How fast, and which way

Speed

How fast something covers distance: distance travelled divided by the time taken, in metres per second (m/s). A scalar.

Take the corridor again, with a phone stopwatch and a chalk mark every metre. Walk six metres in three seconds. Your speed was 6 m ÷ 3 s = 2 m/s, two metres every second. That is the first and simplest number about motion: speed is distance divided by the time it took. A car that covers 150 km in 3.2 hours averaged 47 km/h. A student who walks 205 m at a steady 1.4 m/s takes 205 ÷ 1.4 = 146 s, about two and a half minutes. A cricket ball, a train, a planet: speed is always distance over time, and its unit in physics is metres per second.

Instantaneous speed

The speed at one instant, found by taking the average speed over a smaller and smaller time around that instant. It is what a speedometer shows.

But “the car averaged 47 km/h” hides everything that happened on the way: traffic, a stop for chai, a fast stretch on the Sea Link. The speedometer shows something different, the speed right now. To get at that, physicists take the distance covered in a shorter and shorter time: the last minute, the last second, the last hundredth of a second. As the interval shrinks, the average over it settles down to one value, the instantaneous speed, the speed at that instant. Every speedometer is an instrument for doing that sum.

Velocity

Displacement divided by the time taken: speed together with a direction. A vector. A round trip has an average velocity of zero whatever its average speed.

Now bring back the vector from Section 1.1. An auto-rickshaw takes you 3 km to the market and 3 km back in half an hour. Its average speed is 6 km ÷ 0.5 h = 12 km/h. Its average velocity is zero. Velocity is displacement divided by time, and the auto’s displacement was zero: it ended where it began. Velocity is the vector version of speed, with a direction attached: 1.7 m/s north; 2 m/s towards the front of the carriage; 12 km/h, but which way? The distinction matters because the laws of motion in the next chapters are about velocity, direction included. A thing that turns a corner at a steady speed has changed its velocity, and Section 1.3 takes that further.

The best tool for seeing all of this at once is a graph with time along the bottom and position up the side.

Read Figure 1.2 slowly. For the first three seconds the line climbs steadily: two metres of position for every second of time, which is a velocity of 2 m/s. Then the line goes flat: time passes but position does not change, so you were standing still. Then it slopes downwards: position is decreasing, so you were walking back, and it drops 3 m in 3 s, a velocity of 1 m/s in the backward direction, which we would write as −1 m/s if forward is positive. The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity. Steep means fast; flat means still; downhill means going the other way. If the line were curved, with its slope changing from moment to moment, the slope at any one point would be the instantaneous velocity there.

The story behind this

Reading a motion graphA graph of a walk down a corridor is not a picture of the corridor. Learn to read its slope and the area under it, and every motion graph in the book opens up.

Predict first

In Figure 1.2 your line and your friend’s dashed line cross at 4 seconds. At that moment, which of these is true?

  1. You are at the same place
  2. You are moving at the same speed
  3. Both

What happens

Only the first. Crossing lines mean the same position at the same time, nothing more. Your speed is the slope of your line, which is flat: zero. Your friend’s slope is 0.5 m/s. You are standing still as she walks past you. The same thing happens at 8 seconds, when you overtake her on your way back, walking twice as fast as she does. Being in the same place at the same time says nothing about how fast either of you is going.

Careful

“The graph shows the path the walker took.”

The horizontal axis is time, not a direction in space. The walk in Figure 1.2 happened along one straight corridor; the graph’s rising and falling shows position changing as the seconds pass. A curved position–time graph does not mean a curved path. When you meet the graph of a thrown ball in Section 1.5 this will matter.

At school

Cambridge Lower Secondary calls this a distance–time graph, with speed as its gradient; IGCSE topic 1.2, Motion, uses the same graphs. Ours is a position–time graph, which is why it can slope downwards when you walk back. A graph of distance travelled can only ever climb.

Understand itVelocity

What does it measure?

How fast an object’s position is changing and in which direction: displacement divided by time taken, measured in metres per second (m/s).

Why is it called this?

From the Latin velocitas, swiftness, from velox, swift. Everyday English uses velocity as a grand word for speed, which is misleading: in physics, velocity always includes the direction of travel.

What problem did it solve?

Speed alone cannot tell you where a moving thing will end up: walking at 2 m/s north and walking at 2 m/s south have the same speed and take you to opposite ends of the street.

Why does it work?

Because treating motion as an arrow with both a size and a direction lets you add motions in different frames of reference and read velocity straight off the slope of a position–time graph.

How does it help?

It lets you work out where two trains on the Western line will meet, how a boat crosses a flowing river, and why turning a corner at steady speed still counts as a change of motion.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Every frame-transformation experiment, from walking down a moving train carriage to tracking aircraft in a crosswind, shows that positions and velocities add as directed arrows (vectors), not as plain numbers.

What it isn’t

It is not average speed along a winding path: an auto-rickshaw that drives 3 km to the market and 3 km home in half an hour has an average speed of 12 km/h and an average velocity of zero.

Where does it stop working?

Adding velocities by simple addition works for walks, trains and rockets, and breaks down only when speeds approach the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s), where Einstein’s relativity takes over.

Your turn

Explain Velocity to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

Does a car’s odometer measure distance or displacement? Does its speedometer show speed or velocity?

Answer at the back of the book

1.3Speeding up, slowing down and turning

Back in the local. At a steady 60 km/h you feel nothing; you could be sitting in your kitchen. What you do feel is the pull-away from the platform and the brake coming into the next station: the moments when the velocity is changing. The rate of that change is what physicists call acceleration, and getting it right needs more care than the everyday word suggests.

Acceleration

The change in velocity divided by the time taken for the change, in m/s². It is a vector: it points in the direction the velocity is changing, which is not always the direction the object is moving.

Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time the change took. Say a train starts from rest and reaches 30 km/h, which is 8.3 m/s, in 20 s. Its velocity changed by 8.3 m/s in 20 s, so its acceleration was 8.3 ÷ 20 = 0.42 metres per second per second: every second, it gained another 0.42 m/s. The unit is written m/s², “metres per second squared”, which just means (metres per second) per second. Now say the same train, running at 30 km/h, brakes to a stop in 8 s. Its velocity changed by 8.3 m/s again, this time downwards, in 8 s: an acceleration of about 1.0 m/s², pointing backwards, against the direction of motion. If forward is the positive direction we write it as −1.0 m/s².

Pulling away: 0 → 8.3 m/s in 20 s
acceleration = 8.3 m/s ÷ 20 s = 0.42 m/s²
Braking: 8.3 → 0 m/s in 8 s
acceleration = −8.3 m/s ÷ 8 s = −1.0 m/s²

So slowing down is an acceleration too. Everyday English keeps the word for speeding up and uses “deceleration” for slowing, and you may use that word if you like; in physics it just means an acceleration that points against the velocity. What you must not do is read the minus sign as “slowing down”. The sign only tells you which way the acceleration points along the axis you chose. Figure 1.3 shows the four cases.

Now the part that surprises almost everyone. Velocity is a vector, so it changes when its size changes or when its direction changes. An auto taking a roundabout at a steady 20 km/h is accelerating the whole way round, because its velocity is swinging from north to west to south even though the speedometer never moves. The acceleration points towards the inside of the bend, which is where the velocity is being pulled. You know this in your body: on the roundabout you lean, and when the auto straightens out you stop leaning. The same thing that lets you feel braking lets you feel turning, and in Chapter 3 it will be the same thing that lets a force do its work.

Predict first

An auto-rickshaw goes all the way round a roundabout at a perfectly steady 20 km/h. Is it accelerating?

  1. No: its speed is constant, so its acceleration is zero
  2. Yes: its direction keeps changing, so its velocity keeps changing
  3. Only on the parts where the driver speeds up

What happens

Yes, the whole way round. Its velocity is changing because its direction is changing, even though its size is not. You can feel it: your body leans towards the outside the entire time you are on the curve.

Careful

“A negative acceleration means slowing down.”

Look at car (c) in Figure 1.3: it moves left and its velocity arrow is getting longer, so it is speeding up, yet its acceleration is negative because it points left and we called right positive. The sign depends on a choice you made. The arrows do not. Compare the directions of v and a: the same way means speeding up, opposite ways means slowing down, every time.

At school

The IGCSE syllabus says a resultant force “may change the velocity of an object by changing its direction of motion or its speed”. Both of those are changes of velocity, so both are accelerations. That is why physicists count turning a corner as accelerating.

Understand itAcceleration

What does it measure?

How quickly velocity is changing, whether in speed, in direction, or in both, measured in metres per second every second (m/s²).

Why is it called this?

From the Latin accelerare, to hasten or quicken (ad- towards + celer swift). The everyday name misleads you into thinking it means only speeding up; in physics, slowing down and turning a corner are accelerations too.

What problem did it solve?

Before Galileo, thinkers tried to link falling speed to distance fallen and got into tangles. Defining acceleration as the change in velocity per unit of time made the law of falling simple: every falling body gains the same 9.8 m/s of downward velocity each second.

Why does it work?

Because forces in nature do not set an object’s velocity directly; they set the rate at which its velocity changes from moment to moment.

How does it help?

It explains why a ball at the very top of its throw still has a downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s² even at the instant its velocity passes through zero, and predicts the 1, 4, 9, 16 square-law distances on Galileo’s ramp.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Stroboscopic photographs, slow-motion phone video against bathroom tiles, and Galileo’s inclined-plane timings all show consecutive position gaps changing by a constant amount in every equal time step.

What it isn’t

It is not velocity: a ball at the top of a toss has zero velocity and full acceleration, while a train cruising at 80 km/h on a straight track has high velocity and zero acceleration.

Where does it stop working?

The constant-acceleration formula d = ½at² holds only while the acceleration stays steady; when air drag grows on a fast-falling raindrop, acceleration shrinks toward zero and you must step through the motion bit by bit.

Your turn

Explain Acceleration to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A train is moving to the left and comes smoothly to a stop. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the direction of its acceleration, and what is its sign?

Answer at the back of the book

1.4Galileo’s ramps

Padua, about 1604

Galileo Galilei, working in Padua, wanted to know exactly how a falling thing speeds up. Does its speed grow steadily with time? Does the distance it has fallen grow steadily? Something else? A dropped ball reaches the floor in well under a second, far too fast for anything he had to time it. So he did something that looks like cheating and is actually one of the great ideas in physics: he slowed the fall down. A ball rolling down a gentle slope gathers speed in the same way as a falling ball, only more lazily. Make the slope shallow enough and you can watch the whole thing happen, and time it with a steady beat.

The story behind this

The man who slowed down fallingFrom his father’s lute strings in Florence to inclined ramps in Padua and the moons of Jupiter, Galileo turned physics into an art of measurement.

Predict first

A ball starts from rest at the top of a long ramp. In the first second it rolls 10 cm. How far from the start is it after two seconds?

  1. 20 cm: twice the time, twice the distance
  2. 30 cm
  3. 40 cm: twice the time, four times the distance

What happens

40 cm. After three seconds it is 90 cm from the start, and after four seconds 160 cm. Doubling the time multiplies the distance by four; trebling it, by nine. Almost everyone’s first instinct is 20 cm, and the next few paragraphs explain why that instinct is wrong.

Here is what Galileo found, and what you can find on your own floor. Mark where the ball is after one beat, two beats, three beats and four. The marks are not evenly spaced. If the first mark is one unit from the start, the next are at 4, 9 and 16 units: the square of the number of beats. Look instead at the gaps between the marks: 1, then 3, then 5, then 7. The odd numbers, one after another. Every extra beat adds the next odd number to the distance.

Why squares? Because what grows steadily is the velocity, not the distance. With a constant acceleration the ball gains the same extra speed in every beat: say 20 cm/s per beat. During the first beat its speed rises from 0 to 20 cm/s, averaging 10 cm/s, so it covers 10 cm. During the second beat it rises from 20 to 40, averaging 30, and covers 30 cm; that is the gap of 3. During the third beat, 40 to 60, average 50, gap 5. The distances from the start are 10, 40, 90, 160 cm: the squares. A graph of velocity against time is a straight line climbing from zero, and the distance covered is the area under that line, a triangle, which is why it comes out as half of the acceleration times the time squared.

distance from rest = ½ × acceleration × time²

Speed gained each second: 20 cm/s
After 1 s: speed 20 cm/s; average over the second 10 cm/s; distance 10 cm
After 2 s: speed 40 cm/s; distance = ½ × 20 × 2² = 40 cm
After 3 s: speed 60 cm/s; distance = ½ × 20 × 3² = 90 cm
After 4 s: distance = ½ × 20 × 4² = 160 cm

The slope of the ramp changes only how big the acceleration is. Gentler slope, smaller acceleration, longer beats; but the marks still fall at 1, 4, 9, 16, and the gaps still go 1, 3, 5, 7. That is what let Galileo claim his ramp was telling him about falling: tilt it steeper and steeper and nothing in the pattern changes, so the pattern must hold for the steepest “ramp” of all, straight down. The numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 are ours to check, by the way: neither of this book’s main sources prints them, so we computed them from distance ∝ time², and you can too.

How do we know? Galileo’s ramps Padua, about 1604

Galileo’s inclined-plane experiments are well documented; it was with ramps, not with drops from towers, that he worked out how falling things speed up. How he kept time is less certain. The historian Stillman Drake concluded that he sang a steady beat, with small gut frets fixed across the ramp so that the ball clicked as it passed each one, and that he moved the frets until the clicks fell exactly on the beats. The frets then sat at 1, 4, 9, 16. The story goes that way; it is one historian’s reconstruction, and the ramps themselves are the part that is certain.

Galileo’s ramp with coins for bells

You need a straight board about 2 m long, such as a plank or a long shelf, a marble or a smooth small ball, and masking tape. Prop one end of the board on a single book, so that the slope is as gentle as it can be while the marble still rolls all the way down; a gentle slope makes the beats long and easy to hear. Put tape marks at 10, 40, 90 and 160 cm from the top, measuring with a tape. At each mark, tape a small folded tab of stiff paper or kitchen foil so its tip hangs down and gives a crisp tick as the marble brushes past, or set a coin just to the side of the marble’s line so the marble grazes its rim (if the marble has to climb over a coin at the 10 cm mark, it is still moving so slowly that the coin’s edge will stop it). Release the marble from rest at the top, with no push, and listen: the four clicks should come at an even beat, like a slow clock. If the beats bunch up, the release was a push or the board is not straight. Filming it in slow motion and counting frames between clicks is a stricter test, and the markers are optional: with video you can mark where the marble is at equal time steps instead. Everything here is kitchen-safe; keep the marble away from small children.

Careful

“The ball speeds up steadily, so the distance must grow steadily too.”

The speed grows steadily: 20, 40, 60 cm/s. The distance does not, because a faster ball covers more ground in each beat than it did in the last. Distance grows with the square of the time: 1, 4, 9, 16. Mixing these two up is the commonest slip in all of kinematics, and Galileo’s marks are the cure.

Check yourself

A ball starts from rest and its speed grows by 4 m/s every second. After 2 seconds, is its speed 8 m/s or 16 m/s? How far has it travelled?

Answer at the back of the book

1.5The top of a throw

Now the puzzle this chapter opened with. A physics lecture at MIT begins exactly this way: the lecturer tosses a marker into the air and asks, at the highest point, is its velocity zero? And is its acceleration zero? The first answer is easy. For one instant at the top the marker is going neither up nor down, so its velocity is zero. The second answer is where 44% of students go wrong, and where everything you have learnt in this chapter pays off.

Predict first

At the very top of a toss the ball’s velocity is zero. What is its acceleration at that instant?

  1. Zero: it has stopped, so nothing is changing
  2. 9.8 m/s² downwards, exactly as it is on the way up and on the way down
  3. 9.8 m/s² upwards, because the ball was going up
  4. Something smaller than 9.8 m/s², because the ball is barely moving

What happens

9.8 m/s² downwards, the same as at every other instant of the flight. Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, and at the top the velocity is changing as fast as ever: from a little upward to a little downward. It passes through zero without pausing there. The ball’s position stops changing for an instant. Its velocity never stops changing at all.

Think about what acceleration means: how fast the velocity is changing, which is a different thing from speed. Use the numbers for a toss that rises about one metre. The ball leaves your hand at about 4.4 m/s. Every tenth of a second, gravity takes almost 1 m/s off its upward velocity: 4.4, then 3.5, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, then −0.5, −1.5, −2.4 and so on, where the minus sign means “downwards”. Read along that list and find the top. It is somewhere between 0.5 and −0.5, around 0.45 s, and nothing special happens there. The velocity does not slow its change, hesitate or pause. It goes through zero at the same steady rate, 9.8 m/s every second, that it had all the way up and keeps all the way down. Zero velocity, for an instant; full acceleration, the whole time.

You can see the same thing in the positions, which is what a camera records. Figure 1.5 marks the ball every tenth of a second. Going up, the gaps between marks are 39 cm, then 30, 20 and 10. At the top the ball barely moves: 0.2 cm between the 0.4 s and 0.5 s marks. Coming down, the gaps are 10, 19, 29, 39. Now subtract each gap from the one before it: the gaps shrink by 9.8 cm every tenth of a second, on the way up, over the top and on the way down, with no break in the pattern. That steady shrinking of the gaps is the acceleration, made visible. A ball that really stopped changing at the top would have two equal gaps there. It never does.

A toss that rises 1.0 m leaves the hand at 4.4 m/s and reaches the top after 0.45 s.
Height every 0.1 s: 0, 39, 69, 89, 99, 99, 89, 70, 41, 2 cm (the two 99s are 98.7 and 98.9 cm before rounding).
Gaps: 39, 30, 20, 10, 0.2, −10, −19, −29, −39 cm.
Change in each gap: about −9.8 cm every 0.1 s, the whole way.

Free fall

Motion under gravity alone, with nothing pushing, holding or throwing, and air resistance small enough to ignore. A tossed ball is in free fall from the moment it leaves the hand, going up as well as coming down.

g, the acceleration of free fall

About 9.8 m/s², downwards, everywhere near the Earth’s surface (9.78 to 9.83 depending on where you are). Every object in free fall changes its velocity by 9.8 m/s every second.

Why 9.8? Once the ball has left your hand, nothing is pushing it up any more. The only things acting on it are the Earth’s pull and a little air. The Earth’s pull does not switch off at the top of the flight, or weaken, or wait for the ball to stop; it is the same pull at the top as everywhere else, and it changes the ball’s velocity at the same rate everywhere: 9.8 m/s every second, downwards. Physicists call this motion free fall, and it includes the way up as well as the way down, because the ball is in the grip of gravity alone from the moment it leaves your hand. The number 9.8 m/s² is written g, the acceleration of free fall. It is 9.78 at some places on Earth and 9.83 at others, so 9.8 is a good average for anywhere, including Mumbai.

Film your own toss

Find a wall with tiles, or stick strips of tape on a plain wall at measured 10 cm intervals, and measure a tile with a ruler so you know its real height. Set the phone camera to its slow-motion mode, which on many phones films at 120 or 240 frames a second; check what yours does. Prop the phone against a book a few metres back, in bright light, so that it does not move. Toss a ball about a metre straight up, catch it, and stop filming. Now step through the clip. Do not compare one frame with the next: at 240 frames a second the gap changes by less than a fifth of a millimetre per frame, which no camera will show you against a tile. Instead, mark the ball’s height every tenth of a second, which is every 24th frame at 240 frames a second, every 12th at 120, every 3rd at 30. Write down the heights in tiles and work out the gaps. Going up they should shrink by about one tile each time, pass through almost nothing at the top, and grow by about one tile each time coming down. The live version of Figure 1.5 does the marking for you, frame by frame, and plots the graph; the video stays on your phone.

Careful

“At the top it has stopped, so nothing is happening to it. It just hangs there for a moment.”

It does not hang. The heights at 0.4 s and 0.5 s differ by 0.2 cm, and that is the nearest it ever comes to a pause. Its velocity is changing at 9.8 m/s every second through that instant, exactly as it was a moment before and will be a moment after. Zero velocity and zero acceleration are different things: one says the ball is not moving right now, the other would say its motion is not changing, and the second is false. There is a related wrong idea, that the push of your hand “runs out” at the top. Once the ball has left your hand there is no upward push on it at all, from the first instant of its flight. What carries it upwards is a question for Chapter 2.

At school

IGCSE writes “the acceleration of free fall g is approximately 9.8 m/s²”, which is exactly the number used here. You will also meet g written as 9.8 N/kg; that is the same number read from a different side, and Chapter 4 explains how.

Check yourself

A ball thrown almost straight up passes a coconut on the way up, misses it, and passes it again on the way down. Ignoring air, how do its speeds compare at the coconut the two times?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 1

Two trains on the Western line

You are on a local heading north at a steady 60 km/h, by the window, with a clear view out of both sides of the carriage.

  1. On one side, a train on the next track appears beside you and slides slowly past, so slowly that you watch one passenger reading his newspaper for five or six seconds before his window leaves yours behind. Relative to your window it is moving at about 10 km/h, forwards.
  2. On the other side, a train flashes past in the opposite direction. Relative to your window it passes at about 120 km/h.
  3. The passenger with the newspaper looks up, sees your carriage drifting backwards past his window, and says to his neighbour: “Look, that train is going backwards.”

What is each of the other two trains doing relative to the track: how fast, and which way? And is the man with the newspaper wrong?

Show the solution

To change frames, add the frame’s own velocity, as in Section 1.1. The slow train moves at 10 km/h forwards relative to you, and you move at 60 km/h north relative to the track, so relative to the track it is doing 60 + 10 = 70 km/h north: the same direction as you, slightly faster, which is why it overtakes so gently. The flashing train moves at 120 km/h relative to you, the other way; relative to the track that is 120 − 60 = 60 km/h south. It is doing exactly your speed, in the opposite direction, and the two speeds add up to the 120 km/h you saw. In metres per second, 10 km/h is about 2.8 m/s, a brisk walk, and 120 km/h is about 33 m/s.

The man with the newspaper is not wrong. In his train’s frame your carriage really does move backwards, at 10 km/h. In the track’s frame his train does 70 km/h north and yours 60. In your frame his train creeps forward at 10. Every one of those statements is a complete and correct description of the same motion, each in its own frame. What would be wrong is to say that one of them is what is “really” happening and the others are illusions. For steady motion, no frame has that right.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You can now say exactly how something moves: its position in a chosen frame, its velocity, and its acceleration, and you have seen that a ball at the top of its flight has zero velocity and full acceleration at the same instant. But a question has been left hanging since the top of the throw. After the ball leaves your hand, nothing pushes it upwards, yet it keeps rising for almost half a second. What carries it? Every twelve-year-old has an answer to that, and so did Aristotle, and they are the same answer, and it is wrong. Chapter 2 is about why things keep moving.
