Where this chapter comes from

2

Chapter 2

Why things keep moving

The big questionWhen a local train brakes hard, everyone standing in the compartment lurches forward. What pushed them?

  1. 2.1Aristotle’s world
  2. 2.2The arrow problem
  3. 2.3The ball that never stops
  4. 2.4Newton’s first law
  5. 2.5Friction is a force

In Chapter 1 you learned to describe motion without asking where it came from: where a thing is, how fast it is going and in which direction, and how its velocity changes from one moment to the next. You filmed a ball at the top of its throw and found that even at the instant it hung still, its velocity was changing. Describing is one job. Explaining is another, and this chapter starts on it.

Here is the puzzle to carry with you. A local train is slowing into a station, and the driver brakes harder than usual. Everyone standing lurches towards the front of the compartment. A school bag slides along the floor. A man dozing against the pole wakes with a jolt, looking round for whoever shoved him. Nobody did. The train has no arms. Nothing in the carriage reached out and pushed those people forward, and yet they all moved. By the end of this chapter you will be able to say exactly what happened to them, and the answer turns out to be the most important single idea about force in the whole book: a force changes how something moves. Keeping it moving needs no force at all.

2.1Aristotle’s world

Mumbai, a weekday evening

Start with something you can do before you read another line. Put a book flat on the table and give it a shove. It slides a hand’s width, slows, and stops. Shove it harder and it slides further, and stops. Flick a steel katori across the kitchen counter: the same. Everything you have ever pushed has behaved this way, and from all that experience you have built a rule without ever writing it down. It goes something like this: things move while something pushes them. Take the push away and they slow down and stop. Moving needs a mover.

That rule has a famous author. Aristotle, in ancient Greece, reasoned his way to the same conclusion from the same kind of evidence: a cart moves while the ox pulls it, and stops when the ox stops. Everything that moves, he said, is moved by something. For nearly two thousand years this was physics, and it deserves respect. Aristotle described what really happens on Earth, where every moving thing is rubbing against a floor or pushing through air. He was right about the facts. He was wrong about the cause, and the mistake is so natural that most people make it today. In 1985 two physicists, Halloun and Hestenes, gave a careful test to 478 university students in the United States before their first physics course. Sixty-five per cent agreed that every motion has a cause, something that keeps it going; only 17 per cent reasoned the way Newton did.

Force

A push or a pull on an object, with a size and a direction. It is always exerted by some other object. Measured in newtons (N), a unit you meet in Chapter 3.

A force is the physicist’s word for a push or a pull. It has a size and a direction, and, as you will see in Chapter 3, it always comes from some other object: a hand, a rope, the floor, the Earth. The question this chapter asks is what forces actually do. Aristotle’s answer was that they make things move. Hold that answer up against the sliding book and see whether it survives.

Predict first

You shove a book across the table and let go. It slows down and stops. Why does it stop?

  1. The push you gave it has been used up.
  2. Nothing is pushing it any more, so it stops on its own.
  3. Something is pushing it backwards the whole time it slides.

What happens

Something is pushing it backwards: the table, through friction. You cannot see that push, and that is exactly why it took two thousand years to notice. Aristotle would have chosen the second answer, and most students today choose the first. The rest of this chapter earns the third one, and Section 2.5 puts friction on the scales to prove it is a real force.

The hard thing about the sliding book is that the slowing-down is so ordinary that it hides in plain sight. Nobody asks why a book stops, any more than they ask why water is wet. To see the question at all you have to do what Chapter 0 taught: separate what you observe from the model you use to explain it. “The book slid thirty centimetres and stopped” is an observation. “It stopped because its push ran out” is a model, and so is “it stopped because the table pushed it backwards”. Two models, one observation. The next three sections decide between them.

Back from Chapter 0

In Chapter 0 you kept observations and models apart. Sort these three sentences about a katori flicked across the counter: “it slid about 40 cm and stopped”; “it stopped because the push you gave it ran out”; “it stopped because the counter pushed back on it”.

Answer at the back of the book

Check yourself

Think of three things you pushed today that stopped after you let go. For each one, name what was touching it while it slowed down.

Answer at the back of the book

2.2The arrow problem

Alexandria, 6th century

Aristotle’s rule had one awkward case, and thinkers argued about it for a thousand years. An archer draws a bow and lets go. The string pushes the arrow for a fraction of a second, and then the arrow is on its own, flying across a field with nothing touching it. If moving needs a mover, what is moving the arrow? Aristotle’s own answer was that the air behind it pushes it along. In Alexandria, in the sixth century, a scholar named John Philoponus found that hard to believe, and argued instead that the bow must give the arrow something that stays with it as it flies. Five hundred years later, in Bukhara, Ibn Sina discussed the idea in his Book of Healing and gave the something a name, mayl, an inclination. In the fourteenth century, in Paris, Jean Buridan called it impetus, and worked out that it grows with the arrow’s speed and with the quantity of matter in it. (The Paris scholars almost certainly never read Philoponus directly. The idea reached them through Arabic.)

Impetus

A medieval idea: a kind of force that a mover puts into a moving object, which the object carries along and uses up. A forerunner of momentum, but a force is exactly what a moving object does not carry.

This is good thinking, and the impetus idea is not simply wrong. Buridan was right that a moving thing carries something, and right that the something depends on both speed and amount of stuff; in Chapter 3 that quantity gets its modern name, momentum. The mistake was in what kind of thing it is. Buridan’s impetus is a force stored inside the arrow, a push that the arrow carries and spends. That is the idea Halloun and Hestenes found in 65 per cent of their students before the course, and in 44 per cent of them after it. It feels right. It is the picture most people have of a thrown ball: the throw is “in” the ball, and the ball slows as the throw runs out.

Here is the test that modern physics applies to every force, and it is the most useful habit in this book. For any force you name, you must be able to name the other object that exerts it. A force is an interaction between two things. Your hand pushes the book: two things. The Earth pulls the arrow down: two things. So look at the arrow in mid-flight and ask what is touching it or pulling on it. The string has gone. The archer has gone. Only two things are left: the air it flies through, and the Earth beneath it. Those two can exert forces on the arrow. A “force of the throw” has nobody to exert it, so it is not a force at all.

Predict first

While the arrow flies, which way does the air push on it?

  1. Forward, from behind, carrying it along (Aristotle’s answer).
  2. Backward, against its motion.
  3. Not at all; the air does nothing.

What happens

Backward. Newton put it plainly when he explained his first law: a flying projectile keeps moving except in so far as the air’s resistance slows it and gravity pulls it down. Ride a bicycle fast and you feel on your face which way air pushes on something moving through it. The air is the arrow’s brake, and the planets, which meet almost no air, keep moving for ages.

So nothing pushes the arrow forward. The arrow does not need anything to push it forward. What it got from the bowstring is not a stock of force to spend; it is motion, and motion simply continues until a force changes it. The air and the Earth are the only forces acting, and both are busy changing the motion: the air slowing it, the Earth bending its path downward into the familiar arc. Take those away (fire the arrow in empty space) and it would fly in a straight line for ever at the speed it left the string. That is a strange claim, and Section 2.3 shows how Galileo convinced himself of it.

How do we know? The students who thought like Buridan 1985

Halloun and Hestenes gave a diagnostic test to 478 university students in the United States before and after their first physics course, then interviewed some of them. On the pretest, 65 per cent showed the impetus belief: that a moving object carries a force that keeps it going. Forty-seven per cent believed an object slows down when no force acts on it at all. Sorting each student by their overall pattern, the researchers found 65 per cent impetus-thinkers, 18 per cent Aristotelians and 17 per cent Newtonians. After a semester of lectures, 44 per cent still held the impetus view, and in the interviews students “held firm to mistaken beliefs even when confronted with phenomena that contradicted those beliefs”. Showing someone a demonstration is not enough. That is why this book asks you to predict first.

The story behind this

The arrow problem: two thousand years of a wrong ideaWhy an arrow keeps flying after it leaves the bow puzzled thinkers from Alexandria to Paris, and the answer they settled on is the one most people still believe today.

Careful

“The ball carries the force of my throw inside it, and when that force is used up it stops.”

Apply the two-object test. After the ball leaves your hand, who is exerting “the force of your throw”? Not your hand: it is no longer touching the ball. There is no second object, so there is no such force. What the ball carries is motion, and motion only ever gets changed, by the air, by the Earth’s pull and, finally, by the floor. A ball thrown in empty space would carry the same motion for ever.

Check yourself

A crumpled paper ball flies across the classroom. While it is in the air, list every force acting on it, and for each force name the object that exerts it.

Answer at the back of the book

2.3The ball that never stops

Padua, about 1604

Galileo Galilei spent years rolling balls down ramps in Padua, because falling is too fast to time and a ramp slows it down to a speed he could measure. You met those ramps in Chapter 1. Later, in the books he wrote as an old man, he described an experiment that he could only do in his head, and it is one of the great arguments in science. Imagine two ramps facing each other, like a letter V, and let a ball roll down one of them. It rolls up the other and climbs to very nearly the height it started from, falling a little short because of friction. Now make the second ramp less steep. The ball must travel further along it to climb back to its starting height, and it does. Make the ramp shallower still and the ball rolls further still, always climbing to the same height. Now lay the second ramp perfectly flat. The ball can never climb back to its starting height, however far it rolls. So, Galileo reasoned, it never stops.

Thought experiment

An experiment reasoned through in the head because it cannot be done for real, built on a trend that has been measured as far as it can be. Galileo’s flat ramp is the classic one.

Notice what kind of argument that is. No ramp is perfectly smooth, so no real ball ever rolls for ever; Galileo did not claim to have watched one. He watched the trend. Every time he reduced the steepness, the ball went further, and the only thing stopping the pattern from continuing was friction. Reasoning about where a trend points when you remove the thing that spoils it is called a thought experiment, and it works only when every step of the trend has first been checked against real ramps.

Predict first

A steel katori is sliding across the kitchen floor. Imagine that at this instant someone switches friction off completely, like a light, so that the floor and the air no longer rub on it at all. What does the katori do?

  1. Slows down and stops, a little later than it would have.
  2. Slows down more gently, but still stops eventually.
  3. Keeps sliding at exactly the same speed, in a straight line, for ever.

What happens

It keeps the same speed in a straight line, for ever. Of the 478 students in Halloun and Hestenes’ study, 47 per cent chose one of the first two kinds of answer. If you did too, you are in large company, and the reasoning below is aimed at you.

You can walk Galileo’s trend yourself, on a floor instead of a ramp. Slide a katori across a rough floor and it stops quickly. Dust the floor with talcum powder and it slides further. Smear a little oil on the floor and it slides further still. Each change does the same thing, which is to reduce the rubbing between the katori and the floor, and each time the stopping takes longer. Follow the trend to its end: take the rubbing away entirely and the stopping takes for ever. An air-hockey table does nearly this. With the fan off, the puck stops in a moment. With the fan on, a cushion of air lifts the puck off the surface, almost all the friction is gone, and the puck glides from one end to the other at very nearly constant speed, as if nothing had happened to it. Nothing did.

Put numbers on the kitchen version to see how big the effect is. An ice cube is a wonderful low-friction object: skating on ice is possible because steel slides over ice with a friction coefficient of only about 0.02, measured in laboratories and listed in physics textbooks (Section 2.5 explains the coefficient). Suppose an ice cube leaves your fingers at 1 metre per second, which is a gentle flick. On a wet steel thali it would slide about 2.5 metres before stopping, if the thali were that long. On a cotton cloth, whose friction coefficient nobody has published but which is probably around 0.3, the same flick carries it about 17 centimetres. One flick, two surfaces, fifteen times the distance. The two speeds and the cloth’s coefficient are guesses you can improve on; the ratio is the lesson.

Ice on a thali, ice on a cloth

Wet a large steel thali and set it flat on the counter. Lay a folded cotton cloth beside it. Take an ice cube from the freezer, let it sit for half a minute so its surface starts to melt, and flick it gently across the cloth. Note where it stops. Now flick it the same way across the wet thali. Keep a hand ready at the far edge. Predict first: how many times further will it go on the steel? Then try a third surface (the tiled floor, a plastic tray) and arrange the three in order of friction. What you are watching is Galileo’s trend. The less the surface rubs, the longer the cube keeps the motion you gave it. Wipe up the water afterwards: a wet tile is slippery for people too.

Here, then, is the result that Aristotle could not have reached without a frictionless floor, and that Galileo reached by imagining one. A moving thing on which nothing pushes or pulls keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed. It does not need a force to keep going. It only needs the absence of a force to stop it. Physicists call such a thing an isolated body: one that is cut off from every push and pull, as far as that can be arranged. An isolated body keeps a constant velocity, and that velocity may be zero. Rest is simply the special case of a steady speed that happens to be nought.

Investigation 2.3

Use the ramp model with its friction slider. Set the second ramp at 30° and release the ball: note the height it reaches. Lower the ramp to 15°, then 5°, then flat, and write down how far along the ramp it travels each time. Then set friction to zero and repeat. Which setting lets the ball reach exactly its starting height? What happens on the flat ramp when friction is zero, and what happens when it is not?

Careful

“The ball never stops” means balls never stop.

Every real ball stops, because every real ball meets friction and air. Galileo’s claim is about what would happen with those removed: nothing would slow the ball, so nothing would stop it. The claim is tested not by watching a ball roll for ever, which is impossible, but by watching the stopping fade exactly as the friction fades. Talc, oil, air cushion, ice: each step confirms it.

Check yourself

You push a box across the floor and let go. It slides on for a moment, slowing down. While it slides, which way does the total force on it point: forward, backward, or nowhere?

Answer at the back of the book

2.4Newton’s first law

A local train, Mumbai

Now go back to the braking train, and watch it from two places at once. First stand on the platform. The train is coming in at a steady speed. Everyone inside is moving at that same speed, feet, body and bag together. Then the brakes grip the wheels and the train slows. What slows the passengers? Think about what is touching each one. The floor touches their feet, and the floor is part of the train, so it drags their feet to a slower speed by friction. Nothing is touching their heads, shoulders or hands. Those parts carry on at the speed the train had a moment ago, exactly as Galileo’s ball would. So each passenger’s feet slow with the train while the rest of them keeps going, and from the platform you watch a whole compartment of people tilt towards the front. The bag on the floor had less grip than a pair of shoes, so it slides further before friction stops it.

Predict first

The train brakes hard. Watching from the platform, what happens to a passenger standing in the aisle?

  1. A forward push throws her forward.
  2. Her feet are slowed by the floor, while the rest of her carries on at the speed the train had.
  3. Nothing happens to her until she hits something.

What happens

Her feet are slowed and the rest of her carries on. There is no forward push; there is a backward force, friction on her shoes, and it acts only on her feet. The top of her keeps the old velocity because nothing has yet acted to change it. That is why braking feels like a shove from behind, and why the dozing man looked round for the shover.

Now step inside the train and feel it. From in here, as the brakes bite, it genuinely feels as if something pushes you forward, and if you shut your eyes you would swear to it. Physicists have a name for that feeling: a fictitious force. Inside anything that is speeding up, slowing down or turning, everything seems to be pushed the opposite way. But apply the two-object test. What object is doing the pushing? There is none. The feeling is real; the force is not. It is what the first law looks like from inside a carriage that is changing its velocity while you try not to change yours.

Newton’s first law

A body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion keeps the same speed in the same straight line, unless a force acting on it changes that state. Also called the law of inertia.

Isaac Newton wrote the rule down in 1687, in the book usually called the Principia, as the first of his three laws of motion. In today’s words: every body keeps its state of rest, or of steady motion in a straight line, unless forces acting on it compel it to change that state. Galileo had grasped the idea first, with his ramps, and Newton never acknowledged him; but Newton made it the foundation of everything that followed. Notice how exact the law is. A body left alone does not “tend” to keep moving, as if it might wear out eventually. It keeps its velocity exactly, for as long as the total force on it is zero. Speed and direction both stay fixed, and the only thing that can change either is a force.

Inertia

The tendency of an object to stay at rest, or to keep moving in a straight line at constant speed. It is a property, measured by mass. It is not a force.

Mass

How much matter an object contains, and so how much inertia it has. Measured in kilograms (kg). The same everywhere in the universe, unlike weight (Chapter 3).

The tendency that the law describes, to stay at rest or to keep moving in a straight line at a steady speed, is called inertia, and every object has it. Rest and motion are covered alike: a parked bus has inertia just as much as a moving one, which is why it is hard to get moving. How much inertia a thing has is measured by its mass, the quantity of matter in it. Try to shove a basketball and it goes; try to shove a boulder the same way and it barely moves. A kilogram of puffed rice and a kilogram of steel bolts have the same mass and the same inertia, though one fills a bag and the other fits in your palm; what differs is how much space the matter takes up. Mass is the same on Earth, in orbit and on the Moon. It is a count of stuff, not a pull.

One more thing the law does not say. It does not say that moving at constant speed is impossible while a force acts. Push a heavy trunk across the floor at a steady walking pace and you are certainly pushing, perhaps with 50 newtons. But friction is pushing back with 50 newtons, and the total force on the trunk is zero. Your push cancels the friction that would otherwise stop it; the moving itself needs nothing from you. Take away both, and the trunk would slide on by itself.

The coin, the card and the glass

Stand an empty glass on the table, lay a stiff card (a playing card or an old visiting card) flat across its rim, and put a coin on the card right above the middle of the glass. Flick the card sharply sideways with a finger, hitting its edge. Done well, the card shoots away and the coin drops straight into the glass. Now do it badly on purpose: pull the card away slowly. The coin rides along with it. The physics is the first law plus a very short time. While the card moves, its friction drags the coin sideways, but a sharp flick is over in a few hundredths of a second. If it lasts 0.05 seconds and the card’s friction coefficient on the coin is about 0.3 (a guess), the coin picks up a sideways speed of only about 0.15 metres per second and has slipped about 4 millimetres, far less than the glass is wide, before there is no card under it and the Earth’s pull takes over. Pull for half a second instead and the slip grows a hundredfold, to about 37 centimetres: the coin simply goes with the card. Short time, small change in motion. Keep that thought for the chapter’s case file.

Back from Chapter 1

In Chapter 1 you threw a ball straight up and watched the very top of its flight, where for an instant it is still. Suppose you toss your keys up on the platform while you wait for the next train. At the top, is any force acting on them? And does Newton’s first law say they should stay there?

Answer at the back of the book

Investigation 2.4

Take two identical toy cars, and load one with ₹5 coins taped on top. Give each the same gentle push with a ruler laid flat and released from the same bend. Which is harder to get moving? Which rolls further once it is going, and why might that be a trickier question than it looks? (Think about friction on the wheels.)

At school

Your IGCSE syllabus words the first law as: an object either remains at rest or continues in a straight line at constant speed unless acted on by a resultant force. “Resultant force”, “net force” and “unbalanced force” all mean the same thing, which is what is left over after the pushes and pulls cancel. The syllabus also defines mass as a measure of the quantity of matter in an object.

Careful

“The book kept sliding because of its inertia.”

Try the test from Chapter 0: swap the word for a made-up one. “The book kept sliding because of its movability.” The sentence says exactly as much, which is nothing. Inertia is a name for the fact that motion continues until a force changes it. The explanation of why the book kept sliding is that nothing stopped it yet: the floor’s friction was small, so it took a while to bring the book to rest. Name the forces, or the absence of them. Never let the word do the explaining.

The story behind this

The ball that never stopsGalileo imagined a ramp that never climbs, Descartes wrote the rule down, and Newton made it his first law: a moving thing keeps its velocity until a force changes it.

Understand itInertia

What is it?

The property of every piece of matter that keeps it at rest if it is at rest, or moving in a straight line at constant speed if it is already moving, unless a net force acts on it.

Why is it called this?

From the Latin inertia, idleness or sluggishness, from iners, unskilled or inactive. Kepler introduced the word into physics for a body’s reluctance to start moving, and Newton widened it to cover keeping moving as well, so the “lazy” name is half misleading: a fast-moving planet has inertia too.

What problem did it solve?

For two thousand years people followed Aristotle in assuming that every moving thing needs a continuing push to keep going, which left nobody able to explain why an arrow keeps flying after it leaves the bowstring.

Why does it work?

Because steady motion in a straight line and rest are the same physical state seen from two different steadily moving reference frames; neither needs a cause, and only a change of velocity requires a force.

How does it help?

It explains why passengers lurch toward the front of a braking Mumbai local train (their feet are slowed by the floor while their upper bodies keep the train’s old velocity), and how spacecraft cruise across the solar system with their engines off.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Galileo’s facing ramps, ice cubes sliding across a wet steel thali versus a cloth, air-hockey pucks, and spacecraft in deep space all show that as rubbing and air resistance are removed, stopping fades away toward never.

What it isn’t

It is not a force stored inside the moving object (that was the medieval impetus mistake), and saying “it kept moving because of inertia” is a label, not a cause: it kept moving because nothing stopped it yet.

Where does it stop working?

Newton’s first law holds in any non-accelerating (inertial) reference frame; inside a braking train or a spinning merry-go-round, objects appear to veer on their own unless you account for the frame’s own acceleration.

Your turn

Explain Inertia to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A friend says: “Newton’s first law means that a moving object keeps a constant acceleration unless a force acts on it.” Fix the sentence, and say why the fix matters.

Answer at the back of the book

2.5Friction is a force

Mumbai, the kitchen counter

Friction

The part of the contact force between two touching surfaces that acts along the surfaces and opposes their sliding over each other. It is a real force, with a size you can measure and a direction you can predict.

Rest your palm flat on the table and press down. The table presses up into your hand; you can feel it. Now keep pressing and slide your hand forward. A new push appears, dragging backward along your skin. Push down and forward at once and you feel both together. What you are feeling is the table’s contact force, and it has two parts: one straight out of the surface, holding your hand up, and one along the surface, resisting the slide. The first part is the subject of Chapter 3. The second is friction, and this chapter has been leaning on it since the first page without ever checking that it deserves the name. It does. Friction is as real a force as a shove, and it obeys rules you can measure in a kitchen.

The rules for sliding friction were first written down by Leonardo da Vinci in his notebooks, between about 1493 and 1515, then forgotten; Amontons found them again on his own and published them in 1699. First, friction grows in proportion to how hard the surfaces are pressed together: double the pressing force and you double the friction. Second, it hardly depends on the area of contact: a brick slides just as reluctantly on its narrow end as on its broad face. Third (Coulomb added this), for ordinary speeds it hardly depends on how fast the surfaces slide. The ratio of friction to pressing force is a number called the coefficient of friction, written μ, and it depends only on the pair of materials. Rubber on dry concrete has a sliding coefficient of about 0.7, wood on wood about 0.3, steel on ice about 0.02. Those numbers are rough by nature; friction is complicated, and physicists admit it is still not completely understood.

The second rule puzzled people for centuries, and the answer is under the magnifier in the figure. Surfaces that look smooth are, up close, ranges of tiny hills, and two surfaces touch only where hill meets hill. Pressing harder squashes more hills into contact and raises the friction. Spreading the same weight over a bigger face lowers the pressure, so fewer hills touch per square centimetre, and the two effects cancel. Even surfaces polished until no hills remain are not friction-free, because the molecules of one surface cling to the molecules of the other.

Friction behaves differently before anything slides. Put a book on a level table and nobody pushes it sideways: the friction on it is zero. Push it gently and it does not move, because friction has grown to match your push exactly. Push harder and friction grows to match again, up to a limit. Past that limit the book breaks free and slides, and the friction drops to a slightly smaller, roughly steady value. You can feel the drop with a luggage scale hooked to a heavy bag on the floor: pull gently, watch the reading climb and climb while nothing moves, then feel the bag lurch as the reading falls back. That lurch is also why chalk squeals on a blackboard and why a violin bow makes a string sing: stick, slip, stick, slip, over and over, very fast.

Predict first

You walk forward across the kitchen floor. Which way does the floor’s friction push on the sole of your shoe?

  1. Backward, against the way you are walking.
  2. Forward, the way you are walking.
  3. Nowhere: there is no friction while you walk normally.

What happens

Forward. As you step, your foot tries to slide backward against the floor, and friction opposes that slide, which means it pushes your foot forward. Friction is what lets you walk at all; on wet ice it is nearly gone, and so is your ability to go anywhere. Friction opposes the sliding of surfaces across each other, which is not always the same as opposing the direction you happen to be moving.

Friction makes things warm, as you know from rubbing your hands on a cold morning or touching a bicycle brake after a long downhill. School books say friction “produces heating”, and that is right. What it does not do is destroy anything. The motion that friction takes away does not vanish; it spreads out into the warmth of the two surfaces, and Chapter 7 follows every bit of it.

Investigation 2.5

Put a ₹5 coin on a closed hardback atlas and tilt the book slowly until the coin, once nudged, slides down at a steady speed. Hold that angle and measure it with a phone app (phyphox has an inclinometer). The sliding coefficient of friction is the tangent of that angle: 15° gives about 0.27, 20° gives about 0.36. Try a plastic cover, a cloth cover and a steel thali, and rank them. Then stand the coin on its edge and check the second rule: does the angle change?

At school

The IGCSE syllabus describes solid friction as the force between two surfaces that may impede motion and produce heating. Notice the word “may”. Friction impedes a sliding book, and it also lets you walk and a car accelerate; it opposes sliding between surfaces, whichever way that works out for the object.

Careful

“Friction always acts against the direction I’m moving.”

Friction acts against the sliding of the two surfaces over each other. When you walk, your sole tends to slide backward along the floor, so friction on it points forward, and that forward friction is what moves you. When a car’s wheels spin on wet mud, friction is too small to push the car forward, and the car stays put. The direction of friction is set by the surfaces, not by the direction of travel.

Understand itFriction

What is it?

The force along two touching surfaces that opposes their sliding, or tending to slide, across each other.

Why is it called this?

From the Latin frictio, a rubbing, from fricare, to rub.

What problem did it solve?

On Earth, pushed books and rolling balls always slow down and stop, which fooled observers for centuries into thinking motion dies out on its own. Recognising friction as an invisible backward push from the floor rescued the law of inertia.

Why does it work?

Even surfaces that look polished are microscopic mountain ranges that touch only at their tips; pressing the surfaces together squashes more tips into contact and lets surface molecules tug on one another, resisting any slide.

How does it help?

It lets you calculate how far a braking car or a flicked coin will slide, explains why a magician must yank a tablecloth fast, and shows why your shoes can push you forward when you walk.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Leonardo da Vinci and Guillaume Amontons measured the pull needed to drag blocks across tables and found that friction grows in proportion to the pressing force and barely changes when a brick is turned from its broad face onto its narrow edge.

What it isn’t

It does not always oppose an object’s overall motion (forward friction from the ground is what accelerates a runner or a bicycle), and static friction before sliding is not fixed at its maximum value: it matches whatever sideways push is applied, up to the slip limit.

Where does it stop working?

The simple rule that friction equals a constant coefficient times the normal force (f = μN) is a working approximation that breaks down when surfaces melt, peel, lubricate, or stick at the atomic scale.

Your turn

Explain Friction to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A book rests on a level table and nobody touches it. How much friction acts on the book?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 2

The tablecloth trick

A magician at a birthday party lays a cloth on a table, sets out plates, glasses and a vase of flowers, grips the edge of the cloth and yanks. The cloth is gone and the dishes stand where they were, barely rattled. Afterwards, Kym and two friends argue about how it works.

  1. One says the plates have to be heavy: “the heavier the plate, the more it stays put”.
  2. One says the cloth has to be slippery and without a hem.
  3. One says the pull has to be fast and straight down over the table’s edge, and that a slow pull would drag everything off.

Kym notices that the plates did move, a centimetre or so, in the direction of the pull.

Which of the three is right, and why did the plates move a little but not a lot? Does a heavier plate help?

Show the solution

The second and third are right. The first is the popular explanation, and it is wrong.

While the cloth slides under a plate, the only sideways force on the plate is the cloth’s friction, which drags the plate the way the cloth is going. The plate starts to move, exactly as the first law says it must when a force acts. How far it moves depends on two things: how big that friction is, and how long it acts. A slippery cloth makes the friction small. A fast pull makes the time short.

Put in numbers, with inputs that are guesses. A sliding coefficient of 0.3 between cloth and plate and a pull that takes 0.1 seconds give the plate a speed of about 0.3 metres per second and a slip of about 1.5 centimetres while the cloth is under it. Once the cloth is gone the plate slides on the bare table and stops within about another 1.5 centimetres. Halve the pulling time to 0.05 seconds and the slip drops to about 4 millimetres, a quarter as much. Stretch the pull to half a second and the plate slides about 37 centimetres: off the table. That is Kym’s centimetre, explained, and the magician’s speed, explained.

Now the heavy plate. Friction grows in proportion to how hard the surfaces press together, so a plate twice as heavy feels twice the friction from the cloth. But it also has twice the mass, so twice the force produces exactly the same change in motion. The acceleration of a plate dragged by a cloth is the coefficient times 9.8 metres per second squared, whatever the plate weighs. Heavy plates do not help. Smooth plates, a smooth hemless cloth, and a short, sharp pull do.

If you try it, use plastic plates and a tea towel, and ask an adult first.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You can now say what a force does: it changes motion. You cannot yet say how much. Why does the same shove send a basketball flying and barely move a boulder? Why does the table push up on a book, and how hard? And what about the pair of hands in every push: when you shove the katori, does the katori shove you? Chapter 3 answers all three, and finishes with a rocket launched from a fishing village in Kerala.

Where this chapter comes from

3

Chapter 3

Forces come in pairs

The big questionA mosquito hits the windscreen of a car doing 90 km/h. Which one feels the bigger force, the mosquito or the car?

  1. 3.1Adding forces
  2. 3.2Why heavy things are hard to start
  3. 3.3Can a table push?
  4. 3.4Every push has a partner
  5. 3.5Momentum and rockets

Chapter 2 settled what a force does. It does not keep things moving; a book sliding on a frictionless table would slide for ever with nobody pushing it. A force changes motion, and when nothing changes a thing’s motion, nothing is acting on it. That leaves three questions hanging, and this chapter takes them in turn. How do you add up several forces acting at once? How much does a given force change the motion, and why is a loaded truck so much slower off the mark than a scooter? And who, exactly, is doing the pushing when a table holds up a book?

The last question leads somewhere strange. A mosquito meets the windscreen of a car on the Sea Link at 90 km/h. The mosquito is destroyed; the car does not notice. Ask anyone which one felt the bigger force and they will say the mosquito, obviously. In a test of about 900 university students, 73 per cent said the bigger object pushes harder in a collision. Every one of them was wrong, and by the end of this chapter you will be able to work out by how much.

3.1Adding forces

A school sports ground, Mumbai

Sports day, and the tug of war is on. Two teams dig their heels into the dry ground, lean back and pull. For a long moment the rope does not move; then one team gives, and the other hauls them over the line. Think about the rope, or better, think about a loaded cart with a rope tied to each side and two teams pulling it in opposite directions, which is the same contest with a clearer middle. Two forces act on the cart at once. What does it do?

Net force

The total of all the forces acting on an object, after opposing forces have cancelled. Your school syllabus calls it the resultant force. If it is zero, the object’s velocity does not change.

You already know the answer from experience. If the pulls are equal, the cart stays put. If one side pulls harder, the cart goes that way, and the harder the difference, the more briskly it goes. A force has a size and a direction, and when several forces act on one object at the same time, forces in the same direction add up and forces in opposite directions cancel. What is left over after the cancelling is called the net force, and it is the net force, never any single push on its own, that decides how the motion changes.

Put made-up numbers on the cart. Four children pull it to the left with 120, 100, 90 and 80 newtons: 390 newtons altogether. Three bigger children pull it to the right with 150, 130 and 110 newtons: also 390. Net force: 390 − 390 = 0, and the cart’s velocity does not change. If it was at rest it stays at rest, and Chapter 2 reminds you that if it was already rolling it would keep rolling at the same speed. Now a fourth child joins the right-hand side with 100 newtons. Net force: 100 newtons to the right, and the cart begins to move that way. (A newton, written N, is the unit of force; Section 3.2 says exactly how big it is. A 100 gram packet of biscuits resting on your palm pushes down with about 1 N.)

Predict first

You push a loaded trolley along a smooth level corridor at a steady walking pace. While it moves at that steady speed, the forces on it are:

  1. Unbalanced, with more force forward than backward; that is why it keeps moving.
  2. Balanced: the net force is zero.
  3. Unbalanced, with more force backward; the trolley is always fighting friction.

What happens

Balanced. Steady speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing, and Chapter 2 says that happens only when the net force is zero. Your forward push is being cancelled by friction and air pushing back. Balanced forces do not mean “not moving”. They mean “not changing its motion”.

It is worth asking how anyone knows that forces add like this. It is not a definition; it is a measured fact. Apply one force to a cart on a smooth track and measure how its velocity changes. Apply a second force on its own and measure again. Then apply both at once. The change in velocity you get is exactly what you would get by laying the two force-arrows end to end and reading off the single arrow from start to finish. Physicists check this kind of thing before they trust it, and arrows that add end to end are called vectors; velocity is one too, as you saw in Chapter 1.

Two habits make force problems easy, and both come from the tug of war. First, decide which object you are talking about, and draw only the forces acting on that object, never the forces it exerts on other things. For the cart, that means the pull of each rope, the Earth’s pull downward, the ground’s push upward, and friction. Second, draw the object as a dot and each force as an arrow from the dot, with its length showing its size. That sketch is called a free-body diagram, and it turns a crowded scene into a sum.

Investigation 3.1

Make your own force meter. Hang a small plastic bag from a rubber band and put one ₹5 coin in it; measure how far the band stretches. Then two coins, then four. Is the stretch for four coins twice the stretch for two? Now loop two identical rubber bands side by side and hang four coins from the pair: predict the stretch before you look. This is how a spring balance turns a stretch into a force reading.

At school

IGCSE writes “resultant force” where this book says “net force”; some school sheets say “unbalanced force”. All three mean the same thing: what is left after the pushes and pulls have cancelled. The syllabus also says a resultant force may change the velocity of an object by changing its direction of motion or its speed.

Careful

“If the forces on it are balanced, it must be standing still.”

Balanced forces mean the velocity is not changing. A parked car and a car cruising at a steady 60 km/h on a straight road both have zero net force on them. The second one is moving; it is just not speeding up, slowing down or turning. “Balanced” describes the forces, not the speed.

Check yourself

Two friends push a stalled scooter in the same direction with 200 N and 150 N. Friction and the rough road resist with 350 N. What is the net force on the scooter, and what does it do?

Answer at the back of the book

3.2Why heavy things are hard to start

A traffic signal, Mumbai

The light goes green. A scooter is away before you have finished looking at it; a loaded truck beside it rolls forward so slowly that you could keep pace on foot for the first few metres. Both engines are working hard. The difference is in what the force has to move. Here is your probable explanation: heavy things are hard to get going because they are heavy. It sounds like it cannot be wrong, and it mixes up two different things, which this section separates.

Start with a cleaner experiment than a traffic signal. Put a cart on a smooth track where friction barely matters, and push it with a steady force, the same every second. What does the cart do?

Predict first

You push a cart along a very smooth track with a steady force, never bigger, never smaller. What does the cart do?

  1. Moves at a steady speed set by how hard you push.
  2. Speeds up, and keeps speeding up for as long as you push.
  3. Speeds up at first, then settles at a steady speed.

What happens

It keeps speeding up. A steady force gives a steady change in velocity, every second the same extra speed. Two-thirds of Halloun and Hestenes’ 478 students chose the first answer, and so did 44 per cent of more than 2,000 American school students on a national test. If the cart settled at a steady speed, the net force on it would have to be zero, which means something else, friction or air, had grown to cancel your push. On a very smooth track, nothing does.

Newton’s second law puts a number on it. Push a cart with a certain net force and it gains speed at a certain rate; double the net force and it gains speed twice as fast. Keep the force the same and double the mass by loading the cart, and it gains speed only half as fast. In symbols, with a for the rate of gaining speed (the acceleration from Chapter 1), F for the net force and m for the mass:

net force = mass × acceleration, or F = ma

Newton (N)

The unit of force. One newton is the net force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². On Earth, a 100 g mass weighs about 1 N.

The newton is defined by this rule: 1 N is the net force that makes a 1 kg mass gain 1 m/s of speed every second. The law is the reason a push on a basketball sends it flying while the same push on a stalled car barely moves it: the force is the same, and the free-body diagrams look identical, but the car has a thousand times the mass and gets a thousandth of the acceleration. It is also the reason the loaded truck crawls away from the signal. Suppose, with made-up round numbers, that a scooter with its rider has a mass of 200 kg and a loaded truck 10,000 kg, and that each engine manages a net forward force of 2,000 N. The scooter accelerates at 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10 m/s², and the truck at 2,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.2 m/s², fifty times less, for the same force. A real example from a textbook: a 51 N net force on a 240 kg lawn mower gives 51 ÷ 240 = 0.21 m/s².

Now the two things that “heavy” mixes up. The truck is hard to get going because of its mass, the quantity of matter in it, which is what the m in the law measures. That is the inertia from Chapter 2. The truck is also heavy, which means the Earth pulls down on it hard. The pull of the Earth on an object is called its weight, and weight is a force, measured in newtons like any other. The two are linked but different. If the Earth’s pull is the only force on something, the second law gives its acceleration as weight ÷ mass, and that acceleration, for everything near the Earth’s surface, comes out at 9.8 m/s². Turn it round and you get the rule for weight:

weight = mass × 9.8 N/kg

Weight

The force with which the Earth (or whatever planet you are on) pulls an object down. It equals the mass times the local strength of gravity: on Earth about 9.8 newtons for every kilogram.

A 1 kg bag of sugar has a weight of 9.8 N on Earth. On the Moon, where gravity is weaker, the same bag weighs about 1.7 N, yet its mass is still 1 kg and it is exactly as hard to start moving sideways. Take the truck into orbit, where it floats weightless, and it is still 10,000 kg and still needs 2,000 N to accelerate at 0.2 m/s². Mass is the thing that resists being accelerated. Weight is a particular force that happens to act on it. “Heavy things are hard to start” is true on Earth only because things with lots of mass also have lots of weight.

A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg (a round number; real ones are close to this):
weight = 0.16 kg × 9.8 N/kg
weight = 1.57 N, about one and a half newtons

One small puzzle for the bathroom. A weighing scale cannot measure mass directly. What it feels is the force pressing on it, your weight, through springs or sensors inside, and it divides by 9.8 before it shows you a number in kilograms. Stand on it, reach out and press down on the edge of the basin, and the number drops, though your mass has not changed by a gram. Section 3.3 explains why.

Investigation 3.2

Stand on a bathroom scale next to a sturdy table. Read the scale. Predict what the reading will do when you press down on the table with one hand, then do it. Now lift gently on the underside of the table instead (do not pull it over). What happens to the reading, and what does that tell you about which force the scale is measuring?

At school

Your syllabus says weight is a gravitational force on an object that has mass, and gives g = 9.8 two ways: as 9.8 N/kg (the pull on each kilogram) and as the acceleration of free fall, 9.8 m/s². They are the same number seen from two sides. When someone says they “weigh 40 kg” they mean their mass; in a physics answer, write mass in kg and weight in N.

Careful

“A steady push gives a steady speed. My bicycle goes at a steady speed when I pedal steadily.”

Your bicycle does, and the reason is the forces you cannot see. Pedalling steadily on level ground, you are pushed forward by the road and pushed back by air and rolling friction, and the two cancel: net force zero, steady speed. Stop pedalling and the backward forces win, so you slow. Pedal harder and you win, so you speed up. A steady net force always gives a steady change of speed. The bicycle feels like a counter-example only because the net force on it is zero.

Understand itNewton’s second law (F = ma)

What is it?

The rule that an object’s acceleration equals the net force acting on it divided by its mass, pointing in the direction of the net force.

Why is it called this?

Isaac Newton placed it second among the three laws of motion at the front of his Principia in 1687; Leonhard Euler first wrote it in its modern algebraic dress, F = ma, in the eighteenth century.

What problem did it solve?

Knowing that forces change motion is only half the story: you need to know how much a given push changes the motion of a light scooter compared with a loaded truck, and how to combine several pushes acting at once.

Why does it work?

Because every force acting on a body contributes independently to changing its velocity, while the body’s mass measures how much matter must be accelerated together.

How does it help?

With one equation you can work out the acceleration of anything from a mosquito hitting a windscreen to a rocket lifting off from Thumba, once you add up all the forces on it and divide by its mass.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Cart-and-pulley experiments on low-friction tracks show that doubling the net force doubles the acceleration, while doubling the cart’s mass halves the acceleration to within experimental uncertainty.

What it isn’t

F in F = ma is never a single push in isolation when other forces act; it is always the net (resultant) force left after opposing forces such as friction and air drag have cancelled.

Where does it stop working?

It holds for objects whose mass stays constant and whose speeds are small compared with the speed of light; for a rocket burning half its mass as fuel, or a particle near light speed, you must write the law in terms of rate of change of momentum.

Your turn

Explain Newton’s second law (F = ma) to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A trolley and its load have a mass of 60 kg. You push with 80 N, and friction pushes back with 50 N. What is the trolley’s acceleration?

Answer at the back of the book

3.3Can a table push?

Kym’s desk, Mumbai

A book lies on the desk. The Earth pulls it down with its weight, about 10 newtons for a big textbook. It does not move. By everything in this chapter so far, the net force on it must be zero, so something must be pushing it up with 10 newtons, and the only thing touching it is the desk. Ask people whether a desk can push and about half say no. “The desk is just in the way. It stops the book falling, but it doesn’t push; pushing is something living things do.” A researcher named Minstrell, who studied high-school students’ ideas about forces, found that only around half of them would say a table pushes up on a book. The other half are not foolish. A desk looks utterly passive. Where would a push come from?

Predict first

A book lies still on the desk. Which is true?

  1. The desk pushes up on the book, exactly as hard as the Earth pulls it down.
  2. The desk does not push; it just blocks the book from falling.
  3. The desk pushes up, but less than the book’s weight, which is why the book presses into it.

What happens

The first. Zero net force needs an upward push equal to the weight, and the only candidate is the desk. The rest of this section shows where the push comes from, because “it must” is a poor reason to believe anything.

Here is a chain of four steps, each one a small move from the last, and it was designed by a researcher named Clement to walk people from what they already believe to what is true.

The spring, the foam, the ruler and the table

Step 1. Press your palm down on a spring, or a rubber ball, or a folded sponge. It squashes, and you can feel it pushing back; the harder you press, the harder it pushes. Nobody doubts that a spring pushes. Step 2. Lay a book on a thick sponge or a folded towel. The sponge dents under it and stays dented. The dent is the sponge’s way of pushing up with exactly the book’s weight: it squashed until its push matched the load, and there it stopped. Step 3. Lay a 30 cm steel ruler across the gap between two stacks of books, and put a ₹5 coin in the middle. Add more coins, one at a time, with your eye level with the ruler. It sags, visibly, a little more with every coin, and for every coin it holds. The ruler is doing exactly what the sponge did: bending until its push upward matches the weight on it. Step 4. Now lay the book on the table. The table is a ruler that is very, very stiff. It sags under the book by an amount far too small to see, and that tiny sag is its push. Make the load bigger (sit on the table) and it sags a little more and pushes a little harder, just as the ruler did. Keep the ruler on the desk for a day: it is the table’s argument in a form you can watch.

What is bending, down at the bottom? The atoms of the table top. Press on them and they are squeezed a tiny bit closer together than their normal spacing, and the electrons around each atom push back against the electrons of its neighbours. That push is the same thing that stops your hand passing through the desk. Squeeze harder, and the atoms are squeezed closer and push harder. A table is a spring made of atoms, so stiff that its squash is invisible, and no more passive than a spring.

Normal force

The push of a surface on anything resting on it, directed straight out of the surface (at right angles to it). It takes whatever size is needed to stop the object passing into the surface. It equals the weight only for an object at rest on a level surface with nothing else pushing on it.

The push that any surface gives straight out of itself, at right angles to the surface, is called the normal force. “Normal” here is the old mathematical word for at right angles; it does not mean ordinary. The normal force is a strange kind of force, because no formula tells you its size in advance. It grows to whatever size is required to stop the object sinking in: 10 N for the book, more if you press on the book, less on a slope. A skier of mass 60 kg standing on a 25° slope presses on the snow with only part of her 588 N weight, and the snow pushes back with about 533 N at right angles to the slope. A book lying on a level desk with nothing else touching it gets a normal force equal to its weight, and that is the only case where the two are equal; the moment anything else pushes or pulls on the book, or the desk accelerates, the normal force changes to match.

This is also what your hand feels when you hold a cricket ball. You do not feel the Earth’s pull on the ball; you feel the ball pressing on your palm, and your palm pressing back with 1.57 N, which is the normal force from your hand. Lift the ball a little with your other hand and the first palm feels less, because it is now providing less of the support. Toss the ball up and, while it is in the air, nothing supports it at all: the normal force is gone, and the ball is weightless in exactly the sense that an astronaut is. Gravity has not switched off for either of them. Chapter 5 comes back to that.

At school

At school you may see the table’s push called the normal force, the normal contact force or the normal reaction. “Normal” means at right angles to the surface. Whatever the name, it is the surface pushing back because it has been squashed, never a force the object carries with it.

Careful

“The table doesn’t push. It just gets in the way.”

Getting in the way is pushing. The table bends under the book, by far too little to see, and the bent table pushes up like a bent ruler. If it did not, the book would keep moving downward through the wood, because a force (the Earth’s pull) would be acting with nothing to balance it. Put a ruler across two book stacks and load it with coins, and you can watch the push being made.

Check yourself

When you jump off a low wall, for the moment you are in the air you feel weightless. Has gravity switched off? What has changed?

Answer at the back of the book

3.4Every push has a partner

London, 1687

In the Principia, after the first two laws, Newton wrote a third, and it is the one that people find hardest to believe. Press a stone with your finger, he said, and the stone presses your finger. Whenever one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts a force of the same size, in the opposite direction, on the first. Forces never come singly. Every push has a partner, and the two partners act on different objects.

Your finger on the stone is easy to accept, because you can feel the stone pressing back. The law bites when the two objects are very different. A marble hits a moving train. Which feels the bigger force at the instant they meet, the marble or the train? Almost everyone says the marble, because the marble is the one that gets smashed. Newton says the forces are exactly equal. The marble is smashed because it is small and fragile and the same force gives it an enormous acceleration, while the same force on a train of vastly greater mass changes its motion by an amount nobody could measure. Equal forces; wildly unequal effects. That is the rule you need for the mosquito.

Predict first

Kym and her father hook two luggage scales together and pull against each other. Dad is stronger and pulls harder. Which scale shows the bigger reading?

  1. Dad’s scale.
  2. Kym’s scale.
  3. Both read the same.

What happens

Both read the same, whoever “pulls harder”. The pull of each scale on the other is one pair of forces, equal and opposite. Of about 900 university students asked the truck-and-car version of this question before their physics course, 73 per cent said the bigger object pushes harder. After the course, 39 per cent still did. Do the experiment.

Two luggage scales

Borrow the two hanging luggage scales (the kind for weighing suitcases at the airport) that most homes have at least one of; a neighbour will have the other. Hook them together and pull against a partner, gently at first, then as hard as you both can. Read both dials at the same moment. They agree, to about 0.1 kg. Now hook one scale to a door handle and pull the other as hard as you like: it still reads the same as the one on the handle, and the handle is not pulling at all in any way you would recognise. Finally, pull “harder than your partner” on purpose. You cannot; the readings move together. The dial says kg, which is a weight reading divided by 9.8: a reading of 10 kg means the hook is being pulled with about 98 N.

Why can the scales never disagree? Follow the forces along a rope in a tug of war. Each short piece of rope pulls on the next piece, and the next piece pulls back on it with the same force; every link in the chain is a pair. The size of that pull is the rope’s tension, and it is the same all along a light rope, which is why both teams feel the same pull however the contest is going. The luggage scales are two links in such a chain, and each reads the tension in the chain at its own position. There is no way to make your link pull harder than the link next to it.

Now the subtle part, which textbooks still get wrong. Look at yourself standing on the floor. Two forces act on you: the Earth pulls you down (your weight, about 392 N if your mass is 40 kg), and the floor pushes you up with the normal force, also 392 N. They are equal and opposite, and they cancel, which is why you stay put. They are not a Newton pair. Both act on the same object, you, and a pair always acts on two different objects. The partner of the Earth’s pull on you is your pull on the Earth: you attract the whole planet upward with 392 N, and it responds with an acceleration of about 7 × 10⁻²³ m/s², which is why nobody has noticed. The partner of the floor’s push on you is your push on the floor. Four forces, two pairs, and the two forces that happen to cancel belong to different pairs.

Once you see pairs everywhere, moving about makes a new kind of sense. You walk by pushing the floor backward with your foot, and the floor pushes you forward: that forward friction from Chapter 2 is the partner of your backward push. A swimmer shoves the wall of the pool and the wall shoves her off. A car’s tyres push the road backward and the road pushes the car forward. A helicopter pushes air down; the air pushes the helicopter up. An octopus squirts water backward and the water pushes the octopus forward. In every case the thing that moves off is the one that is free to move, and the force that moves it is the partner of the push it gave.

The story behind this

Every push has a partnerNewton’s third law in his own examples, a finger on a stone and a horse on a rope, and why a truck and a car in a collision feel exactly the same force.

At school

This is Newton’s third law. School books often say “every action has an equal and opposite reaction”. Two words make that safe: the two forces act on different objects, and they act at the same instant. There is no first push followed by a reply. “Reaction” is a name, not a delay.

Careful

“The truck pushes the car harder than the car pushes the truck. It’s bigger and it’s going faster.”

At the moment they touch, the force of the truck on the car and the force of the car on the truck are equal and opposite, always. What differs is what the equal forces do: the car, with less mass, gets the much bigger acceleration and the much bigger damage. “Going faster” cannot matter either, because speed depends on who is watching: from the truck driver’s seat, it is the car that is rushing at the truck.

Check yourself

If every pull your tug-of-war team gives the rope is matched by an equal pull from the rope on your team, how can your team ever win?

Answer at the back of the book

3.5Momentum and rockets

Thumba, Kerala, 21 November 1963

Momentum

How much motion an object has: its mass multiplied by its velocity, in kg·m/s. It points the way the object is moving. Hard to stop means a lot of momentum.

Before any formula, feel it. A cricket ball comes at you at 20 km/h and you catch it: easy. The same ball at 100 km/h: your hands sting, and the keeper wears gloves for a reason. Now a tennis ball at 100 km/h: the same speed, far less sting. There is a quantity here that is bigger for a faster ball and bigger for a heavier one, and the simplest way to think of it is how hard the thing is to stop. Newton called it the quantity of motion. Buridan, back in Chapter 2, had almost found it: his impetus grew with speed and with the amount of stuff, and so does this. We call it momentum, and it is simply mass times velocity. A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m/s carries 0.16 × 30 = 4.8 kilogram-metres per second of it. Momentum has a direction, the direction of the velocity, and that matters in a moment.

Impulse

A force multiplied by the time it acts. It equals the change in momentum it produces. The same change can come from a big force for a short time or a small force for a long time.

What changes momentum? A force, acting for a time. Catch the fast ball with stiff arms and your hands stop it almost instantly, with a large force; let your hands ride back with the ball and the same momentum is removed over a longer time, with a smaller force, which is the whole of the keeper’s art. The product of force and time is called impulse, and it equals the change in momentum. You met it without the name at the end of Chapter 2: the tablecloth’s friction acted on the plate for so short a time that it gave the plate almost no momentum. Bending your knees when you land from a jump is the same trick in the other direction.

Now put the third law next to impulse and something remarkable drops out. When two things push on each other, the forces are equal and opposite, and they act for the same time (they start and stop touching together). So the two impulses are equal and opposite, and the two changes in momentum cancel exactly. Whatever momentum one object gains, the other loses. Add up the momentum of both objects before they touch and after, and the total is the same. This is the conservation of momentum, and it holds for any set of objects on which nothing from outside is pushing: in a collision, however violent, the total momentum of the colliding things does not change. A textbook example: a 0.350 kg cart moving at 2 m/s meets a 0.500 kg cart coming the other way at 0.5 m/s. Before, the total is 0.350 × 2 − 0.500 × 0.5 = 0.45 kg·m/s. After the collision the first cart is measured bouncing back at 0.94 m/s, and the second must therefore be moving forward at 1.56 m/s, so that the total is still 0.45. Measure it, and it is.

Back from Chapter 2

A spacecraft far from any planet switches off its engines. It keeps going at the same speed. A friend says: “The push from the engines is stored inside it, and it will slow down when that push runs out.” What is wrong with that, and what does the spacecraft actually carry?

Answer at the back of the book

Momentum is where the rocket comes from. The question people have always asked is: in empty space, with nothing to push against, how does a rocket move at all? The answer is that it carries the thing it pushes against. The engine throws hot gas backward out of the nozzle at enormous speed; by the third law, the gas pushes the rocket forward with an equal force, and that forward push is the thrust. By momentum, the gas going backward and the rocket going forward keep the total exactly what it was. A rocket does not push on the air behind it, and it does not push on the launch pad. It works better in a vacuum, where no air gets in the way of the exhaust. A balloon is the same engine in rubber: the stretched balloon squeezes its air out of the neck, and the air pushes the balloon the other way.

The balloon rocket

Thread a drinking straw onto a long piece of string and tie the string tight between two chairs, or a door handle and a chair, a few metres apart. Blow up a balloon, hold the neck pinched, and tape the balloon to the straw with the neck pointing backward along the string. Let go. The balloon runs the length of the string with its air jetting the other way. Try a bigger balloon, and a balloon with the neck pinched half shut so the air leaves more slowly: which goes further, and which goes faster? The balloon is not pushed by its air hitting the room. It is pushed by the air it is throwing out, at the moment of throwing.

On 21 November 1963, at Thumba, a fishing village on the Kerala coast, India launched its first rocket. It was an American-made Nike-Apache, and it went up beside the church of St Mary Magdalene, which the village had given over to the new space programme: the church became the control and assembly building, and rockets stood about where the altar had been. The story goes that parts were carried to the launch site by bicycle and bullock cart. The scientist behind it was Vikram Sarabhai, and the space programme that grew from that church is the one that put Chandrayaan-3 on the Moon in 2023. Every one of its engines works by the rule in the figure: throw gas one way, go the other.

The story behind this

Rockets from a churchIndia’s first rocket rose from beside a village church in Kerala in 1963, and it climbed by throwing things away: the idea of momentum, and why a rocket needs nothing to push against.

Investigation 3.5

On a glass table or a large wet steel thali, flick one ice cube into another that is at rest, head on. Watch what happens to each. Then try a big cube into a small one, and a small cube into a big one. In which case does the first cube stop dead, and in which does it bounce back? Avoid glancing hits and spinning cubes, which make the result hard to read.

At school

IGCSE has a topic called Momentum (1.6). Expect to use momentum = mass × velocity and to work out the total before and after a collision. The habit to keep from this book is to decide first which objects you are counting, because only the total for the whole group stays the same.

Careful

“The rocket pushes against the air behind it, so it can’t work in space.”

Rockets work better in space. The thing a rocket pushes against is its own exhaust, which it carries with it as fuel. Push gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward: a Newton pair, with the air playing no part. In the atmosphere the air only gets in the way of the exhaust and adds drag.

Understand itMomentum

What does it measure?

How much directed motion an object carries, and how hard it is to stop: its mass multiplied by its velocity (p = mv), in kg·m/s.

Why is it called this?

From the Latin momentum, movement or moving power, contracted from movimentum (from movere, to move). Newton called it quantitas motus, the quantity of motion.

What problem did it solve?

Collisions between carts, billiard balls or a mosquito and a car involve forces that spike and vanish in a millisecond, too fast to track instant by instant. Momentum lets you relate the motion after a collision to the motion before without knowing the messy details in between.

Why does it work?

Because by Newton’s third law, when two objects push on each other, they exert equal and opposite forces for the exact same time, so whatever momentum one loses (F × t), the other gains.

How does it help?

It explains why a wicket-keeper draws her hands back to catch a fast cricket ball over a longer time, how recoil speeds can be predicted after a collision, and how a rocket accelerates in empty space by throwing exhaust gas backward.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

From Christopher Wren and Christiaan Huygens’ colliding-pendulum tests in the 1660s to modern air-track carts and particle accelerators, the vector sum of mv before and after an isolated collision always matches.

What it isn’t

It is not kinetic energy (½mv²), which has no direction and can be turned into heat during an inelastic crash even while total momentum stays strictly unchanged.

Where does it stop working?

Conservation of momentum never stops working anywhere in physics, provided you include all interacting parts of the system (even the small momentum carried away by light or electromagnetic fields).

Your turn

Explain Momentum to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

An astronaut is floating in the middle of a space-station module, out of reach of every wall, holding a spanner. She wants to drift to the window. What should she do?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 3

The mosquito and the windscreen

A car on the Bandra–Worli Sea Link is doing 90 km/h, which is 25 metres every second. A mosquito drifting the other way meets the windscreen. In about a thousandth of a second, the mosquito goes from drifting to travelling with the car. The driver notices nothing.

  1. A mosquito’s mass is about 10⁻⁵ kg, a hundredth of a gram.
  2. The car’s mass is about 1,200 kg.
  3. Newton’s third law says the force of the windscreen on the mosquito and the force of the mosquito on the windscreen are equal and opposite.

Which feels the bigger force? And if the forces are equal, why is only the mosquito destroyed?

Show the solution

They feel exactly the same force. The third law allows no exception for size or speed.

Estimate it. The mosquito’s momentum changes by about 10⁻⁵ kg × 25 m/s = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m/s, in about 0.001 s. Force × time = change in momentum, so the force is about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 0.001 = 0.25 N: a quarter of a newton, about the weight of a 25 g biscuit, on each of them.

Now the second law, separately for each. The mosquito gets an acceleration of 0.25 N ÷ 10⁻⁵ kg = 25,000 m/s², about two and a half thousand times the acceleration of a falling stone. The car gets 0.25 N ÷ 1,200 kg, about 0.0002 m/s², a change of speed too small for any instrument in the car to register. The ratio of the two accelerations is the ratio of the two masses, about a hundred million to one. The mosquito is destroyed not because it felt a bigger force but because its body is tiny and fragile and the same force wrenched it to the car’s speed in a millisecond.

Notice, too, that “the car was going faster” explains nothing. From the driver’s seat the car is still and the mosquito is the one travelling at 90 km/h. Speed belongs to a point of view; the pair of forces does not.

(The mosquito’s mass is an order-of-magnitude figure from a physics textbook; the car’s mass and the thousandth of a second are our guesses. Change them and the conclusion does not move.)

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You can now add forces, turn a net force into an acceleration, find the partner of any push, and keep the books on momentum. One force has appeared in every section without ever being explained: the Earth’s pull. Why does it give every falling thing the same 9.8 m/s², heavy or light, when the same push gives a truck far less acceleration than a scooter? Chapter 4 drops a cricket ball and a ₹1 coin together, and starts with the two people who did that experiment four hundred years ago.
