Chapter 4

Falling

The big questionDrop a cricket ball and a ₹1 coin from the same height at the same moment. Which lands first, and why do you think so?

  1. 4.1Heavier falls faster?
  2. 4.2Air gets in the way
  3. 4.3On the Moon
  4. 4.4Thrown sideways
  5. 4.5Going round

Chapter 3 ended with a mosquito on a windscreen and a rule that surprises almost everyone: the two of them push on each other equally hard. Forces come in pairs, and a force changes motion rather than keeping it going. This chapter takes those two rules to the most familiar force there is, and the one most people have wrong since they were five years old: the pull of the Earth on everything near it.

Here is the puzzle to carry with you. Hold a cricket ball in one hand and a ₹1 coin in the other, at the same height, and let go of both at the same instant. Which hits the floor first? Nearly everyone says the ball, because it is heavier. The chapter will give you the answer, and then something better than the answer: the reason, which turns out to be the same reason the Moon stays up and a spacecraft can coast to it with its engine off.

4.1Heavier falls faster?

Delft, 1586

Picture a church tower in a Dutch town, and two men at the top with lead balls in their hands. Simon Stevin was an engineer and mathematician who thought the way to settle an argument was to try it. His friend Jan Cornets de Groot had climbed the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk with him. One ball weighed ten times as much as the other. About 30 feet below them, roughly 9 m, lay a wooden board. They let go of both balls at the same moment, and listened.

The argument they were settling was nearly two thousand years old. Aristotle had taught that heavier things fall faster, and faster in proportion to their weight. If that were right, the heavy ball should hit the board when the light one was still only a tenth of the way down, about 8 m above it, and the listeners would hear two thuds well apart. A few people had doubted this. In Alexandria in the sixth century, John Philoponus wrote that when you drop two very different weights, the difference in their fall times is tiny. But almost nobody had done the experiment carefully and written it down.

They heard one thud.

Stevin printed the result in 1586, three years before Galileo reached Pisa. You may have heard that Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. The only account of that comes from Vincenzo Viviani, his assistant late in life. Galileo himself never describes doing it, and most historians think it was a thought experiment, or at most a private test. So the famous drop is probably a legend, and the real drop happened in Delft. Galileo’s reasoning about falling, though, was real and brilliant, and we will meet it again in a moment.

Before the explanation, take your own idea seriously, because it is Aristotle’s idea and it is held by very clever people. In one well-known survey, 82% of university students starting a physics course believed that an object’s own properties change how fast it falls, even with no air at all. The idea is not foolish. A feather does drift down slowly; a sheet of paper does lag behind a stone. What the idea gets wrong is which thing is doing that. So separate the two questions: what does the air do, and what does the Earth do? This section is about the Earth. The next one is about the air.

Predict first

You drop a cricket ball and a ₹1 coin from the same height at the same moment. Which lands first?

  1. The cricket ball, because it is heavier
  2. The coin, because it is smaller and slips through the air
  3. They land together, or so nearly that you cannot tell

What happens

They land together, or so nearly that you cannot tell. Both are small and heavy for their size, so from a table’s height the air hardly touches either of them. Try it over a steel thali: you hear one clink. The feeling that the ball should win comes from watching light, wide things like paper and feathers, which are a different story.

Free fall

Motion with nothing acting but the pull of the Earth: no air resistance, no hand, no string. A ball thrown upward is in free fall too, on the way up, at the top, and on the way down.

Acceleration of free fall (g)

How fast a freely falling object speeds up: about 9.8 m/s² near the ground, which means its speed grows by 9.8 m/s every second. It points towards Earth’s centre, and that direction is what we call “down”.

With the air out of the way, everything near the ground speeds up at the same rate as it falls: about 9.8 metres per second, every second. Let go of a stone. After one second it is moving at 9.8 m/s and has fallen 4.9 m. After two seconds it is moving at 19.6 m/s and has fallen 19.6 m. After three, 29.4 m/s and 44 m. Those numbers do not care what the stone is made of or how heavy it is. Falling with nothing but Earth’s pull acting is called free fall, and the rate of speeding up, 9.8 m/s², is the acceleration of free fall, written g. It is not quite the same everywhere. Around the world it runs from about 9.78 to 9.83 m/s², depending on where you stand, so we round it to 9.8.

Why should a heavy ball and a light one speed up at the same rate? This needs Chapter 3, and it is the simplest true explanation there is. Earth pulls a heavier object harder: its weight is bigger. But Chapter 3 also said that a heavier object is harder to get moving. The same push gives a truck far less acceleration than a scooter. Double the mass of a falling ball and you double the pull on it, and you also double its stubbornness. The two doublings cancel exactly, and the acceleration comes out the same. The cricket ball is pulled many times harder than the coin, and it is exactly that many times harder to speed up. Stevin’s two balls told the same story in lead.

How do we know? Timing a fall a laboratory measurement

To measure g, let a dense steel ball fall exactly 1.0000 m and time it with an electronic timer: it takes 0.4517 s. In free fall the distance fallen is half of g times the time squared, so g is twice the distance divided by the time squared: 2 × 1.0000 ÷ 0.4517² = 9.80 m/s². Repeat it with a heavier ball and the time does not change. The ball has to be dense so that the air does not matter, and the timer has to be electronic, because a thumb on a stopwatch is late by your reaction time, which can be a large part of such a short fall. You can measure that reaction time yourself: a friend holds a 30 cm ruler hanging between your open finger and thumb and lets go without warning. If you pinch it after 20 cm have passed, it fell for 0.20 s; 10 cm means 0.14 s, and the full 30 cm means 0.25 s.

At school

At school you will see g written two ways: 9.8 m/s², the acceleration of free fall, and 9.8 N/kg, the gravitational field strength, the pull on each kilogram. They are the same number seen from two sides. IGCSE calls the pull on an object its weight, “a gravitational force on an object that has mass”, measured in newtons.

Careful

“Heavier things fall faster.”

With the air out of the way, they do not: everything speeds up at 9.8 m/s per second, whatever it weighs, because a heavier thing is pulled harder and is harder to get moving by exactly the same factor. In air a light, wide object can lag, but that is the air’s doing, not the weight’s. A coin and a cricket ball from a table’s height land together, and you can hear it.

Understand itFree fall

What is it?

Motion under the pull of gravity alone, with no air resistance, hand, floor or string pushing on the object.

Why is it called this?

Free here means free of every other force besides gravity. The word fall misleads people into thinking it applies only on the way down: a ball thrown straight up is in free fall on the way up, at the very top, and on the way down, from the instant it leaves your hand.

What problem did it solve?

Everyday falls in air mix two things together, Earth’s downward pull and the air’s upward drag, so a feather lags behind a stone and people concluded for two millennia that heavier things naturally fall faster.

Why does it work?

Earth pulls a body of ten times the mass with ten times the gravitational force, and by Newton’s second law (a = F/m) ten times the mass also takes ten times the force to achieve the same acceleration; the two factors of ten cancel out completely.

How does it help?

It tells you that every dense object near Earth’s surface changes its vertical velocity by 9.8 m/s every second downward, letting you time the depth of a well or predict the arc of any thrown ball.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot dropped two lead balls of 10-to-1 weight 30 feet onto a board at Delft in 1586 and heard a single thud, and David Scott dropped a 1.32 kg geological hammer and a falcon feather in the Moon’s vacuum on 2 August 1971 and watched them hit the lunar soil side by side.

What it isn’t

It is not motion at terminal speed: once air drag grows to balance a raindrop’s weight, the drop is no longer in free fall and falls at a steady speed instead of accelerating.

Where does it stop working?

Near Earth’s surface g ≈ 9.8 m/s² stays nearly constant over everyday heights, and weakens noticeably only when you climb hundreds of kilometres toward orbit.

Your turn

Explain Free fall to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A friend drops a glass marble and a cricket ball together from a first-floor balcony about 4 m up, and says the ball will land first because it is heavier. What do you say, and how long does the fall take?

The single thud at DelftTwo lead balls, a church tower in Delft and a single thud, three years before Galileo reached Pisa; then a hammer and a feather on the Moon finished the argument.

4.2Air gets in the way

Mumbai, a monsoon afternoon

Stand under a balcony in July and watch the rain. Those drops have fallen from clouds that can be a few kilometres up. If a drop kept speeding up all the way down at 9.8 m/s every second, from 4000 m it would arrive at about 280 m/s, over 1000 km/h. The monsoon would be a hail of bullets. A big drop does sting a little, but it arrives at the speed of a bicycle, not a rifle shot. Something stops the speeding up. That something is the air, and this section is about what it does and when it matters.

Drag (air resistance)

The force a fluid, such as air or water, puts on an object moving through it, pointing against the motion. It grows with speed and with the area facing the motion. Unlike the weight, it is zero when the object is still.

Start with a feeling. Fill a bucket with water, hold your hand flat and sweep it through, then turn your hand edge-on and sweep again. Flat, the water fights you; edge-on, it hardly does. Your hand has to shove the water out of its way, and the faster you move, the more water you must shove each second and the harder you must shove it. Air does the same thing to anything moving through it, more gently, because air is far thinner than water. The force is called drag. Drag always points against the motion, and it grows with speed: for most everyday objects, roughly with the speed squared, so doubling the speed makes the drag about four times as big. It also grows with the area facing the motion, which is why your edge-on hand slipped through.

Predict first

Take two identical sheets of paper. Crumple one into a tight ball and leave the other flat. Hold them at the same height and let go together. Which lands first?

  1. The flat sheet, because it is spread out
  2. The crumpled ball, by a lot
  3. Together: they weigh the same, so the Earth pulls them the same

What happens

The crumpled ball, by a lot. The Earth does pull them the same: same paper, same weight. The difference is the air. The flat sheet pushes a wide area of air out of its way and the drag soon matches its tiny weight; the ball slips through. Same weight, different fall. So weight was never the whole story.

Terminal speed

The steady speed a falling object reaches when the drag on it has grown to equal its weight, so the net force is zero. Both forces are still there; they cancel.

Now follow a raindrop from the moment it forms. At first it is barely moving, so there is almost no drag, and the only force is its weight: it speeds up at the full 9.8 m/s². As it gets faster, the drag grows. The weight does not change, so the net force downward shrinks, and the drop speeds up more and more slowly. Eventually the drag grows until it exactly matches the weight. Now the two forces cancel. Remember Chapter 2: balanced forces do not mean the drop stops; they mean its velocity stops changing. From here down it falls at a steady speed, its terminal speed.

For a drop about 2 mm across, that steady speed is about 6.5 m/s, 23 km/h, which is bicycle speed. Bigger drops fall faster, because a bigger drop has more weight for each bit of area the air can push on. But there is a ceiling. Above about 4.5 mm a drop flattens into a parachute shape and breaks up, so the largest drops reach only about 10 m/s, 36 km/h. Even those take at least 400 s, nearly seven minutes, to fall from 4000 m. And while we are on raindrops: they are not teardrop-shaped. Small ones are nearly round, and drops of 2 to 3 mm are flattened underneath, like a bun.

How do we know? The speed of a raindrop course notes and NASA

Physics courses work out a raindrop’s terminal speed by setting drag equal to weight. The MIT course notes take a drop of mass 4 milligrams with a cross-section of 3 square millimetres, which is a drop about 2 mm across, and get 6.5 m/s. NASA, which measures rain from satellites, reports that a drop’s speed in still air rises with its size up to a maximum of about 10 m/s for the largest drops. The two agree where they overlap. The same sum gives about 20 m/s for a small hailstone, and for people it gives the speeds skydivers report: roughly 350 km/h falling head-down and about 200 km/h spread-eagled, because spreading out puts more area in the way of the air.

The same rule explains a lot. Two sheets of paper crumpled together into one ball weigh twice as much as one crumpled sheet but push on about the same air, so the double ball reaches a higher steady speed and lands first. A small animal has little weight for the area it presents to the air, so its terminal speed is low, and it can survive a fall that would kill a large one. A feather has almost no weight for its area, so its terminal speed is tiny, and it drifts.

Four sheets of paper

Take four identical sheets of paper, A4 from the printer is ideal, and clear a space on the floor. Predict first, every time. First: one sheet flat against one sheet crumpled into a tight ball; drop them together from shoulder height. Second: one crumpled sheet against two sheets crumpled together into one ball, so the second ball has twice the weight but about the same size and shape. Drop them together several times and watch which lands first. The weights are the same in the first race and different in the second, yet the air decides both. Write down what you saw.

Careful

“At terminal speed the drop has stopped speeding up, so gravity has stopped pulling on it.”

Gravity is pulling exactly as hard as ever. The drag has simply grown until it pulls back equally hard, so the two forces cancel and the speed stays constant. Take the air away, as on the Moon, and the drop would go on speeding up all the way down.

Check yourself

Two skydivers jump in the same spread-eagled position, one much heavier than the other. The heavier one ends up falling faster. Why, if both are pulled towards Earth with the same acceleration at the start?

Answer at the back of the book

At school

IGCSE calls drag through air “air resistance”. The rule you will need is the one from Chapter 2: an object keeps a constant speed in a straight line unless a resultant force acts. At terminal speed the resultant force is zero, so the speed is constant.

Investigation 4.2

In the live figure for this section, set the air to zero and drop a feather and a hammer: they fall together. Now slide the air up a little at a time. Predict which separates from the other first, and whether the heavier object’s final speed is higher or lower than the lighter one’s, before you look.

4.3On the Moon

Hadley Rille, the Moon, 2 August 1971

The last moonwalk of Apollo 15 was nearly over. David Scott, the mission’s commander, stood in front of the television camera with a geological hammer in one hand and a falcon’s feather in the other. The hammer had a mass of 1.32 kg. He held them out at about the same height, roughly 1.6 m up, in front of the camera, and let go of both at the same moment.

Predict first

On the Moon there is no air. A hammer and a feather are let go together from the same height. Which lands first?

  1. The hammer: it is far heavier
  2. The feather: it is lighter and the Moon’s pull is weak
  3. They land together

What happens

They land together. With no air to hold the feather back, nothing separates them: the Moon pulls the hammer much harder, and the hammer is exactly that much harder to get moving. NASA’s transcription of the moment has Scott saying that “Mr Galileo was correct in his findings”.

Three things happened in that drop, and it is worth taking them apart. First, the hammer fell. Many people are sure that there is no gravity where there is no air. In one survey, 81% of 13-year-olds did not think there is gravity in space. But the hammer fell, and so did the feather: the Moon pulls. Second, they fell together, which is Stevin’s single thud with the Moon supplying the vacuum. Third, they fell slowly. From 1.6 m the pair took about 1.4 s to land, where on Earth a hammer takes 0.57 s. The Moon is a smaller, lighter world, and its pull at its surface gives an acceleration of about 1.6 to 1.7 m/s², roughly one sixth of Earth’s.

Notice which fact explains which. The feather kept up with the hammer because there is no air. The two of them fell slowly because the Moon’s pull is weaker. People often tangle these: “things fall in slow motion on the Moon because there is no air to push them.” But air can only slow a fall. Take it away and a fall gets faster, not slower. The slow motion is all the Moon’s gentle pull.

Scott gave the credit to Galileo. As we saw, the Leaning Tower drop is probably a legend, but the idea he was testing really was Galileo’s, and Stevin’s and Philoponus’s before him: with the air out of the way, everything falls together. It took three and a half centuries and a journey to another world to see it done with a feather.

You can make a small vacuum of your own with a coin. Cut a paper disc a little smaller than a ₹5 coin and lay it flat on top of the coin. Drop the pair. The coin shields the paper from the air, so the paper rides down with it and the two land together, where the paper alone would flutter.

Careful

“There’s no gravity on the Moon, because there’s no air.”

The hammer fell. The Moon pulls everything near it, at about a sixth of Earth’s rate. Air and gravity have nothing to do with each other: air is the stuff that gets in the way of falling, and taking it away lets things fall freely, which is why the feather kept up.

Check yourself

Suppose Stevin and de Groot had done their experiment on the Moon, dropping their two lead balls about 9 m onto a board. What would they have heard, and when?

Answer at the back of the book

The story behind this

A hammer, a feather and the MoonAt the end of the last moonwalk of Apollo 15, an astronaut dropped a hammer and a falcon’s feather for the television cameras, and an argument 385 years old ended in about 1.2 seconds.

4.4Thrown sideways

At home, at the kitchen table

Put two coins at the edge of a table. Nudge one so that it just drops off the edge. At the same instant, flick the other hard so that it flies out sideways. The flicked coin travels much farther before it lands. Does it stay in the air longer? Most people feel that it must: it was moving faster, it had more “force” behind it, so surely it had more to carry it. That feeling has a name, and you met it in Chapter 2.

Back from Chapter 2

“The flicked coin keeps going forward because it carries the push of your finger with it, and when that runs out it falls.” What is wrong with this picture?

Answer at the back of the book

Predict first

Two coins leave the edge of a table at the same instant. One is nudged so that it just drops; the other is flicked so that it flies out sideways. Which hits the floor first?

  1. The dropped coin: the flicked one is going faster and stays up longer
  2. The flicked coin: it hits the floor harder and sooner
  3. Both at the same moment

What happens

Both at the same moment. Listen: one clink. From a table about 75 cm high, both are in the air for 0.39 s, however hard you flick. Flicking changes how far the coin goes, not how long it takes to fall.

Here is the idea that unlocks this, and it is one of the most useful ideas in the whole book. A flying coin has two motions at once: a sideways one and a downward one. Treat them separately. Sideways, after the coin leaves your finger, nothing pushes it or pulls it (the air, over a short flight, is too little to notice). So its sideways speed stays whatever the flick gave it. Downward, the Earth pulls, and the coin is in free fall: it speeds up downward at 9.8 m/s², exactly like the dropped coin beside it. The two motions do not interfere. The sideways motion does not hold the coin up, and the fall does not slow the sideways motion. All they share is the clock.

Projectile

Anything thrown or launched that then moves under the pull of the Earth alone. Its sideways speed stays constant and it falls at g, and the two motions are independent, so its path is a curve.

So the dropped coin and the flicked coin fall in step, and they land together. The flicked coin simply covers ground while it does so. Flick it at 2 m/s and it lands 78 cm from the table; flick it at 4 m/s and it lands 1.56 m out, but still after 0.39 s. Put the two motions together and the path is a curve, the smooth arc that any thrown ball follows. An object moving under gravity alone like this is called a projectile, and its path is its trajectory.

The physics course at MIT shows this with a trick that looks impossible. A gun is aimed straight at an apple hanging across the room, and the moment the gun fires, the apple is released. The bullet does not fly straight; it falls as it flies. But the apple falls too, at exactly the same rate, so the bullet meets it in mid-air, every time, however fast or slow the shot. Both fall together; the only thing that matters is pointing straight at the apple.

Now, the curved paths. In 1980 three researchers asked university students to draw the path of a ball coming out of a curved tube lying flat on a table. A third drew the ball still curving after it left a C-shaped tube, and half did so for a spiral tube. But with nothing to push it round any more, the ball goes straight. A path curves only while something is bending it: the tube’s wall, or the Earth’s pull. There is no “curviness” stored in the ball, just as there is no push stored in the coin.

One honesty note. All this ignores the air, and for a flicked coin or a tossed ball across a room that is fine. For a long, fast throw it is not. In the MIT course notes a ball thrown at 30 m/s lands at only about 72% of the distance the no-air curve predicts, and it comes down more steeply than it went up. A spinning ball can also curve sideways in the air, which is the drift a spin bowler gets before the ball even reaches the pitch. The clean two-motion picture is the skeleton; air adds the flesh.

Careful

“The flicked coin stays up longer because it is going faster.”

Going faster sideways has no effect on falling. Both coins start with no downward speed and both are pulled down at 9.8 m/s², so they reach the floor together. Speed sideways only decides where the coin lands, not when.

Check yourself

A ball is thrown horizontally from a balcony and takes 1.2 s to reach the ground. The same ball is then thrown horizontally from the same spot at twice the speed. How long does it take to reach the ground now, and what changes?

Answer at the back of the book

Investigation 4.4

In the live figure, launch two balls from the same height at the same instant, one dropped and one thrown sideways. Predict which lands first and where, then run it. Then double the sideways speed and predict again. Finally set the launch angle upward and watch the sideways steps: do they change size while the ball rises and falls?

4.5Going round

Mumbai, on a local train

The train takes a curve and everyone standing sways the same way, outward from the bend, grabbing the handles. It feels exactly like being pushed. Ask anyone what pushed them and they will say “centrifugal force”, the force that flings you outward when you go round a corner. The feeling is real. The force, as we will see, is not what it seems, and the test is simple enough to do on the kitchen floor.

Cut a gap about 5 cm wide in the rim of a paper plate. Put a marble inside and roll it round and round against the rim, fast. It circles until it reaches the gap.

Predict first

A marble rolls round the inside of a paper plate with a gap cut in its rim. When the marble reaches the gap, which way does it go?

  1. Outward, away from the centre of the plate, flung by the spinning
  2. Straight on, along the direction it was moving at that instant
  3. It keeps curving round for a while, then straightens out

What happens

Straight on, along the line it was moving on at that instant: a tangent to the circle. It does not fly outward, and it does not keep curving. In the 1980 study, 30% of students drew a curved path for a ball let go from a string; the marble disagrees with them every time.

Think about what the rim was doing before the gap. A marble rolling in a straight line at a steady speed needs no force at all; Chapter 2 settled that. But the marble was not going straight. Its direction was changing every instant, and a change of direction is a change of velocity, which only a force can cause. Which force? The rim, pushing the marble inward, towards the centre, all the way round. Take the rim away and there is no inward push, so there is no more turning. The marble does what everything does when nothing acts on it: it carries straight on.

Centripetal force

The inward force, towards the centre, that keeps an object moving in a circle by continually changing its direction. It is always some ordinary force doing the job: tension, friction, gravity, the push of a wall.

That is the whole secret of going round. Anything moving in a circle is being pulled or pushed towards the centre, and that inward force is doing the turning. For a stone on a string it is the string’s pull. For a car on a bend it is the friction of the road on the tyres. For the ping-pong balls in a bucket swung fast in a vertical circle, an MIT lecture demonstration, it is the bucket’s bottom pressing on them, which is why they stay in even when the bucket is upside down at the top. For the Moon going round the Earth, it is gravity, which is where the next chapter begins. The inward force needed grows quickly with speed: on the same bend, a car at 100 km/h needs four times the sideways grip of a car at 50 km/h, because the needed acceleration goes as the speed squared. That is why fast cornering is dangerous. Physicists call any force doing this job centripetal, which is Latin for “centre-seeking”. It is a role, not a new kind of force: the string’s tension, the road’s friction or Earth’s gravity plays it.

So what pushed you on the train? Nothing pushed you outward. When the train turned, your body did what the marble did at the gap: it carried straight on, while the train swung round under you. The handle, or the side of the carriage, then pushed you inward to bring you round with it. The outward “force” is the feeling of your own straight-line motion meeting a vehicle that is turning. A washing machine’s spin cycle works on the same fact. The drum wall pushes the clothes inward, round and round. Water at a hole in the drum has nothing pushing it inward, so it carries straight on, through the hole and out.

At school

Your syllabus never uses the word “centrifugal”. IGCSE describes circular motion as “motion in a circular path due to a force perpendicular to the motion”. In an exam, name the real inward force: the tension in the string, the friction of the road, or the gravitational pull of the Sun.

Now the honest part about “centrifugal force”, because you will keep hearing the words. Someone who insists on describing the world from inside the turning train, treating the carriage as if it were standing still, finds that Newton’s rules do not quite work there: things seem to slide outward with nothing pushing them. To make the rules work in that spinning view, they have to add an outward force by hand. Physicists call that a fictitious force. It has no source; nothing is doing the pushing. Seen from the platform, there is no such force, just a passenger carrying straight on and a train turning. Both descriptions can be made to agree, but the one from the platform is the simpler and truer one, because in it every force has something causing it.

A marble, a paper plate and a gap

Cut a gap about 5 cm wide in the rim of a paper plate and put the plate on a smooth floor, a tiled one is best. Roll a marble round the inside, fast enough that it hugs the rim. Predict first: which way will it leave at the gap? Mark your guess on the floor with a coin. Then watch, several times, from different starting points. It always leaves straight along the rim’s direction at the gap, never outward. If you have a bucket with a sturdy handle, ask an adult to do the swing: a little water in the bucket, swung fast in a vertical circle outdoors, stays in even at the top, because the bucket’s bottom keeps pushing the water inward, towards the centre of the swing.

Careful

“A force throws me outward when the train goes round a bend.”

Nothing pushes you outward. Your body carries straight on while the train turns, and then the handle or the carriage wall pushes you inward to bring you round. The only real force in the turning is the inward one. The outward feeling is your own straight-line motion meeting a turning vehicle.

Understand itCentripetal force

What is it?

Any net force that points inward toward the centre of a curve and keeps an object moving along a circular path by continually turning its velocity vector.

Why is it called this?

Isaac Newton coined vis centripeta in 1687 from Latin centrum (centre) and petere (to seek), to contrast with Christiaan Huygens’ earlier vis centrifuga (centre-fleeing).

What problem did it solve?

People felt tugged outward on a bend or when whirling a sling and assumed circular motion was driven by an outward push, which left them unable to explain why a stone released from a sling flies along the tangent rather than straight out from the centre.

Why does it work?

By Newton’s first law, a body with no force on it goes straight at constant speed; to bend that straight path into a circle at speed v and radius r requires an inward acceleration of v²/r toward the centre at every instant.

How does it help?

It lets you calculate the road grip a car needs on a bend (four times as much grip at twice the speed), why water stays in an overhead swinging bucket, and how gravity holds the Moon and satellites in orbit.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Roll a marble round the inside of a paper plate with a gap cut in its rim: the instant the rim’s inward push ends at the gap, the marble travels straight along the tangent, never outward.

What it isn’t

It is not a new fifth force of nature to add alongside tension, friction or gravity on a free-body diagram; it is simply the job description for whichever real force (string tension, road friction, or gravity) is pointing toward the centre.

Where does it stop working?

If the required inward force mv²/r exceeds what the string or road friction can supply, the string snaps or the tyres skid and the object leaves the circle along a straighter path.

Your turn

Explain Centripetal force to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

A racing car goes round a bend at a perfectly steady 120 km/h. Is it accelerating? If so, which way?

Investigation 4.5

In the live figure, whirl the ball on its string and press “release” at three different points of the circle. Before each release, point to where you think the ball will go. Then switch on the “from the ball’s seat” view and see the same event from inside the turning: notice that the pretend outward force appears there and nowhere else.

Bandra–Worli Sea Link, Mumbai

Case file 4

The ball off the Sea Link

The Bandra–Worli Sea Link is a 5.6 km cable-stayed bridge with a main span of 250 m. Imagine standing at its railing, high above the water, with three identical tennis balls and a friend who is sure of herself.

  1. You drop the first ball straight down.
  2. At the same instant your friend throws the second ball out horizontally, gently.
  3. Also at the same instant, a third ball is thrown out horizontally, as hard as possible.
  4. Your friend says: “The hard-thrown ball has the most force, so it stays up longest. The dropped one hits first.”
  5. A car is driving along the bridge beside you at a steady speed. Its passenger holds a fourth ball out of the window and simply lets go of it.

Ignore the air. Which of the first three balls hits the water first? Where do they land, compared with one another? And where does the fourth ball land: behind the car, beside it, or ahead of it?

Show the solution

The first three balls hit the water at the same instant. Each starts with no downward speed, and each is pulled down at 9.8 m/s² from the moment it is released; a sideways throw changes nothing about the fall (Section 4.4). Your friend has the impetus idea from Chapter 2: there is no “force” stored in the hard-thrown ball, only a larger sideways speed that stays constant. The dropped ball lands straight below the railing; the gently thrown one lands some way out; the hard-thrown one lands farther out still, each in proportion to the sideways speed it was given, because all three are in the air for the same time.

The fourth ball lands beside the car, directly below where the passenger’s hand is at that moment. When it was released it already had the car’s forward speed, and nothing acts to slow that sideways motion, so it keeps pace with the car while it falls. Seen from the car it drops straight down; seen from the railing it traces the same kind of curve as the thrown balls. (With air, all four would fall a little short and a little late; the hard-thrown ball would lose the most.)

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Everything in this chapter falls, and everything falls alike. But we have been using the pull of the Earth without asking what it is or how far it reaches. Does it stop at the top of the air? Does it reach the Moon, and if it does, why has the Moon not fallen on us? In Section 4.5 you saw that anything going in a circle must be pulled towards the centre. In the next chapter a young man in a Lincolnshire garden puts those two thoughts together, and the Moon turns out to be falling all the time.

Chapter 5

Gravity and orbits

The big questionAstronauts on the space station float, yet gravity up there is about 89% as strong as it is on the ground. Why do they float?

  1. 5.1The apple and the Moon
  2. 5.2Newton’s cannon
  3. 5.3Ellipses
  4. 5.4Weighing the Earth
  5. 5.5Predicting the sky
  6. 5.6The slow road to the Moon

Chapter 4 left two facts lying side by side. With the air out of the way, everything falls alike: the hammer and the feather landed together on the Moon. And a thing moving sideways falls exactly as a dropped thing does: the flicked coin and the dropped coin clinked at the same instant. Hold on to both. Put together, they lift the Moon into the sky and keep it there, and they explain why a woman in the International Space Station can let go of her pen and watch it hang in front of her face.

That is this chapter’s puzzle. The station circles about 400 km above the ground. Work out how strong Earth’s pull is up there and the answer is about 89% of what it is in Mumbai: not zero, not even small. Yet everything inside floats. Something is wrong with the way most of us picture “weightless”, and fixing it takes a cannon on a mountain, a careful look at the Moon, and a phone dropped onto a pillow.

5.1The apple and the Moon

Woolsthorpe, 1666

In 1666, in the plague years, Isaac Newton was 23 and at home at Woolsthorpe, his family’s farmhouse in Lincolnshire. Sixty years later he told a friend, William Stukeley, that his thinking about gravity had been “occasion’d by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood”. There really was an apple tree in the garden. The apple did not hit him on the head; that detail was added later, and the story itself rests on an old man’s memory, so hold it lightly. But the question he asked is well recorded, and it is a wonderful one.

An apple falls. Everybody knows that. Newton’s question was: how high does the pull that drops the apple reach? To the top of the tree, obviously. To the top of the air? And if it reaches that far, why should it stop? What if it reached the Moon?

Here is why the question had teeth. Chapter 2’s law says a thing left alone moves in a straight line at a steady speed. The Moon does not: it goes round Earth, roughly in a circle, once in about 27.3 days. Chapter 4’s last section says that anything going round must be pulled towards the centre by some force, or it would fly off along a tangent. So something is pulling the Moon towards the Earth, all the time. Newton’s guess was that it is the very same pull that drops the apple, reaching out across 384,000 km of empty space.

Back from Chapter 2

“Nothing is pushing the Moon along its orbit, so it ought to slow down and eventually stop.” What is wrong here?

Answer at the back of the book

Inverse-square rule

A pull that weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter as strong; ten times as far, a hundredth. Gravity follows it, and the same arithmetic will come back later in the book.

A guess is cheap; Newton tested it with numbers. The Moon is about 60 Earth radii away, sixty times farther from Earth’s centre than the apple is. Newton supposed that the pull weakens with distance in a particular way: double the distance and the pull drops to a quarter, treble it and the pull drops to a ninth. This is an inverse-square rule. Sixty times the distance then means 60 × 60 = 3600 times weaker. So at the Moon, each kilogram should be pulled 1/3600 as hard as at the ground, and the Moon should be falling with an acceleration of 9.8 ÷ 3600 = 0.00272 m/s². Now, is it?

Yes. We can check it ourselves, with nothing but the Moon’s distance and its month. Going once round a circle of radius 384,000 km in 27.3 days means the Moon moves at about 1 km/s. A thing moving at 1 km/s in a straight line would, in one second, be 1 km further along and no closer to Earth. The real Moon, in that second, has curved towards Earth by 1.36 mm. That is its fall: 1.36 mm in the first second. An apple falls 4.9 m in its first second, and 4.9 m is 3600 times 1.36 mm. The Moon falls exactly as the inverse-square rule said it should. Newton did this comparison himself and found that the two agreed, as he put it, pretty nearly; the modern figures agree to better than 1%, and the leftover is the slightly oval shape of the orbit and the fact that Earth moves too.

Put another way: in one minute the Moon falls 4.9 m below its straight line, which is what the apple falls in one second. A minute is 60 seconds, so a one-minute fall goes 60 × 60 = 3600 times as far as a one-second fall, and the Moon’s acceleration is 3600 times gentler. The apple and the Moon are doing the same thing, under the same pull.

Gravity (Newton’s law of gravitation)

Every mass pulls every other mass. The pull is bigger for bigger masses, and it weakens with the square of the distance between their centres. It never switches off; it only gets weaker with distance.

So the pull of the Earth is not a special property of the ground. Newton proposed that every piece of matter pulls every other piece, with a pull that grows with both masses and weakens as the inverse square of the distance between them. This is gravity in Newton’s sense, the universal law of gravitation, and it was the first time anyone had said that the rules on Earth and the rules in the sky are the same rules. Remember the luggage scales from Chapter 3, too: the Moon pulls Earth exactly as hard as Earth pulls the Moon. Earth is far more massive, so it moves far less, but it does move: the two of them circle a shared balance point that lies about 1700 km beneath Earth’s surface.

F = G m₁ m₂ ÷ r²

How do we know? Does Earth’s pull reach the Moon? Newton's test, with modern numbers

Two numbers from completely different places. From the Moon’s distance and its month alone, its path curves towards Earth at 0.00272 m/s². From a falling apple and the inverse-square rule, the pull at 60 Earth radii should give 9.8 ÷ 3600 = 0.00272 m/s². They match to better than 1%, and that match is the evidence that one pull does both jobs. The MIT course notes run the sum the other way: from the law and the Moon’s distance they predict the length of the Moon’s month, and get 27.2 days.

Careful

“The Moon falls 1.36 mm closer to Earth every second.”

It falls 1.36 mm below the straight line it would otherwise have followed. But in that same second it also moves about 1 km sideways, and the straight line leads slightly away from Earth, so the two effects cancel and the Moon’s distance stays about the same. It is always falling and never arriving.

Understand itUniversal gravitation

What is it?

The law that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres (F = Gm₁m₂/r²).

Why is it called this?

From the Latin gravitas, heaviness or weight (from gravis, heavy), combined with universal because Newton showed in 1687 that one and the same attraction governs falling stones on Earth and planets in the sky.

What problem did it solve?

Since antiquity, Earth and the heavens were thought to obey different laws: heavy things fell toward the Earth while planets moved in eternal circles for reasons of their own. Nobody knew what held the Moon in its path or why Kepler’s three laws held.

Why does it work?

Because gravitational influence spreads out across three-dimensional space so its strength thins out with the surface area of a sphere (4πr²), weakening as 1/r² while pulling in proportion to how much mass each body has.

How does it help?

It lets us weigh the Earth in a shed (Cavendish, 1798), weigh the Sun and Jupiter from the periods of their satellites, predict the return of Halley’s comet, and discover Neptune by pen and paper from the wobble of Uranus.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Newton’s apple-and-Moon test showed that the Moon’s inward acceleration at 60 Earth radii (0.00272 m/s²) is 1/60² = 1/3600 of g at Earth’s surface (9.8 m/s²), and Cavendish directly measured the tiny attraction between lead spheres in 1798.

What it isn’t

It is not a force that requires air or stops at the top of the atmosphere: at the International Space Station 400 km up, Earth’s gravity is still 89% as strong as on the ground in Mumbai.

Where does it stop working?

Newton’s inverse-square law is extraordinarily accurate across the solar system and gives way to Einstein’s general relativity only in very strong gravitational fields, such as near the Sun (where Mercury’s orbit precesses by an extra 43 arcseconds per century) or around black holes.

Your turn

Explain Universal gravitation to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

Suppose Earth kept the same mass but swelled to twice its radius, and you stood on the new surface. By what factor would your weight change?

Answer at the back of the book

The story behind this

The apple and the MoonA young man at a farmhouse wondered whether the pull that drops an apple reaches all the way to the Moon, and worked out that it does, exactly 3,600 times weaker.

5.2Newton’s cannon

In orbit, 400 km above Mumbai

The International Space Station circles about 400 km above the ground; on some evenings it can be seen from Mumbai as a bright, steady point crossing the sky in a few minutes. Use Section 5.1’s rule to find Earth’s pull up there: the station is at 6771 km from Earth’s centre against 6371 km for us, and the square of 6371/6771 is 0.885. Gravity on the station is 89% of gravity in Mumbai. And yet the astronauts float. Before reading on, decide what you think is going on.

Predict first

Gravity at the space station’s height is about 89% of its strength on the ground. Why doesn’t the station fall down?

  1. Its engines keep pushing it up
  2. It is above the air, and gravity cannot act where there is no air
  3. It is falling, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground keeps curving away beneath it
  4. There is no gravity in space, whatever the sum says

What happens

It is falling, and it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away as fast as it falls. The station is in free fall all the time, exactly like the dropped hammer, and it never lands because Earth is round. Its engines are off almost all the time, and gravity has nothing to do with air.

Orbit

The path of something falling freely under gravity but moving sideways fast enough never to land. A satellite in orbit is not held up; it is falling and missing.

Newton saw this with a cannon. Imagine a cannon on a mountain so tall that it stands above the air, firing horizontally. Fire a slow shot and it curves down and lands a little way off, like the flicked coin. Fire faster and it lands farther round the Earth. Keep increasing the speed and the landing point moves farther and farther away, because the ground is curving away under the falling shot. At one particular speed, about 8 km/s at Earth’s surface, the ground curves away exactly as fast as the shot falls. The shot never lands. It falls all the way round the Earth and comes back to the cannon from behind, and if the cannon has been moved away, it carries on falling round for ever. That is an orbit. Faster still, and the path stretches into a long loop. At about 11 km/s the shot never comes back at all: it has escaped.

Now the station. At 400 km up, the speed that makes the ground curve away as fast as you fall is about 7.7 km/s, and that is how fast the station moves: NASA puts it at about five miles a second, once round the Earth in about 90 minutes, sixteen sunrises a day. Check the two numbers against each other. In one second the station falls about 4.3 m towards Earth, from the 8.7 m/s² of gravity up there. In that same second it moves 7.7 km sideways, and over 7.7 km the round Earth’s surface curves away by, as it happens, 4.3 m. The fall and the curve match, so the station’s height never changes. It is the Moon’s story again, closer in and faster.

Back from Chapter 4

In Chapter 4 you dropped a cricket ball and a coin. Now an astronaut of 70 kg and a space station of 420 tonnes are both falling round the Earth. Does the heavier one fall faster and pull away from the lighter one?

Answer at the back of the book

Weight, and feeling weightless

Weight is the pull of gravity on an object: a force, in newtons. You feel your weight only through whatever pushes back on you, like the floor. Fall freely, and nothing pushes back, so you feel weightless although your weight is unchanged. Astronauts in orbit are in this state all the time.

That recall is the whole answer to the chapter’s puzzle. The astronaut floats not because gravity is absent, but because she and the station are falling together. Think of a lift whose cable has just snapped: for the moments before it hits the bottom, everything in it falls at the same rate, so the floor no longer presses on your feet and a dropped pen hangs beside you. The station is that lift, except that it is falling around the Earth instead of into it, so the moments never end. There is a word people use for this, and it needs care. In the language of your syllabus, the astronaut still has weight: Earth pulls on her mass, at 89% of the pull in Mumbai. What she has lost is the feeling of weight, which comes from a floor pushing up on you. Nothing pushes up on her, so she feels weightless. Physicists say she is in free fall, or in microgravity; “zero gravity” is a phrase to avoid, because it is simply false.

The scenes of floating in the film Apollo 13 were filmed in an aircraft that climbs and then falls freely along a great arc: NASA’s version gives about 25 seconds of free fall each time. A phone falling onto a pillow gives a third of a second, which is enough.

The phone that reads zero

Install the free phyphox app, which uses the phone’s own motion sensor, and open “Acceleration (with g)”. Held still, it reads about 9.8 m/s²: that is the sensor feeling the phone’s weight, the way you feel yours through your feet. Put a thick, soft pillow on the floor. Hold the phone flat above it, no higher than your knee, about 40 cm, start recording, and let it drop. Then look at the graph. For about 0.29 s, while the phone was falling, the reading dropped to about zero. Nothing was pushing on the sensor, so it felt no weight, although the Earth’s pull on it never changed. For that third of a second your phone was an astronaut. The live figure for this section does the same thing with the book’s own sensor reading.

One more thing follows from the cannon. Once a satellite is above the air, it needs no engine to stay up: it is simply falling round, and nothing slows it. The hard and expensive part is getting it up there and up to speed. Very low orbits do slowly decay, because a little air still brushes past at that height and drags on the craft.

Careful

“There’s no gravity in space. That’s why astronauts float.”

At the station’s height gravity is about 89% of its strength on the ground, and it is what keeps the station from flying off in a straight line. The astronauts float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together, so nothing pushes up on them. They still have weight; they do not feel it.

Understand itOrbit

What is it?

The closed or open path of a body falling freely under gravity while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the body it circles.

Why is it called this?

From the Latin orbita, the wheel-rut or track left by a cartwheel (from orbis, a wheel or ring), adopted by medieval and Renaissance astronomers for the track of a planet across the sky.

What problem did it solve?

Ancient astronomers imagined solid crystal spheres carrying the Moon and planets around, and modern intuition still imagines rockets must keep their engines firing to hold a satellite up.

Why does it work?

Because at orbital speed (about 7.7 km/s at 400 km altitude), in each second the satellite falls toward Earth by the exact same 4.3 metres that the round Earth’s surface curves away beneath it.

How does it help?

It explains why astronauts float weightless inside the Space Station (craft and crew fall together with no floor pressing up), and how ISRO raised Chandrayaan-3 to the Moon using short engine burns at perigee and days of engine-off coasting.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Every satellite ever launched switches its main engine off once it reaches orbital speed and coasts for years, and a phone dropped 40 cm onto a pillow reads 0 m/s² on its accelerometer during the fall for the exact same reason.

What it isn’t

An orbit is not a place where gravity has switched off; without gravity pulling inward at every instant, the spacecraft would fly off in a straight line into deep space.

Where does it stop working?

In low Earth orbit below a few hundred kilometres, wisps of thin upper air slowly drag on a satellite and bleed off its speed, causing the orbit to spiral down unless boosted from time to time.

Your turn

Explain Orbit to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

Anna says a satellite in orbit is in free fall. Tom says it cannot be, because its acceleration is not 9.8 m/s². Who is right?

Answer at the back of the book

At school

IGCSE defines weight as “a gravitational force on an object that has mass”, so in an exam an astronaut in orbit has weight; say that she “feels weightless” because she is in free fall. When the syllabus says that gravity “keeps an object in orbit”, think of a satellite that keeps falling towards the Earth and keeps missing it. The orbital speed formula is v = 2πr/T: the circumference divided by the time for one circuit.

Investigation 5.2

In the live figure, fire Newton’s cannon at increasing speeds and watch where each shot lands. Predict the speed at which it will stop landing at all, then find it. Then go a little faster and look at the shape of the path: where is it moving fastest, and where slowest?

The story behind this

Falling around the EarthNewton imagined a cannon on a mountain so high that its ball never came down, and in doing so explained why astronauts float while gravity still pulls on them at nearly full strength.

5.3Ellipses

Hven, 1576

Newton’s law was the explanation. The thing it explained had been found a lifetime earlier by two men who could hardly have been more different. Tycho Brahe built an observatory, Uraniborg, on the small island of Hven, and for about twenty years measured the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, without a telescope, more carefully than anyone before him. His positions disagreed with the printed tables, and his were the better ones.

Prague, 1600

Johannes Kepler arrived in Prague to work for Tycho in February 1600. Tycho died in October 1601, and Kepler got his data: twenty years of Mars. Kepler believed, as everyone did, that a planet moves in a circle, and he set out to find the circle that fitted Tycho’s Mars. He could not. His best circle missed some of Tycho’s positions by eight minutes of arc, a little more than an eighth of a degree. That is a tiny angle, small enough that many would have blamed the measurements. Kepler trusted Tycho. Eight minutes of arc, he decided, were enough to throw out two thousand years of circles.

Predict first

Mars’s orbit, drawn to scale on a page, looks like which of these?

  1. A clearly squashed oval, like a rugby ball seen from the side
  2. A perfect circle with the Sun at its centre
  3. Almost a circle, but with the Sun noticeably off-centre

What happens

Almost a circle, with the Sun noticeably off-centre. Mars’s orbit is only slightly stretched (its eccentricity is about 0.09), so the outline looks round. But the Sun is not at the middle: it sits about 9% of the way from the centre to the edge, so Mars is about 17% closer to the Sun at one end of its orbit than at the other.

Ellipse and focus

An ellipse is the closed curve you get when a loop of string is kept taut round two pins: from any point on it, the distances to the two pins add up to the same total. The pins are its two foci. A circle is an ellipse with its two foci in the same place.

The shape that fitted was an ellipse. You can draw one with two drawing pins and a loop of string: the pencil keeps the string taut and goes round, and the two pins are the ellipse’s two foci, a word Kepler invented. Push the pins together and the ellipse becomes a circle; pull them apart and it stretches. Kepler’s first law is that each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The other focus is empty. Mars’s ellipse is nearly a circle: pull the pins apart by only 9% of the ellipse’s half-length and you have it. But that 9% puts the Sun clearly off-centre, and it was enough to break the circles.

Kepler was lucky in his planet. Among the planets other than Mercury, Mars has the most stretched orbit; Earth’s is far rounder, with a stretch of only about 0.017, so our distance from the Sun varies only between about 147 and 152 million km over a year. Had Tycho spent twenty years on Venus, no naked-eye data could have revealed the ellipse. (That small change in Earth’s distance, by the way, is not what makes seasons. Chapter 14 settles that.)

Kepler found two more rules in the same data. The second: a planet moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther away, in such a way that a line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. The first two laws were published in 1609, in his book The New Astronomy. The third came ten years later, in 1619: the square of a planet’s year is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. Measure time in Earth years and distance in Earth-distances (one astronomical unit, about 150 million km) and the rule is simply P² = a³. Mars takes 1.88 years to go round; 1.88² is 3.53, the cube root of 3.53 is 1.52, so Mars is 1.52 times as far from the Sun as we are, about 228 million km. Kepler got the distances of all the planets from their years, with a pencil.

Notice what these laws are. They describe the orbits with great precision. They do not say why the orbits are ellipses, or why the planet speeds up near the Sun, or why the squares and cubes should match. Kepler tried hard to explain them and could not. The explanation waited eighty years for Newton: an inverse-square pull from the Sun forces exactly these shapes and exactly these speeds, and nothing else. Keep the two apart in your mind. Kepler’s laws are what the sky does; Newton’s law is why.

Two pins and a loop of string

Ask an adult for two drawing pins and push them into a flap cut from a cardboard box, about 5 cm apart. Tie thread into a loop that fits loosely round both pins, put a pencil inside the loop, pull it taut and trace all the way round. You have drawn an ellipse, and the pins are its two foci. Now move the pins closer together and draw again, then farther apart. Predict first: what happens to the shape each time? To draw Mars’s orbit to scale, make the loop so that the pencil reaches about 10 cm from the midpoint, and put the pins 0.9 cm either side of the midpoint. Mark one pin “Sun”. It barely looks like an ellipse at all, and that is the point.

Careful

“The Sun sits at the centre of the ellipse, and planets move in long, squashed ovals.”

The Sun sits at one focus, not at the centre, and the other focus is empty. And the planets’ ellipses are very nearly circles: Earth’s distance from the Sun changes by only about 3% over a year. Textbook drawings stretch the ellipse so that you can see its shape; the real thing is round with an off-centre Sun.

Check yourself

A distant object goes round the Sun at an average distance of 50 astronomical units, fifty times Earth’s distance. How long is its year?

Answer at the back of the book

5.4Weighing the Earth

Clapham, 1798

Newton’s law says that every mass pulls every other mass. Not just planets: a book pulls a cup, you pull the person next to you on the train. Nobody notices, because for everyday masses the pull is absurdly small, and for a hundred years after Newton nobody managed to measure it. Then Henry Cavendish, a man in his late sixties who lived at Clapham on the edge of London, and who was so shy that, the story goes, he spoke to his housekeeper only by written notes, set out to catch it.

Predict first

Two 1 kg bags of rice sit on a table 1 m apart. Do they pull on each other?

  1. No. Gravity is something planets and stars have, not bags of rice
  2. Yes, but far too weakly to notice, about a hundred-billionth of their weight
  3. Yes, about as strongly as a fridge magnet pulls a coin

What happens

Yes, far too weakly to notice. Each bag pulls the other with about 0.000 000 000 067 N, roughly 150 billion times less than the weight of either bag. It is real, and Cavendish measured a pull of this kind in 1798.

His instrument, designed by Michell, was a torsion balance: a light rod hanging from a thin wire, with a small lead ball at each end. When a big lead ball was brought close to each small one, the tiny pull swung the rod round a little, twisting the wire until the wire’s resistance balanced the pull. The twist was minute, and anything could spoil it: a draught, a change of temperature, the warmth of a human body. So Cavendish put the whole apparatus in a closed shed, stayed outside, and watched the rod through telescopes poked through holes in the shed wall. From the size of the twist and the stiffness of the wire he got the pull between lead balls whose masses he knew.

Why does measuring the pull between lead balls weigh the Earth? Because you can compare. The Earth pulls a small lead ball with a force you can measure on a scale: its weight. Cavendish now also knew how hard a big lead ball of known mass pulls it from a known distance. Newton’s law says the pull grows with the mass of the puller and weakens with the square of the distance; the Earth’s centre is 6371 km away, and the big lead ball’s centre was a few centimetres away. Knowing both pulls, both distances and the lead ball’s mass, the only unknown left is the mass of the Earth. Cavendish published his answer as a density: the Earth, as a whole, is 5.48 times as dense as water. The modern figure is 5.51. He was within 1%, in a shed, with a wire.

Gravitational constant (G)

The number in Newton’s law that sets how strong gravity is: about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N for two 1 kg masses 1 m apart. It is thought to be the same everywhere in the universe. Do not confuse it with g, the acceleration of free fall, which is different on every world.

Today’s books restate his result as a measurement of G, the gravitational constant in Newton’s law, which is the same information in modern dress. G is about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ in the units of newtons, metres and kilograms, which is why two 1 kg bags a metre apart pull with 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N. It is the least precisely known of all the fundamental constants, because gravity between laboratory masses is so faint. From G, Earth’s radius and the 9.8 m/s² of Chapter 4, Earth’s mass comes out at about 6 × 10²⁴ kg: six million million million million kilograms.

Mass

The amount of matter in an object, in kilograms. It does not change when you move to the Moon or into orbit. Weight does.

This is a good moment to be precise about two words that everyday speech runs together. Your mass is how much matter you are made of, measured in kilograms, and it is the same wherever you go. Your weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons, and it changes from world to world. A person of mass 60 kg weighs about 588 N on Earth. On the Moon the same person, with the same 60 kg, weighs about 100 N, a sixth as much. When someone says “I weigh 40 kg”, they mean their mass; in a physics answer, mass goes in kilograms and weight in newtons. One more fact worth knowing: careful experiments have shown that gravity does not care what a mass is made of. Lead, wood, water or feather, the pull per kilogram is the same, to a few parts in a billion.

Careful

“Gravity is a thing planets and stars have. Small objects don’t have gravity.”

Every mass pulls every other, including you and this book, and Cavendish measured the pull between lead balls in 1798. It is just extraordinarily weak unless one of the masses is enormous. Earth’s pull on you is strong only because Earth has six million million million million kilograms of stuff doing the pulling.

Check yourself

Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, has a radius of 2.58 × 10⁶ m and a mass of 1.35 × 10²³ kg. What is the acceleration of free fall at its surface?

Answer at the back of the book

At school

IGCSE wording: mass is “a measure of the quantity of matter in an object”, and weight is “a gravitational force on an object that has mass”. Write mass in kg and weight in N, and remember that G (the constant in Newton’s law) and g (9.8 N/kg at Earth’s surface) are different things.

5.5Predicting the sky

Cambridge, August 1684

In August 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley visited Newton in Cambridge with a question: if the Sun pulled on a planet with a force weakening as the inverse square of the distance, what path would the planet follow? Newton answered at once: an ellipse. He had worked it out, he said, but he could not find the paper. Halley pressed him to write it up properly. The result, three years later, was the Principia, the book that contains everything in this chapter so far. The Royal Society was supposed to print it, but it had spent its money on a History of Fishes that did not sell, so Halley paid for the printing himself.

What Halley had seen was that a law like Newton’s does more than describe. If you know where a body is and how fast it is moving, the law tells you where it will be next, and next after that, for as long as you care to calculate. Newton’s law and his laws of motion allow only certain paths around the Sun: circles, ellipses, and two open curves for things moving too fast to be held. Find which one a body is on, and its future is written.

Perturbation

A small change in an orbit caused by the pull of bodies other than the main one, such as Jupiter’s tug on a comet or Neptune’s on Uranus. The word means “disturbance”.

The law also lets you weigh things you cannot visit. Kepler’s third law, P² = a³, holds for the planets because they all circle the same Sun. Newton’s version of it includes the mass of whatever is being circled: the heavier the central body, the faster things must go round it at a given distance. Turn that round and an orbit becomes a weighing scale. A planet going round another star at Earth’s distance in 0.71 of a year must be circling a star twice the Sun’s mass, and Jupiter can be weighed from the periods of its moons. That is how the Sun, and every planet with a moon, has been weighed.

There is a catch, and it is what made the next two stories hard. Newton’s law is simple for two bodies. But every body pulls every other, so a comet rounding the Sun is also tugged by Jupiter and Saturn as it passes them, and the planets tug one another. These tugs are called perturbations, and the moment there are three bodies there is no neat formula for the path. The future still follows from the law, but you have to work it out step by step, a small stretch of time at a time, with a very great deal of arithmetic. Halley predicted that a certain comet would return in 1758. He died in 1742 and never saw whether it did; the case file at the end of this chapter tells what happened.

Berlin, 23 September 1846

The second story is about Uranus, the planet beyond Saturn, which refused to stay where the calculations said it should be. Year after year it drifted off its predicted path, by small amounts that grew. Either Newton’s law failed far from the Sun, or something unseen was pulling on Uranus.

Predict first

Uranus kept drifting away from the position that Newton’s law predicted for it. Which of these was the right explanation?

  1. Newton’s law weakens even faster than the inverse square far from the Sun
  2. An unseen planet beyond Uranus was pulling on it
  3. The old measurements of Uranus were simply wrong

What happens

An unseen planet. Urbain Le Verrier treated the drift as a perturbation and calculated, from Newton’s law alone, where a planet must be to cause it. He posted the position to the Berlin observatory. On the night the letter arrived, 23 September 1846, Galle and d’Arrest pointed their telescope at the predicted spot and found Neptune within about a degree of it.

Think about what that night meant. A planet nobody had ever seen was found with a pen, from the pull it exerted on a planet people could see, using a law written down 160 years earlier for apples and the Moon. Another astronomer, Adams, had also tried the calculation; his answer was about 12 degrees off and played no part in the discovery, and Challis had actually seen Neptune twice without recognising it. Neptune is called the first planet discovered through mathematics, and the phrase is exact.

One honesty note. Newton’s law predicts the sky very well, not perfectly: with many bodies tugging, every prediction is a long calculation and carries some uncertainty, as the comet’s story at the end of this chapter shows.

Careful

“Halley discovered Halley’s comet.”

Comets had been seen for thousands of years. What Halley did was new in a different way: he predicted that one of them would come back, in 1758, because a body on a closed orbit under Newton’s law must return. He discovered the comet’s future. The farmer who first spotted it on its return, on Christmas night 1758, was Johann Georg Palitzsch.

Check yourself

Why do astronomers say that Neptune was the first planet discovered through mathematics, when Galle found it with a telescope?

Answer at the back of the book

5.6The slow road to the Moon

Sriharikota, 14 July 2023

At 14:35 on 14 July 2023, an LVM3 rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at Sriharikota, carrying Chandrayaan-3: a propulsion module, a lander called Vikram and, inside the lander, a small rover called Pragyan, about 3.9 tonnes in all. The Moon is about 384,000 km away, and the rocket had put the spacecraft into an orbit whose far point was planned at about 36,500 km. It would not reach the Moon for another three weeks, and it would get there by going round the Earth, again and again, in loops that grew.

Why loops? Why not point the rocket at the Moon and fire? Here is the picture to hold on to from this chapter. Once a rocket’s engine stops, the spacecraft is simply falling, coasting on an orbit under gravity alone, exactly like the cannonball or the Moon. It needs no push to keep going (Chapter 2). An engine firing does not “push it outward”; it changes the spacecraft’s speed along its path, and that moves it onto a different orbit. The whole art of flying to the Moon is choosing a sequence of orbits and the short burns that hop between them. ISRO’s own updates record the sequence, and it is a lesson in Kepler.

The first burn came on 15 July, from the control centre at ISTRAC in Bengaluru, and raised the orbit to 173 km at its low point and 41,762 km at its high point. The second, on 17 July, gave 226 km by 41,603 km. A fourth, on 22 July, gave 233 km by 71,351 km, and one more followed on 25 July. Each burn was made near the low point, the perigee, to speed the craft up along its path. Look at the figure and notice where the effect appears: not at the perigee where the engine fired, but on the far side, half an orbit later. Going faster at the low point means the craft climbs higher before gravity turns it back, so the apogee rises. And because each new orbit is bigger, Kepler’s third law says each takes longer: about 12.5 hours for the 15 July orbit, about 24 hours for the 22 July one. The craft’s “year” was being stretched, burn by burn.

On 1 August came the big one, the translunar injection: a burn at perigee that stretched the orbit to 288 km by 369,328 km, a loop reaching out to where the Moon would be. For four days the craft coasted outward, slowing as it climbed, just as Kepler’s second law says a body does far from what it circles.

Predict first

Chandrayaan-3 arrives near the Moon on 5 August, falling towards it faster and faster. To be captured into orbit around the Moon, what must it do with its engine?

  1. Fire to speed up, so that it can catch the Moon
  2. Fire against its motion, to slow down
  3. Nothing: the Moon’s gravity will capture it by itself

What happens

Fire against its motion, to slow down. Arriving at the Moon it is moving too fast for the Moon’s weak pull to hold: left alone, it would swing past and fly back out, as the fast cannonball did. ISRO’s engine fired backwards for 1835 seconds, about half an hour, starting at 19:12 on 5 August, and the craft dropped into an orbit round the Moon of 164 km by 18,074 km.

That first lunar orbit was itself a long loop, taking about 28 hours to go round. Then the process ran in reverse: burns on 6, 9 and 14 August shrank the far point step by step until, by 16 August, the orbit was 153 km by 163 km, nearly circular, a lap of about two hours. On 17 August the lander separated from the propulsion module, and two more burns brought it down to an orbit of 25 km by 134 km. From there, on 23 August, Vikram fired its engines against its fall one last time and touched down at 18:04 Indian time, near 69° south, in the Moon’s south polar region. The landing site was named Shiv Shakti Point. Pragyan rolled down its ramp the next day.

Every stage of that journey is in this chapter: coasting with the engine off, burns at the low point that lift the far side of the loop, braking to be captured, and the hammer and feather of Chapter 4, since Vikram, Pragyan and every loose bolt inside fell round the Earth and then round the Moon together. ISRO’s pages say what the spacecraft did at each step; they do not say why this route was chosen over a direct one, so we will not guess. You can fly the sequence yourself in The Sky explorer at the front of the book, which has a mission tab built from these ISRO figures.

Careful

“The engine burns pushed Chandrayaan-3 outward, away from the Earth.”

Each burn pushed the craft along its path, making it faster at the low point of its orbit. The effect showed up half an orbit later, on the far side, as a higher high point. Nothing pushed it outward; gravity did the turning, as it always does, and a faster start simply let it climb farther before gravity brought it round.

Check yourself

Once the propulsion module was in its near-circular orbit of about 153 km by 163 km round the Moon, did it need to keep its engine running to stay there?

Answer at the back of the book

Investigation 5.6

Open the Chandrayaan-3 tab in The Sky explorer and step through the burns. Before each one, predict where on the orbit the engine will fire and which part of the orbit will change. Then watch the time for one lap grow from about 12 hours to about 24 hours, and work out from Kepler’s third law roughly how much bigger the orbit’s average size must have become.

The story behind this

The slow road to the MoonForty days from Sriharikota to the Moon’s south polar region in widening loops, a half-hour brake behind the Moon, and a soft landing at 18:04 on 23 August 2023.

Near Dresden, Christmas night 1758

Case file 5

The comet that came back

Edmond Halley, the man who had paid to print Newton’s Principia, predicted that a particular comet would return in 1758. He died in 1742. As 1758 approached, three people in Paris, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, spent months on a calculation Halley had not done, working out step by step how the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn would alter the comet’s path. They announced that it would pass closest to the Sun around the middle of April 1759, some months later than a simple return would suggest.

  1. The comet was first spotted on 25 December 1758 by Johann Georg Palitzsch, a farmer and amateur astronomer near Dresden.
  2. A comet spends almost all of its time far from the Sun, moving slowly, and races through its closest approach in a matter of weeks.
  3. The Paris calculators included the pulls of Jupiter and Saturn, the two giant planets, and no others.
  4. Newton’s law gives an exact formula for the path of one body round the Sun, and no exact formula at all when a third body pulls as well.

A sceptic says: “Halley said 1758. It wasn’t closest to the Sun until 1759. So Newton’s law got it wrong, and the Paris sums were just luck.” Was the comet obeying Newton’s law? Why did the three calculators need months, and what would have happened to the prediction if they had ignored Jupiter and Saturn?

Show the solution

The comet obeyed Newton’s law precisely; that is why the Paris prediction worked. The law says every mass pulls every other, so the comet is pulled not only by the Sun but by Jupiter and Saturn as it passes near them, and over decades in the outer dark, where it moves slowly, those tugs have time to shift its path and its timetable by months. Halley’s prediction used the Sun alone and could only be rough. To do better you must follow the comet step by step, adding up the three pulls at each stage, and in 1758 that meant months of hand arithmetic shared among the three of them. Ignoring the two giant planets would have given a date well off the true one, so the sceptic has it backwards: the months of sums were not luck, they were the law being taken seriously. Palitzsch spotted the comet as it came in, on Christmas night, on its way to the closest approach that the calculators had placed in the spring. The comet carries Halley’s name because he was the first to know it would come back.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

This chapter has used gravity to lift the Moon, weigh the Earth and find a planet, and it has never once said what gravity is, or how a pull crosses empty space. Newton would not guess, and neither will we, yet. There is a nearer puzzle, too. Gravity pulls a steel ship down exactly as it pulls a steel coin, and it pulls the ocean of air down on all of us with a weight you have never felt. Yet the ship floats and the coin sinks, and the air does not crush you. The next chapter is about what pushes back.
