Where this chapter comes from

8

Chapter 8

Heat and temperature

The big questionA steel thali and a wooden board sit in the same room all night. In the morning the steel feels colder. Is it?

  1. 8.1Hot and cold aren’t substances
  2. 8.2Heat vs temperature
  3. 8.3Why metal feels colder
  4. 8.4Sweaters don’t make heat
  5. 8.5Hidden heat
  6. 8.6The matka and the monsoon

In Chapter 7 you followed energy from store to store and found that none of it was ever used up. A bouncing ball lost height, bounce by bounce, and the energy went into the floor, the air and the ball itself as a little warmth that spread out and did not come back. Warmth is where energy ends up. This chapter is about that warmth: what it is, how it moves, and why your own skin is so easily fooled by it.

Here is the puzzle to carry. Tonight, leave a steel thali and a wooden chopping board side by side on the kitchen counter. In the morning, lay one hand on each. The steel will feel colder; it always does. Now ask the question a physicist asks: is it colder? A thermometer laid on each will have something to say about that, and the answer runs through a cannon in Munich, a bucket of bath water, a block of melting ice in Glasgow, and the matka on your own counter.

8.1Hot and cold aren’t substances

Munich, 1798

Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, worked at the arsenal in Munich, among cannon. A cannon barrel starts as a solid metal casting, and the bore is drilled out with a slowly turning borer. Everyone knew the metal got hot. What struck Rumford was that it never stopped getting hot. Drill for an hour, and the metal was hot; drill for another hour, and it was just as hot again.

That was a problem for the best theory of the day. Most scientists then said heat was a fluid, called caloric, that sat inside things and flowed from hot to cold the way water runs downhill. Drilling, they said, squeezed caloric out of the metal, as wringing squeezes water from a cloth. But a cloth runs dry. Rumford fitted a blunt borer to a cannon barrel, sank the barrel in a box of water, and set the borer turning. No fire anywhere.

Predict first

If heat were a fluid stored inside the metal, what should happen as the boring goes on, hour after hour?

  1. The metal runs out of heat, and the water stops warming
  2. The water keeps warming for as long as the borer keeps turning
  3. The water cools, because the borer is scraping heat away

What happens

The water kept warming. After two and a half hours it boiled, and the metal showed no sign of running dry. Whatever the water was getting, the metal was not storing a fixed amount of it. Something else was supplying it, for as long as the borer turned.

What the turning supplied was work. Something pushed the borer round, and the pushing warmed the water. Nearly fifty years later, in Manchester, James Joule measured how much. He let weights fall and turn a paddle wheel in a tub of water, and read a thermometer in the water before and after. So much falling made so much warming, every time he tried it. Heating water with a flame and churning it with a paddle did the same thing to the water. You cannot tell afterwards which happened.

So we drop the idea of a heat fluid. What an object has is internal energy: the energy of its particles jiggling, spinning and vibrating, and of their interactions with one another. Chapter 7 called the store “thermal”. Rubbing an object or warming it with a flame can increase that store. We use the word heat for one thing only: energy transferred from a hotter thing to a colder one because of the difference in their temperatures.

Internal energy

The energy of the particles within an object: their jiggling, spinning and vibrating, and their interactions with one another. Also called thermal energy here. Heating or doing work can increase it.

Heat

Energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder one because of the temperature difference between them. Heat is energy moving; an object does not contain heat.

Heat is a transfer, like a payment; internal energy is the stored amount, like an account balance. A payment changes a balance, but it is not something kept inside the account. In the same way, an object stores internal energy, not heat. Count the water as your system: the turning paddle does work on it, adding energy across its boundary. A flame can add energy by heating instead. Both can increase the water’s internal energy, but only the transfer caused by a temperature difference is called heat. The payment comparison keeps track of amounts; it cannot tell you how hot something is. For that you need the next section.

Try the oldest version of Rumford’s experiment. Rub a pencil eraser hard against your desk for ten seconds and touch it to your lip. It is warm. Nothing hot touched it. Your arm did work against friction, and that work ended up as internal energy in the rubber. The unit tells the story: the energy that warms one kilogram of water by one degree is 4186 joules, which is also what a kilocalorie is. The “calories” on a biscuit packet are kilocalories, so your food is measured in the same currency as Joule’s falling weights.

The story behind this

Boiling water with a blunt drillThe best theory of heat in 1798 said it was an invisible fluid stored inside things. A cannon-maker in Munich showed that the fluid never ran out.

Careful

“When I open the fridge, the cold comes out into the kitchen.”

Nothing comes out. The kitchen air is warmer than the inside of the fridge, so energy flows in, from the warm air to the cold shelves, and the air near the door loses some of its internal energy and feels cool on your legs. There is no cold substance. There is only energy, and it moves from hotter to colder.

At school

At school this topic is called transfer of thermal energy. IGCSE uses “heating” as the name of a process and “internal energy” for what an object holds. The old noun survives in one place: “specific heat capacity”, which you meet in the next section.

Check yourself

Sample A is warmed with a flame until it has gained 10 kJ. Sample B, identical, is stirred hard by a paddle until it has gained 10 kJ. Afterwards, can a thermometer tell you which was which?

Answer at the back of the book

8.2Heat vs temperature

A bucket of warm bath water sits on the bathroom floor at 40 °C. On the kitchen counter is a spoonful of water from the chai pan, at 90 °C. Which one has more “heat” in it? Most people answer “the spoon, obviously”, and the question is a trap, because after Section 8.1 you know that neither has any heat in it. What each one has is internal energy, and that is a different question, with a surprising answer.

Predict first

The bucket (10 kg of water at 40 °C) and the spoonful (5 g at 90 °C) are both left in a room at 30 °C until they match it. Which gives out more energy to the room as it cools?

  1. The spoonful: it is far hotter
  2. The bucket: it holds far more water
  3. About the same: the spoon is hotter, the bucket is bigger, and the two balance

What happens

The bucket, by a very long way. The spoonful cools by 60 °C and gives out about 1,256 J. The bucket cools by only 10 °C and gives out about 418,600 J, roughly 333 times more. Hotter is not the same as having more energy to give.

Temperature

A measure of how fast, on average, the particles of an object are moving. It is what a thermometer reads. Energy flows from higher temperature to lower, whatever the sizes of the objects.

Here is the picture to keep. Temperature is about the average particle: how fast, on average, each one is jiggling. A thermometer reads that average. Internal energy is the total over every particle in the object. The spoonful’s few particles jiggle hard; the bucket’s enormous crowd jiggle more gently, but there are so many of them that their total is far larger. When two objects touch, energy flows from the one whose particles jiggle faster on average to the one whose particles jiggle slower, until the averages match. Then the flow stops. It does not flow from the one with more energy; a bucket of lukewarm water warms a cold spoon, and a hot spoon warms a bucket, each by passing energy from faster particles to slower ones.

Understand itTemperature vs internal energy

What is it?

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of each jiggling particle in an object; internal energy is the total energy added up over all the particles in the object.

Why is it called this?

“Temperature” comes from Latin temperatura, a due measure or proportion, first used by physicians for the balance of warmth in the body. “Internal energy” was coined in nineteenth-century thermodynamics for the energy held inside a body’s particles, to stop people calling it “heat inside”.

What problem did it solve?

People confused “how hot something is” with “how much energy it has to give”, so a spoonful of boiling water seemed to hold more “heat” than a bucket of warm bath water. Separating average per particle from total across the crowd cleared up the muddle.

Why does it work?

When two objects touch, fast-jiggling particles collide with slower-jiggling ones and hand energy across. Direction of flow depends only on which side has the higher average jiggle (temperature), while the total amount of energy transferred depends on how many particles there are and what they are made of.

How does it help?

It tells you both which way energy will flow (always higher temperature to lower) and how much energy is needed to warm a given mass by a given number of degrees (E = mcΔT).

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Leave a 10 kg bucket at 40 °C and a 5 g spoonful at 90 °C in a 30 °C room: a thermometer reads higher in the spoon, yet a calorimeter shows the bucket gives out over three hundred times more energy as it cools.

What it isn’t

Temperature is not a count of joules in an object, and internal energy is not a substance called “heat” sitting in a tank.

Where does it stop working?

During melting or boiling, energy pours into a substance and increases its internal energy without raising its temperature at all, because the energy goes into pulling particles apart rather than speeding them up.

Your turn

Explain Temperature vs internal energy to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Specific heat capacity

The energy needed to warm one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius, in J/(kg·°C). Water: 4186. Aluminium: 900. Steel: about 450. Wood: about 1700. Sand: about 800.

How much energy does it take to warm something? Three things decide it: how much stuff there is, how many degrees you want, and what the stuff is made of. Each kilogram of each substance needs its own amount of energy per degree, called its specific heat capacity. Water needs 4186 J for each kilogram and each degree, which is one of the largest values of any common material. Aluminium needs 900, steel about 450, wood about 1700, glass about 840, and dry sand about 800. Multiply the three together and you have the energy:

energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change

The bucket: 10 kg × 4186 J/(kg·°C) × 10 °C = 418,600 J
The spoonful: 0.005 kg × 4186 J/(kg·°C) × 60 °C ≈ 1,256 J
418,600 ÷ 1,256 ≈ 333

The same arithmetic explains why the sea stays cool while the beach burns your feet. Give one kilogram of sand and one kilogram of water the same sunshine, and the sand’s temperature climbs about five times as far, because 4186 ÷ 800 is about 5.2. Water is slow to warm and slow to cool. That one number is behind the sea breeze at Marine Drive and, as you will see in Section 8.6, behind a three-hundred-year-old argument about the monsoon.

Careful

“A thermometer measures how much heat something has.”

A thermometer measures the average jiggle of the particles touching it, which is temperature. It knows nothing about how many particles there are. The spoonful of chai water reads 90 °C and has about 1,256 J to give; the bucket reads 40 °C and has 418,600 J. To know the energy you need the mass and the material as well as the temperature.

Back from Chapter 7

The bucket of bath water is left overnight and is at room temperature by morning. Its 418,600 J have gone. Were they used up?

Answer at the back of the book

Investigation 8.2

Fill one steel tumbler with dry sand and another with the same mass of water. Stand both in the sun on a windowsill and read a kitchen thermometer in each every five minutes. Predict first: which climbs faster, and by about how many times? Then watch them cool in the shade.

At school

IGCSE writes the specific heat capacity as c = ΔE/(mΔθ), with θ for temperature. It also describes a temperature rise as “an increase in the average kinetic energies of all of the particles”. The word average is the whole of this section.

Check yourself

A block needs 25 kJ to warm from 25 °C to 30 °C. How much does it need to go from 45 °C to 50 °C?

Answer at the back of the book

8.3Why metal feels colder

Morning. The thali and the chopping board have sat on the counter all night, side by side, breathing the same air. You lay a hand on each. The steel is cold. The wood is, if anything, faintly warm. Everyone who has ever stepped from a bathroom’s tiles onto a bedroom rug knows this feeling, and almost everyone draws the same conclusion from it.

Predict first

A kitchen thermometer is laid flat on the thali for a minute, then on the board for a minute. What does it read?

  1. Lower on the steel
  2. Lower on the wood
  3. The same on both

What happens

The same on both. Two objects left together in one room for a night end up at the room’s temperature, both of them. Your hand reported something real, but it was not temperature.

What your skin feels is the rate at which energy leaves it. Your hand is warmer than the room; the counter and everything on it are at the room’s temperature, perhaps 30 °C. Energy flows from your hand into whatever you touch. The steel carries that energy away from the contact point quickly so the surface stays cool and keeps drawing more, and your skin loses energy fast: fast loss is what “cold” means to your nerves. The wood takes energy slowly; the surface under your palm soon warms to nearly skin temperature, the flow dwindles, and your hand reports “not cold”. Same temperature, two different speeds.

Conduction

The transfer of energy through a material, or between two touching materials, by particles colliding with their neighbours. No material moves; only the energy is passed on.

The passing of energy through a material by contact is called conduction. Picture the surface where your palm meets the steel. On your side, skin particles jiggle fast; on the other side, steel particles jiggle more slowly. Where they touch, they collide, and in a collision the faster one tends to lose and the slower one to gain. Energy is handed across the boundary, then handed on, particle to particle, into the metal. In a metal the hand-over is especially quick, partly because metals are full of loose electrons that carry energy between the atoms. That is why the materials that conduct electricity well also conduct heat well, a connection Chapter 12 returns to.

Thermal conductivity

How quickly a material passes energy along by conduction, in W/(m·K). Metals score in the tens and hundreds; wood, wool and air score well below one.

How quickly depends on a number for each material, its thermal conductivity. Aluminium scores about 220, ordinary steel about 80, stainless steel about 14, glass under 1, water 0.6, wood between 0.08 and 0.16, wool 0.04 and still air 0.023. A stainless thali conducts about a hundred times better than the board beside it. The flow also grows with the area in contact and with the temperature difference, and it shrinks as the material gets thicker. Put all of that together and you have the rule engineers use: energy per second = conductivity × area × temperature difference ÷ thickness.

The thali and the board can settle this for themselves. An ice cube is a thermometer that cannot be fooled: it melts only when energy arrives, and the faster the energy arrives, the faster it melts.

Which plate melts the ice?

Take an aluminium kadhai or pan that has been sitting at room temperature (never one from the stove) and turn it upside down. Beside it put the wooden chopping board. Touch both: the metal feels colder. Now predict: on which one will an ice cube melt first? Put one cube from the freezer on each and watch. On aluminium the cube slumps into a puddle within a few minutes; a commercial version of this demonstration melts its cube in under about four minutes. On the wood it is still a cube long after. The “colder” plate melted it faster, because it fed energy into the ice faster. Melting a 10 g cube takes about 3,340 J whichever plate it sits on; the plate only decides how quickly that energy arrives.

Careful

“Metal is colder than wood. You can feel it.”

You can feel energy leaving your hand faster. A thermometer finds the same temperature on both. “Cold” is a report from your nerves about the rate of loss, and metal conducts your hand’s energy away about a hundred times faster than wood does. Nor does the metal pull cold into you: energy only ever flows out of the warmer thing, which is your hand.

At school

IGCSE lists this under 2.3.1 Conduction, and asks you to describe experiments that show which materials are good thermal conductors and which are good insulators. “Insulator” here means a poor conductor, which is the next section.

Check yourself

A cook lifts the steel lid off a boiling pot with a cloth, then picks up the wooden spoon that has been standing in the same pot with bare fingers. Both have been in the same steam. Why does only the lid need a cloth?

Answer at the back of the book

8.4Sweaters don’t make heat

Mumbai gives you about one week a year that calls for a sweater, so the sweater lives in a cupboard and comes out smelling of naphthalene. When you pull it on, it feels warm within a minute. Where did the warmth come from? Ask a class of children and many will tell you the sweater makes heat, or that it keeps the cold out. Both sound right. Both are tested by the same experiment.

Predict first

Two ice cubes come out of the freezer. One is wrapped snugly in a woollen sweater; the other sits bare on a saucer beside it. Which melts first?

  1. The wrapped one: sweaters are warm
  2. The bare one
  3. They melt together: the room is the same for both

What happens

The bare one melts first. The wrapped one lasts far longer. If the sweater made heat it would melt its cube faster. It does the opposite, because what a sweater does is slow down the flow of energy, whichever way that energy is going.

A sweater makes nothing. Your body does: it runs at about 37 °C and gives out energy all day. In the open, that energy conducts into the air next to your skin, and the warmed air drifts away and is replaced by cooler air, so the loss goes on and on. A sweater slows the loss. The wool fibres themselves are poor conductors, scoring about 0.04 on the scale in Section 8.3. More important is what sits between them: air. Still air is one of the worst conductors there is, at 0.023, more than five thousand times worse than aluminium. The trouble with air is that it does not stay still. Free air that is warmed rises and carries energy away with it, which is how a room’s air moves energy from a heater to the ceiling. Wool, fur, feathers and the fibreglass in a building’s walls all work the same trick: they trap air in pockets too small for it to flow. Trapped, the air is only a conductor, and a very poor one.

Thickness counts too. Halve the thickness of a layer and energy flows through it twice as fast; double it and the flow halves. Two layers add their resistance, the way two sweaters do. A lecture course on the physics of energy works through a building wall with a 20-degree difference across it: 20 cm of bare concrete leaks about 5 GJ a day, and a sandwich of 3 cm of fibreglass between boards cuts that to about 160 MJ, roughly thirty times less. The wall, like the sweater, makes nothing. It slows a flow.

One more thing, because this book must not fool you. An answer key in one of the textbooks this chapter leans on says woollen clothes keep you warm because of their “large specific heat”. That is a different quantity (the one from Section 8.2, about storing energy) and it is the wrong reason. Wool insulates because it traps air and conducts badly. A good book can still be wrong in a line, and the test is the ice cube, which does not read answer keys.

The sweater and the ice

Put two ice cubes of the same size on two saucers. Wrap one saucer, cube and all, in a woollen sweater or a thick folded towel; leave the other bare. Predict how long each will take to melt. Check every fifteen minutes. The bare cube goes first. When the wrapped one is finally a puddle, ask: did the wool make heat, or slow it?

Careful

“A sweater keeps the cold out.”

Nothing comes in. Cold is not a substance (Section 8.1). Energy leaks out of you into cooler surroundings, and the sweater slows that leak. Your school book may say woollens “keep warmth close to the body”; read “keep” as “slow its escape”, never “make”.

Check yourself

A Styrofoam box keeps ice cold for a picnic. Does the box make cold, keep cold in, or slow energy flowing in from outside? One such box, with walls 2.5 cm thick, sitting in 35 °C air, still lets about 3.4 kg of ice melt a day. What would make it lose less?

Answer at the back of the book

8.5Hidden heat

Glasgow, 1761

Joseph Black, who lectured at Glasgow, noticed something that everyone before him had walked past. Take a lump of ice that is already melting and warm it steadily. The thermometer does not rise. The ice goes on melting, you get more water, and the water stays at the ice’s temperature until the last of the ice is gone. Only then does the thermometer begin to climb. Energy was flowing in the whole time. Where was it going? Black called it latent heat, from the Latin for hidden. He never properly published the idea; it survives in notes of his lectures.

Predict first

A steel tumbler holds ice and water, well stirred, with a kitchen thermometer in it. Plenty of ice is still floating. Over the next ten minutes, in a warm Mumbai kitchen, the reading will:

  1. Rise steadily, as the warm room heats the water
  2. Stay at 0 °C until the ice is gone, then rise
  3. Fall, as the ice cools the water further

What happens

It stays at 0 °C for as long as there is ice to melt, and only then starts to rise. Energy is pouring in from the kitchen the whole time. All of it is going into melting, and none into raising the temperature.

Latent heat

The energy needed to change the state of one kilogram of a substance (solid to liquid, or liquid to gas) with no change in temperature. For water: 334 kJ/kg to melt, 2256 kJ/kg to boil at 100 °C.

Where does it go? In ice, the water particles hold one another in a fixed pattern. To melt, they must be pulled a little apart and set free to slide, against the attraction that held them. That costs energy, and while the energy is being spent on loosening the pattern it is not being spent on faster jiggling. The thermometer, which reads the jiggling, sees nothing. For water the price is 334 kJ for every kilogram, the latent heat of melting. Compare that with Section 8.2: the same 334 kJ would warm a kilogram of liquid water from 0 °C to nearly 80 °C. Melting is expensive.

Understand itLatent heat

What is it?

The energy required to change one kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid, or from liquid to gas, without any change in its temperature.

Why is it called this?

Joseph Black coined latent heat in 1761 from the Latin latere, to lie hidden, because the energy poured into melting ice or boiling water did not show up on a thermometer.

What problem did it solve?

Everyone before Black assumed that adding heat to a body must always raise its temperature, which could not explain why a pan of melting ice stays stubbornly at 0 °C in a warm room instead of turning into water all at once.

Why does it work?

In a solid or a liquid, particles attract one another. Unlocking them from the rigid lattice of ice (334 kJ/kg) or tearing them completely apart into steam (2256 kJ/kg) costs work against those attractions, so incoming energy goes into potential energy between particles rather than faster jiggling.

How does it help?

It explains why ice cools a drink far better than cold water at 0 °C, why steam burns are far worse than boiling-water burns, and why sweating and a clay matka cool by evaporation.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Heat a weighed block of ice at a steady rate with a thermometer in it: the temperature pauses flat at 0 °C while the ice melts, then climbs, and pauses flat nearly seven times longer at 100 °C while the water boils away.

What it isn’t

It is not energy that disappears: every joule spent melting ice or boiling water is stored in the looser state and comes back out as warmth when the water freezes or the steam condenses.

Where does it stop working?

Evaporation from a liquid surface happens at any temperature below boiling, and the exact latent heat of vaporisation shifts slightly with temperature and pressure (about 2400 kJ/kg for warm sweat, against 2256 kJ/kg at 100 °C).

Your turn

Explain Latent heat to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Boiling is far more expensive still. To turn a kilogram of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C takes 2256 kJ, almost seven times the cost of melting, because the particles must be torn fully apart from one another. The figure below follows one kilogram of ice from −20 °C to steam and draws every stretch to scale. Warming the ice takes 42 kJ; melting it, 334; warming the water from 0 °C to 100 °C, 419; boiling it, 2256. The two flat stretches are the hidden heat, and the boiling stretch is longer than everything else put together.

Hidden heat is only hidden, never lost. When steam condenses on a cold lid, the 2256 kJ for each kilogram come back out and warm the lid. When water freezes, the 334 kJ come back out. Fruit growers in cold places spray their orchards with water on frosty nights for exactly this reason: as the water freezes it gives out energy and keeps the fruit from falling far below 0 °C. In Mumbai you can watch the same accounting in reverse on a glass of iced water. Beads of water form on the outside as vapour from the humid air condenses on the cold glass. Condensing gives out energy, and that energy goes into the glass and melts the ice faster. The sweating glass is helping your ice disappear.

A glass of nimbu pani: 250 g at 20 °C, with three ice cubes of 6 g each at 0 °C.
Melting the ice: 0.018 kg × 334 kJ/kg ≈ 6.0 kJ
The drink has 0.25 kg × 4.186 kJ/(kg·°C) × 20 °C ≈ 20.9 kJ above 0 °C.
After melting, the 268 g of water share the remaining 14.9 kJ above 0 °C: about 13 °C.

For what is going on among the particles when a solid melts or a liquid boils, The Invisible World has the pictures: Chapter 3, on the states of matter. The energy accounting here and the particle story there are two views of the same event.

Careful

“While the ice melts, the heat just disappears.”

It is spent, and stored. It went into pulling the particles out of their fixed pattern, and it is held in the looser arrangement of the liquid. Freeze the water again and every joule comes back out. Nothing disappeared; it changed form, as energy always does.

Investigation 8.5

Stir ice and water in a steel tumbler with a kitchen thermometer in it, and read it every minute for twenty minutes. Plot the readings. Mark the minute the last sliver of ice vanishes. Where on your graph is Black’s hidden heat?

At school

IGCSE puts this under 2.2.3 Melting, boiling and evaporation. Evaporation is the part this section has not touched yet: water leaving as vapour well below 100 °C. It is where the next section begins.

Check yourself

Ice at exactly 0 °C is dropped into water at exactly 0 °C in a perfectly insulated box. Does any ice melt, or any water freeze?

Answer at the back of the book

8.6The matka and the monsoon

Section 8.3 made a promise: nothing left in a room ends up colder than the room. Yet in May, the water in the matka on the counter is cooler than the kitchen air around it, and has been all afternoon. Ask why, and the usual answer is that clay is cold. You now know that cannot be right: clay left in a room is at the room’s temperature, like steel and wood. Something is going on at the surface of that pot that was not going on with the thali.

Predict first

Fill two steel tumblers with tap water. Wrap one in a cloth soaked in water and the other in a dry cloth, and stand both in front of a fan for an hour. Can the wet-wrapped tumbler’s water end up colder than the room’s air?

  1. No. Moving air can only bring something down to the air’s own temperature
  2. Yes, a little below the air temperature
  3. Yes, as cold as a fridge

What happens

Yes, below the air temperature, by an amount that depends on how damp the air already is. Moving air alone never cools anything below its own temperature; a fan on a dry tumbler does nothing. The wet cloth is the whole trick, and the reason is evaporation.

Evaporation

Particles leaving the surface of a liquid as vapour, at any temperature below boiling. The fastest particles leave, so the liquid left behind cools.

Water does not have to boil to become vapour. At any temperature, the fastest particles at a liquid’s surface are moving quickly enough to break free of their neighbours and leave. That is evaporation, and it has a cost. The ones that leave are the fastest, so the average speed of the ones left behind falls, and a falling average speed is a falling temperature (Section 8.2). Each gram that escapes from warm water carries away about 2.4 kJ, slightly more than a gram boiled away at 100 °C takes. A matka is a leaky pot by design. Water seeps through the pores in the fired clay and evaporates from the outside, and every gram that leaves takes energy from the water inside. Cooling ten litres by 10 °C means evaporating about 170 g through the clay. Your body runs the same cooling system: a resting person giving out 120 W must evaporate about 3 g of sweat a minute to carry it away.

Relative humidity

How much water vapour the air has, compared with the most that can be present at that temperature, as a percentage. At 100% there is no net evaporation.

Why, then, does the matka work so poorly in July? Because the air around it is already full of water vapour. At a given temperature, vapour can build up in the air only to a certain amount; beyond that, as many particles return to the water as leave it, and evaporation stops. How close the air is to that limit is its relative humidity: 100% means the limit has been reached. People say the air “holds” water like a sponge, but nothing is holding anything; it is a balance of particles leaving and particles returning. When the humidity is 81%, as it typically is on a Mumbai afternoon in July, the air is already close to the balance point, and the matka’s water barely cools. Warm air has more room: the amount of vapour that can be present at 37 °C is about twice the amount at 25 °C.

Wet-bulb temperature

The lowest temperature that evaporation alone can bring a wet surface to, in air of a given temperature and humidity. Damp air gives a floor only a little below the air temperature; dry air gives a floor far below it.

There is a floor. An evaporating surface can only cool until the air right next to it is at the balance point; the temperature it reaches then is the wet-bulb temperature, and no matka, sweat or wet cloth can go below it. In dry inland air at 38 °C and 20% humidity the floor is about 21 °C, nearly 17 degrees below the air, which is why a matka in a dry town makes water that is almost cold. Mumbai’s damp sea air leaves far less room; how much less, in May and in July, is the case at the end of this chapter. Measured matkas drop their water by anywhere from 5 to 15 °C, depending on the humidity; one measurement in humid Kolkata managed 7 °C. A real pot never quite reaches the floor, because energy also leaks in from the room through the clay. The fan helps because it sweeps away the damp air next to the cloth and brings drier air to take its place, so evaporation keeps going. A fan on your skin feels cool for the same reason: the air is no cooler, and your sweat evaporates faster.

The story behind this

Why the matka works in MayA clay pot with no electricity keeps water cool through the worst of the heat, then stops working the week the rains arrive. The reason is a floor set by the air itself.
Convection

The transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid. Warmer fluid is less dense and is pushed up by the denser fluid around it, so the fluid circulates in loops.

Evaporation moves energy through a wall of clay. Air moves energy across a whole city. Warm a patch of air and it expands, so it is less dense than the air around it, and the denser air pushes it upward, exactly as water pushes up a floating orange in Chapter 6. Cooler air flows in to take its place, warms in turn, and rises too: a loop. That loop is convection, and you have already met its villain in this chapter; it is the reason free air is a poor insulator and trapped air a good one.

Back from Chapter 6

“Hot air rises because heat rises.” Chapter 6 found a floating orange and a sinking peeled one. Use it to say what really pushes warm air up.

Answer at the back of the book

Now think of Mumbai on a May afternoon. Section 8.2 showed that a kilogram of sand warms about five times as fast as a kilogram of water. So by midday the land is hotter than the sea. The air over the land warms, is pushed up, and cooler air from the Arabian Sea flows in to replace it: the afternoon breeze on Marine Drive. At night the land cools faster than the sea, the loop turns the other way, and a gentle wind blows out to sea. Weather services call the pair the sea breeze and the land breeze.

In 1686 Edmond Halley, whom you met in Chapter 5, proposed that the monsoon is this same loop at the scale of a continent: all of India heats up through the summer, the air over it rises, and moist air from the ocean flows in for months and brings the rain. Then the land cools, and the winds turn around. It is a beautiful idea, and it is the one most books still give. In 2021 Sulochana Gadgil and her colleagues argued that it fails several tests, and that the monsoon rains are better understood as a shift of the band of rain that circles the Earth near the equator. The argument is still going on. Nobody disputes the sea breeze; what is in dispute is whether the monsoon is a giant one. You are reading this during an unsettled scientific question, which is the normal condition of science. What is settled is that on a normal year the rains reach Mumbai around 11 June, that the instruments measuring them were standardised for India by the physicist Anna Mani, and that the first week of rain finishes the matka’s season for the year.

The story behind this

The wind that turns aroundEdmond Halley explained the monsoon as a sea breeze the size of a continent. Three centuries later, Indian scientists argue that the picture fails, and the question is still open.

A matka without a matka

Fill two identical steel tumblers with water from the same tap. Wrap one in a cloth soaked in water and wrung out; wrap the other in a dry cloth. Stand both in front of a fan. Read a kitchen thermometer in each every ten minutes for an hour, and keep the wet cloth damp. Write down the room’s temperature too. The wet tumbler ends up below the room; the dry one does not. Do it once in May and once in July, and compare how far below the room each one got.

Careful

“The matka’s water is cold because clay is cold.”

Clay left in a room is at the room’s temperature, like the thali and the board. The water is cooler because of what happens at the pot’s surface: water seeps out and evaporates, and the escaping particles take energy with them. A glazed pot of the same clay, which cannot sweat, does nothing.

At school

IGCSE places evaporation under 2.2.3 and convection under 2.3.2 Convection. Cambridge Lower Secondary calls what the matka does “evaporative cooling”. When an exam asks why evaporation cools, name the escaping particles: the fastest ones leave, so the average energy of the rest falls.

Check yourself

A fan blows air at the room’s own temperature, 30 °C, over your damp skin, and you feel cool. Why, when the air is no cooler than before you switched it on?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 8

May or July?

A cousin visiting from a dry inland town is baffled by Mumbai’s matkas, which never make the water as cold as hers at home. “Mine drops the water by more than ten degrees,” she says. “Yours barely does anything. When does it work best here?” You pull two typical afternoons out of the weather record for the airport at Santacruz:

  • May: air 34.3 °C, relative humidity about 65%. The weather table gives the wet-bulb temperature as 28.7 °C.
  • July: air 29.4 °C, relative humidity about 81%. Wet-bulb temperature 26.7 °C.
  • Her town, for comparison: air 38 °C, humidity 20%, wet-bulb about 21 °C.

A perfect matka could bring its water down to the wet-bulb temperature and no lower; a real one stops a little above it.

Two questions. In which month does a Mumbai matka cool its water further below the air? And in which month is the water in it actually colder? Explain both with the numbers.

Show the solution

Further below the air: May. In May the floor is 34.3 − 28.7 = 5.6 °C below the air; in July it is 29.4 − 26.7 = 2.7 °C below. May has about twice the room to cool, because its air, though hotter, is drier. In her town the gap is 38 − 21 = 17 °C, which is why her matka seems to work and ours seems not to.

Colder water: possibly July. The lowest a perfect matka could reach is 28.7 °C in May and 26.7 °C in July. July’s water can be the colder drink, because July’s air is cooler to begin with; the matka simply adds less to it. Both pots will sit a degree or two above these floors in practice, because energy leaks in through the clay from the room.

So the cousin is right that the matka does very little in July: the air is already close to its balance point, and evaporation is slow. She is wrong that it does nothing in Mumbai. It works in May, and it works best of all in the dry months before the monsoon, when the air has the most room for vapour.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Every transfer in this chapter needed something to carry it: particles colliding in conduction, a fluid flowing in convection, water particles escaping in evaporation. Yet the Sun warms your face across 150 million kilometres of empty space, with nothing to collide and nothing to flow. How energy crosses emptiness is the question of the next three chapters, and the answer begins, in Chapter 9, with a wave crossing the Arabian Sea while the water in it stays almost exactly where it was.

Chapter 9

Vibrations, waves and sound

The big questionA wave crosses the whole Arabian Sea, but the water in it stays where it is. So what travels?

  1. 9.1Things that swing
  2. 9.2Resonance
  3. 9.3What a wave carries
  4. 9.4Sound is a push passed on
  5. 9.5Loud and high
  6. 9.6Why a tabla sings
  7. 9.7The moving whistle

Every transfer of energy in Chapter 8 needed stuff to carry it: particles colliding in conduction, air flowing in convection, water escaping from a matka. This chapter is about a different way for energy to travel, one in which the stuff stays put. A swell rolls in at Marine Drive during the monsoon. It came from far out over the Arabian Sea, and it arrives with enough energy to throw spray over the sea wall. Yet a plastic bottle floating beyond the breakers only bobs as the swell passes under it, and is still there, bobbing, when the next one comes. The water did not make the journey. Something did.

That something is a wave, and this chapter follows the idea from the simplest swinging thing to the sound of a tabla and the horn of a passing local train. Begin with a swing.

9.1Things that swing

Pisa, about 1583

The story goes that a young Galileo, in the cathedral at Pisa, watched a lamp swinging on its chain and noticed that each swing took the same time whether the lamp swung wide or barely moved. It is a lovely story, and it comes from one source only: Viviani, Galileo’s assistant in his old age, writing long afterwards. The lamp that hangs in the cathedral today was installed after Galileo had left Pisa. So treat the lamp as a legend. What is true is that Galileo did study swinging pendulums, carefully and for years, and that what the legend has him notice is real.

Period

The time for one complete repeat of a motion that repeats, such as one full swing out and back. Symbol T, in seconds.

Frequency

How many repeats happen each second, in hertz (Hz). Frequency = 1 ÷ period.

You can notice it yourself on the swing in the building compound. Push off and let it go. Each swing takes the same time as the one before, and as the swing dies down the time between swings hardly changes. The time for one complete swing, out and back, is the period; the number of swings in a second is the frequency, which is one divided by the period. A swing on chains about 2.5 m long has a period of about 3.2 s.

Predict first

Two pendulums hang from strings of the same length. One has a 10 kg bob, the other 100 kg. Both are pulled back 12° and released. Which swings faster?

  1. The heavy one
  2. The light one
  3. Neither: they keep time with each other

What happens

They keep time with each other. Mass makes no difference to a pendulum’s period. The heavier bob is pulled ten times harder by gravity and is ten times harder to get moving, and the two cancel exactly.

What sets the period, then? Watch what pulls the bob back. At the bottom of the swing nothing pulls it sideways, so it sails through the middle at its fastest. Pull it to one side and part of its weight points back along the arc, towards the middle, and the further out it is, the bigger that pull. For small swings the pull back grows in proportion to the displacement, and anything with that property swings in the same regular way, with a period that does not depend on how far you pull it. MIT’s course on vibrations makes a sharp point here: there is no special law behind this. It is what almost any smooth system does when it is nudged a little from a resting place, whether a swing, a plucked string, a bridge or a bell. Nudge it far and the rule breaks down, slowly at first.

For a pendulum the period depends on only two things, its length and the strength of gravity:

period = 2π × √(length ÷ g)

A pendulum one metre long has a period of 2.0 s; one four metres long, 4.0 s. Four times the length gives twice the period, because of the square root. How far you pull it back barely matters: a swing released from 15° takes less than half a per cent longer per swing than a tiny one, which is why the legend’s lamp kept time. At 60° each swing takes about 7% longer, so Galileo’s rule is a rule for small swings. And since the period depends on g, a pendulum measures gravity: 75.000 cm timed at 1.7357 s per swing gives g = 9.83 m/s², within a fraction of a per cent of the accepted value.

Weigh the Earth’s pull with a key

Tie a key to a thread exactly one metre long, measured from the knot you hold to the middle of the key. Hold it against a door frame so the top cannot move, pull it aside less than 10° (about 15 cm at the bottom) and let go. Time ten complete swings with a phone stopwatch and divide by ten; you should get close to 2.0 s. Then work out g = 39.5 × length ÷ (period × period); the 39.5 is 2π squared. With 1.00 m and 2.01 s you get 9.8 m/s². Try a thread twice as long and see what happens to the period.

Careful

“A heavier child makes the swing go faster, because gravity pulls harder.”

Gravity does pull harder on the heavier child, and the heavier child is harder to get moving by exactly the same factor. The period comes out the same. Only the length of the chains (and the strength of gravity) decides how fast a swing swings.

At school

At school, a motion that repeats like this is called an oscillation, and the period and frequency are defined exactly as here. The pendulum formula belongs to IB Diploma physics (topic C.1, simple harmonic motion); IGCSE asks for period and frequency only.

Check yourself

A pendulum clock keeps perfect time in Mumbai. It is moved to a city where g is very slightly larger. It now runs fast. Should its pendulum be lengthened or shortened to fix it?

Answer at the back of the book

9.2Resonance

London, June 2000

The Millennium Bridge, a new footbridge over the Thames, opened on 10 June 2000 with crowds pouring across it. Almost at once it began to sway from side to side, and the engineers closed it two days later. The sway came from the walkers themselves. As the deck moved a little, people adjusted their steps to keep their balance, fell into step with the sway, and pushed it further; the more it swayed, the more of them fell into step. Dampers costing about £5 million were fitted, and the bridge reopened in 2002. One textbook says it was closed “for the same reason” as a famous American bridge you will meet below. It was a different reason, and the difference is the point of this section.

Natural frequency

The frequency at which something oscillates when it is set going and left alone, with nothing driving it.

Resonance

What happens when something is driven at or near its natural frequency: each small push arrives in time with the motion and adds to it, so the motion grows large.

Every swinging thing has a rhythm of its own, the rate at which it swings when you let it go and leave it alone: its natural frequency. The swing in the compound, with its 3.2 s period, has a natural frequency of about 0.3 Hz. Push it once every 3.2 s, each time it comes back to you, and each push adds a little to the last; after ten pushes the child is flying. Push at random, and half your pushes fight the swing. Push very fast, several times a second, and the swing barely moves: it just shivers. Driving something at its own natural frequency, so that small pushes add up into a big motion, is resonance.

Understand itResonance

What is it?

The large build-up of oscillation that happens when a system is pushed repeatedly at a frequency matching its own natural frequency.

Why is it called this?

From Latin resonare, to sound back or echo, first used in acoustics for a musical string or air column that begins to hum in sympathy when its own note is sung nearby.

What problem did it solve?

It explained how very gentle periodic forces, too weak to move an object far in a single push, can selectively make one particular string vibrate, shatter a wine glass, or set a footbridge swaying.

Why does it work?

When each push arrives in step with the object’s natural swing, it always pushes in the direction the object is already moving, so every cycle adds energy instead of cancelling the previous cycle.

How does it help?

Engineers use it to tune radios and musical instruments so they respond strongly to one frequency, and to design dampers on bridges and tall buildings so they do not sway dangerously.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Drive an oscillator across a range of frequencies and measure its amplitude: the swing peaks sharply at the natural frequency, and adding friction (damping) lowers and broadens that peak.

What it isn’t

It is not just shaking something violently at any frequency, and not every bridge failure is resonance: the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a steady wind by aerodynamic flutter, making its own rhythm.

Where does it stop working?

If the swing grows so large that the restoring force is no longer proportional to displacement, the natural frequency itself shifts with amplitude and the simple resonance curve bends over.

Your turn

Explain Resonance to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Predict first

A singer, the story always goes, can shatter a wine glass with her voice. For the glass to break, which matters more?

  1. Being loud enough: any note will do if it is loud
  2. Singing the right note: the glass’s own natural frequency, even at moderate volume
  3. Both equally

What happens

The right note. A glass rings at its own natural frequency. Sing that exact note and each wave of sound arrives in time with the glass’s flexing and adds to it; the rim swings further and further until it cracks. MIT physics lecturers break a glass this way in front of their class, with sound at the glass’s own note. A different note, however loud, just fights itself.

How tall the peak is depends on damping, the friction that drains energy away. With little damping the pushes keep adding up for a long time before the drain catches up, so the peak is tall and narrow: you must hit the frequency almost exactly. With heavy damping the peak is low and broad. That is why the Millennium Bridge’s cure was dampers: they drain the sway’s energy faster than the walkers can feed it.

The story behind this

Pushing a swingA legend about a swinging lamp, the true thing Galileo found in swinging weights, and why a small push at the right moment builds a huge swing while a big push at the wrong moment does nothing.

How do we know? Why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge fell 1940

Film of the suspension bridge at Tacoma Narrows, in the state of Washington, twisting itself to pieces in a steady wind in 1940 is shown in physics courses everywhere, usually with the explanation that gusts of wind happened to match the bridge’s natural frequency. MIT’s course on differential equations, following a 1991 analysis by Billah and Scanlan, calls that explanation “worthless”: the wind was not gusting. A steady wind made the deck twist slightly; the twisted deck changed how the wind pushed on it; and the changed push drove the next twist. The bridge was pushing itself, using the wind’s energy, the way a flag flaps in a steady breeze. Engineers call this flutter. Resonance needs a driver with the right rhythm; flutter makes its own. One car and one dog, Tubby, were lost; Tubby bit the professor who tried to rescue him.

Back from Chapter 7

A parent gives a swing one small push every 3.2 s, and after a minute the child is swinging two metres high. Is energy being made from nothing?

Answer at the back of the book

Careful

“Resonance is just a fancy name for shaking something hard.”

Shaking in time is the point. A loud wrong note leaves the glass intact, and a modest right note breaks it. Nor is every violent oscillation resonance: the Tacoma bridge drove itself with a steady wind, which is flutter, and the Millennium Bridge was driven by walkers who adjusted their steps to it.

Check yourself

Soldiers crossing a bridge are ordered to break step and walk out of rhythm. Why?

Answer at the back of the book

9.3What a wave carries

Fill a bucket to the brim and wait for the water to go still. Float a scrap of paper in the middle. Now dip a finger in at the edge, once. Rings spread out across the surface, reach the paper, and pass under it. Watch the paper.

Predict first

As the ripples reach the paper scrap and pass it, the scrap will:

  1. Be carried along with the ripples to the far side of the bucket
  2. Bob up and down, and stay roughly where it was
  3. Be pushed backwards, away from the ripples

What happens

It bobs and stays. Each ripple lifts it, moves it a little forward and then a little back, and sets it down almost exactly where it was. The ripples cross the bucket; the water, and the paper riding on it, does not.

Wave

A disturbance that travels away from where it was made, carrying energy. The material it travels through moves back and forth, or round in small loops, and ends up where it started.

A wave is a disturbance that travels away from the place where it was made. Your finger pushed the water down in one spot. That water pushed its neighbours, which pushed theirs, and the push travelled outward in a ring while each bit of water went up and down and came back to where it started. Out at sea it is the same on a bigger scale: a bit of water near the surface moves round in a small loop as a swell passes, forward at the crest, back in the trough, and ends up where it began. The swell crosses the whole sea; the water goes round in circles. What travels is the shape, and the energy. That answers the chapter’s question, and it is the third big idea of this book: waves carry energy without carrying stuff.

Understand itWave

What is it?

A travelling disturbance that carries energy and information from one place to another without carrying matter along with it.

Why is it called this?

From the Old English wagian, to move to and fro, first applied to the ridges on the sea and then extended by physicists to sound, ripples on strings, and light.

What problem did it solve?

It showed how energy can cross a bucket, a concert hall, or an ocean while the water or air stays in its own neighbourhood, and gave one mathematical rule (v = fλ) for ripples, sound and light alike.

Why does it work?

Each piece of the medium is coupled to its neighbours: displace one bit and it pulls or squeezes the next bit, handing the motion and energy onward while restoring forces pull the original bit back to its resting place.

How does it help?

Knowing a wave’s frequency and wavelength gives its speed immediately, and knowing that waves add where they meet explains echoes, beats, musical notes, and interference.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Float a scrap of paper on rippled water or track air in a sound tube: the crests race across from one side to the other while the paper scrap only bobs in a small loop about the same spot.

What it isn’t

It is not a stream of water or air travelling from source to receiver: wind and ocean currents move matter, whereas sound and sea swells move only a pattern of motion and energy.

Where does it stop working?

When a water wave runs into shallow water near a beach, the bottom slows the trough while the crest overtakes it and topples forward as surf; there the wave breaks and really does throw water up the sand.

Your turn

Explain Wave to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Wavelength

The distance from one crest to the next (or trough to trough). Symbol λ, in metres.

Amplitude

The largest displacement from the resting position: for a water wave, the height of a crest above the still level.

Three numbers describe any wave. The distance from one crest to the next is the wavelength. The height of a crest above the still level is the amplitude. And the time between one crest passing and the next is the period, exactly as for the swing; its inverse is the frequency. A crest moves one wavelength in one period, which gives the wave’s speed: if swells pass the paper scrap every 5.0 s and the crests are 10.0 m apart, the swell is travelling at 10.0 ÷ 5.0 = 2.0 m/s. For every wave there is, from ripples to sound to light:

wave speed = frequency × wavelength

The energy a wave carries goes with the square of its amplitude: a swell twice as high carries four times the energy, and one three times as high carries nine times. It is also why the rings in the bucket fade as they spread: the energy of one ring is shared around a longer and longer circle, so the amplitude must fall.

Back from Chapter 2

“The swell carries the water along, the way a thrown ball carries its push inside it.” Chapter 2 had something to say about pushes carried inside things. What really travels in the swell?

Answer at the back of the book

Transverse wave

A wave in which the material moves across the direction the wave travels, like ripples on water or a flicked rope.

Longitudinal wave

A wave in which the material moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels, like a push running down a line of people. Sound is longitudinal.

Waves come in two kinds. In the bucket the water moves up and down while the ripple moves outward, across the direction of travel: a transverse wave. A rope flicked at one end makes the same kind. In the other kind the material moves back and forth along the direction of travel, like a push running down a line of people standing close together: a longitudinal wave. Sound is one of these. Two waves can also cross. Where they meet their displacements simply add, and then they carry on as if nothing had happened; the ripples from two fingers in the bucket pass straight through one another.

Measure a ripple

In a bucket or a wide parat of still water, float a paper scrap and dip one finger at the edge at a steady rhythm, once a second. Watch the scrap stay put. Estimate the distance between crests with a ruler held above the water, and the time between crests from your dipping; divide one by the other for the speed. Does dipping harder change the spacing of the crests, or only their height?

Careful

“Waves at the beach push the water up the sand, so waves do carry water.”

At the shore, yes: when a wave runs into shallow water it breaks, and the water in it tumbles forward. That is a wave falling apart. Out at sea, where the wave is a wave, the water goes round in loops and stays.

At school

IGCSE puts all of this under 3.1 General properties of waves, with the same words: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, and the two kinds, transverse and longitudinal. Learn to draw a wave and label the first two.

Check yourself

Drop a stone into still water. The rings spread out and, as they spread, get lower. Why?

Answer at the back of the book

9.4Sound is a push passed on

Tie a steel spoon to the middle of a metre of string. Wind the two ends of the string round your index fingers and press those fingertips gently into your ears. Now let the spoon swing and knock against the edge of a table. Through the string you hear a deep, clear bell, as if from inside your head. Let the string go slack and tap the spoon again: a faint tink. The spoon vibrated the same way both times. What changed was the road the vibration took to your ear.

Predict first

A friend taps one end of a long steel railing with a coin. You are at the other end, 100 m away, with one ear pressed against the rail and the other in the air. Which ear hears the tap first?

  1. The ear in the air
  2. The ear on the rail
  3. Both at once

What happens

The ear on the rail, by a clear margin. Sound travels through steel at about 5960 m/s and through warm air at about 349 m/s, so the rail delivers the tap in about 0.017 s and the air takes 0.29 s. The vibration travels about eighteen times faster in the steel.

Compression

A region where the material a sound passes through is momentarily squeezed closer together. Between compressions come rarefactions, where it is stretched apart.

Here is what sound is. The spoon, struck, vibrates: its surface moves out and back many times a second. Each time it moves out it squeezes the layer of air next to it; each time it moves back it leaves that layer stretched. The squeezed layer pushes on the next, which pushes on the next, and a pattern of squeezed and stretched air, compressions and rarefactions, runs outward at the speed of sound. No air travels from the spoon to your ear. Each layer shoves its neighbour and swings back, like the line of people in Section 9.3. Sound is a longitudinal wave of pushes passed on, and at your ear the pushes set your eardrum moving in step with the spoon.

Take the air away and there is nothing to pass the push on. A bell ringing inside a jar goes silent as the air is pumped out. You cannot do that at home: a bag with the air sucked out is nowhere near empty, so do not trust that test. Trust the spoon. The string carried the vibration better than air did because a tight string is stiff and passes a push along almost without loss, and that is the rule everywhere: stiffer material, faster sound; and, for a given stiffness, denser material, slower sound. Sound crosses water at about 1480 m/s and steel at 5960, eighteen times its speed in cold air. Lead, which is very dense, carries it at only 1960 m/s, slower than aluminium at 5120; so “denser is faster” is wrong and “stiffer is faster” is right.

In air the speed depends on the temperature: 331 m/s at 0 °C, about 343 m/s at 20 °C, and 349 m/s on a 30 °C Mumbai afternoon. A clap aimed at a building 50 m away comes back as an echo 0.29 s later, because the sound has to go there and back, 100 m, at 349 m/s.

How do we know? The speed of sound, measured in a glass tube MIT, 2016

Newton worked out what the speed of sound in air should be, assuming the air’s temperature stays fixed while it is squeezed, and got a number about 15% too low (with today’s values for air, about 290 m/s). Laplace saw what was missing: a sound wave squeezes the air so quickly that the warmth made by the squeeze has no time to flow away, as Chapter 8 would lead you to expect, and warm squeezed air pushes back harder. His correction gives about 342 m/s. In an MIT lecture on waves the class sets up a standing sound wave in a glass tube, measures a wavelength of 34 cm at a known frequency, and gets 340 m/s, within 1% of Laplace’s value.

The spoon bell

Tie a steel spoon to the middle of a metre of thread. Wrap the ends round your index fingers, press those fingertips lightly into your ears, lean forward and let the spoon knock the edge of a table. Then take your fingers out and knock it again. Try a fork, a steel ladle and a wooden spoon: which gives the deepest bell?

Careful

“The air from the loudspeaker travels across the room to my ear.”

Each layer of air moves back and forth a tiny distance about its own place and shoves the next layer. The push travels; the air stays. It is the paper scrap in the bucket again, a thousand times a second.

At school

IGCSE topic 3.4 Sound asks for this: sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions, it needs a medium, and an echo is a reflection. Cambridge Lower Secondary puts it as “no sound in a vacuum”.

Check yourself

On Diwali night you see one firework burst and hear its bang at the same instant. Another, further off, bursts in silence, and the bang arrives a moment later. Why?

Answer at the back of the book

9.5Loud and high

A baby wails in the next seat of the local train; a whistle shrieks on the platform; a friend hums in your ear. Each sound has two things you can tell at once: how loud it is, and how high. Children, and plenty of adults, run the two together, and say that a high sound is a loud one. The microphone in your phone can take them apart.

Predict first

You sing one steady note into a phone app that draws the sound wave, and then sing the same note twice as loud. On the screen, the wave becomes:

  1. Taller, with the same spacing
  2. The same height, with the crests closer together
  3. Both taller and closer together

What happens

Taller, with the same spacing. Loudness is the size of the vibration, the wave’s amplitude. The spacing of the crests is set by how often your vocal cords vibrate, which is the note, and you did not change the note.

Pitch

How high or low a sound seems. It is the ear’s reading of the frequency of the sound wave.

What you hear as pitch is the frequency of the vibration reaching your ear: how many compressions arrive each second. Human ears work from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound, above 20,000 Hz ultrasound, and you hear neither. The ear is remarkably fine about pitch: two notes only about 0.3% apart in frequency can be told apart.

Decibel

A unit for how loud a sound is. Every 10 dB more means ten times the sound energy arriving per second; 20 dB more means a hundred times.

What you hear as loudness is mostly the amplitude of the vibration, and, as for any wave, the energy goes with the amplitude squared. The ear copes with an enormous range: the loudest sound you can stand delivers about a million million times the energy of the faintest you can hear. A scale running straight from one to a million million would be useless, so loudness is measured in decibels (dB), on a scale in which every step of 10 dB means ten times the energy. The threshold of hearing is 0 dB; a whisper a metre away is about 20 dB; ordinary conversation, 60 dB; busy traffic, 70 dB, which is where a Mumbai road sits. The step from 40 dB to 70 dB is three tens, so it is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times the energy. Doubling the amplitude adds just 6 dB.

The sensor lab for this section is your own voice: the live version of the figure above listens through the phone’s microphone and draws the pressure against time, the way an oscilloscope does. Hum louder and the trace grows taller; hum higher and the crests crowd together. Nothing is recorded and nothing leaves the phone.

One wrinkle, which is why the paragraph above says “mostly”: loudness depends a little on frequency as well, because the ear is less sensitive at the extremes of its range, so a very low or very high note has to carry more energy to sound as loud as a middle one.

Investigation 9.5

Put a phone playing music face down on a light table or a cardboard box and rest your fingertips on the surface. Turn the volume up: you feel the surface vibrate harder, and the vibration you feel is the amplitude. Turn it down until you can only just feel it, then listen: is that also the point where you can only just hear it?

Careful

“That whistle is so high it’s deafening. High sounds are loud sounds.”

Height and loudness are different properties of the same wave. A whistle can be high and faint; a drum can be low and deafening. The ear is more sensitive to some frequencies than others, so a modest amplitude at a frequency it likes can sound loud; the loudness still comes from the amplitude.

At school

Cambridge Lower Secondary states it as “loudness ↔ amplitude, pitch ↔ frequency”, which is this section in six words. IGCSE adds the decibel scale under 3.4 Sound.

Check yourself

A mayor announces that the new trains will add “only 30 dB” to the noise beside the line. Should the residents be reassured?

Answer at the back of the book

9.6Why a tabla sings

Calcutta, 1920

Strike an ordinary drum and you get a thud with a vague sense of height, and no note you could hum. Strike a tabla and a clear, singing note rings out. In 1920 C. V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar published a short paper in Nature explaining why. Most drums, they showed, give out overtones that are out of tune with one another, so the sound is a clash with no clear pitch. The tabla and the mridangam are different: their overtones fall in tune, at whole-number multiples of the lowest one, as a string’s do, and the reason is the syahi, the black loaded patch on the drumhead, which tunes the drumhead’s modes into line. To see why that is remarkable, start with a string.

Florence, about 1589

The old story says Pythagoras discovered the laws of harmony by hearing blacksmiths’ hammers and weighing them. It was first written down about six centuries after his time, and the physics in it is wrong: the weight of a hammer does not set its note. The true version has Galileo’s father in it. Vincenzo Galilei, in Florence, hung weights from strings to tighten them and measured what he heard. To raise a string’s note by an octave, doubling its frequency, you must pull it with four times the weight. Four times the pull for twice the pitch: the pattern is a square root, found by measuring.

Fundamental

The lowest frequency at which a string, pipe or drumhead can vibrate. It sets the note you hear.

Overtone

Any of the higher frequencies at which something can vibrate, above its fundamental.

Harmonic

An overtone that is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental: 2×, 3×, 4× and so on. Strings and open pipes have only harmonics; most drums do not.

A string fixed at both ends cannot vibrate any way it likes. Its ends are held still, so the only patterns that fit are the ones with a whole number of half-wavelengths between the ends: one bump, two bumps, three. The one-bump pattern has the lowest frequency, the fundamental, and gives the note you hear. The two-bump pattern vibrates at exactly twice that frequency, the three-bump at three times, and so on: the string’s higher patterns, its overtones, are all whole-number multiples of the fundamental, which is what makes them harmonics. Pluck a string and it vibrates in many of these patterns at once, added together as in Section 9.3, and the mixture is what reaches your ear.

Timbre

The quality that makes two instruments playing the same note sound different: the particular mix of overtones each one produces.

The mix of overtones gives an instrument its character. A violin and a harmonium playing the same note have the same fundamental and different mixes, which is why you can tell them apart with your eyes shut; the word for it is timbre. Air in a pipe has modes too. A pipe open at both ends behaves like a string, with every multiple present. A pipe closed at one end can only hold patterns with a still point at the closed end, which allows only the odd multiples: 1, 3, 5. A straight tube 30 cm long, closed at one end and blown across the open end on a warm day, sounds at about 290 Hz, with overtones near 870 and 1450 Hz; the same tube open at both ends would sound an octave higher, at about 580 Hz.

Predict first

Blow across the mouth of an empty glass bottle and you get a low toot. Pour water into the bottle, so the air column above the water is shorter, and blow again. The note:

  1. Goes up
  2. Goes down
  3. Stays the same, because the bottle is the same bottle

What happens

It goes up. The note comes from the air inside, and a shorter column of air fits a shorter wavelength, which is a higher frequency. The water simply shortens the air.

Now the drum. A drumhead is a flat circular skin held still all round its rim, and its modes are patterns across a surface rather than bumps along a line: one hump in the middle, then two halves rocking, then rings and quarters. Work out the frequencies of an ideal flat drumhead and they come out at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65 times the lowest. None of those is a whole number, so the overtones do not fit the fundamental, and when you strike the drum you hear a clash that soon dies into a thud. Raman and Kumar found that the tabla’s syahi weighs down the middle of the skin and shifts its modes until the overtones sit at whole-number multiples of the lowest. The drum becomes, acoustically, a kind of string, and sings a note. Whole-number overtones are the sound of a note; out-of-tune overtones are the sound of a thud, and the live version of the figure above lets you build both from the same ingredients.

The story behind this

How a tabla singsWhy a plucked string sounds like a note, why most drums only thud, and how the black patch on a tabla turns the thud into music, as Raman and Kumar showed in 1920.

A bottle organ

Line up three identical glass bottles. Leave one empty, half-fill the second with water and nearly fill the third. Blow gently across the mouth of each (practise: a thin, steady stream of air just over the rim). Predict which gives the highest note before you blow. Then tap the bottles with a spoon instead: is the order the same? Blowing sounds the air inside; tapping sounds the glass and the water in it, which is a different vibration altogether.

Careful

“All overtones are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.”

That is true for an ideal string and for a pipe open at both ends. A pipe closed at one end gives only the odd multiples, and a plain drumhead’s overtones are not whole-number multiples at all; that is why most drums have no clear note. The tabla is the exception, and the syahi is the reason.

Check yourself

Two wind instruments are the same length. One is a pipe open at both ends; the other is closed at one end. Which can play the lower note?

Answer at the back of the book

9.7The moving whistle

Utrecht, 1845

In 1842 Christian Doppler, in Prague, read a short paper to a handful of members of the Royal Bohemian Society. If a source of waves moves towards you, he argued, the waves should reach you more often and the pitch should rise; if it moves away, the pitch should fall. His main example was the colours of double stars, and it was wrong. Three years later a Dutch scientist, Christophorus Buys Ballot, tested it. On the railway line between Utrecht and Maarssen he had horn players stand on an open wagon pulled by a locomotive, sounding one steady note, while musicians with perfect pitch stood by the track and wrote down what they heard. The note rose as the wagon came towards them and fell as it went away. A well-known textbook credits Doppler himself with the train. It was Buys Ballot.

You have done his experiment on every station platform. Stand behind the yellow line as a fast local comes through with its horn sounding. The note holds steady while the train is far off, then, as it passes, drops, and holds a new, lower note as it recedes. The driver, meanwhile, hears none of this.

Predict first

The driver of the train hears the horn, which is mounted on the train with her. Compared with the horn’s true note, she hears:

  1. A higher note, because the train is moving fast
  2. A lower note
  3. The true note

What happens

The true note. She and the horn move together, so each compression reaches her exactly as often as the horn makes it. The shift happens only between things moving towards or away from each other.

Doppler effect

The change in the frequency of a wave heard or seen when the source and the observer are moving towards or away from each other. Approaching: higher. Receding: lower.

Here is why the note changes. The horn makes compressions at a steady rate, say 300 a second, and each one spreads out through the air at the speed of sound from the point where it was made. But the horn does not stay at that point. By the time it makes the next compression it has moved forward, so the new compression starts a little closer to you than the last. Ahead of the train the compressions are bunched together: a shorter wavelength. Behind, each one starts further away than the last, so they are stretched out. The compressions still travel at the fixed speed of sound, so bunched-up ones arrive more often, which your ear reads as a higher note, and stretched-out ones arrive less often, a lower note. This is the Doppler effect, and it is as real as a thermometer reading: a microphone measures the changed frequency, so it is no trick of the ear.

How big is the change? For a horn of frequency f on a train moving at speed v towards you, with sound travelling at c, the frequency you hear is f × c ÷ (c − v); moving away, it is f × c ÷ (c + v). A textbook example first: a 150 Hz horn at 35 m/s, with sound at 340 m/s, is heard at 167 Hz approaching and 136 Hz receding. The rise (17 Hz) is bigger than the fall (14 Hz): the two shifts are never quite symmetric. Now a Mumbai local. Nobody has published its horn’s frequency or its speed through a station, so take a 300 Hz horn at 80 km/h, which is 22 m/s, on a 30 °C afternoon when sound travels at 349 m/s:

Approaching: 300 Hz × 349 ÷ (349 − 22) ≈ 320 Hz
Receding: 300 Hz × 349 ÷ (349 + 22) ≈ 282 Hz
The ratio 320 ÷ 282 ≈ 1.14, a drop of about 2.2 semitones: a bit more than a whole tone.

That matches what your ear tells you on the platform: a drop of about a tone as the train passes. The drop is quick because, while the train is far off, almost all of its motion is straight towards you, and as it passes, that part shrinks to nothing and then reverses. A source that moves at the speed of sound catches up with its own compressions, which pile into one great pressure wall, the start of a sonic boom.

The story behind this

Horn players on a trainDoppler’s idea was right and his favourite example was wrong; three years later a Dutch scientist tested it the only way he could, with horn players on an open railway wagon.

Investigation 9.7

With an adult, stand on a platform well behind the yellow line as a fast local passes with its horn sounding. Hum the note you hear as it approaches, then the note as it recedes, into a tuner app, and read off the two frequencies. Does the ratio come out near 1.14? Trains differ, so your number will be your own.

Careful

“The horn gets louder as the train comes, and that is why it sounds higher.”

Louder and higher are separate (Section 9.5). The pitch rises because the compressions arrive more often, and that depends on the train’s speed, never on how loud the horn is.

At school

IGCSE leaves out the Doppler effect for sound. Under 6.2.3 it asks for redshift: the increase in the wavelength of light from galaxies that are moving away from us, which is the horn’s falling note, for light. IB Diploma physics covers both as topic C.5. You will meet redshift again in Chapter 15.

Check yourself

Two cars sound identical horns as they drive towards you, one at 20 m/s and one at 40 m/s. Which horn sounds higher?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 9

The echo off the building

A hot afternoon, 30 °C. You stand in the compound facing the building across the open ground and clap once, hard. The clap comes back to you from the wall. Your cousin says the wall “makes a new sound” when the clap hits it. You set the phyphox app’s acoustic stopwatch going and clap again. It reads 0.29 s between the clap and its return.

Two questions. How far away is the wall? And is the echo a new sound?

Show the solution

Distance. The sound went to the wall and came back, so it travelled twice the distance in 0.29 s. At 30 °C sound travels at about 349 m/s, so the round trip is 349 × 0.29 ≈ 101 m, and the wall is about 50 m away.

Not a new sound. The compressions you made with your hands ran to the wall, pushed on it, and were pushed back: the same pattern of pushes, turned around. The wall adds nothing of its own, which is why an echo repeats what you said and never says anything else.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Every wave in this chapter needed something to wave: water, a string, the air. Take the air away and the bell in the jar goes silent. Yet sunlight crosses 150 million kilometres of emptiness to reach Marine Drive, and the light of the stars crosses far more. If light is a wave, what is waving, when there is nothing there? Chapter 10 begins at the near end of that question, with your own eyes, in a completely dark room, and asks whether anything comes out of them.
