Chapter 15

Atoms, stars and the universe

The big questionThe Sun has “burned” for about four and a half billion years. What could possibly keep a fire going that long?

  1. 15.1Light comes in packets
  2. 15.2The nucleus and radiation myths
  3. 15.3E = mc² and the Sun’s fire
  4. 15.4What stars are made of
  5. 15.5How far are the stars?
  6. 15.6How stars die
  7. 15.7The stretching universe

Chapter 14 leaned on the Sun at every turn. It lights the Moon, it drives the seasons, and twice a month its pull joins the Moon’s to send the biggest tides over the causeway at Haji Ali. It has been doing all this, as far as the rocks can tell, for about four and a half billion years. And in Chapter 7 you learned to keep accounts of energy: nothing comes from nowhere. A bonfire the size of the Sun would be ash in a few thousand years. So what is the Sun doing?

The answer needs the smallest things in the book and the largest, in that order. It starts with light, which turns out to arrive in packets. It goes down into the centre of the atom, where Chapter 1 of The Invisible World left off, and finds there the thing that keeps the Sun shining. Then it turns outward: what stars are made of, how far away they are, how they end, and what the whole universe is doing. Two of the people on this road were told, at first, that they must be wrong.

15.1Light comes in packets

Bern, 1905

In 1905 a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein, published four papers in the journal Annalen der Physik. One of them changed how we measure space and time; another gave the world E = mc², which you will meet in Section 15.3. But the Nobel Prize he was eventually given was for the first of the four, which was about something that looks small: what happens when light falls on a metal.

Photoelectric effect

Electrons being knocked out of a material by light falling on it. Each electron is freed by one packet of light; the packet must carry at least the energy that binds the electron.

Here is the effect. Shine light on a clean metal surface and, for some metals and some colours of light, electrons come flying out of it. That is the photoelectric effect, and after Chapter 11 you have a ready picture of it. Light is a wave; a wave carries energy; the energy shakes electrons loose. A brighter light is a bigger wave, so it should shake them out harder, and a very dim light should need a little time to build up enough energy before any electron can leave.

Predict first

Two lamps shine in turn on the same clean metal: a very bright red lamp and a dim violet one. Which knocks electrons out?

  1. The bright red lamp, because it delivers far more energy
  2. Both, the red one more strongly
  3. Only the violet one, however dim it is

What happens

Only the violet one, for most metals, and it works the instant it is switched on, however dim it is. Make the red lamp as bright as you like and nothing comes out. Make the violet lamp brighter and more electrons come out, each with the same top speed as before. Measured carefully, the effect breaks the wave picture in five places at once: a threshold colour below which nothing happens, whatever the brightness; no delay; a number of electrons that follows the brightness; a top energy that does not; and a top energy that rises in a straight line with the light’s frequency.

Photon

A packet of light. Its energy is E = hf: Planck’s constant times the frequency. Brighter light means more photons per second, never bigger ones.

Einstein’s explanation was that light delivers its energy in packets. Each packet, now called a photon, carries an energy fixed by the light’s frequency: E = hf, where h is a very small number called Planck’s constant, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. Violet light has a higher frequency than red, so each violet photon carries more energy. When light meets the metal, one photon gives its whole energy to one electron. If that is more than the energy binding the electron to the metal, the electron leaves with the difference; if it is less, the electron stays, and no number of such photons will help, because they arrive one at a time. Brightness is simply how many photons arrive each second. Brighter red means more too-small packets. Dim violet means a few packets that are each big enough.

Understand itPhoton

What is it?

A single quantum packet of light (or any electromagnetic radiation), carrying an energy proportional to the wave’s frequency: E = hf.

Why is it called this?

Einstein called the packets light quanta in 1905; the physical chemist Gilbert Lewis coined photon in 1926 from the Greek phos (phot-), light, to match electron and proton.

What problem did it solve?

In the photoelectric effect, dim violet light knocks electrons out of calcium instantly while blazing red light never knocks out a single one; waves that spread their energy smoothly could not explain why colour alone sets a sharp threshold.

Why does it work?

Whenever light is emitted or absorbed by matter, it hands over its energy one whole packet at a time to one electron; if a single packet (hf) is smaller than the energy binding the electron, the electron cannot leave, no matter how many packets arrive per second.

How does it help?

It explains the photoelectric effect, why ultraviolet light causes sunburn while infrared from a remote control cannot, how solar cells and camera sensors count light, and why atoms emit and absorb sharp spectral lines.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Shine monochromatic light on a clean metal in a vacuum and measure the stopping voltage of the freed electrons: below a threshold frequency no electrons appear at any brightness, and above it their maximum kinetic energy rises in a straight line with frequency, with slope h.

What it isn’t

A photon is not a tiny hard marble with mass: it has zero rest mass, always travels at c in empty space, and still produces wave interference patterns when sent through two slits.

Where does it stop working?

In everyday lamps and radio antennas where trillions of photons arrive together, the individual packets blur into the smooth classical electromagnetic wave of Chapter 13.

Your turn

Explain Photon to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Electronvolt (eV)

A unit of energy for atoms and light: the energy an electron gains when pushed through one volt, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Visible photons carry 1.63 to 3.26 eV.

The energies involved are tiny, so physicists use a small unit, the electronvolt. Visible photons carry between about 1.63 eV, for deep red, and 3.26 eV, for violet. A clean calcium surface holds its electrons with 2.71 eV. A violet photon of 3.26 eV, as drawn below, frees one and leaves it with up to 3.26 − 2.71 = 0.55 eV of motion. A photon from your television remote, which flashes infrared light at a wavelength of about 940 nm, carries 1.32 eV: not enough, so the remote could shine on calcium all day and nothing would leave. Everyday light is a torrent of these packets: if a tenth of a 100-watt bulb’s output were yellow light, it would throw out about 3 × 10¹⁹ photons a second, so many that they blur into the smooth flow of energy you kept accounts of in Chapter 7.

See the invisible

Point a television remote at your phone’s camera in a dim room, look at the screen, and press a button. The remote’s tip flashes a pale light on the screen that your eyes cannot see in the room: infrared, at about 940 nm, a colour just beyond red. Only some cameras show it; if the back camera shows nothing, try the front one. This is light from a small lamp, a torch at a colour you cannot see. It is not the heat of a warm object, and the phone is not “seeing heat”. Each of these photons carries about 1.32 eV, less than any visible photon, which is one reason the remote cannot hurt you.

So is light a wave or a stream of packets? Young’s card in Chapter 11 gave fringes that only waves make. The photoelectric effect gives thresholds that only packets make. Both experiments are right, and the honest statement is both at once: light travels like a wave and delivers its energy in packets. Nobody has a picture of a single thing that does both. The equations do both, and they have never been caught out.

Dacca, 4 June 1924

Nineteen years later a physics lecturer in Dacca, Satyendra Nath Bose, worked out a new way of counting photons that gave Planck’s formula for the light from a hot body. The Philosophical Magazine in London had not replied to his paper. So he wrote to Einstein, beginning “Respected Sir”, and asked him, if he thought the work worth it, to arrange its publication, since he did not know enough German to do so himself. Einstein translated the paper with his own hand, sent Bose a postcard on 2 July, and had it printed in August with a note of his own. Particles that can be counted Bose’s way are now called bosons, and photons are the first of them.

The story behind this

Light in packetsA patent clerk in Bern explained why a dim violet lamp can knock electrons out of a metal when a blinding red one cannot, and nineteen years later a teacher in Dacca wrote to him with a better way to count the packets.

Back from Chapter 11

“Light is a wave, full stop.” Chapter 11 showed you Young’s fringes and Arago’s spot. Does the photoelectric effect mean Chapter 11 was wrong?

Answer at the back of the book

Careful

“A brighter light must give each electron more energy.”

Brighter light means more photons each second, and each photon’s energy is fixed by the colour alone. So a brighter lamp frees more electrons, each with the same energy as before. If the colour is below the metal’s threshold, a brighter lamp frees more of nothing. Remember the remote: it cannot free an electron from calcium however hard you press the button.

At school

The photoelectric effect is not in IGCSE; it arrives in IB Diploma physics under E.2, Quantum physics. IGCSE topic 3.3 does ask for the electromagnetic spectrum: the remote’s infrared is one rung of Chapter 11’s ladder of light.

Investigation 15.1

In the free PhET simulation Photoelectric Effect (through Further adventures at the back), set a colour just below the metal’s threshold. Predict first: what does turning the brightness to maximum do?

Check yourself

A made-up metal needs 2.3 eV to free an electron. Red light, 1.63 eV per photon, is shone on it ten times more brightly than before. Does anything come out? What about dim violet light at 3.26 eV per photon?

Answer at the back of the book

15.2The nucleus and radiation myths

Kenilworth, Peddar Road, Bombay, 19 December 1945

A few minutes’ walk from Haji Ali, in a house called Kenilworth on Peddar Road, a new institute opened its doors on 19 December 1945. Its founder, Homi Bhabha, had written to his father from Cambridge in 1928 that business and engineering were not for him and that he was burning to do physics; the bargain they struck was an engineering degree first. In March 1944 he wrote to the Sir Dorab Tata Trust proposing an institute for fundamental research, and the Tata Institute, TIFR, began in Bangalore that June before moving to Bombay. Among those who joined it was Bibha Chowdhuri, who had spent the war years leaving photographic plates on mountains at Darjeeling and Sandakphu so that cosmic rays, particles raining in from space, would streak across them, and had found in them the curved tracks of a new kind of particle.

Radiation

Anything that streams outward from a source: light of every colour, radio waves, X-rays, and the particles and gamma rays that some nuclei throw out. Most radiation is harmless; the harmful kinds carry enough energy per packet to knock electrons off atoms.

Particles from space pass through you every day. The word for anything that streams out of a source, from radio waves and the remote’s infrared to X-rays and the fragments of atoms, is radiation, and it is a word that frightens people. Two fears are common. One is that all radiation is dangerous. The other, held by somewhere between 63% and 75% of students asked, is that anything that has been near radiation becomes radioactive itself. The remote has answered the first fear. The second needs the inside of the atom.

Nucleus

The tiny, heavy centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons held by the strong nuclear force. About 10⁻¹⁵ m across, 100,000 times smaller than the atom.

The Invisible World told you how Rutherford’s students fired alpha particles at gold foil and found that about one in eight thousand bounced back. An atom is almost entirely empty space around a nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ m across, a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself. If the nucleus were a marble one centimetre across, the atom would be a kilometre wide. Inside it, protons and neutrons are held together by the strong nuclear force, which is very strong and reaches only a very short way. Chemistry, burning and cooking never touch it.

Radioactive

A nucleus is radioactive if it changes by itself, throwing out an alpha particle, a beta particle or a gamma ray as it does so. Most nuclei never do.

In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that a lump of uranium ore, left on wrapped photographic plates in a drawer, darkened them through the paper. Some nuclei are unstable: of their own accord, now and then, they throw out a particle or a flash of light and change into something else. Such nuclei are radioactive. Each event carries around a million electronvolts, against a few electronvolts for anything an atom does with its electrons, which is why this radiation can do what light cannot: knock electrons clean off the atoms it passes. That is what “ionising” means, and ionising radiation is the kind that can harm living tissue. Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper or your skin; beta particles go farther; gamma rays, which are photons of very high energy, go farthest of all.

Predict first

After a chest X-ray, is the patient radioactive?

  1. Yes, for a few hours
  2. Yes, very slightly, for ever
  3. No

What happens

No. An X-ray is a beam of high-energy photons; they pass through the body, some are absorbed, and when the machine switches off there is nothing left behind. Being exposed to radiation and being contaminated with radioactive material are different things, and the difference is the whole answer to the second fear.

Contamination

Radioactive material where it should not be: on skin, hair or clothing, or inside the body. It keeps emitting until it is removed. Being exposed to a beam is not contamination.

Think of sunlight and mud. Stand in sunlight and you are exposed to radiation; step into the shade and it stops, and nothing of it stays on you. Walk through mud and some of it comes with you until it is washed off. Radioactive material is the mud: dust on your skin or clothes, or breathed in or swallowed, which keeps emitting wherever it is. That is contamination. X-rays, gamma rays and light are the sunlight: they pass, and are gone. Spices and other foods are routinely irradiated with gamma rays to kill insects and germs, and are left with no radioactivity at all, because photons and electrons do not change nuclei. One honest exception: a beam of neutrons can make the atoms it hits radioactive, which is exactly why neutrons are never used on food. The true rule is about which radiation, and the everyday kinds are in the clear.

You are a little radioactive yourself, and always have been. Cosmic rays from space give the average person about 0.40 millisieverts a year of dose; a twelve-hour flight adds 0.02 to 0.03; the rocks under your feet and your food add more, and in some places the ground gives ten times the average. A dose below 100 millisieverts counts as low. The question with any radiation is never “is it there?” but how much, of what kind, and for how long.

The story behind this

Radiation is not catchingMost students think a chest X-ray leaves you radioactive. It does not, and the difference between being hit by radiation and carrying radioactive dust is the whole of radiation safety.

Careful

“Anything that has been near radiation becomes radioactive.”

Being hit by light, X-rays or gamma rays does not change a nucleus, so it cannot make anything radioactive: the patient after an X-ray and the irradiated spices are as they were. Two things do: radioactive material on you or in you, and neutron beams, which are rare and kept away from people and food. Keep “exposed” and “contaminated” apart and most of the fear goes.

At school

IGCSE topic 5.1 is the nuclear model of the atom and 5.2 is radioactivity: the three types of emission, half-life and safety. When the syllabus says “ionising”, it means knocking electrons off atoms, and “contamination” there means what it means here: radioactive material where it should not be.

Investigation 15.2

Put a marble on the floor as a nucleus and work out, at that scale, how far away the edge of the atom would be. Then pace it out with an adult along a straight road. Everything between the marble and you is where the electrons are, and nothing else.

Check yourself

A packet of chilli powder has been irradiated with gamma rays to kill insects. Is the chilli radioactive?

Answer at the back of the book

15.3E = mc² and the Sun’s fire

Kungälv, Sweden, Christmas 1938

Fission

A heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter ones. The pieces have a little less mass than the original, and the difference comes out as energy.

Lise Meitner had fled Germany that summer. She spent Christmas in the small Swedish town of Kungälv with her nephew Otto Frisch, and brought with her a letter from her old colleague Otto Hahn in Berlin. He had been firing neutrons at uranium and had found, among the products, barium: an atom only about half as heavy as uranium. It made no sense. Nuclei chipped; they did not halve. The story goes that the two of them walked out into the snow to think about it, and on that walk they saw what Hahn had done. The uranium nucleus had split in two. They called it fission, and they worked out that the two pieces together have slightly less mass than the nucleus they came from, and that the missing mass had become about 200 million electronvolts of energy, more than a hundred thousand times what any chemical reaction releases per atom. Their paper appeared in Nature in February 1939.

The mass had become energy by the rule from the third of Einstein’s 1905 papers, E = mc². Mass and energy are two names for one thing, and the exchange rate is the speed of light squared: 9 × 10¹⁶ joules for every kilogram, so that one gram of mass, fully converted, is 9 × 10¹³ J, about 25 million kilowatt-hours on the bill from Chapter 7. Nothing ordinary converts mass to energy at anything like that rate. A nucleus can, because the strong force that binds it is so strong that the binding itself has a measurable mass.

E = mc²

Now the Sun. Astronomers of the nineteenth century had two candidates for its energy, and both fail.

Predict first

If the Sun were a giant ball of coal, burning, how long could it keep shining as brightly as it does now?

  1. About as long as it already has: billions of years
  2. A few million years
  3. A few thousand years

What happens

A few thousand years. Burning is chemistry, a few electronvolts per atom, and no chemical fuel the size of the Sun could last longer than that; besides, nothing like coal could survive at the Sun’s temperature. The other old idea, that the Sun shines because it is slowly shrinking under its own gravity, reaches only about a hundred million years, and the rocks say that there was liquid water on the Earth nearly four billion years ago. Something far richer than burning is going on, and it is the opposite of fission.

Fusion

Light nuclei joining to make a heavier one. In the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus and 0.71% of their mass becomes energy. It needs a temperature above about 12 million degrees.

In the centre of the Sun the temperature is about 15 million degrees, and the matter there is hydrogen nuclei, which are bare protons, rushing about. Protons repel each other, as Chapter 12’s charges do, so only the very fastest can get close enough to touch, which is why the centre must be hotter than about 12 million degrees for this to happen at all. In several steps, four protons and two electrons become a helium nucleus and two neutrinos. That is fusion. For the complete mass account, compare four hydrogen atoms with one helium atom: the helium atom has about 0.71% less mass. The difference leaves as energy, by E = mc². The neutrinos carry some straight out of the Sun; most of the energy eventually escapes as sunlight, after a journey of a hundred thousand years or more being passed between particles on the way out.

Understand itNuclear fusion

What is it?

The joining of two light atomic nuclei into a heavier nucleus whose mass is slightly less than the sum of the pieces, releasing the mass difference as energy according to E = mc².

Why is it called this?

Nuclear refers to the atom’s nucleus; fusion comes from Latin fusio, melting together, borrowed in the 1930s as the opposite of nuclear fission (splitting).

What problem did it solve?

Neither chemical burning (which would last a few thousand years) nor gravitational shrinking (about a hundred million years) could explain how the Sun has shone for 4.5 billion years; fusing hydrogen into helium releases millions of times more energy per kilogram than any chemical reaction.

Why does it work?

The strong nuclear force binds the final helium nucleus. Across the full reaction chain, four protons and two electrons become a helium-4 nucleus and two neutrinos. Comparing the masses of four hydrogen atoms with one helium atom accounts for the electrons: about 0.71% of the starting mass becomes released energy, yielding about 6.4 × 10¹⁴ J per kilogram of hydrogen.

How does it help?

It explains what powers the Sun and every main-sequence star, how stars forge heavier elements out of hydrogen and helium, and why the Sun has used only about 0.03% of its mass in 4.5 billion years.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

We measure the Sun’s luminosity (3.8 × 10²⁶ W), compare hydrogen and helium atomic masses to verify the 0.71% mass difference, and detect the neutrinos streaming straight out of the Sun’s core from the fusion reactions.

What it isn’t

It is not chemical burning (which only rearranges outer electrons and leaves nuclei untouched), and it is not nuclear fission (which splits heavy nuclei like uranium).

Where does it stop working?

Because protons carry positive charge and fiercely repel each other, fusion cannot happen at ordinary temperatures; it requires temperatures above about 12 million degrees and enormous density so protons collide fast enough to touch, and building nuclei heavier than iron absorbs energy instead of releasing it.

Your turn

Explain Nuclear fusion to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Put numbers on it and the Sun’s fire makes sense at last. Every second the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and about 4 million tonnes of that mass leaves as light. That sounds like a catastrophe until you weigh the Sun: it has about 2 × 10³⁰ kg, and in four and a half billion years of this it has used up about 0.03% of itself. Most of its protons have never fused at all.

Energy from one kilogram of hydrogen fused: 0.0071 × (3 × 10⁸ m/s)² ≈ 6.4 × 10¹⁴ J
The Sun’s output: 3.8 × 10²⁶ J every second
Mass turned into energy each second: 3.8 × 10²⁶ ÷ (3 × 10⁸)² ≈ 4.3 × 10⁹ kg, about 4 million tonnes
Hydrogen fused each second: 4.3 × 10⁹ ÷ 0.0071 ≈ 6 × 10¹¹ kg, about 600 million tonnes

Back from Chapter 7

“Energy is never created. So where does the Sun’s energy come from?” Chapter 7 kept a ledger with stores and transfers. What has to go in the ledger to make the Sun’s accounts balance?

Answer at the back of the book

Since January 2024 a spacecraft has been watching all this without a blink. ISRO’s Aditya-L1 flies in a loop around a point in space called L1, about 1.5 million km from the Earth towards the Sun, one per cent of the way there, where the pulls of the Sun and the Earth balance with the motion round the Sun so that a craft keeps pace with the Earth all year, with the Sun always in view and the Earth never in the way. It does not sit still at the point; it circles it in a halo orbit once every 178 days, and it arrived there on 6 January 2024.

The story behind this

A fire that has lasted four and a half billion yearsNo fire could shine for four and a half billion years, and the Sun is not burning at all; the walk in the snow that explained a split nucleus also explains where sunlight comes from.

The story behind this

A spacecraft that never stops watching the SunOne and a half million kilometres sunward of Earth there is a spot where the Sun’s pull and Earth’s pull combine so neatly that a spacecraft can keep pace with us for years; India parked a Sun-watcher there in January 2024.

Careful

“The Sun is burning, like a huge fire.”

Burning is a chemical change: atoms swap partners and their electrons rearrange, and the nuclei are never touched. A coal Sun would be ash in a few thousand years. The Sun shines by fusion, which changes the nuclei themselves, hydrogen into helium, and releases about a million times more energy per atom than any flame. Say “shining”, or “fusing”, and keep “burning” for the kitchen.

At school

IGCSE 1.7.1 lists “nuclear” among the energy stores, and 6.2.1 treats the Sun as a star. The nuclear store is the mass of the Sun’s hydrogen, released a little at a time as it becomes helium.

Investigation 15.3

Open The Sky and its mission tab for Aditya-L1. Watch the craft keep pace with the Earth as both go round the Sun.

Check yourself

The Sun loses 4 million tonnes of mass every second. Is it in danger of running out soon? Use its mass, 2 × 10³⁰ kg, and its age.

Answer at the back of the book

15.4What stars are made of

Calcutta, 1920

Nobody can visit a star, and yet by 1920 astronomers had been reading the recipe of the Sun for sixty years. The trick is the spectrum from Chapter 11. Spread a star’s light into a rainbow and it is crossed by dark lines, hundreds of them in sunlight; Joseph von Fraunhofer counted about 600 in 1815. Each kind of atom swallows its own set of colours, so each element leaves its own pattern of lines, like a barcode. In 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff matched one of the Sun’s patterns to sodium, the first element ever identified in a star. Helium was found in the Sun’s light before anyone had found it on Earth.

But the stars’ barcodes differ. Some show strong hydrogen lines; some, the hottest and bluest, show almost none. The first guess was the obvious one: different lines, different ingredients. In Calcutta a young physicist, Meghnad Saha, saw another possibility. The lines an atom can make depend on where its electrons are sitting, and that depends on how hot the gas is. Heat a gas enough and its atoms lose electrons altogether; an atom with no electron cannot make its usual lines at all. In 1920 Saha wrote the equation that says, for any temperature and pressure, what fraction of the atoms have lost their electrons. Alfred Fowler hosted him at Imperial College in London that year and helped him revise the papers, and the equation has been the key to every star’s spectrum since.

Predict first

A hot blue star shows almost no hydrogen lines in its spectrum. Does that mean it contains almost no hydrogen?

  1. Yes: no lines, no hydrogen
  2. No: it is so hot that its hydrogen atoms have lost their electrons, and cannot make the lines
  3. The lines are there but drowned out by the blue light

What happens

No. In the hottest stars nearly every hydrogen atom has been stripped of its electron, so there is nothing left to swallow the hydrogen colours, and the lines vanish. In the coolest stars the lines are weak for the opposite reason: the electrons all sit in their lowest level, and the visible lines need an electron one step up. The hydrogen lines are strongest in stars of middling temperature, and that is the trap: “different-looking spectrum” was read as “different stuff” when it mostly meant “different temperature”.

At Harvard, Annie Cannon had spent years sorting the spectra of stars into classes by their lines; put in order of temperature, hottest first, the classes run O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Then, in 1925, a young astronomer at Harvard, Cecilia Payne, took Saha’s equation and asked it the question nobody had asked properly: allowing for temperature, how much of each element is really there? The answer was that the Sun and the stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, with everything else a trace. It was so unexpected that the astronomer Henry Norris Russell told her it was clearly impossible, and her thesis went to print with the hydrogen result labelled “spurious”. It was confirmed within three years, by Russell among others. Later the astronomer Otto Struve called it “the most brilliant PhD thesis ever written in astronomy”.

Plasma

A gas so hot that its atoms have lost electrons, leaving charged nuclei and free electrons mixed together. Stars are made of it.

Absorption lines

Dark lines in a spectrum where atoms in a cooler gas have swallowed particular colours. Each element has its own set, but how strong the lines are depends on temperature as much as on how much of the element there is.

The modern figures: about 73% of the Sun’s mass is hydrogen and 25% is helium, leaving about 2% for everything else. The Earth’s crust, by contrast, is mostly oxygen, silicon and aluminium, which is why everyone had expected the Sun to be made of the same. And the stuff of a star is not fire, and not gas as you know it. At those temperatures atoms are broken into nuclei and loose electrons, a state called plasma; the Sun’s absorption lines are made in its cooler outer layers, where some atoms still hold their electrons.

The story behind this

What the stars are made ofA Calcutta physicist worked out why hot stars hide their hydrogen; a Harvard student used his equation to show that stars are almost nothing but hydrogen, and was told to call her own result spurious.

Careful

“Different lines in two stars’ spectra mean they are made of different things.”

Mostly they mean the stars are at different temperatures. Nearly all stars are made of the same stuff, hydrogen and helium with a sprinkling of everything else; what changes with temperature is which atoms still have the electrons they need to make their lines. Saha’s equation lets you allow for that, and when Payne did, the differences in recipe almost vanished.

Investigation 15.4

Hold a CD at a slant under a white LED lamp, as in Chapter 11, and look at the rainbow it throws. Then try an old orange street lamp, if you can find one, and see where the light is and where it is missing. Never point a CD, or anything else, at the Sun.

Check yourself

Why did astronomers expect the Sun to be made of the same stuff as the Earth’s crust, and what did they get wrong?

Answer at the back of the book

15.5How far are the stars?

Parallax

The apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when you look from two places. The farther the object, the smaller the shift. For a star, the two places are the Earth six months apart.

Hold up your thumb at arm’s length against the far wall of the room. Close one eye, then the other. The thumb jumps against the wall. Bring it closer to your face and the jump is bigger; hold it farther away and the jump shrinks. The jump is called parallax, and it is the only direct way we have of measuring the distance to a star.

Predict first

You hold a pen at arm’s length and note how far it jumps against the wall when you switch eyes. A friend holds it twice as far from your eyes. How big is the jump now?

  1. Twice as big
  2. The same
  3. About half as big

What happens

About half as big. The shift depends on how far apart your eyes are compared with the distance to the pen, and doubling the distance halves the angle. Now imagine the pen is a star. Your eyes, 6 or 7 centimetres apart, are hopeless. The farthest apart two viewpoints can ever be, for anyone on the Earth, is the two sides of its orbit round the Sun, 300 million kilometres apart: look in January and again in July.

Even with that baseline the nearest stars shift by a hair. Astronomers define a star’s parallax as half the total shift, the angle you would get from a baseline of one Earth–Sun distance, and measure it in arcseconds, each 1/3,600 of a degree. How small is that? A ₹1 coin is 22 mm across. It would look one arcsecond wide from about 4.5 km away, a little less than the length of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, has a parallax of 0.77 arcseconds, the coin seen from about 6 km, and every other star shows less. Friedrich Bessel was the first to measure one, in 1838, for a star called 61 Cygni. Today the satellite Gaia measures them for nearly a billion stars, to a few millionths of an arcsecond.

Parsec and light-year

A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m. A parsec is the distance at which a star’s parallax is one arcsecond: 3.26 light-years. Both are distances, never times.

The distance at which a star’s parallax would be exactly one arcsecond is called a parsec, and it is 206,265 times the Earth–Sun distance, or 3.26 light-years, a light-year being the distance light travels in a year. Proxima is 1.3 parsecs away, 4.25 light-years: its light takes four and a quarter years to reach you, where the Sun’s takes eight minutes (Chapter 10). The arithmetic is simple: distance in parsecs is one divided by the parallax in arcseconds. The difficulty is all in the measuring, and it sets a limit.

Parallax measured to ±0.001″. For the distance to be good to 10%, the parallax must be at least 0.01″.
Distance = 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100 parsecs, about 326 light-years.
Beyond that, this method alone becomes too rough.

Harvard, 1912

Cepheid

A large, pulsing star whose brightness rises and falls over days or weeks. The slower the pulse, the brighter the star really is, so its pulse gives its distance.

Our galaxy is far bigger than 100 parsecs, and the other galaxies are far beyond it, so another way was needed. Henrietta Leavitt was one of the “computers” at Harvard College Observatory, women hired to measure photographic plates at a third or a quarter of what the men were paid. She was studying the Small Magellanic Cloud, a cloud of stars so far away that all its stars are at very nearly the same distance from us, and in it a kind of star that pulses, brightening and fading over days or weeks: Cepheids, named for the first one found, Delta Cephei. In 1912 she reported that the brighter-looking Cepheids always had the longer pulses. Because all the stars in the Cloud are at about the same distance, brighter-looking meant truly brighter. So a Cepheid’s pulse told you its true brightness, and comparing that with how bright it looked told you how far away it was, anywhere you could find one. Leavitt could not set the scale herself, because nobody then knew the distance to the Cloud; others did that later. With her measuring tape, Edwin Hubble found the distances to other galaxies, and then found something stranger, which is Section 15.7.

The story behind this

A measuring tape to the starsA Harvard “computer” noticed that the slow blinkers among the stars of one small cloud were always the bright ones, and gave astronomers a tape that reaches far beyond anything a surveyor’s triangle can measure.

Careful

“A light-year is a length of time.”

It is a distance: how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million kilometres. Proxima Centauri is 4.25 light-years away, which also tells you that its light took 4.25 years to arrive, so you see it as it was four years ago. But the unit measures the road, not the journey.

At school

IGCSE 6.2.2 uses the light-year as the unit for the distances of stars and galaxies. Write it, and think of it, as a distance.

Investigation 15.5

On a terrace, with an adult, pick a water tank on a nearby building and a tall building far behind it. Sight the tank from one end of the terrace and note what it lines up with on the far building; walk to the other end and sight again. Pace out your baseline and estimate the tank’s distance.

Check yourself

Leavitt’s brighter-looking Cepheids pulsed more slowly. Why could she trust that “brighter-looking” meant “truly brighter”?

Answer at the back of the book

15.6How stars die

At sea, Bombay to England, 1930

In 1930 a nineteen-year-old from Madras, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, nephew of the C. V. Raman of Chapter 11, boarded the SS Pilsna at Bombay for England, where he was to study. He had finished college at nineteen. On the long voyage he began working on a problem that sounds harmless: what happens to a star like the Sun when its fuel runs out?

White dwarf

What is left of a Sun-like star when its fuel is gone: a core held up by the pressure of electrons that cannot be squeezed closer together. This degeneracy pressure is a quantum effect, far stronger than electric repulsion.

The answer begins with the squeeze. When the core of a Sun-like star has turned its hydrogen into helium, nothing holds it up against its own gravity, and it shrinks. The electrons in it are pressed closer and closer. Then a rule from the quantum world takes over, the Pauli principle: no two electrons can be in the same place at the same time doing the same thing. Press them closer than that rule allows and they push back, with a pressure that has nothing to do with their electric charge and is far stronger than ordinary repulsion. Think of a local at rush hour, where every seat is taken; however hard the crowd pushes at the doors, the seats do not get smaller. The electrons’ rule is like that, only stricter. The shrinking stops, and what is left is a white dwarf: the dead core of a star, held up by the refusal of its electrons to be crowded further.

Predict first

A white dwarf is held up by its crowded electrons. Add more mass to it. Does it get bigger or smaller?

  1. Bigger: more stuff takes up more room
  2. Smaller
  3. The same size: the electrons are already as close as they can be

What happens

Smaller. More mass means more gravity, and the extra gravity crushes the electrons closer still. The more massive the white dwarf, the smaller it is, the opposite of everything you handle in daily life. Chandrasekhar’s question on the Pilsna was where that ends.

Chandrasekhar limit

The greatest mass a star can end its life with and still become a white dwarf: about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, about 2.8 × 10³⁰ kg. Heavier cores collapse further.

He added the new physics of relativity to the calculation, and the answer was a limit. As the mass goes up, the radius comes down, faster and faster, and the models give a radius of zero at about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun. That is the Chandrasekhar limit, and it means that no white dwarf can exist above it: for anything heavier, even the electrons’ refusal cannot stop the collapse, and the star must end some other way. Those other ways have names you may have heard, neutron stars and black holes, and they belong to another book. In 1935 the astronomer Arthur Eddington ridiculed the idea in public. Chandrasekhar was right, and in 1983 he was given the Nobel Prize for it.

The Sun has one solar mass, under the limit, so this is its future: in the very far future, its core will become a white dwarf. Many stars born far heavier than 1.4 Suns shed much of their mass as they age and still end below the limit. The ones that cannot are the ones Chandrasekhar’s limit was really about.

The story behind this

The limit worked out at seaA nineteen-year-old on a ship out of Bombay worked out that a dead star heavier than about 1.4 Suns cannot hold itself up; the astronomer who had made Einstein famous called the idea absurd, and the Nobel committee sided with the teenager forty-eight years later.

Careful

“The electrons hold the star up because they are all negative and repel each other.”

Electrons do repel each other, but that is not what holds a white dwarf up. The pressure comes from the Pauli rule, that no two electrons can be in the same place doing the same thing, and it is a different effect, far stronger than electric repulsion. Squeeze a white dwarf and it is the rule, not the charge, that pushes back.

Check yourself

Will the Sun become a white dwarf?

Answer at the back of the book

15.7The stretching universe

Redshift

A stretching of light waves, so that every line in a spectrum appears at a longer wavelength than in the laboratory. It shows a source moving away, or, for distant galaxies, space stretching while the light travels.

In Chapter 9 the horn of a local dropped in pitch as the train passed you: the sound waves from a source moving away are stretched, so their frequency falls. Light does the same. The lines in the spectrum of a star moving away from us sit at slightly longer wavelengths than they would in a laboratory, shifted towards the red; a star coming towards us shows them shifted towards the blue. The first is called a redshift, and it is the hinge on which the biggest discovery in this book turns.

Hubble’s law

A galaxy’s speed away from us is proportional to its distance: v = H × d, with H about 22 km/s for each million light-years.

From 1912 Vesto Slipher measured the light of the spiral “nebulae”, the faint smudges that Leavitt’s tape would soon show to be other galaxies, and found nearly all of them redshifted: racing away, some at 1,800 km/s. Then Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason, in 1929 and 1931, put Slipher’s speeds next to Cepheid distances and found a plain rule, now Hubble’s law: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, in proportion. The current value is about 22 km/s for every million light-years of distance, so a galaxy 100 million light-years away recedes at about 2,200 km/s.

Predict first

Every galaxy we measure, in every direction, is moving away from us, and the farther ones faster. Does that put us at the centre of the universe?

  1. Yes: everything is moving away from here
  2. No: an observer in any galaxy would see exactly the same thing
  3. Only the nearby galaxies are really moving

What happens

No. Draw ants on a ruler at the 2, 4, 7 and 12 cm marks, and stretch the ruler so that it doubles in length in one minute. The ant at 2 cm sees the others move away at 2, 5 and 10 cm per minute: speed in proportion to distance, exactly Hubble’s law. Now sit on the ant at 7 cm instead: it sees the others recede at 5, 3 and 5 cm per minute, the same law again. Every ant sees itself at the centre, and none of them is. None of the ants moved of its own accord. The ruler stretched.

A loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven does the same in three dimensions: every raisin sees every other raisin move away, faster if farther. Notice what does not happen: the raisins do not grow. Neither do galaxies. Gravity holds each galaxy together, and only the space between them stretches. That is the better way to picture the redshift too. The light from a distant galaxy has been travelling for hundreds of millions of years through space that was stretching; the waves were stretched with it, and arrive longer than they left. The galaxies are passengers. The stretching of space is the thing.

Big Bang

The name for the beginning of the universe’s stretching, about 13.8 billion years ago, when everything we can see was far closer together. It happened everywhere; there is no place in space where it was.

That is what the Big Bang means, and it is not an explosion. An explosion happens at a place and throws things out into the empty space around it. There is no place where the universe began and no empty space it is expanding into: the stretching happens everywhere at once, and every observer, in every galaxy, sees it spreading away from them. Run it backwards and everything we can see was once far closer together, hotter and denser, everywhere. Run Hubble’s rule backwards and the simple sum gives about 13.6 billion years; the careful figure, allowing for how the stretching has changed its pace, is 13.8 billion years.

A balloon universe

Draw a dozen dots on an uninflated balloon with a marker, and draw one short wavy line, a wave, between two of them. Inflate the balloon slowly. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and the dots farthest apart separate fastest; no dot is the centre, and the dots themselves do not grow. Watch the wave: it stretches as the balloon grows, which is what happens to light crossing a stretching universe. Remember the balloon’s limits: it has an inside and an outside, and the universe has neither.

The story behind this

The stretching universeEvery distant galaxy’s light is stretched towards the red, and the farther the galaxy the more it is stretched; the right picture is not galaxies flying apart through space but space itself growing between them.

Careful

“The Big Bang was an explosion at a point in space, and the galaxies are flying away from it.”

Nothing is flying out from a point into empty space. Space itself is stretching, everywhere, and the galaxies are carried apart with it, like the ants on the ruler. Every galaxy sees all the others receding, so none is at the centre, and there is no spot you could visit where it began. The rulers, balloons and loaves all have an edge and a middle; the universe has neither.

At school

IGCSE 6.2.3 describes redshift as an increase in the observed wavelength of light from “receding” galaxies, evidence that the universe is expanding and “supports the Big Bang Theory”. A careful way to picture “receding” is space stretching between the galaxies. The syllabus also says all the matter in the universe was once “present at a single point”; read that as “far closer together, everywhere”, because there is no point in today’s space where it happened. It writes Hubble’s law as H₀ = v/d; our 22 km/s per million light-years is about 72 km/s per megaparsec. “Theory” there means a well-tested explanation, never a guess.

Investigation 15.7

Redo the ruler sum for the ant at 12 cm: how fast does it see each of the others recede? Then explain to someone why it would be wrong for that ant to conclude it was at the edge of everything.

Check yourself

As the raisin bread rises, do the raisins grow? Do galaxies grow as the universe stretches?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 15

The star that’s mostly hydrogen

An astronomer in 1920 lays three spectra on the desk. Star A is hot and blue, and shows almost no hydrogen lines. Star B is a little hotter than the Sun, and its hydrogen lines are the strongest thing in its spectrum. Star C is cool and red, and its hydrogen lines are faint again. Many of the dark lines in all three match metals known on Earth.

The astronomer concludes that Star B is made largely of hydrogen, Stars A and C of something else, and that the Sun, like the Earth’s crust, is mostly the familiar heavy stuff.

Use Saha’s idea and Payne’s result to say what all three stars are really made of, and where the reasoning went wrong.

Show the solution

All three are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun: about 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with about 2% left for everything else. Star A’s hydrogen is so hot that it has lost its electrons, so it cannot make the lines. Star C is so cool that its electrons sit in the lowest level, and the visible hydrogen lines need an electron one step up. Star B is at the temperature where hydrogen shows best. The astronomer read line strength as amount, when it depends on temperature as much as on quantity. That is the mistake Saha’s equation corrects and Payne’s thesis exposed: the stars are mostly hydrogen, and the Earth is the odd one out.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

This is where the book stops, and it stops where physics does: in front of questions nobody can answer yet. What is light, between the wave that makes Young’s fringes and the packet that frees an electron? The equations do both; a picture that does both is missing. What makes the monsoon come, the giant sea breeze or the shifting rain belt? Chapter 8’s argument is still going on, and you are living inside the evidence. Does hot water really freeze first? Nobody agrees. And the stretching universe: the model says that everything was once far closer together, and says nothing about what, if anything, came before, or whether “before” is even a question.

Every answer in this book was once a question like these, held by someone who did not know the answer and refused to pretend: Aryabhata in his boat, Bose at his desk in Dacca, Payne over her plates with “spurious” written across her best result, a nineteen-year-old at the rail of the Pilsna. They looked, they guessed, they predicted before they checked, they kept what they saw apart from what they thought, they did the sum, and they said plainly what they did not know. You have done all of that in this book, in a kitchen in Mumbai, with a torch, an orange, a marble and a balloon.

Further adventures lists where to go next: MIT’s lectures and OpenStax’s Astronomy for when you are older, the planetarium at Worli, the phone in your pocket, and your own notebook, which is the oldest instrument of all. The world is still moving. Go and look.

A

Aryabhata

The boy who put the sky in a boat

476 CE to c. 550 CEExplained that the stars seem to move because the Earth turns, and that eclipses are shadows

Kusumapura, Patna, 499 CE

In 499 CE, in Kusumapura near modern Patna, a twenty-three-year-old astronomer and mathematician named Aryabhata finished a short work in Sanskrit verse called the Aryabhatiya. We know his age because he wrote it into a verse of the book: twenty-three years had passed since his birth when that age of the world reached 3,600 years, which places his birth in 476 CE. Some historians date the final text nearer 510 CE, and its arguments survived across India in commentary after commentary.

The river shore that slides backwards

Anyone who watches the night sky for an hour sees the stars drift steadily from east to west. To almost every astronomer of the ancient world, the explanation seemed obvious: the Earth sits still in the middle, and the dome of the sky spins around it once a day.

Aryabhata offered a different picture, and he explained it with a boat. When a person in a boat moves forward down a river, he wrote, the stationary trees and stones on the bank appear to move backwards in the opposite direction. In the same way, the stationary stars appear to drift westwards from Lanka, at the equator, because the Earth itself turns towards the east.

The boat analogy separates what your eyes see from what is actually moving. Watching the stars rise and set cannot by itself tell you whether the sky turns around a still Earth or the Earth turns inside a still sky. Both models give the same view from the ground. You do not feel the Earth’s spin for the same reason you do not feel a steady glide in a boat or a local train cruising at constant speed: as you saw in Chapter 2, your body detects changes in velocity, not steady motion itself.

Shadows in place of Rahu

Aryabhata applied the same geometry to eclipses. Popular tradition blamed eclipses on Rahu, a demon head that swallowed the Sun or the Moon. Aryabhata wrote that the Moon shines by sunlight and that eclipses are shadows. When the Earth stands between the Sun and the Moon, the Earth casts a long cone of shadow into space, and the Moon grows dark as it passes through it. When the Moon passes directly between the Sun and the Earth, the Moon covers the Sun and casts its own shadow onto the ground. From the widths and angles of those shadow cones, astronomers could calculate in advance when an eclipse would start and how long it would last.

What he claimed, and what he did not

Because Aryabhata was right about the turning Earth and the geometry of eclipses, modern websites often credit him with claims he never made. He did not propose a heliocentric solar system with the Earth orbiting the Sun; his planetary model was still geocentric, using epicycles, smaller circles riding on larger circles, to track the planets. Even later Indian astronomers, including Brahmagupta, rejected his rotating Earth, asking why tall buildings and birds in flight were not left behind. Direct mechanical proof that the ground turns beneath us waited until Léon Foucault’s pendulum in Paris in 1851. Nor is there any historical basis for the “99.4 per cent accuracy” figures repeated online. What Aryabhata actually did at twenty-three needs no exaggeration: he looked at the turning sky and saw a moving boat.

In Chapter 14 you will use Aryabhata’s turning Earth and shadow cones to see how day and night and eclipses work.

HB

Homi Bhabha

The Bargain at Cambridge

1909 to 1966Cosmic-ray physicist who founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Bombay

Bombay, 19 December 1945

In the drawing rooms of Kenilworth, a rented bungalow on Peddar Road in Bombay where Homi Jehangir Bhabha had been born thirty-six years earlier, the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) opened its doors. Glassblowers, cosmic-ray experimentalists, and young mathematicians shared the veranda and the converted garages. Within twenty years that household laboratory would grow into a seaside campus at Colaba and launch India’s programmes in particle physics, radio astronomy, and computing.

A Letter to His Father

Born in Bombay on 30 October 1909, Bhabha grew up painting in oils, listening to classical music, and reading physics books in his grandfather’s library. In 1927 he sailed to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, because his father and his uncle Dorabji Tata wanted him to take an engineering degree and return to manage the Tata steel mills at Jamshedpur.

After a year in Cambridge, Bhabha wrote home to his father on 8 August 1928: “I seriously say to you that business or a job as an engineer is not the thing for me. It is totally foreign to my nature and radically opposed to my temperament and opinions. Physics is my line. I know I shall do great things here… I am burning with a desire to do physics.” His father made a counter-offer: if Homi earned a First Class in the Mechanical Sciences Tripos, the family would support two further years at Cambridge for theoretical physics. Bhabha took his First in June 1930 and joined the Cavendish Laboratory.

Cosmic Showers and Bhabha Scattering

Working in Cambridge, Zurich, Rome, and Copenhagen during the 1930s, Bhabha calculated in 1935 the quantum cross-section for an electron scattering off its antimatter twin, the positron (e⁻ + e⁺ → e⁻ + e⁺). Particle collider teams still use Bhabha scattering as the standard ruler to calibrate their beam luminosity.

With Walter Heitler in 1937, Bhabha explained how a single primary cosmic ray striking the upper atmosphere cascades into a shower of electrons, positrons, and gamma rays. In 1938 he showed in Nature that unstable cosmic-ray muons survive the trip to sea level only because Albert Einstein’s relativistic time dilation slows their internal clocks near the speed of light.

Building the School Before the Machines

Home on holiday in 1939 when the Second World War broke out, Bhabha stayed in India to work alongside C. V. Raman at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore, flying high-altitude cosmic-ray balloon payloads near the geomagnetic equator.

On 12 March 1944 Bhabha wrote to the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust proposing an institute that would train India’s own physicists and mathematicians before big machines were built. Backed by J. R. D. Tata, TIFR started at Bangalore in June 1945, was inaugurated at Kenilworth in Bombay on 19 December 1945, and later moved to Colaba. Bhabha died on 24 January 1966 when Air India Flight 101 crashed on Mont Blanc.

We meet Bhabha’s work on relativistic particles and nuclear physics in Chapters 14 and 15.

BI

Bhaskara II

A hundredth part of the circumference

c. 1114 to 1185Head of the Ujjain observatory and author of the Siddhanta Shiromani on the sphere of the Earth and sky

Ujjain, about 1150

Around 1150, at the age of thirty-six, the mathematician and astronomer Bhaskara II (often called Bhaskaracharya, “Bhaskara the teacher”) finished his four-part work, the Siddhanta Shiromani, or Crown of Treatises. Born around 1114 in Vijjadavida in the Deccan region of India, he headed the astronomical observatory at Ujjain, the city that served for centuries as the prime meridian of classical Indian astronomy.

Four books in verse

The Siddhanta Shiromani was written in Sanskrit verse so that students could memorise the rules, accompanied by Bhaskara’s own prose explanations and worked examples. Its first two parts, the Lilavati (on arithmetic and geometry) and the Bijaganita (on algebra), became the standard mathematics textbooks across India for centuries. The Lilavati poses its problems as riddles about swarms of bees, flocks of swans, and lotus flowers blown sideways in a pond, turning geometry and quadratic equations into stories.

The third and fourth parts, the Grahaganita and the Goladhyaya, turn to the motions of the planets and the sphere of the sky and Earth.

Why a round Earth looks flat

In the Goladhyaya (Chapter on the Sphere), Bhaskara tackled a question every student asks when first told that the Earth is a ball: when we walk outside and look across a field, the ground looks flat. How can we be standing on a sphere?

Bhaskara answered with scale and geometry. Draw a huge circle, he wrote, and look at just a hundredth part of its circumference. That short arc curves so gently that to the eye it looks like a straight line. A person standing on the Earth sees only a tiny fraction of its circumference at once, far less than a hundredth part of the globe, and so the ground appears flat to us even though the whole Earth is a sphere.

He also addressed the puzzle that Brahmagupta had discussed five centuries earlier: if the Earth is a sphere hanging in space without a pillar underneath it, why does it not fall, and why do people and oceans on the opposite side not drop off into the sky? Bhaskara argued that if the Earth fell simply by being heavy, an arrow shot into the sky and the Earth itself would fall together, and one would have to ask which way “down” even points in open space. Instead, the Earth holds things to its surface by its own attractive power, so that people standing on opposite sides of the globe each feel “down” as towards the Earth’s centre beneath their own feet, and nobody is upside down.

Instruments and honest history

In the final chapters of the Goladhyaya, Bhaskara described the instruments (yantras) of an astronomer’s observatory: armillary spheres of rings to model the sky, vertical rods (shanku) to cast noon shadows for latitude and time, water clocks, and a sighting board called the phalaka-yantra that he designed to measure the Sun’s altitude.

One caution is needed when reading about Bhaskara online. Non-scholarly websites often quote a verse on attraction and claim that Bhaskara discovered the law of gravity. As with Brahmagupta, that confuses a qualitative statement with a mathematical law. Bhaskara wrote in the Siddhanta tradition that the Earth draws heavy things in the air down to its surface, but he gave no inverse-square formula and no link between falling bodies and planetary orbits, which he still modelled with epicycles. What he gave his readers was a clear, geometric explanation of life on a giant sphere.

In Chapter 5 and Chapter 14 you will meet the geometry of the round Earth and the sky that Bhaskara taught at Ujjain.

B

Brahmagupta

Zero, negative numbers, and the nature of heavy things

598 CE to 668 CEMathematician and astronomer at Ujjain who wrote of the Earth's nature to attract heavy bodies

Ujjain, 628 CE

In 628 CE, at the age of thirty, the mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta completed his treatise Brahmasphutasiddhanta, the Correctly Established Doctrine of Brahma. Born in 598 CE, likely at Bhillamala in Rajasthan, he worked in the astronomical tradition of Ujjain in central India, the city through which Indian astronomers drew their prime meridian of longitude.

Fortunes, debts, and zero

Today Brahmagupta is remembered first for mathematics. Before him, zero was used mostly as an empty placeholder in positional numbers, so that you could tell 205 apart from 25. In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, Brahmagupta treated zero as a number in its own right and wrote down explicit rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers, which he called “debts” (rina), alongside positive numbers, which he called “fortunes” (dhana).

His rules read like modern algebra in everyday words. The sum of two fortunes is a fortune, and the sum of two debts is a debt. The sum of a fortune and an equal debt is zero. Subtracting a debt is the same as adding a fortune, and the product of two debts is a fortune. Only at division by zero did his rules falter, a trap that took centuries more to untangle. Every time you use a negative sign in Chapter 1 to tell a westward velocity from an eastward one, or a downward acceleration from an upward one, you are using Brahmagupta’s bookkeeping.

The Earth’s nature to attract

Brahmagupta also asked why things fall, and why people and oceans stay on a round Earth instead of dropping off. Around 1030 CE, four centuries after the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, the scholar Al-Biruni travelled through India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote a survey of Indian science. In it, Al-Biruni reported Brahmagupta’s statement on falling bodies: heavy things fall to the Earth by a law of nature, for it is the nature of the Earth to attract and to keep things, as it is the nature of water to flow.

To someone standing on a spherical Earth, “down” means towards the Earth’s centre. People on the opposite side have their feet pointed towards the same centre. Brahmagupta was arguing that objects do not fall toward some universal bottom of space; they are drawn toward the Earth itself from every side around the globe.

The gap between a word and a law

Because of Al-Biruni’s report, some accounts claim that Brahmagupta discovered the law of gravity a thousand years before Isaac Newton. That confuses two very different steps in science.

Saying that the Earth’s nature is to attract heavy things is a qualitative idea, a sentence in words. It has no mathematics for how the pull changes with distance, and no link to planetary orbits. In fact, Brahmagupta rejected Aryabhata’s rotating Earth, arguing that if the Earth spun, stones and birds would not come straight back down to the spot below them.

A thousand years later, Newton did not merely say that the Earth attracts the apple. He showed that if the pull weakens with the square of the distance from the Earth’s centre, then at the Moon’s distance of 60 Earth radii the pull is weaker by 60² = 3,600, predicting an acceleration of 0.00272 m/s² that matches the Moon’s orbit. Brahmagupta stated a true physical intuition about the round Earth, and that idea waited ten centuries for a mathematical law.

In Chapter 5 you will see how Newton turned the qualitative idea of attraction into the inverse-square law that links falling stones to the orbits of moons and planets.

SC

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar

The Calculation on the Ship

1910 to 1995Worked out at age nineteen on a ship from Bombay that white dwarf stars have a maximum mass

Bombay, July 1930

On 31 July 1930, nineteen-year-old Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar boarded the steamship SS Pilsna at Ballard Pier in Bombay, bound for Venice and a graduate scholarship at Cambridge. In his trunk he carried Ralph Fowler’s 1926 paper explaining how burnt-out stars called white dwarfs support themselves against gravity. During the voyage across the Arabian Sea, working in pencil on deck, Chandrasekhar added one piece of physics Fowler had left out: Albert Einstein’s speed limit for fast-moving electrons. His notepad calculation showed that no white dwarf heavier than about 1.4 solar masses could hold itself up.

From Madras to the Pilsna

Born in Lahore on 19 October 1910 (his uncle was C. V. Raman), Chandrasekhar grew up in Madras and studied at Presidency College, where he published his first paper in the Proceedings of the Royal Society at eighteen and won a scholarship to Trinity College, Cambridge.

Fowler had explained how white dwarfs like Sirius B pack the mass of the Sun into a sphere the size of the Earth, a million times denser than water. Wolfgang Pauli’s exclusion principle forbids two electrons from sharing the same quantum state; squeezed together, the electrons are forced into high momentum states, creating a quantum electron degeneracy pressure that resists gravity even at zero temperature.

Adding Special Relativity

On the Pilsna, Chandrasekhar worked out how hard the core of a white dwarf is squeezed as you add mass. In a white dwarf as heavy as the Sun, the fastest electrons move at speeds approaching the speed of light c.

In non-relativistic mechanics, kinetic energy grows with momentum squared (E = p² / 2m), stiffening the gas enough to halt gravity at any mass. In special relativity, however, no electron can outrun c, so energy grows only in proportion to momentum (E ≈ pc). That softens the pressure law (P ∝ ρ⁴/³ instead of ρ⁵/³), matching the scaling of gravity itself. Above the Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.44 solar masses), electron degeneracy pressure fails and the star must collapse further.

The Ambush in Burlington House

London, 11 January 1935

After four years refining the exact equation of state at Cambridge, twenty-four-year-old Chandrasekhar presented his full curve of white-dwarf masses and radii to the Royal Astronomical Society in London.

Speaking immediately after him, Arthur Eddington attacked the relativistic formula as “stellar buffoonery”. “I think there should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way,” Eddington declared, objecting to the unchecked collapse that would leave behind what physicists later called a black hole.

Although Bohr, Pauli, and Dirac privately agreed that Chandrasekhar’s mathematics was right, none challenged Eddington in public before astronomers. Chandrasekhar wrote up his stellar theory in a 1939 book, moved to the University of Chicago, and spent the next five decades writing the definitive treatises on radiative transfer, hydrodynamic stability, and black holes, receiving the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics fifty-three years after his voyage from Bombay.

We trace the life cycle of stars, white dwarfs, and the Chandrasekhar limit in Chapter 15.

KC

Kalpana Chawla

From Karnal to Orbit

1962 to 2003Aeronautical engineer from Karnal who flew twice in orbit aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia

Karnal, 1976

On summer evenings in the town of Karnal in Haryana, the Chawla family slept on string charpoys on the flat roof of their house, looking up at the Milky Way and the occasional bright point of an artificial satellite gliding from horizon to horizon. By day, whenever her brother drove her past the Karnal Aviation Club, fourteen-year-old Kalpana Chawla pressed against the fence to watch single-engine Pushpak trainer aeroplanes lift off from the grass strip, and pestered her father until he took her up for a flight in a cockpit.

The Only Girl in the Wind-Tunnel Lab

Born in Karnal on 17 March 1962, the youngest of four children of Banarsi Lal Chawla and Sanyogita Chawla, who had crossed from Pakistan during the 1947 Partition, she chose her own name, Kalpana (“imagination”), on her first day at Tagore Baal Niketan school. Her bedroom walls were covered with drawings of biplanes and jets.

When she decided in 1978 to study aeronautical engineering at Punjab Engineering College in Chandigarh, professors tried to steer her toward electrical engineering or medicine. Out of a hundred students admitted that year, only seven were women, and Kalpana was the first and only woman in the Aeronautical Engineering department. She organised fluid-mechanics study clubs and graduated at the top of her department in 1982.

Simulating Airflows and Ground Effect

Moving to the United States in 1982, Chawla earned a master’s degree in aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Arlington and a PhD in 1988 at the University of Colorado Boulder. At NASA Ames Research Center in California, she specialised in computational fluid dynamics (CFD), programming supercomputers to solve the equations of airflow around vertical and short take-off aircraft such as the Harrier jump-jet. When a hovering jet blasts exhaust downward against a runway, the rebounding air curls into low-pressure vortices beneath the wings so that the higher-pressure air above pushes the aircraft down; Chawla wrote numerical simulations to map those three-dimensional flows while earning pilot licences for aeroplanes and gliders.

Weightless Aboard Columbia

In orbit, November 1997

Selected as a NASA astronaut in December 1994, Chawla lifted off from Florida on 19 November 1997 aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia on mission STS-87, becoming the first Indian-born woman in space.

Orbiting 280 kilometres above the Earth at 7.7 kilometres per second, the shuttle circled the globe every ninety minutes. Inside, the crew floated weightless not because gravity had disappeared (Earth’s pull at 280 km is still 92 per cent as strong as on the ground in Karnal), but because both shuttle and crew were in continuous free fall around the curve of the Earth.

In January 2003 she returned to orbit on STS-107, running more than eighty microgravity experiments in fluid physics, combustion, and crystal growth. On 1 February 2003, sixteen minutes before landing, Columbia broke apart during atmospheric re-entry after superheated air entered a wing leading edge damaged at launch. Chawla died with her six crewmates, and India renamed its meteorological satellite series Kalpana-1 in her memory.

We study drag and terminal speed in Chapter 4, circular orbits and free fall in Chapter 5, fluid pressure in Chapter 6, and kinetic energy and heating in Chapters 7 and 8.

BC

Bibha Chowdhuri

Star Tracks on Sandakphu

1913 to 1991Captured tracks of cosmic-ray mesons on photographic plates high in the Himalaya at Darjeeling and Sandakphu

Darjeeling, 1940

High on the Singalila ridge along the Bengal-Nepal border, at Darjeeling (2,130 m) and Sandakphu (3,660 m), Bibha Chowdhuri packed light-tight wooden boxes holding glass plates coated with photographic emulsion. Some batches sat in the thin mountain air under the open sky; others lay beneath twenty centimetres of water or paraffin wax to slow incoming cosmic rays. Carried back to the Bose Institute in Calcutta, developed, and examined millimetre by millimetre through a binocular microscope, the emulsions revealed tiny strings of blackened silver grains: the curving footprints of unstable subatomic particles from space called mesotrons (now known as muons and pions).

The Only Woman in the MSc Class

Born in Calcutta in 1913 into a Brahmo Samaj family where her father was a physician and her aunt had founded a girls’ school, Bibha Chowdhuri studied physics at the Rajabazar Science College of the University of Calcutta, graduating in 1936 as the only woman in her MSc physics class.

She persuaded Debendra Mohan Bose, who had succeeded his uncle Jagadish Chandra Bose as director of the Bose Institute, to let her join his cosmic-ray group and took charge of exposing and reading the mountain plates.

Measuring Particle Mass with a Microscope

In 1935 Hideki Yukawa had predicted that atomic nuclei are held together by a middleweight particle about two hundred times heavier than an electron. Before giant post-war accelerators existed, the only source of such particles was the cosmic rays striking Earth’s upper atmosphere.

While cloud chambers captured only brief snapshots, photographic emulsions acted as continuous traps. Between 1939 and 1942, Bose and Chowdhuri published four papers in Nature turning microscopic tracks into quantitative detectors. As a charged particle ploughs through gelatin emulsion, it ionises silver bromide crystals and leaves a trail of silver grains. Slower, heavier particles scatter more often and leave closer-spaced grains than fast, light ones. By calibrating their Ilford half-tone plates against known proton tracks and comparing exposures at Darjeeling and Sandakphu, Chowdhuri and Bose measured the grain spacing and scattering angles along curved tracks and calculated a mesotron mass of roughly 160 to 220 electron masses.

Wartime Limits, Manchester, and TIFR

In their 1941 and 1942 Nature papers, Chowdhuri and Bose noted that wartime supply restrictions prevented them from obtaining fuller-tone emulsions with denser silver grains. After the war, Cecil Powell in Bristol used those improved Ilford nuclear emulsions with the same grain-counting method to distinguish the pion from the muon and won the 1950 Nobel Prize, crediting Bose and Chowdhuri’s 1941 method in his 1959 book.

Chowdhuri completed her PhD on cosmic-ray air showers in Patrick Blackett’s laboratory at Manchester, and in 1949 Homi Bhabha recruited her as the first woman scientist at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Bombay. She later studied deep underground muon bundles in the Kolar gold mines. In 2019 the International Astronomical Union named the star HD 86081 Bibha (“beam of light”) in her honour.

We trace cosmic rays, magnetic deflection, and subatomic particles in Chapters 13 and 15.

ÉC

Émilie du Châtelet

Four times the dent in the clay

1706 to 1749Championed mv² alongside momentum in the Institutions de physique and translated Newton's Principia into French

Cirey, France, 1740

In the 1730s, a woman in France could not enrol at the University of Paris, attend meetings of the Royal Academy of Sciences, or enter the Paris cafés where mathematicians gathered to argue about physics (when Gabrielle Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil, Marquise du Châtelet, was turned away at the Café Gradot, she had a man’s suit tailored and walked back in). To do serious research, she and her partner, the writer Voltaire, renovated her family’s château at Cirey-sur-Blaise in north-eastern France, equipping it with twenty thousand books and a laboratory.

The argument over moving force: mv or mv²?

In 1740 du Châtelet published Institutions de physique (Foundations of Physics), begun as a textbook for her teenage son after she found that no French book explained the newest physics clearly.

In the final chapter of the Institutions, she entered a fierce dispute in European mechanics. Everyone agreed that a heavier or faster object is harder to stop, and that a moving object carries some “force of motion.” Followers of René Descartes and Isaac Newton said the true measure of motion is mass times velocity, mv (what we now call momentum). Double a ball’s speed, and its mv doubles. Followers of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz argued instead for vis viva (“living force”), which goes with mass times velocity squared, mv² (twice what we now call kinetic energy, ½mv²). Double a ball’s speed, and its mv² grows by 2² = 4.

Brass balls in soft clay

How do you test mv against mv² by experiment? Du Châtelet pointed to the experiments carried out in Leiden in 1722 by the Dutch physicist Willem ‘s Gravesande. He had dropped solid brass balls from different heights onto soft potter’s clay and measured the dents they left behind.

Suppose you want a ball to hit the clay at twice the speed. Because a falling ball’s speed grows with the square root of the drop height (v = √(2gh)), dropping a ball from four times the height makes it hit the clay at twice the speed. If the effort needed to stop the ball went with mv, the twice-as-fast ball would sink twice as deep into the clay. Instead, ‘s Gravesande found that a ball hitting at twice the speed made a dent four times as deep; a ball hitting at three times the speed (from nine times the height) made a dent nine times as deep.

Du Châtelet did not claim to have invented the clay experiment or to have “proved” the law alone, but she built ‘s Gravesande’s measurements into a clear, public argument for mv². Today we know that both sides had hold of a real physical quantity: momentum (mv) measures how a force acts over time, whereas kinetic energy (½mv²) measures how a force acts over distance, such as the depth of a dent in clay.

Translating the Principia against the clock

From 1745 onwards, du Châtelet translated Newton’s Latin Principia into French, adding an algebraic commentary that recast Newton’s geometry in modern calculus. Discovering in 1748 that she was pregnant at forty-two, an age then perilous for childbirth, she worked late into the night to finish the manuscript, posted the parcel to the royal library days before giving birth, and died six days later in September 1749. Her two-volume translation remains the standard French edition of Newton’s Principia.

In Chapter 3 you will meet momentum (mv), and in Chapter 7 you will drop marbles to see why kinetic energy goes with mv².

MF

Michael Faraday

The bookbinder's apprentice and the invisible lines

1791 to 1867From bookbinder's apprentice to the discoverer of the electric motor, electromagnetic induction, and the field picture

The Royal Institution, London, 1831

Michael Faraday was born in 1791 in Newington Butts, south London, the son of a blacksmith who had moved to the city looking for work. The family was poor, and Michael’s schooling ended at thirteen with little more than reading, writing, and basic arithmetic.

Seven years in a bookshop

At fourteen he became an apprentice to a French bookbinder and bookseller named George Riebau on Blandford Street. For seven years Faraday stitched leather covers onto other people’s books, and after hours he read what he was binding: the electricity article in the Encyclopædia Britannica and Jane Marcet’s Conversations on Chemistry. With pocket pence he bought glass vials and zinc discs to repeat the experiments at the back of the shop.

In 1812 a customer gave the twenty-year-old apprentice tickets to hear the chemist Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution. Faraday wrote out three hundred pages of neat notes with hand-drawn diagrams, bound them in leather, and sent the book to Davy, asking for any job in science. When a laboratory assistant was dismissed in 1813, Davy hired Faraday in his place.

The spinning wire and the iron ring

In April 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted in Copenhagen found that an electric current in a wire makes a nearby compass needle twitch: electricity produces magnetism.

On 3 and 4 September 1821, in his basement laboratory at the Royal Institution, Faraday set a vertical magnet in a dish of conducting mercury (never touch mercury yourself) and hung a free wire above it. When current flowed through the wire, the wire circled continuously around the magnet. By turning an electric current and a magnet into continuous rotation, Faraday had built the world’s first electric motor.

Then he asked the reverse question: if electricity makes magnetism, can magnetism make electricity? For ten years he tried placing magnets beside coils of wire and saw nothing.
