The answer came on 29 August 1831. Faraday wound two separate coils of insulated copper wire around opposite sides of a heavy iron ring. When he connected the first coil to a battery, a compass needle attached to the second coil jumped for an instant and settled back to zero. When he disconnected the battery, the needle jumped the opposite way. A steady magnet makes no current; only a changing magnetic field induces a current in a wire. Within weeks he showed that pushing a bar magnet in and out of a hollow coil, or spinning a copper disc between the poles of a magnet, generates a continuous current. Every power-station generator and street transformer in Mumbai descends from those experiments.

Lines of force and the Christmas Lectures

In 1836 Faraday built a twelve-foot wooden cube covered in metal foil, stepped inside with sensitive charge detectors while sparks struck the outside, and found not the least electrical influence inside: the Faraday cage.

Because he had no university algebra, Faraday pictured the space around magnets and charges as filled with curved lines of force, like the patterns iron filings trace on a card over a magnet. James Clerk Maxwell later turned Faraday’s lines into the equations of electromagnetism, praising Faraday’s physical reasoning as a mathematical method of the highest order.

Remembering his own youth, Faraday founded the Royal Institution’s Friday Evening Discourses and, in 1825, its Christmas Lectures for children. In Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 you will trace his circuits, his motor, his iron ring, and his field lines.

GG

Galileo Galilei

The man who slowed down falling

1564 to 1642Slowed falling motion down on ramps, turned a spyglass on Jupiter's moons, and argued from measurement

Padua, 1604

Drop a stone from head height and it hits the floor in less than half a second. In 1604, when Galileo Galilei taught mathematics at Padua in northern Italy, no clock could measure half a second. To discover the mathematical rule of falling bodies, Galileo had to slow falling down without changing its nature.

Strings, balances, and the habit of testing

Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564. His father, Vincenzo Galilei, was a lutenist and music theorist who tested ancient claims by experiment. An old legend said that Pythagoras had discovered musical intervals from the weights of blacksmiths’ hammers and that doubling the weight pulling a string raises its pitch by an octave. Around 1589 in Florence, Vincenzo hung weights on lute strings and showed that an octave requires four times the weight, not twice.

Young Galileo shared that habit. In 1586, aged twenty-two, he wrote La Bilancetta (The Little Balance), pointing out that Vitruvius’s tale of Archimedes checking King Hiero’s crown by bathtub overflow would need impossible precision, and designing a hydrostatic balance to weigh metals in water instead (Chapter 6).

As for the Leaning Tower of Pisa, that tale comes only from Galileo’s late-life secretary Vincenzo Viviani; Galileo never describes dropping balls from the tower himself. Instead, he gave a sharp thought experiment: tie a heavy stone and a light stone together. If the light stone really fell slower, it would drag back on the heavy stone and make the pair fall slower than the heavy stone alone; yet the tied pair is heavier than either one, so by the same rule it should fall faster.

Ramps and the odd-number rule

At Padua, Galileo replaced vertical dropping with a smooth wooden groove tilted at a gentle angle. A bronze ball rolling down a slight incline is pulled by gravity just like a falling ball, only much more slowly.

In a reconstruction by historian Stillman Drake, the story goes that Galileo tied movable gut frets across the ramp like lute frets and sang a steady beat, sliding the frets until the ball clicked over one fret on each beat. Whether he timed the rolls by beats or by weighing water pouring from a thin pipe into a cup, his measurements revealed a clear rule. In the first beat of time, the ball rolled 1 unit of distance; in the second beat, 3 units; in the third, 5; in the fourth, 7. Add those odd numbers up (1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16) and the total distance from the start grows as the square of the time (d ∝ t²). That meant the ball’s speed grew by the same amount in every equal beat: constant acceleration.

Four moons around Jupiter

Venice, August 1609

In May 1609 Galileo heard of the new Dutch spyglass. Grinding his own lenses, he showed an eight-to-nine-power telescope to the Venetian Senate from the bell tower of San Marco on 25 August 1609. Turning a stronger telescope on the sky on 7 January 1610, he saw three tiny “stars” beside Jupiter; a fourth soon appeared, and by 15 January he realised they were four moons orbiting Jupiter (Sidereus Nuncius, March 1610). Critics had argued that a moving Earth would lose its Moon, yet here was Jupiter moving across the sky with four moons in tow.

In his final book, Two New Sciences (1638), written under house arrest near Florence, Galileo brought together his work on motion, ramps, and projectiles. You will meet his work across Chapters 1, 2, 4, 9, and 10.

EH

Edmond Halley

The man who bet on a comet he would never see

1656 to 1742Coaxed and paid for the Principia, predicted the return of a comet he would not live to see, and published the first physical map of the monsoon

London, 1684

In August 1684, the twenty-seven-year-old astronomer Edmond Halley travelled from London to Cambridge to ask Isaac Newton a question that had stumped Robert Hooke and Christopher Wren: if the Sun pulls on a planet with a force that weakens with the square of the distance, what shape of path will the planet follow?

A fish book and a masterpiece

Born in London in 1656, Halley had never been content to stay indoors. At twenty, before finishing his degree at Oxford, he sailed to St Helena in the South Atlantic and spent a year charting 341 southern stars that European astronomers could not see from home.

When Halley asked his orbit question in Cambridge in 1684, Newton answered at once: an ellipse. Asked how he knew, Newton replied that he had calculated it years earlier, rummaged through his papers, and could not find the proof. He promised to write it out afresh and send it to London.

What arrived a few months later led Halley to coax a full three-volume book out of the secretive professor. Yet the Royal Society had no money left to print it. The Society had just spent its funds printing an expensive illustrated volume called De Historia Piscium (The History of Fishes) by Francis Willughby, which sold so poorly that the Society paid Halley’s clerk salary partly in unsold copies of the fish book. So Halley paid to print Newton’s Principia (1687) out of his own pocket, edited the text, calmed Newton down when Hooke quarrelled with him, and saw the book through the press.

The comet of 1531, 1607, and 1682

Once Newton’s laws were in print, Halley applied them to comets, which people had assumed were one-off visitors travelling on straight lines or open curves. Computing the orbits of twenty-four comets, Halley noticed that three bright comets, seen in 1531, 1607, and 1682, shared almost identical paths around the Sun at intervals of 75 to 76 years.

They were not three comets, he concluded, but one comet on a long elliptical orbit, due back around late 1758. Halley died in 1742, aged eighty-five. As 1758 approached, three French mathematicians, Alexis Clairaut, Joseph-Jérôme Lalande, and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, spent months calculating how the gravitational pulls of Jupiter and Saturn would delay the comet, predicting perihelion around mid-April 1759. On Christmas night, 25 December 1758, a farmer and amateur astronomer named Johann Georg Palitzsch near Dresden spotted the comet returning on schedule.

The first theory of the Indian monsoon

In 1686 Halley also published the first meteorological map of the trade winds and the first physical theory of the Indian monsoon. Because land heats up faster in summer sunshine than the ocean does, he argued, warm air over Asia rises and cooler, moist air from the Indian Ocean flows in to replace it, bringing the monsoon rains; in winter the flow reverses.

For three centuries Halley’s “giant sea breeze” was the textbook explanation of the monsoon. In recent decades, meteorologists such as Sulochana Gadgil and her colleagues have shown that the real monsoon is driven even more by the seasonal northward shift of the equatorial rain belt (the Intertropical Convergence Zone) than by a simple land-sea breeze alone. Even where later data revise it, Halley’s paper started the physics of the monsoon.

In Chapter 5 you will trace the orbit of Halley’s comet, and in Chapter 8 you will meet his monsoon theory alongside modern Indian meteorology.

I

Ibn al-Haytham

The man in the dark room

c. 965 CE to c. 1040 CEProved that vision happens when light enters the eye, and tested optical ideas with dark-room experiments

Cairo, about 1015

Hasan Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin Europe as Alhazen, was born around 965 CE in Basra, in modern Iraq, and spent much of his working life in Cairo. Between about 1011 and 1021 he wrote his seven-volume Kitab al-Manazir, the Book of Optics. How he got the quiet years to write it is a famous tale: the story goes that he promised Caliph al-Hakim he could control the flooding of the Nile, saw upriver that the task was impossible, and feigned madness so the Caliph would keep him under house arrest rather than execute him. Historians treat the madness story with caution as a legend, but the experiments in his book are real.

Do your eyes send out beams?

For more than a thousand years before Ibn al-Haytham, Greek and Arab thinkers had argued over how we see. Mathematicians such as Euclid and Ptolemy taught the extramission theory: your eyes send out invisible rays, like feelers, that touch an object and report back. That idea still tempts us today; in psychology studies, most children and a majority of adults sketch something leaving the eyes when asked to draw how vision works.

Ibn al-Haytham overturned the eye-beam theory with observations that anyone can check. First, if you look at a very bright light, your eyes hurt. If you stare at a bright window and close your eyes, a coloured afterimage lingers in the dark for seconds afterwards. Why would a beam going out of your eye hurt your eye or leave an imprint behind? Something from outside is clearly coming in and acting on the eye. Second, when you walk outside at night and open your eyes, you see the distant stars at once. How could a substance from your tiny eye rush out and fill the whole sky to the stars in an instant?

Every point sends out rays

Instead, Ibn al-Haytham argued that luminous bodies such as the Sun or a candle flame send light out in straight lines from every point on their surface, and non-luminous objects reflect the light that hits them in every direction. You see your hand or this page only when some of that reflected light enters the pupil of your eye. He recognised that light enters through the lens of the eye and passes to the optic nerve, though how the retina forms a focused image was worked out only centuries later.

The dark room and the pinhole

To test whether light travels in straight lines and whether crossing rays mix, Ibn al-Haytham used a darkened room (bayt al-muzlim, the ancestor of the camera obscura or pinhole camera). Hang several candles in a row outside a dark room with a single tiny hole in the shutter. On the wall opposite the hole, an image of each candle appears, upside down and in reversed order: the right-hand candle makes a spot on the left, and the left-hand candle makes a spot on the right.

Block one candle outside, and only its matching spot on the wall vanishes. Uncover it, and the spot returns. That simple experiment proved two things at once: light from each candle travels in a straight line through the hole to its own place on the wall, and when light beams cross inside the tiny hole, they pass right through one another without tangling or mixing their colours.

In Chapter 10 you will test your own eyes in the dark, build a pinhole camera, and trace Ibn al-Haytham’s straight rays through mirrors and lenses.

JB

Jagadish Chandra Bose

Millimetre waves through the walls of Calcutta

1858 to 1937Built millimetre-wave radio transmitters and semiconductor receivers in Calcutta in the 1890s

Calcutta, 1895

In 1895, at Calcutta Town Hall, the physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose stood before an audience chaired by the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, Sir Alexander Mackenzie, and triggered an electric spark in a small metal box. Invisible electromagnetic waves travelled about 75 feet across the building, passed through walls and the Lieutenant-Governor’s own body in between, and tripped a detector that rang a bell and set off gunpowder.

Three years without taking a rupee of pay

Born in 1858 in Munsiganj in Bengal (now in Bangladesh), Bose studied at St Xavier’s College in Calcutta before travelling to England, where he learned physics at Cambridge under Lord Rayleigh. When he returned to India in 1885, the colonial education service appointed him Professor of Physics at Presidency College in Calcutta, but on the reduced “Indian tier” of pay: two-thirds of the salary paid to a European professor, cut in half again because his appointment was marked officiating.

Bose protested in the quietest way possible. He taught all his classes every day, and he refused to touch his salary cheque. For three years he worked without taking a rupee of pay, until the college authorities relented, granted him the full rate, and paid all three years of arrears at once.

Shrinking the waves to five millimetres

In 1888 Heinrich Hertz in Germany had confirmed James Clerk Maxwell’s prediction by generating electromagnetic waves in the laboratory. But Hertz’s waves were metres long, about the length of a dining table. Try to study how a wave reflects from a small mirror or bends through a prism when the wave is three metres long, and the wave washes right around your apparatus.

Working in a twenty-four-foot room next to a bathroom at Presidency College, with no government grant and the help of a skilled local tinsmith, Bose built spark transmitters that generated electromagnetic waves as short as 5 millimetres, at a frequency of about 60 GHz (3 × 10⁸ m/s ÷ 0.005 m = 60 × 10⁹ Hz). Because his waves were tiny, his whole apparatus could fit into a carrying case. He invented pyramid-shaped horn antennas to collect the waves, lenses of sulphur to focus them, wire-grid polarisers, and even a stack of Bradshaw’s Railway Timetable with tin-foil pages interleaved to twist the waves’ polarisation just as crystals twist visible light.

The coherer and the patent story

To detect his millimetre waves, Bose built a spiral-spring coherer using fine contacts of iron with a drop of mercury, and later semiconductor crystals such as galena (lead sulphide). When a wave arrived, the contact’s electrical resistance dropped and clicked a receiver. In January 1897, at Lord Rayleigh’s invitation, Bose demonstrated his compact millimetre-wave apparatus at the Royal Institution in London.

You will often read that Bose refused to patent any of his inventions. The true story has an extra layer. Bose disliked commercial secrecy and published his designs openly so anyone could use them, including Guglielmo Marconi. However, two of Bose’s friends, the American philanthropist Sara Bull and the Irish writer Sister Nivedita, persuaded him to sign a patent application for his galena crystal detector. US Patent 755,840 was filed in 1901 and granted in 1904, though Bose never enforced it commercially and allowed it to lapse. Today the 60 GHz band he opened in Calcutta is used in high-speed wireless links, radar, and radio astronomy.

In Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 you will meet the electromagnetic spectrum and see how Bose’s millimetre waves bridge the gap between radio and light.

HL

Henrietta Leavitt

The blinking stars in the southern cloud

1868 to 1921Discovered the period-luminosity law of Cepheid variable stars that let astronomers measure distances across the universe

Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1912

At the start of the twentieth century, astronomers could measure the distances to only the nearest stars by watching them shift slightly as the Earth orbits the Sun (parallax). Beyond a few hundred light-years, that shift becomes too tiny to measure from the ground. Nobody knew how large our Milky Way galaxy was, or whether the spiral patches in the sky were small gas clouds inside our galaxy or whole island universes millions of light-years away. The astronomer who found the yardstick to answer both questions could not choose her own research topic or use the observatory’s telescopes at night.

Glass plates from Peru

Henrietta Swan Leavitt was born in Massachusetts in 1868 and educated at what became Radcliffe College. After an illness left her with progressive hearing loss, she joined the Harvard College Observatory in the 1890s, first as a volunteer and later as a staff member.

At Harvard, Director Edward Pickering hired a group of skilled women known as “computers” (because a computer was then a person who computed) to measure and classify stars on glass photographic plates, paying them a third to a quarter of what men in equivalent posts earned. Leavitt’s assignment was to find variable stars, stars whose brightness rises and falls over days or weeks, on plates taken at Harvard’s southern station at Arequipa in Peru.

To spot a variable star among thousands of tiny black silver dots on a glass negative, Leavitt laid a transparent positive copy of one night’s plate directly over a negative plate from a different night. A steady star left a neat white ring around a dark core; a star that had brightened or dimmed stood out to her practised eye.

A swarm of bees at the same distance

In 1908 Leavitt published a list of 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds, two misty companion galaxies in the southern sky. Among sixteen of those stars for which she could measure the cycle time, she noticed a hint of a rule: the brighter ones took longer to complete each pulse from bright to dim and back.

Normally, seeing a bright star in the sky tells you nothing about its true luminosity: a dim bicycle lamp ten metres away looks brighter than a lighthouse ten kilometres away. You cannot tell whether a star looks bright because it is truly luminous or merely close.

Leavitt saw that the Small Magellanic Cloud solved that trap. Because all the stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud belong to the same distant cluster, they all sit at nearly the same distance from Earth, like a swarm of bees across a field. Any star in that cloud that looks four times brighter on the plate really is giving out four times more light.

In 1912, using 25 Cepheid variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, Leavitt plotted their brightness against the logarithm of their period and drew a smooth, tight line: brighter Cepheids always pulse more slowly.

Measuring the universe

Once other astronomers calibrated the distance to a few nearby Cepheids, Leavitt’s period-luminosity law became a cosmic measuring tape: time how many days a distant Cepheid takes to blink, read off its true brightness, and compare that with how faint it looks to find its distance. Harlow Shapley used her law to measure the Milky Way, and from 1923 to 1929 Edwin Hubble used Cepheids in distant galaxies to show that the universe is vast and expanding. Leavitt died in 1921, four years before a Swedish mathematician wrote to nominate her for the Nobel Prize.

In Chapter 15 you will use Leavitt’s blinking stars to step out from nearby stars to the expanding universe.

AM

Anna Mani

The Woman Who Measured the Wind

1918 to 2001Standardised nearly a hundred weather instruments so India could measure its own wind, sunshine and ozone

Pune, 1948

When thirty-year-old Anna Modayil Mani walked into the Instruments Division of the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in Pune in 1948, a year after Independence, the country’s weather stations still ordered their barometers, anemometers, rain gauges, and sunshine recorders from Britain. Even simple thermometers were imported. Working with a workshop of Indian machinists and glassblowers, Mani set out to design, calibrate, and standardise the drawings for nearly a hundred meteorological instruments so that India could measure its own sky.

Britannica Instead of Diamonds

Born on 23 August 1918 in Peermade in the Western Ghats of Travancore (now Kerala), the seventh of eight children of a civil engineer, Anna famously asked her parents for the Encyclopædia Britannica instead of the customary pair of diamond earrings on her eighth birthday.

After graduating with an honours degree in physics and chemistry from Presidency College in Madras in 1939, she won a scholarship in 1940 to work in C. V. Raman’s laboratory at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore. For five years she recorded the fluorescence, absorption, and Raman spectra of hundreds of diamonds and rubies over sixteen-hour photographic exposures, publishing five single-authored papers. Although she submitted a complete doctoral dissertation, Madras University denied her a PhD on the technicality that she held an honours BSc rather than an MSc.

Precision by Design

In 1945 Mani sailed to London on a government scholarship, spending three years at Imperial College and the British Meteorological Office learning how weather sensors are built and calibrated in wind tunnels.

Joining the IMD at Pune in 1948 under S. P. Venkiteshwaran, Mani knew that atmospheric physics is only as honest as its instruments: if two anemometers on two hills have different bearing friction, the wind map they produce is fiction. Rising to Deputy Director General, she oversaw Indian Standards specifications for nearly a hundred weather instruments, built a national calibration wind tunnel, and established networks mapping solar radiation and wind energy across India long before renewable power became an industry.

Rockets and Ozone

In 1962 Vikram Sarabhai called on Mani to build the wind towers and weather instrumentation at Thumba for India’s first rocket launch in November 1963. Encouraged by K. R. Ramanathan, she also developed the balloon-borne Indian ozonesonde, giving India a twenty-year vertical record of tropical atmospheric ozone before the Antarctic ozone hole made world headlines.

Try it at home

Why standards matter. Set a narrow straight-walled glass and a wide straight-walled pot side by side in the rain. Both collect the exact same water depth in millimetres, because a wider opening catches more drops in exact proportion to its base area. Standardising straight vertical walls lets a rain gauge in Kerala be compared directly with one in Assam.

We meet Anna Mani’s philosophy of honest measurement in Chapter 0 and her solar-radiation and monsoon networks in Chapter 8.

IN

Isaac Newton

The apple, the prism, and the falling Moon

1643 to 1727Linked the fall of a stone to the orbit of the Moon, set out the three laws of motion, and split white light with a prism

Woolsthorpe, 1666

In the summer of 1665, plague broke out in England, and Cambridge University closed. A twenty-two-year-old student named Isaac Newton packed his notebooks and went home to his family’s manor house at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire, where he spent the next two years with his calculations and experiments.

Two prisms in a darkened room

At that time, most scientists believed that white sunlight was the purest, simplest kind of light, and that when a glass prism threw a rainbow onto a wall, the glass itself was staining the white light to create the colours.

Newton tested that belief in a darkened room by cutting a small hole in his window shutter and holding a triangular prism in the sunbeam. Across the room, the prism threw an elongated band of colours, from red at one end to violet at the other. Then came what he called his experimentum crucis, the decisive test at the crossroads. He placed a board with a small hole in it so that only a single colour, say blue or red, could pass through, and sent that single colour through a second prism.

If a prism worked by adding colour to light, the second prism should have spread the single colour into a fresh rainbow. Instead, the blue ray bent further and stayed blue; the red ray bent less and stayed red. White sunlight was already a mixture of all the colours, and the glass simply sorted them out because violet bends more strongly in glass than red does. He published this result in a letter to the Royal Society on 6 February 1672.

The apple and the sixty Earth radii

At Woolsthorpe, Newton also thought about gravity. Sixty years later, in 1726, he told his biographer William Stukeley over tea under some apple trees that the idea of gravitation had come to him earlier in just such a setting, “occasion’d by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood.” There really was an apple tree at Woolsthorpe, though the cartoon version where the apple hits his head is an invention; a Royal Society librarian calls the story “an 18th-century sound bite.”

The question was genuine: how high does the Earth’s pull reach? It stays just as strong on the highest mountain top. What if the same pull reaches sixty times farther than the Earth’s surface, all the way to the Moon?

By Newton’s first law of motion, a Moon with no force on it would fly off along a straight line. Instead, the Moon’s path bends continually around the Earth. Newton guessed that Earth’s pull weakens with the square of the distance from the Earth’s centre. At the Moon’s distance of about 60 Earth radii, the pull per kilogram should be weaker than at the ground by 60² = 3,600. An apple near the ground accelerates at 9.8 m/s² and falls 4.9 m in its first second. Divided by 3,600, the Moon’s acceleration towards the Earth should be 0.00272 m/s², dropping about 1.36 mm below a straight line in one second and 4.9 m in one minute. Comparing that prediction with the Moon’s 27.3-day orbit, Newton found they agreed “pretty nearly.”

The Principia

Newton kept the calculation in his papers until Edmond Halley visited him in Cambridge in August 1684 and urged him to publish. Three years later came the Principia (1687), uniting the three laws of motion and universal gravitation.

You will meet Newton’s laws of motion in Chapters 2 and 3, his falling Moon in Chapter 5, and his prisms in Chapter 11.

CP

Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin

What the Stars Are Made Of

1900 to 1979Used Saha's equation on Harvard's stellar spectra to show that the stars are made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium

Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1925

In the brick library of the Harvard College Observatory, twenty-five-year-old Cecilia Payne sat surrounded by thousands of glass photographic plates, each striped with the dark barcode of a star’s spectrum. For two years she had measured the strengths of those spectral lines and fed them into the thermal ionisation equation published in Calcutta by Meghnad Saha. Common metals from silicon to iron came out in roughly the same relative proportions as in the crust of the Earth. Hydrogen and helium did not. According to her equations, hydrogen was roughly a million times more abundant in the stars than astronomers believed.

A Ticket to Eddington’s Lecture

Born in Wendover, Buckinghamshire on 10 May 1900, Cecilia Payne entered Newnham College, Cambridge on a scholarship in 1919. That December she attended a lecture in Trinity College by Arthur Eddington on the May 1919 solar eclipse expedition that had confirmed Albert Einstein’s general relativity. She wrote the lecture out from memory that night and switched her main study to physics.

At the Cavendish Laboratory she attended lectures by Ernest Rutherford and Niels Bohr, sitting alone in the front row by regulation as the only woman in the advanced course. Because Cambridge did not grant degrees to women until 1948, and Britain offered her little prospect beyond schoolteaching, she won a fellowship in 1923 to work under Harlow Shapley at the Harvard College Observatory.

Decoding the Glass Archive

Harvard’s women computers, led by Williamina Fleming and Annie Jump Cannon, had classified more than two hundred thousand stellar spectra into the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Yet leading astronomers, including Eddington and Henry Norris Russell, assumed that a vaporised Earth would show the same spectrum as the Sun, and that the Sun’s strong iron and calcium lines meant the stars were made mostly of heavy elements.

Combining Cavendish atomic physics with Cannon’s plate archive, Payne applied Saha’s equation across eighteen elements to establish the first accurate stellar temperature scale. She also saw why solar hydrogen lines looked deceptively modest: at the Sun’s surface temperature of 5,800 K, fewer than one hydrogen atom in a hundred million sits in the second energy level (n = 2) needed to absorb visible Balmer light. For the Balmer lines to appear as strong as they do when almost all the hydrogen sits unseen in the ground state, the star had to consist overwhelmingly of hydrogen.

The Caveat Added Under Pressure

When Payne sent her draft thesis, Stellar Atmospheres, to Henry Norris Russell in January 1925, he warned her that a hydrogen-dominated universe was “clearly impossible”. Payne published all of her data tables and abundance figures in her 1925 dissertation, earning Radcliffe College’s first astronomy PhD, while adding a reluctant sentence stating that the enormous hydrogen and helium abundances were “almost certainly not real”.

Four years later, Russell arrived at the same result by an independent calculation and confirmed in 1929 that Payne had been right all along. The astronomer Otto Struve called her 1925 monograph “undoubtedly the most brilliant Ph.D. thesis ever written in astronomy”. In 1956 Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin became the first woman promoted to full professor in Harvard’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences and the first woman to chair a Harvard department.

We trace how Saha’s equation and Payne-Gaposchkin’s thesis revealed the composition of the stars in Chapter 15.

CR

C. V. Raman

Five Weeks in Calcutta

1888 to 1970Explained why the tabla sings in tune, why the deep sea is blue, and how molecules shift the colour of scattered light

Calcutta, February 1928

In a darkened room at 210 Bowbazar Street, C. V. Raman and his research student K. S. Krishnan directed a beam of sunlight, narrowed by a telescope lens and filtered through violet glass, into flasks of purified benzene and sixty other liquids. Looking through a second green filter that blocked the incoming violet beam, they still saw a faint, shifted glow. On the evening of 27 February 1928, Raman looked through a direct-vision spectroscope and saw the shifted colour separated from the incident line by a dark gap. The next morning, 28 February, they photographed the spectrum with a small quartz spectrograph.

The Accountant After Hours

Born on 7 November 1888 near Tiruchirappalli, Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman entered Presidency College in Madras at fourteen and published his first optics papers in Philosophical Magazine while still an undergraduate. Because research posts for Indian scientists scarcely existed under colonial rule, he sat the Indian Finance Department examination in 1907, placed first, and went to Calcutta as an Assistant Accountant General.

Riding a tram home from work, Raman spotted the signboard of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS) at 210 Bowbazar Street. For the next decade he worked double hours: in the Bowbazar laboratory from half past five until quarter to ten each morning, at his Finance Department desk all day, and back in the laboratory until late at night. In 1917 he gave up his high civil-service salary to take the Palit Chair of Physics at the University of Calcutta.

The Tabla’s Black Patch

An ordinary circular drumhead vibrates at frequencies that do not form whole-number ratios (1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30), so it gives an unpitched thud. Working with Sivakali Kumar, Raman studied the Indian mridangam and tabla, whose makers weight the centre of the skin with a layered black paste called syahi (iron filings, charcoal, and rice starch). Sprinkling fine sand on the drumhead to trace its nodal lines, Raman and Kumar showed in Nature on 15 January 1920 that the heavy central patch slows the inner membrane just enough to pull the vibration modes into five clean harmonic overtones (1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : 5).

Pocket Instruments at Sea

Mediterranean Sea, September 1921

Sailing home from England aboard the SS Narkunda, Raman climbed onto deck with a pocket spectroscope and a Nicol polarising prism.

Lord Rayleigh had explained the blue sky by molecular scattering, yet argued that the blue sea was merely the reflection of the sky in water. Using his Nicol prism at Brewster’s angle to cancel the surface reflection, Raman saw the sea glow an even richer indigo from below. By the time the ship docked in Bombay, he had posted a Nature letter showing that water molecules themselves scatter sunlight.

The New Radiation

Back in Calcutta, Krishnan recorded in his diary between 5 and 28 February 1928 that every pure liquid they tested showed a weak polarised glow of altered wavelength, which Raman and Krishnan discussed on 9 February as the Raman-Krishnan effect. Roughly one scattered photon in ten million gives a packet of energy to a molecule’s vibration or takes one away, emerging with a shifted colour that serves as a fingerprint of its chemical bonds. The discovery won Raman the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and India celebrates 28 February as National Science Day.

We meet Raman’s work on the tabla in Chapter 9, and we follow his sea voyage and the Raman effect in Chapter 11.

MS

Meghnad Saha

The Thermometer of the Stars

1893 to 1956Linked the spectral lines of stars to their temperature and pressure with the thermal ionisation equation

Calcutta, 1920

At the University College of Science in Calcutta, twenty-six-year-old Meghnad Saha puzzled over a question that had stalled astronomers for decades. When starlight is spread out through a prism, cooler yellow stars like the Sun show strong dark absorption lines of calcium and iron, whereas hotter white and blue stars show strong lines of helium and hydrogen and almost no metals. Most astronomers assumed different stars were made of different proportions of chemical elements. Working with paper, pencil, and German journals delayed by the First World War, Saha proved that the stars were not changing their ingredients; they were changing their temperature.

From Seoratali to Presidency College

Meghnad Saha was born on 6 October 1893 in the village of Seoratali near Dacca (now Dhaka), the fifth child of a village grocer. Because the nearest English middle school lay ten kilometres away in Simulia, a local doctor, Ananta Kumar Das, boarded the boy free of charge in his own home while Saha walked between villages and won a scholarship to Dacca Collegiate School.

Expelled from that school in 1905 after joining a silent student boycott during the British governor’s visit, Saha continued at a private school and entered Presidency College in Calcutta in 1911. There he studied alongside Satyendra Nath Bose and learned under Prafulla Chandra Ray and Jagadish Chandra Bose. Recruited as young lecturers at Calcutta in 1916, Saha and S. N. Bose taught themselves quantum theory and relativity from German papers and in 1920 published the first English translation of Albert Einstein’s and Hermann Minkowski’s papers on relativity.

The Ionisation Equation

Reading Walther Nernst’s physical chemistry alongside Niels Bohr’s atomic model, Saha saw a bridge between thermodynamics and spectroscopy. Chemists knew how furnace heat splits molecules into atoms in reversible equilibrium. What if the extreme heat inside a stellar atmosphere strips electrons off atoms according to the same thermodynamic laws?

In four papers drafted in Calcutta in 1919 and 1920, beginning with “Ionization in the Solar Chromosphere” in Philosophical Magazine, Saha derived his thermal ionisation equation. It links the fraction of ionised atoms to the gas temperature, the electron pressure, and the atom’s ionisation potential, the energy required to knock an electron free.

Suddenly the Harvard stellar sequence (O, B, A, F, G, K, M) made sense as a single temperature scale. In a cool 3,000 K star, hydrogen atoms sit in their ground state and cannot absorb visible Balmer light. Around 10,000 K, collisions boost hydrogen into its second level so the Balmer lines blaze across the spectrum. Above 25,000 K, nearly every hydrogen atom has already lost its electron (H⁺), so the lines fade again. Working with Alfred Fowler in London in 1920 and 1921, Saha verified these predictions against laboratory spectra.

Rivers and Calendars

Returning to Calcutta in 1938 after fifteen years at Allahabad, Saha founded the Institute of Nuclear Physics and was elected to Parliament in 1952. Having grown up amid Bengal’s river floods, he wrote the hydrological plan for the Damodar Valley Corporation and chaired the committee that reformed the Indian national calendar.

We trace Saha’s thermal ionisation equation and how it decoded the spectra of the stars in Chapter 15.

VS

Vikram Sarabhai

The Church on the Magnetic Equator

1919 to 1971Founded India's space programme from a fishing-village church on the magnetic equator at Thumba

Thumba, Kerala, 21 November 1963

At dusk on 21 November 1963, in a coconut grove beside the Arabian Sea at Thumba near Trivandrum, a two-stage Nike-Apache sounding rocket roared off its pad and climbed 200 kilometres into the twilight sky, releasing a glowing orange trail of sodium vapour that drifted with the upper-atmosphere winds. The launch control room was a local cattle shed, the bishop’s house served as the drawing office, and the village church of St Mary Magdalene was the rocket assembly workshop.

Cosmic Rays in Ahmedabad

Born in Ahmedabad on 12 August 1919 into a family of textile philanthropists who supported Mahatma Gandhi and ran a Montessori school in their garden, Vikram Ambalal Sarabhai studied natural sciences at St John’s College, Cambridge. Returning to India when the Second World War broke out in 1939, he researched cosmic-ray time variations under C. V. Raman at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore alongside Homi Bhabha, setting up Geiger counters in Bangalore and at 4,000 m in Kashmir. After completing his Cambridge doctorate, the twenty-eight-year-old Sarabhai founded the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad in November 1947.

Why Thumba?

About 100 kilometres above the ground flows a narrow ionospheric ribbon of electric current called the equatorial electrojet, concentrated right along the Earth’s geomagnetic equator. That magnetic line clips the southern tip of India directly through the fishing village of Thumba.

In 1962 Sarabhai and his young engineers, including A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, met the Right Reverend Peter Bernard Pereira, Bishop of Trivandrum. Invited to Sunday Mass, Sarabhai explained the scientific station to the fishing congregation, and Bishop Pereira told the villagers that science and faith both sought truth to uplift human life. Within a hundred days the community relocated to a new village and handed their church over to become the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS).

Careful

Bicycles and bullock carts. Famous photographs show a rocket nose cone wheeled past coconut palms on a bicycle and a payload carried on a wooden bullock cart. Both really happened at Thumba: nose cones were pedalled from the church to the pad, and wooden carts were used so that iron chassis parts would not disturb sensitive magnetometers inside the payload. As ISRO’s own photo archive notes, however, the surviving photographs were re-staged for a press photographer a few months after the first launch.

Satellites for the Villages

Leading India’s space programme (which became ISRO in 1969) and chairing the Atomic Energy Commission after Bhabha’s death in 1966, Sarabhai explained in Vienna in 1968 why a developing nation belonged in space: not for prestige or Moon races, but to forecast the monsoon, survey crops and groundwater, and broadcast classroom lessons to half a million villages by satellite. He died in his sleep near Trivandrum on 30 December 1971, aged fifty-two, just after reviewing the SLV-3 satellite launcher design at Thumba.

We connect Sarabhai’s rockets and satellites to Newton’s laws in Chapter 3, circular orbits in Chapter 5, and Earth’s magnetic field in Chapter 13.

SB

Satyendra Nath Bose

A Four-Page Letter to Berlin

1894 to 1974Derived Planck's radiation law by counting indistinguishable light packets, giving his name to bosons

Dacca, 4 June 1924

In his study at the University of Dacca, thirty-year-old Satyendra Nath Bose enclosed a four-page typescript with a brief covering letter to Albert Einstein in Berlin. “Respected Sir,” Bose wrote, “I have ventured to send you the accompanying article for your perusal and opinion. I am anxious to know what you think of it. You will see that I have tried to deduce the coefficient 8πν²/c³ in Planck’s Law independent of the classical electrodynamics.” If Einstein thought the paper worth publishing, Bose asked whether he would arrange for its translation into German for the Zeitschrift für Physik. “Though a complete stranger to you, I do not feel any hesitation in making such a request. Because we are all your pupils though profiting only by your teachings through your writings.”

The Classroom Puzzle

Born in Calcutta on 1 January 1894, the son of an East Indian Railway accountant, Bose topped every university mathematics examination at Presidency College, just ahead of his classmate and friend Meghnad Saha. Together the two young lecturers taught themselves modern physics and translated Einstein’s relativity papers into English in 1920.

In 1921 Bose moved to the new University of Dacca as Reader in Physics. Lecturing to postgraduate students in 1924 on Max Planck’s blackbody radiation law, he was dissatisfied with every textbook proof. Planck’s formula assumed energy comes in discrete quanta of size E = hf, yet to count how many radiation modes exist at each frequency, every derivation fell back on classical electromagnetic waves before bolting the quantum hypothesis on at the end. Bose wanted a derivation that treated light as particles from the first line.

Two Identical Coins

Counting how packets of light share energy across tiny phase-space cells of volume h³, Bose noticed why classical probability failed. Toss two distinct coins, a rupee and a paisa, and there are four equally likely outcomes: (H, H), (H, T), (T, H), and (T, T).

If two light quanta of the same frequency have no private labels at all, however, then “first photon in cell A, second in cell B” and “second in A, first in B” are the exact same physical state. Counting only how many particles sit in each cell gives three equally likely arrangements (two in A, two in B, or one in each). From this new rule of counting, Planck’s radiation law dropped out in four pages without a single reference to classical wave electrodynamics.

The Postcard from Berlin

After Philosophical Magazine ignored his manuscript, Bose posted it to Einstein on 4 June 1924. On 2 July, Einstein sent a handwritten postcard to Dacca calling Bose’s paper “a most important contribution”. Einstein translated the paper into German himself, published it in the August 1924 Zeitschrift für Physik with a praising note, and extended Bose’s counting rule to massive atoms to predict the Bose-Einstein condensate.

After working in Europe with Marie Curie and meeting Einstein in Berlin, Bose returned to teach in Dacca and Calcutta and championed teaching science in Bengali. In 1945 Paul Dirac named every particle that obeys Bose’s statistics and shares a single quantum state, including photons and gluons, a boson.

We explore photons, quantum statistics, and how Bose’s counting rule divides particles into bosons and fermions in Chapter 15.

SS

Simon Stevin

The single thud at Delft

1548 to 1620Dropped two lead balls of tenfold different weight from the church tower at Delft and heard a single thud

Delft, 1586

In 1586, in the Dutch town of Delft, the Flemish engineer and mathematician Simon Stevin and his friend Jan Cornets de Groot climbed with two lead balls, one ten times heavier than the other, to drop them from a height of 30 feet (about 9.1 metres) onto a wooden board below. Tradition places their drop at the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk, the New Church of Delft.

Testing a two-thousand-year-old claim

Everyone who had studied university natural philosophy knew what was supposed to happen. According to Aristotle, heavier bodies fall faster than lighter ones in proportion to their weight. If a ten-times-heavier lead ball fell ten times faster, it would hit the board when the lighter ball had fallen only 3 feet, and a listener below would hear two distinct bangs separated by a long gap.

Stevin and de Groot let the two lead balls go together. Down on the wooden board below, the two balls struck so closely that their impacts sounded like a single thud.

Most people have heard the story of Galileo Galilei dropping weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Yet that story comes only from a biography written long afterwards by Galileo’s last pupil, Vincenzo Viviani, and Galileo himself never mentioned doing it. Stevin actually performed the drop with de Groot and published the result in Dutch in 1586, in De Beghinselen der Weeghconst (The Principles of the Art of Weighing), three years before Galileo arrived to teach at Pisa.

Why did Stevin use lead balls and a wooden board? In air, a wide, light sheet of paper is slowed by air resistance much more than a compact metal ball. Choosing two dense spheres of lead kept air drag tiny compared with weight, and dropping them onto a sounding board let the human ear judge whether they landed together.

The wreath of spheres on a ramp

In the same 1586 book, Stevin solved another puzzle: how hard do you have to pull to hold a heavy load still on a ramp?

He drew a triangular ramp with a gentle slope on the left and a steep slope, half as long, on the right. Over the triangle he draped a closed loop of fourteen identical, evenly spaced balls on a string, like a wreath (clootcrans). Four balls lie along the gentle slope and two along the steep slope, while eight hang symmetrically underneath.

If the four balls on the gentle side did not balance the two on the steep side, the loop would slide round by itself, placing four new balls on the left and two on the right in the exact same arrangement, and spin forever in perpetual motion. Because a loop of weights cannot drive itself forever, it must hang still. Cut away the symmetrical hanging piece at the bottom, and the four balls on the gentle ramp must balance the two balls on the steep ramp. Stevin put this diagram on the cover of his book with the Dutch motto Wonder en is gheen wonder: “Wonder is no wonder.” Once you see the mechanism, the mystery vanishes.

Decimal fractions for everyone

Born in Bruges in 1548, Stevin worked as a bookkeeper before designing windmills, sluices, and fortifications in the Netherlands. In 1585 he published a short booklet called De Thiende (The Tenth), which introduced decimal fractions (0.1, 0.01, 0.001) to everyday European arithmetic so surveyors and merchants could calculate without awkward fractions.

In Chapter 2 and Chapter 4 you will hear Stevin’s single thud again and see why heavy and light objects fall together when air drag is small.

GS

Govind Swarup

A Hillside and Thirty Wire Dishes

1929 to 2020Designed the Ooty Radio Telescope on a hillside tilted to match India's latitude and the thirty-dish Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune

Khodad, near Pune, 1996

Rising out of fields of sugarcane and onions around Khodad, eighty kilometres north of Pune, stand thirty parabolic dishes, each 45 metres across, wide enough to hold a cricket pitch inside its rim. Look up through one of the bowls against the blue Deccan sky, however, and you see clouds right through the reflector. Rather than heavy steel plates, Govind Swarup and his engineers wove the dishes of the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) out of thin stainless-steel wire mesh stretched over rope trusses like a bicycle wheel. To metre-long radio waves from distant galaxies, that wire grid looks like a solid mirror; to the monsoon wind, it is an open screen through which the air blows with barely a push.

From Thakurdwara to Sydney and Stanford

Born on 23 March 1929 in Thakurdwara in Uttar Pradesh, Govind Swarup completed his MSc at Allahabad University in 1950, trained in solar radio astronomy under Joseph Pawsey in Sydney on a Colombo Plan fellowship, and earned his doctorate at Stanford University in 1961. When Swarup and three fellow Indian radio astronomers abroad wrote to Homi Bhabha offering to return and build a radio astronomy group at home, Bhabha cabled back within days inviting them to the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Bombay, which Swarup joined in 1963.

Tilting a Telescope with a Hill

To track a star across the sky as the Earth spins once every twenty-four hours, an equatorially mounted telescope must have its rotation axle pointed parallel to the Earth’s axis, tilted at an angle equal to the observatory’s geographic latitude. Tilting a 500-metre steel structure to 40° or 50° in Europe or North America is prohibitively expensive.

Swarup noticed that southern India sits only 11° north of the equator. If he laid a long cylindrical radio reflector along a natural hillside sloping north-to-south at 11°, its axle would automatically stand parallel to the Earth’s rotation axis. A single mechanical drive turning the trough east to west could then track radio sources across the sky for ten hours a day at low cost.

In 1965 Swarup found the exact 11.4° north-south hill slope he needed near Ooty (11.4° N latitude) in the Nilgiris. Completed in 1970, the 530-metre Ooty Radio Telescope (ORT) measured the structures of hundreds of distant radio galaxies by timing the exact moments when the Moon passed in front of them.

The Bicycle-Wheel Dish

In the 1980s Swarup proposed building the world’s largest telescope at longer metre wavelengths (150 MHz to 1,420 MHz), the band that detects redshifted 21 cm signals from neutral hydrogen gas in the early universe and millisecond pulsars.

Because a wave cannot pass through holes much smaller than its wavelength, a one-metre radio wave reflects cleanly off a wire mesh with centimetre openings. Swarup invented the SMART design (Stretch Mesh Attached to Rope Trusses): 0.55 mm stainless-steel wire mesh pulled into a parabola by tensioned steel ropes like bicycle spokes. Completed in 1996 near Pune, the thirty-dish GMRT array spans 25 kilometres and serves astronomers worldwide.

We explore wavelengths in Chapter 10, the electromagnetic spectrum and diffraction in Chapter 11, and radio astronomy in Chapter 15.

CW

Chien-Shiung Wu

The Mirror That Cracked

1912 to 1997Designed and carried out the cobalt-60 beta-decay experiment proving that nature distinguishes left from right

Washington, December 1956

In a low-temperature basement at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington, Chien-Shiung Wu and four cryogenic physicists watched the count rate from a thin crystal of radioactive cobalt-60 cooled to 0.003 degrees above absolute zero (0.003 K). A strong magnetic field lined the spinning cobalt nuclei up like tiny tops turning the same way. If nature’s laws were indifferent between left and right, as every textbook assumed, the beta-decay electrons shooting out of those nuclei would fly off equally toward the north and south poles of the magnet. Instead, most of the electrons shot out opposite to the nuclear spin. Nature’s mirror had cracked.

From Mingde School to Columbia

Chien-Shiung Wu was born on 31 May 1912 in Liuhe near Shanghai, where her father founded the Mingde Vocational Continuing School for Girls so that local girls could learn mathematics and science. Boarding at the Suzhou Women’s Normal School from age eleven, she graduated in physics from National Central University in Nanjing in 1934 and sailed to California in 1936 to earn her PhD at Berkeley under Ernest Lawrence and Emilio Segrè.

At Columbia University during the Second World War, her work on radioactive xenon-135 explained why the first plutonium reactor at Hanford kept shutting down as xenon swallowed slow neutrons. After the war she became the world authority on beta decay (in which a nucleus turns a neutron into a proton while emitting an electron and an antineutrino), using ultra-thin radioactive films to confirm Enrico Fermi’s beta-decay spectrum.

The Question from Lee and Yang

In the spring of 1956, Columbia theorist Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang of Princeton visited Wu’s office in Pupin Hall. They suspected that parity conservation (the rule that the mirror image of any physical process behaves identically to the original) had never been tested in the weak nuclear interaction governing beta decay.

Wu saw how to test it: align the spins of cobalt-60 nuclei in a magnetic field and check whether beta electrons emerge equally along and opposite to the spin axis. To stop thermal jiggling from scrambling the nuclear spins, the crystal had to be cooled below 0.01 K.

Cancelling the Voyage Home

Wu and her husband, Luke Chia-Liu Yuan, held tickets on the Queen Elizabeth for their first trip home to China in twenty years. Wu cancelled her passage, partnered with Ernest Ambler’s cryogenic team in Washington, and commuted by train from Columbia all autumn.

Over Christmas 1956, whenever the team reversed the magnetic field, the electron count flipped with it. In a mirror, a spinning nucleus reverses its sense of rotation while an outgoing electron’s path does not; the asymmetry proved that the weak interaction distinguishes left-handed from right-handed. Lee and Yang received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics; Wu was omitted despite twenty-three nominations, and later won the first Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978.

We meet Wu’s experiment and the four fundamental interactions in Chapter 15.

1798

Weighing the world through a hole in the wall

Henry Cavendish, John Michell

Clapham, near London, 1798

In a big house on the edge of Clapham Common, south of London, lived one of the richest men in Britain and one of the shyest. Henry Cavendish had turned the upper rooms into an observatory and the drawing room into a laboratory. The one social event he never missed was the dinner before the Royal Society’s weekly meeting, and anyone who went up to speak to him there was likely to get a high-pitched squeak and a view of his back. The story goes that he left notes for his housekeeper in the hall rather than speak to her, and that a second staircase was built so that he need never meet his women servants on the stairs. He wore the same old-fashioned suit for years and was sometimes seen after dark walking down the middle of the road.

In 1798, in his late sixties, this man did the most delicate experiment anyone had yet attempted.

Michell’s machine

The idea was not his. A clergyman and scientist named John Michell had designed the apparatus and built it, then died in 1793 before he could use it. It came to Cavendish, who rebuilt it carefully and kept to Michell’s plan.

A wooden rod, six feet long, hangs by its middle from a thin wire. At each end is a small lead ball, five centimetres across and 0.73 kg. Beside each small ball, on opposite sides of the rod, Cavendish could swing in a big lead ball, thirty centimetres across and 158 kg. Newton’s rule says every lump of matter pulls on every other lump. So the big balls should pull the small ones towards them, the rod should swing round, and the wire should twist. The pull would be absurdly small. Two one-kilogram bags of sugar a metre apart attract each other with about 0.000 000 000 07 newtons.

A pull that small can be swamped by anything: a draught under the door, the warmth of a hand, a person breathing. So Cavendish sealed the apparatus in a mahogany case, put the case in a closed shed, and stayed out. He cut two holes in the shed walls, set a telescope in each, and watched the ends of the rod from outside, reading their position against a scale to better than a hundredth of an inch.

What he saw

The rod turned. Not much, but it turned, and it swung slowly back and forth about its new position, taking about fifteen minutes for each swing at first and about seven and a half after he fitted a stiffer wire. From the size of the twist he could work out the force the big balls were exerting: about 0.000 000 17 newtons, or 1.74 × 10⁻⁷ N.

Two pulls on the same small ball. The big lead ball, sitting about 22 cm away, pulls the small ball with 1.74 × 10⁻⁷ N.
The Earth, whose centre is about 6,400 km away, pulls the same small ball with its weight: 0.73 kg × 9.8 N/kg = 7.2 N.
7.2 ÷ 0.000 000 174 ≈ 41,000,000. The Earth pulls forty-one million times harder than a 158 kg ball of lead.
The rule of gravity says exactly how a pull depends on mass and on distance. Knowing both pulls, both distances and the mass of the lead, Cavendish could work out how much matter the Earth contains, and, since its size was known, how dense it is.

His answer: the Earth is 5.448 times as dense as water. His paper printed it as 5.48, because of a small arithmetic slip that nobody noticed until 1821. The modern value is 5.51. He was within about one per cent, in a shed, with a wooden rod and some lead.

Think about what that means. The rocks at the Earth’s surface are far less dense than that. A planet averaging 5.5 must have something much denser deep inside it, and Cavendish’s number was the first measurement to say so, made without anyone digging a single hole.

Careful

“Cavendish measured G, the gravitational constant.”

That is how many textbooks put it, and it is not what he did. His paper is called Experiments to determine the Density of the Earth, and a density is what it gives. The constant G, the number in the modern formula for gravity, does not appear in print until about 1873, seventy-five years later. What Cavendish measured was the pull between two lumps of lead, and from it he weighed the world.

Why he needed the shed

Hang a drinking straw from a single thread taped to a shelf, in a room with the fan off, and wait until it is perfectly still. Now walk up to it slowly and hold one hand a few centimetres from one end, without touching. Watch the straw begin to turn. The warmth of your hand makes the air beside it rise, and that gentle current is enough to push the straw round. A pull of a ten-millionth of a newton would have been lost in a disturbance like that, which is why Cavendish stayed outside and looked in through a hole.

In Chapter 5, Section 5.4, you meet the rule Cavendish used and see that the two bags of sugar on your kitchen counter are pulling on each other too, with a force he would have recognised.

1919 to 1980

The eclipse that made Einstein famous, and the argument after

Arthur Eddington, Frank Dyson, Andrew Crommelin, Charles Davidson, Edwin Cottingham, Albert Einstein, Daniel Kennefick

Príncipe, an island off West Africa, 29 May 1919

It rained all morning. Arthur Eddington and his companion Edwin Cottingham had sailed from England, set up a telescope on a plantation on the island of Príncipe, and waited weeks for an eclipse that was due at two in the afternoon. Now the sky was full of cloud. When the Moon’s shadow arrived, the Sun showed through gaps, and Eddington took sixteen photographs of whatever he could see, hoping that a few stars had come out on the plates beside the blacked-out Sun.

He was not there to look at the eclipse. He was there to see whether the Sun bends light.

The prediction

In 1915 Einstein had finished a new theory of gravity, and it made a prediction nobody could check in a laboratory. A ray of starlight passing close to the Sun should be bent by the Sun’s pull, by 1.75 seconds of arc for a star right at the Sun’s edge. The older way of reckoning, treating light as something that falls like a stone under Newton’s gravity, gave about half that. A test had to tell 1.75 from 0.87, and that is a very small angle.

How small is 1.75 seconds of arc? A degree has 60 minutes, a minute 60 seconds, so 1.75 seconds is 1.75 ÷ 3600 of a degree, or 0.000 008 5 in the units mathematicians use for angles (radians).
A one-rupee coin is about 22 mm across. It looks 1.75 seconds wide from 0.022 ÷ 0.000 008 5 = 2,600 m away: a coin seen from two and a half kilometres.
The Sun itself looks about 1,900 seconds wide, so the shift to be measured was about a thousandth of the Sun’s own width.

Stars next to the Sun can be photographed only when the Sun is blotted out, so the test needed a total eclipse, and 29 May 1919 was a good one: the Sun would sit in front of the Hyades, a cluster of bright stars. Frank Dyson, the Astronomer Royal, organised two expeditions. Eddington and Cottingham went to Príncipe. Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson went to Sobral, in northern Brazil, where they had a clear sky, 5 minutes and 13 seconds of totality, and two instruments: a large telescope fed by a mirror, and a small 4-inch telescope brought as a backup.

Three answers

Back home, the plates were measured against photographs of the same stars taken months later with the Sun elsewhere. Príncipe, through its clouds, yielded two usable plates with five stars each and a shift of 1.61 arcseconds. Sobral’s small backup telescope gave the clearest pictures of all: 1.98 arcseconds. Sobral’s main telescope gave 0.93, close to the old prediction, but its images were blurred; the heat of the day had distorted the mirror and thrown the stars out of focus. Dyson’s team set that result aside, for reasons they described in their report, and kept the other two.

On 6 November 1919, at a joint meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society in London, the result was announced: the light bends, and it bends by Einstein’s amount, not Newton’s. The newspapers took it up within days. Einstein, until then known mainly to physicists, became the most famous scientist in the world.

The argument, sixty years on

In 1980 two historians of science, John Earman and Clark Glymour, looked again at the three numbers and made an accusation. The expedition had thrown away the one measurement that disagreed with Einstein and kept the two that agreed. Eddington, they noted, had believed in the theory before he sailed. The charge spread, into a popular book, into Stephen Hawking’s A Brief History of Time, which called the result “sheer luck, or a case of knowing the result they wanted to get”, and into a thousand classrooms.

Then people checked. In 1978 and 1979 staff at the Royal Greenwich Observatory re-measured the surviving Sobral plates with modern machines. The blurred plates that had been set aside gave 1.55 ± 0.34 arcseconds, in agreement with Einstein after all; the blurring had spoiled the original measurement, not the sky. The physicist Daniel Kennefick then went through the expedition’s own papers and found that the decision to drop the blurred plates was Dyson’s, not Eddington’s, and Dyson was cautious about Einstein’s theory and had no reason to tilt the result. Eddington, analysing separately, refused Dyson’s later suggestion to average all three numbers, which would have let the suspect plates in. Another physicist, Clifford Will, put it simply: in Eddington’s place, “I would have done the same thing”.

So the plates were dropped for a reason that was written down before anyone knew whether it mattered, which is the only honest way to drop data. Later measurements, with better instruments, have confirmed the bending many times since. And the argument itself is part of the story: the Royal Society’s motto is nullius in verba, “take nobody’s word for it”, and that applies to Eddington, to Earman and Glymour, and to this page.

Careful

“The 1919 eclipse proved Einstein right.”

One measurement never proves a theory. The eclipse agreed with Einstein’s number and disagreed with the old one, within its errors, and the suspect plates, re-measured, agreed too. What turned a result into knowledge was repetition by other people with other instruments over the following decades.

In Chapter 5 you meet the pull that bends the light, the same pull that drops a mango and steers Chandrayaan; and Eddington returns in Chapter 15, where he is on the wrong side of a different argument.

1955 to 1998

The brain in the jars

Albert Einstein, Thomas Harvey

Princeton, New Jersey, 18 April 1955

Albert Einstein died in hospital in Princeton on 18 April 1955, at the age of 76. He had asked to be cremated, and he was. But the pathologist who examined his body that morning, Thomas Harvey, removed the brain first and kept it. He had no permission to do so, from Einstein or from his family. When the family learned what had happened, Einstein’s son Hans Albert agreed, reluctantly, after the fact, on one condition: the brain must be used only for science, and anything learned from it must be published in proper scientific journals.

What Harvey did

Harvey weighed the brain, 1,230 grams, which is an ordinary size, photographed it from every side, preserved it, and divided it into about 240 small blocks so that thin slices could be put on microscope slides. He sent slides to a few scientists he hoped would study them. Then, for the most part, nothing happened. Harvey moved house several times across the United States, and the blocks went with him, in two large glass jars packed in a cardboard box that had once held cider.

In 1978, twenty-three years later, a young journalist named Steven Levy tracked Harvey down and found the box. In 1997 Harvey drove the brain across America in the boot of a car with a writer, Michael Paterniti, who wrote a book about the journey. In 1998, forty-three years after the death, Harvey gave what remained to the pathology department of the hospital in Princeton where it had started. His heirs later passed the rest, and fourteen never-published photographs, to a medical museum in the United States, and a museum in Philadelphia shows thin slices of it on microscope slides.

What the scientists found

Every few years a study of Einstein’s brain makes the news. In 1985 a researcher reported that one small region had more supporting cells per nerve cell than in eleven other brains she compared it with. In 1999 a team working from Harvey’s photographs said one of the lobes was unusually shaped. In 2012 another team found extra folds in the frontal lobe. In 2013 another reported a thicker band of fibres joining the two halves.

Each of these has critics, and the criticisms are worth more to you than the findings, because they are the same criticisms you will learn to make of any claim. The eleven brains in the first study came from people whose average age was 64; Einstein was 76. Nobody measured the slides without knowing whose they were. And the deepest objection, made by the psychologist Terence Hines, is about counting. Every brain has features that are unusual in some way, because every brain is different. If you have one brain and you know in advance that its owner was a genius, you will find something unusual in it, and you will remember the unusual things that fit your story and forget the ones that do not. To learn what makes a genius you would need many brains of geniuses and many brains of everyone else, measured by people who do not know which is which. That study has never been done, and one brain in two jars cannot stand in for it.

Careful

“There must be something special in Einstein’s brain. That is where the genius was.”

Perhaps, but no one has shown it, and a single brain cannot. This is the lesson of Chapter 0 in its hardest form: an observation only means something against a model of what you expected to see, and with a sample of one, you can fit any model you like. The honest statement is that his brain was an ordinary weight and that studies of it disagree with one another.

Where the physics was

What made Einstein Einstein is not in the jars. In 1905, as a 26-year-old clerk in a patent office in Bern, he published four papers in one year: that light comes in packets, which won him the Nobel Prize and which you meet in Chapter 15; that the jiggling of pollen grains in water proves atoms are real; that space and time are not what they seem; and that mass and energy are two forms of one thing, which is the fire inside the Sun. In 1919 his prediction that the Sun bends starlight was tested at an eclipse, and that tale is told on its own page.

None of that came from an unusual fold. It came from a habit of taking a simple question seriously for years: what would you see if you rode beside a beam of light? The hospital kept the organ. The method is in his papers, which anyone can read, and in the chapters that follow.

Careful

“Harvey was a villain who stole the brain.”

He took it without permission, and that was wrong by the rules of 1955 as much as by today’s, when nothing like it could happen without consent in advance. But he was not a thief who sold it. He kept it for forty years, gave slides to anyone who asked seriously, and handed it back. The story is a lesson in consent, not a crime thriller.

Chapter 15, Section 15.1, begins with the first of those four papers, light in packets; and Chapter 0 is where you learn why one measurement, or one brain, is never enough.

1836

The man in the foil box

Michael Faraday

The Royal Institution, London, 1836

By 1836 Michael Faraday had already built the first electric motor and discovered how to make electricity from magnetism. Now he wanted an answer to a simpler-sounding question. When you put electric charge on a hollow metal object, where does the charge go, and does anything at all happen inside?

He did not do it with a tin can. He built a cube twelve feet along each side, about 3.7 metres, a wooden frame covered all over with metal foil, big enough to stand in. He connected the outside to an electrostatic generator, a machine that builds up charge by friction, and charged the cube so strongly that sparks jumped from its surface. Then he went inside, carrying an electroscope, a little instrument with two thin gold leaves that spring apart when the slightest charge reaches them. He walked round inside his charged box, holding the electroscope to the walls, the corners, the air in the middle. The leaves never moved. Outside, sparks; inside, as he put it, not “the least influence”.

Why the inside is quiet

A metal is a material in which some of the electric charge is free to move. Put extra charge on a lump of metal and the charges push each other apart, as like charges do, and spread out as far from one another as they can get, which is over the outside surface.

Now ask what would happen if there were any electric push left inside the hollow. The free charges in the metal would feel it and move. They keep moving, rearranging themselves on the surface, until there is nothing left to move them, and that happens only when the inside is completely quiet. So the charges always end up arranged in exactly the pattern that cancels every push inside. It is not that the metal “blocks” anything. The charges on the shell build a push of their own that undoes the one from outside, wherever it comes from and however strong it is. That is a Faraday cage, and any closed metal shell is one.

Cages you have been inside

A car is a Faraday cage with wheels. If lightning strikes it, the charge runs round the metal body and down to the ground, and the people inside, surrounded by metal, feel nothing. The same is true of an aeroplane, and aeroplanes do get struck. Mumbai’s monsoon thunderstorms are a good moment to remember that a hard-topped car is one of the safer places to be, and an open field one of the worst.

A microwave oven is a cage turned inside out: the box keeps the microwaves in, and the mesh in the glass door is a wall to them even though you can see through it. The bags that computer parts are shipped in are flimsy Faraday cages against stray charge. Hospital scanner rooms are lined with metal so that radio noise from outside cannot get in.

The phone in the foil

Wrap a phone completely in two layers of kitchen foil, with no gaps, and ask someone to call it from another phone. It does not ring. Radio waves, which are made of the same electric and magnetic pushes Faraday was studying, cannot reach the antenna through a closed metal shell. Unwrap it and it rings. The foil is not thick, and it does not need to be: what matters is that the shell is closed.

Careful

“The metal blocks the electricity, like a wall blocks rain.”

Nothing is blocked. Charge on the metal shell moves about until its own push exactly cancels the outside push everywhere inside. Faraday did not find a weakened effect inside his cube; he found none. A wall against rain always leaks a little. This does not, because the cancellation is not a barrier but a balance.

Faraday himself was the least cage-like of men. He had little schooling, taught himself from the books he bound as a bookbinder’s apprentice, and became the greatest experimenter of his century. Sitting inside a box he had charged to spark-point, watching two gold leaves not move, is exactly the kind of thing he found delightful.

In Chapter 12, Section 12.1, you make charge with a balloon and find out why that is hard in the monsoon; in Chapter 13, Section 13.6, you meet the radio waves that the foil kept out of your phone.

1684 to 1687

The book that nearly sank the *Principia*

Edmond Halley, Isaac Newton, Francis Willughby, John Ray

The Royal Society, London, January 1684

In January 1684 the young astronomer Edmond Halley showed the Royal Society a neat piece of reasoning. Kepler had found, sixty-five years earlier, that the planets farther from the Sun take longer to go round in a particular way. Halley showed that this pattern follows if the Sun pulls each planet with a force that weakens with the square of the distance: four times as far, a quarter of the pull.

Three of the Society’s members, Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke, then asked the harder question. If the force is like that, what path would a planet follow? Would it be the ellipse that Kepler had found? Nobody could prove it. Wren offered a prize, a book worth forty shillings, to whoever could. Hooke said he already had the proof. Two months went by and he produced nothing.

The ride to Cambridge

In August 1684 Halley rode to Cambridge to put the question to Isaac Newton. What curve would the planet follow? An ellipse, said Newton. He had worked it out years before. He looked for the paper and could not find it. He promised to send the proof.

Three months later a nine-page treatise in Latin arrived, De Motu, “On Motion”. Halley saw at once what it was and asked for more. Newton, who disliked appearing in print, expanded the nine pages over the next eighteen months into three volumes. The Society agreed to publish. Then it looked in its accounts.

The fish

The Royal Society had just spent its money on a book about fish. De Historia Piscium, “The History of Fishes”, had been begun by the naturalist Francis Willughby, who died in 1672, and finished by his friend John Ray. It was a serious work of natural history and a very expensive one to print: five hundred copies had cost the Society £400, which comes to sixteen shillings a copy. And it did not sell. The Society was broke.

So Halley paid for the Principia himself. He was not a rich man. He paid the printer, corrected the proofs, and put his own work aside to push the printing through. The Society, which owed Halley his salary as its clerk, settled what it owed him and Hooke in copies of the fish book instead of money. Later, when Halley was asked to measure the length of a degree of the Earth, the Society voted him “£50 or fifty Books of Fishes”. In the end his costs were paid back from the sales, because the Principia, unlike the fish, sold.

Prize money and fish money. Wren’s prize was a book worth 40 shillings. A copy of the fish book had cost the Society 400 pounds ÷ 500 copies = 0.8 pounds, and there are 20 shillings in a pound, so 16 shillings.
So the prize for proving the ellipse would have bought two and a half fish books. Newton’s proof, when it came, filled three volumes and was paid for by the man who asked the question.

What was in the book

Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, “The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy”, came out in 1687. In it are the three laws of motion you meet in Chapters 2 and 3: a moving thing keeps moving unless a force changes its motion; a force changes motion in proportion to its size; every push has a partner push back. And in it is the rule that a single pull, weakening with the square of the distance, drops an apple, holds the Moon in its orbit and steers every planet, which is Chapter 5. One set of rules for the Earth and the sky. That is the book that a history of fishes nearly stopped.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The fish book was not a bad book, and the Society was not foolish to print it. It simply ran out of money at the wrong moment, as institutions do. The Principia exists because one person happened to ask the right question, recognised the answer when he saw nine pages of it, and was willing to pay for the rest. Ideas do not publish themselves.

Careful

“Newton worked alone and the world just received his book.”

Newton did the physics alone, and that part is as remarkable as it sounds. But the book exists because Halley asked, pushed, edited, proof-read and paid. Most of what you will read in this book reached you by a chain like that: someone who saw the point, and someone who found the money.

In Chapter 2 you meet the first of Newton’s laws through a braking local train; in Chapter 3 the pairs of forces; and in Chapter 5 the pull that Halley rode to Cambridge to ask about.

1849

A cogwheel across Paris

Hippolyte Fizeau, Léon Foucault

Suresnes, outside Paris, July 1849

Hippolyte Fizeau was 29. His father was a professor of medicine, his family had produced doctors for generations, and he had started at the Paris medical school himself in 1840, until migraines drove him out. He travelled, recovered, and came back to a different subject. He sat in Arago’s lectures at the Observatory, took a course on optics, borrowed his brother’s engineering notes, and with his school friend Léon Foucault learned the new art of photography and took the first photograph of the Sun, sunspots and all. By 1849 he had a question that nobody had answered on the ground: how fast does light go?

The problem

Rømer had shown in 1676, from the late eclipses of one of Jupiter’s moons, that light takes time to travel; that story is in Chapter 10. But that was a measurement across the solar system. On Earth, across a room, across a city, light seemed instant. No clock of 1849 could be started as a flash left and stopped as it returned.

Fizeau’s answer was to make the light stop itself.

The wheel
