Take a wheel with 720 teeth around its rim, and so 720 gaps. Shine a brilliant light, a limelight, through one gap and out through a telescope. Fizeau set his telescope in the bell tower of his father’s house at Suresnes, on the western edge of Paris, aimed at a mirror on the hill of Montmartre, 8,633 metres away. The light crossed the city, hit the mirror, and came straight back towards the wheel.

Spin the wheel slowly, and the returning light comes back through the same gap it left by, and you see it, as a point of light in an eyepiece. Spin it faster. At some speed, by the time the light has made its round trip, the wheel has turned just far enough for a tooth to have moved into the gap’s place. The returning light hits the tooth. The point of light vanishes. Spin faster still and the next gap arrives in time; the light reappears. Fizeau drove the wheel with falling weights through gears that multiplied its speed five hundred times, and for the last 110 seconds of each run it held a steady rate while he watched.

The arithmetic

The first blackout came at 12.6 turns per second. One turn passes 720 teeth and 720 gaps, so moving from a gap to the next tooth is 1/1440 of a turn.
At 12.6 turns a second that takes 1 ÷ (1440 × 12.6) = 0.000 055 1 s, about 55 millionths of a second.
In that time the light went to Montmartre and back: 2 × 8,633 m = 17,266 m.
Speed = 17,266 m ÷ 0.000 055 1 s ≈ 313,000,000 m/s, about 313,000 km/s. With his own readings Fizeau published about 315,000 km/s.
The modern value is 299,792.458 km/s. He was about five per cent high, with a cogwheel, a lamp and a mirror on a hill.

The light’s round trip across Paris took about 58 millionths of a second. That is why it had always looked instant. Nothing in ordinary life happens that fast, and nothing in 1849 could time it, except a wheel that chopped the beam into pieces shorter than the journey.

Afterwards

Fizeau’s friend and rival Foucault found a better way, with a spinning mirror instead of a wheel, and by 1862 had the speed within about 0.6 per cent. The two of them also settled, in 1850, an old argument about whether light travels faster or slower in water than in air (slower, which is why a straw looks bent in a glass; see Chapter 10). Foucault got there first, and Fizeau confirmed it seven weeks later with his own apparatus.

Today nobody measures the speed of light. Since 1983 it has been fixed by definition at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, and the metre is defined from it: the distance light goes in one 299,792,458th of a second. Fizeau’s number was the first step from “too fast to notice” to a quantity so well known that we build our ruler out of it.

Careful

“Light gets there instantly.”

Too fast to notice is not the same as instant. Across Paris and back took 58 millionths of a second. Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Mumbai, and the Sun you see at sunset over Marine Drive is where it was eight minutes ago.

In Chapter 10, Section 10.6, you follow the whole chain from Rømer’s late eclipses to Fizeau’s wheel, and work out how old the sunlight on your hand is.

1851

Have you seen the Earth turn?

Léon Foucault, François Arago

Paris, January 1851

Léon Foucault had no degree in physics. He had started in medicine and given it up, and his only training in science was what he had taught himself and picked up as a journalist, reporting the meetings of the Académie des sciences for a Paris newspaper. With his school friend Hippolyte Fizeau he had made the first photograph of the Sun, and in 1850 he had shown, a few weeks ahead of Fizeau, that light goes more slowly through water than through air.

The idea came from a workshop. A thin, flexible rod clamped in the axis of a lathe, when plucked, vibrates in one plane, and when the lathe turns, the plane of vibration does not turn with it. The rod keeps its direction while its support goes round. Foucault saw what that meant for a pendulum, and for the Earth.

The three pendulums

Everyone educated in 1851 accepted that the Earth turns; Aryabhata had said so in 499, and after Newton nobody serious doubted it. But nobody had ever shown it, in a room, to the eye. Foucault’s idea was this. A pendulum swings in a plane, and nothing about a hanging weight can twist that plane round. So if you hang a pendulum and the plane of its swing slowly turns, it is not the pendulum turning. It is the floor.

He tried it first in his cellar, with a two-metre wire. The plane of the swing drifted, exactly as he expected. Then, with the backing of Arago, the director of the Paris Observatory, he hung an eleven-metre pendulum there and showed it to the scientists. He reported it to the Académie on 3 February 1851.

A month later came the public version. Under the dome of the Panthéon, the great domed building in the heart of Paris, he hung a hollow brass sphere 17 cm across, filled with lead to a mass of 28 kg, from a wire 67 metres long. A stylus under the bob brushed through ridges of sand on each swing. Each swing shifted the line it drew by about 2.3 millimetres, and the crowd could watch the lines creep round the floor. Paris came to look. The story goes that the newspapers asked their readers, “Have you seen the Earth turn?”

How much it turns, and why not the same everywhere

The Panthéon pendulum. A pendulum’s time for one swing there and back is 2π√(L ÷ g). With L = 67 m and g = 9.81 m/s²: 2π × √(67 ÷ 9.81) = 16.4 s. A slow, grand swing.
The turning of the floor. The Earth turns 360° in 23 h 56 min, a shade under 15° an hour. At the North Pole the floor under a pendulum would turn the full 15° an hour and the swing-line would come round once a day.
Anywhere else, the floor turns less about the vertical. The rule is 15° × sin(latitude) per hour.
Paris, latitude 48.85°: 15 × 0.753 = 11.3° an hour, a full circle in about 32 hours.
Mumbai, latitude 19.08°: 15 × 0.327 = 4.9° an hour, a full circle in about three days.
On the equator: nothing. The swing-line never turns.

That last line puzzles everyone, and it puzzled the Paris public, so here is the picture. Stand at the North Pole and the ground under your feet spins like a turntable, once a day. Stand on the equator and the ground does not spin under you at all; it tips over, carrying you round the Earth’s axis the way a point on the rim of a wheel goes round, and tipping does not twist the direction of a swing. Mumbai is in between: the ground does a bit of spinning and a lot of tipping, and the bit of spinning is what the pendulum reveals.

The Earth turns everywhere

By the summer of 1851 the experiment had been repeated in Rennes and in the cathedral at Reims, and in at least 25 cities in the United States. The next year Foucault built a cleaner proof, a spinning wheel on gimbals that holds its direction while the Earth turns beneath it, and he gave it the name it still has, the gyroscope. The original pendulum is in the Musée des Arts et Métiers in Paris, and since 2015 one has hung again in the Panthéon. You can stand under it and watch the floor go round.

Careful

“The pendulum turns slowly on its wire.”

It does not turn. Nothing is there to turn it: the wire hangs from a point and the weight swings under gravity, and gravity has no twist in it. The pendulum keeps its plane, and the building, the city and the ground turn under it. The hard part of the experiment is believing which thing is moving, which was Aryabhata’s whole point thirteen and a half centuries earlier.

A Foucault pendulum cannot be built in a flat; the effect at Mumbai’s latitude is slow and the slightest flaw in the hanging spoils it. But if you are ever in a science museum with a tall atrium, look for the sand or the row of toppled pegs on the floor. You are watching the one experiment that answers Chapter 14’s first question, and that story, Aryabhata’s boat, is told in Section 14.1.

1737 to 2009

Galileo's fingers

Galileo Galilei, Giovanni Targioni Tozzetti

The basilica of Santa Croce, Florence, 12 March 1737

Galileo died in 1642, old, blind and under house arrest. Nine years earlier the Church had tried him for teaching that the Earth moves round the Sun, and a man condemned like that could not be given a grand public tomb. So he was buried quietly, in a small room off the side of the basilica of Santa Croce in Florence, and there he stayed for ninety-five years.

On 12 March 1737 the city finally moved him. His remains were carried to a new monumental tomb in the main body of the church, directly opposite the tomb of Michelangelo, where they still lie. It was a solemn occasion, and not everybody present behaved solemnly. A historian named Giovanni Targioni Tozzetti, and others, took souvenirs. From the body of the most famous scientist in Europe they removed three fingers, a tooth and a bone from his spine.

Where the pieces went

The pieces travelled. One finger, the middle finger of the right hand, ended up in Florence’s museum of the history of science, standing upright inside a glass egg, where it has been on show for the best part of a century. The vertebra went to Padua, the university town where Galileo had taught for eighteen years and done his best work. The other two fingers and the tooth passed into the hands of a noble family, the Capponi, and in 1905 they disappeared. For a hundred years they were presumed lost.

In 2009 a strange lot came up at an auction: a tall wooden case of unusual shape, made in the nineteenth century and topped with a carved wooden bust of Galileo. Inside was a blown-glass vase from the eighteenth century, and inside the vase, two fingers and a tooth. An anonymous collector recognised what they might be, bought the lot and traced its history back through the Capponi family to the night of 1737. The experts of Florence, led by Cristina Acidini and Paolo Galluzzi, confirmed it. The newspaper reports disagree about which two fingers they are, a thumb and the index finger or a thumb and the middle one, which tells you something about how carefully souvenirs were labelled in 1737. The following spring the museum reopened with a new name, the Museo Galileo, and put all three fingers and the tooth on display.

It happened to be four hundred years since 1609, the year those fingers first held a telescope.

What the hands did

It is the hands that are worth thinking about, not as relics but as tools. On 25 August 1609 Galileo climbed the bell tower of San Marco in Venice and showed the Doge a spyglass he had built that made things look eight or nine times closer; the city gave him a pay rise. On the night of 7 January 1610 he pointed a better one at Jupiter and saw three small “stars” in a line beside it. By 15 January he had watched them long enough to know that they were moons going round the planet. The little book he rushed out on 13 March 1610, the Starry Messenger, changed what people thought the sky was.

A few years earlier, in Padua, those hands had rolled bronze balls down a grooved ramp to slow falling down enough to time it, the experiment you repeat in Chapter 1. They had swung weights on strings and found that a pendulum’s time depends on its length and not on how wide it swings, which is Chapter 9. They had built a balance to weigh things in water, at the age of 22, to show that the famous story of Archimedes and the crown could not have worked as told.

Relics and reasons

Florence keeps the fingers the way churches keep the relics of saints, in glass, with labels, for pilgrims. There is something odd in that for a man the Church once condemned, and something odder still. A finger in a glass egg tells you nothing about why Galileo matters. His bones are no different from anyone’s. What made him Galileo was a habit: look for yourself, measure, argue it through, and say plainly when the test does not come out clean, as he did when his two dropped balls “did not quite fall together”. That habit is not in a museum case. You can pick it up free, and this whole book is an attempt to hand it to you.

Careful

“Galileo was a genius, so he saw things nobody else could.”

The spyglass was a Dutch invention he heard about and improved. The moons of Jupiter were there for anyone with a telescope and the patience to watch for a week. What he had was not special eyes but a special method: point the instrument, write down what you see night after night, and let the record decide. The fingers that did the pointing are in a glass case; the method is yours if you want it.

In Chapter 1, Section 1.4, you roll a ball down Galileo’s ramp; in Chapter 9, Section 9.1, you time a pendulum as he did, and learn why the famous cathedral lamp is a legend.

1971

A hammer, a feather and the Moon

David Scott, Joe Allen

Hadley Rille, the Moon, 2 August 1971

It is the last few minutes of the third and final moonwalk of Apollo 15. Commander David Scott stands in front of the television camera in his white suit, holding something in each gloved hand.

“Well, in my left hand, I have a feather; in my right hand, a hammer,” he tells the camera. He explains that a long time ago a gentleman named Galileo made a discovery about falling objects, and that there could be no better place to confirm it than on the Moon. “And I’ll drop the two of them here and, hopefully, they’ll hit the ground at the same time.”

He lets go. The hammer and the feather fall side by side, slowly, and land together in the grey dust.

“How about that!” says Scott.

“How about that,” says Joe Allen in Houston, over applause in the control room.

“Which proves that Mr Galileo was correct in his findings,” says Scott.

“Superb,” says Allen.

Whose idea it was

The idea was Allen’s: he was the astronaut in Houston whose voice the crew heard during their moonwalks, and Scott later said plainly that the demonstration was his. The hammer was the real thing: the 1.32 kg aluminium geological hammer Scott had been using to break rocks. The feather was chosen with care. The lunar module that had carried the two astronauts down to the surface was named Falcon, so the feather was a falcon’s, from a bird kept at the United States Air Force Academy, whose mascot is the falcon.

The honest numbers

The official science report says the two objects were released from about 1.6 metres. People who have since gone through the television film frame by frame put it closer to 1.2 metres, judging from Scott’s posture and the known length of the hammer. Nobody on the Moon measured it. On the film, the fall lasts 36 frames at 30 frames a second: about 1.2 seconds. The report also gives a mass for the feather that is a misprint, far too heavy; a feather like that weighs about a gram.

Does 1.2 seconds make sense? On the Moon, falling things speed up at about 1.62 m/s² (often rounded to 1.67 m/s², a sixth of the 9.8 m/s² on Earth). A thing dropped from rest falls a height h in a time √(2h ÷ g).
From 1.2 m on the Moon: √(2 × 1.2 ÷ 1.62) = 1.22 s (or 1.20 s using 1.67 m/s²). The film says about 1.2 s. It fits.
The same drop on Earth would take √(2 × 1.2 ÷ 9.8) = 0.49 s, for the hammer. The feather, on Earth, would still be drifting down long after the hammer had landed.

Why it worked

On Earth a feather loses to a hammer because of the air. Anything moving through air is pushed back by it, and a feather is nearly all surface and almost no weight, so the air’s push stops it speeding up almost at once. The Moon has no air worth mentioning. Take the air away and there is nothing left to tell a feather from a hammer. The Moon pulls the feather with a tiny force, but the feather is also tiny, and the two go together exactly: twice the mass, twice the pull, and twice the sluggishness. Everything speeds up at the same rate. Chapter 3 gives you the sluggishness half of that argument and Chapter 5 the pull half.

Allen wrote in the mission’s science report that the hammer and the feather “were observed to undergo the same acceleration and strike the lunar surface simultaneously”, and he added something that is easy to miss. The result, he said, was reassuring, because the journey home depended on that theory. The same rule of gravity that dropped the feather was steering their spacecraft.

Careful

“There is no gravity on the Moon. That is why astronauts bounce.”

The hammer fell. It fell at about a sixth of the rate it would on Earth, because the Moon pulls about a sixth as hard, but it fell. Astronauts bounce because, with a sixth of the pull, each step carries them higher and keeps them up longer before they come down, not because nothing is pulling them down.

Careful

“Things fall in slow motion on the Moon because there is less air.”

Slow because the pull is weaker. No air is a separate fact, and it is the reason the feather kept up with the hammer, not the reason both fell slowly.

A feather with a shield

Cut a disc of paper a little smaller than a ₹2 coin. Drop the disc on its own and watch it flutter down. Now lay it flat on top of the coin and drop the two together, holding the coin level. They land together. The coin pushes the air out of the way and the paper rides in its shadow, which is as close to the Moon as your kitchen gets.

Chapter 4, Section 4.3, takes the Moon drop further, and the drop that started the argument, Stevin’s single thud at Delft in 1586, has its own story.

1889 to 2019

The kilogram that changed

George Matthey, Ian Robinson

Sèvres, near Paris, 20 May 2019

In a basement vault outside Paris, under three nested glass bell jars, behind a door that needs three separate keys held by three separate people, sits a small cylinder of metal. It is 39 millimetres high and 39 millimetres across, about the size of a golf ball, made of nine parts platinum to one part iridium. It was made in London in 1879 by the firm of Johnson Matthey, and in 1889 the first General Conference on Weights and Measures chose it as the kilogram. Not a kilogram. The kilogram. Its official name is the International Prototype Kilogram; everyone calls it Le Grand K.

For 130 years its mass was one kilogram by definition. It could not be wrong, because it was the thing that “kilogram” meant. Every kilo of rice in Crawford Market, every weight on every chemist’s balance, every satellite’s mass traced back through a chain of comparisons to that cylinder. Six sister copies sat beside it in the vault. Countries held their own copies, the United States number 20, India number 57, and brought them to Sèvres about every forty years, in 1889, 1948 and 1989, to be compared with the original.

The problem

The comparisons showed something unsettling. The copies and the original were drifting apart. Over a century the original seemed to have lost about 50 micrograms, fifty millionths of a gram, relative to the average of its copies: roughly the mass of a fingerprint. “Seemed”, because by definition it could not change. If Le Grand K had lost mass, then every kilogram in the world had lost mass with it, and nothing could tell you which had moved.

Nobody found a convincing cause. The copies might have gained from their surroundings; the original might have worn or absorbed something. It had its own cleaning ritual, rubbed with chamois leather soaked in ether and alcohol, steamed with twice-distilled water, then left for a week or more to settle, after which it slowly gained mass again, about a microgram a month at first. A unit that depends on how recently somebody wiped it is not a good unit.

How much is 50 micrograms? 50 µg is 0.000 05 g, and a kilogram is 1,000 g, so the drift is 0.000 05 ÷ 1,000 = 5 × 10⁻⁸ of the whole: fifty parts in a thousand million.
A kitchen scale that reads to 1 g would need 1 ÷ 0.000 05 = 20,000 such drifts piled up before it noticed. For rice, nothing. For the laboratories that compare the constants of nature to ten decimal places, everything.

The fix

The second had already stopped being a fraction of a day and become a count of vibrations of a caesium atom, in 1967. The metre had gone from a fraction of the Earth’s size, to a platinum bar, to the light of a krypton lamp, to the distance light travels in a fixed fraction of a second, in 1983. The kilogram was the last unit still defined by an object.

In November 2018, at Versailles, delegates from sixty countries voted to change it, and the change came into force on 20 May 2019, World Metrology Day, the anniversary of the treaty of 1875 that had created the whole system. The new rule fixes a number of nature instead of a lump of metal. The number is the Planck constant, written h, and it is now exactly 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ kilogram metre² per second. That number links the energy of a packet of light to the light’s frequency, which is Chapter 15, and it is the same in every atom in the universe. Its units contain a kilogram. With the second and the metre already fixed, fixing h fixes the kilogram too. An instrument called a Kibble balance can then weigh an object against an electric force that is measured in terms of h, and any well-equipped laboratory on Earth can make its own kilogram from the rule, without a visit to a vault. On the same day the ampere, the kelvin and the mole were pinned to constants of nature as well.

“The redefinition of the kilogram may seem like a small change, but it will have an enormous impact on science,” said Ian Robinson of Britain’s National Physical Laboratory, who had spent years building one of the balances. He also said this: “There will be no change to the mass scale currently used in trade and industry.” A kilo of rice is still a kilo of rice. Le Grand K is still in its vault, under its three bell jars. It is now just a very well-made lump of metal whose mass can, for the first time, be measured.

Careful

“My weight is 40 kg.”

Kilograms measure mass, the amount of stuff in you, which is the same in Mumbai, on the Moon and in orbit. Weight is the Earth’s pull on that stuff, a force, and it is measured in newtons: about 390 N for 40 kg of you, and about 65 N on the Moon. Chapter 3 keeps the two apart. The cylinder in the vault was never about how hard the Earth pulls; it was about how much is there.

In Chapter 0, Section 0.2, you meet the units, and why measuring anything starts with a promise about what the unit means; Chapter 15 shows you where the Planck constant comes from.

1963 to 1969

The schoolboy and the ice cream

Erasto Mpemba, Denis Osborne, Henry Burridge, Paul Linden, John Bechhoefer, Avinash Kumar

Magamba Secondary School, Tanzania, 1963

The class was making ice cream. You boil milk, stir in sugar, let the mixture cool, and put it in the freezer. Erasto Mpemba, a Form 3 student, put his in while it was still hot. And his froze first, before the mixtures of classmates who had patiently let theirs cool.

He said so. The class laughed. His physics teacher told him, “You were confused. That cannot happen.” Everybody knows that hot water takes longer to freeze than cold water, because it has further to cool. Mpemba had seen what he had seen, and he did not let it go.

The lecturer who listened

A few years later, at Mkwawa Secondary School in Iringa, a physicist from University College in Dar es Salaam, Dr Denis Osborne, came to give a talk. Afterwards Mpemba asked him a question. If you take two equal amounts of water, one at 35 °C and one at 100 °C, and put them in a freezer, the hot one freezes first. Why?

Osborne thought the boy must be mistaken. But he went back to his laboratory and tried it, and it happened. In 1969 the two of them published a short paper together in the journal Physics Education, with the title “Cool?”, Mpemba by then a student at a college of wildlife management. They had put 70 ml of water in beakers on a block of foam in the icebox of an ordinary refrigerator, starting at different temperatures, and timed how long each took to begin freezing. Water starting at 25 °C took longest. Water starting near 90 °C took much less. They checked that the hot water had not simply boiled away, and that dissolved air was not the answer. Osborne called the tests crude and asked for better ones. He got fifty years of them.

An old puzzle

It turned out to be an ancient observation. Aristotle wrote that water which has been warmed freezes more quickly. Francis Bacon wrote that “slightly tepid water freezes more easily than that which is utterly cold”. Descartes had a theory about it. Joseph Black, in 1775, compared water that had been boiled with water that had not. Nobody had settled it, and the schoolboy’s name went on it because he was the one who refused to be laughed out of it.

Why it is so strange

Here is why physicists found it hard to believe, and it is a good piece of reasoning. Temperature is one number. Hot water cooling towards freezing has to pass through the cold water’s starting temperature on its way down. If, at that moment, the hot water were the same as the cold water in every other way, it could not possibly win: from there on the two would be identical, and the hot one would be behind by however long it took to get there.

So if the effect is real, the hot water must arrive at that temperature different in some way that matters. There are candidates. Some of it has evaporated, so there is less to freeze. It has been stirred by currents as it cooled, while the cold water sat still. It holds less dissolved gas. It has melted the frost under its container, so it sits in better contact with the cold shelf. Its molecules may be arranged a little differently. Each of these has been proposed; none has been shown to be the answer.

The argument

In 2016 two physicists at Cambridge, Henry Burridge and Paul Linden, measured the time for water to cool to 0 °C with great care and found that the dramatic effects reported earlier vanished. Worse, they found that a thermometer sitting a single centimetre higher or lower in the water could produce a false effect all by itself, because the top of a cooling cup is not at the same temperature as the bottom. Their verdict was that there is “no evidence to support meaningful observations of the Mpemba effect”, though they noted that the 1969 result was too large to be explained by that mistake.

In 2020, Avinash Kumar and John Bechhoefer showed the effect cleanly, not in water but in the simplest system they could build: a single tiny glass bead, held in water by laser light, nudged thousands of times from a “hot” start and a “warm” start. The hot start settled faster. So something like the effect is real in some systems, and understood there. For water, the honest answer in 2022, from a journalist who asked all of them, was: “Whether hot or cold water freezes faster remains unknown.”

This book promised to say plainly what nobody knows. This is one of those things.

Careful

“Hot water freezes faster than cold. Everyone knows that.”

Nobody knows that. Careful experiments mostly fail to find it, and the ones that find it do not agree about why. The equally confident “that was disproved years ago” is also too strong: it has been found, cleanly, in systems that are not water. The true statement is the uncomfortable one: for water, after fifty years, it is unsettled.

A fair test

Take two identical cups and put exactly the same amount of water in each, say 100 ml, one from the cold tap and one from the warm tap. Put them side by side on the same shelf of the freezer at the same moment and look every ten minutes for the first skin of ice. Then do it again with the cups’ positions swapped. You will probably not see the effect, and that is not the point. The point is what Burridge and Linden learned: anything that differs between the two cups except the starting temperature, their position, their shape, how deep a thermometer sits, can produce a result that looks like physics and is not.

Mpemba went on to a career in wildlife management, and lived to see his question become a field. Chapter 8, Section 8.2, keeps heat and temperature apart, which is the first thing you need to think about this clearly, and Section 8.6 is where evaporation does its cooling.

1586 to 1654

The drop that probably never happened

Galileo Galilei, Vincenzo Viviani, Simon Stevin

Pisa, about 1590

You know the picture. A young professor climbs the Leaning Tower of Pisa with two balls, one heavy and one light. Below him stand the other professors, who believe Aristotle’s rule that heavy things fall faster, and all the students. He lets go. One thud. Two thousand years of physics end in a couple of seconds.

It is a wonderful scene, and it almost certainly did not happen.

Where the story comes from

Every version of it goes back to one man. Vincenzo Viviani was Galileo’s assistant and secretary in the last years of his life, when Galileo was old and blind. In 1654, twelve years after Galileo died, Viviani wrote a life of his master, and it was printed in 1717, seventy-five years after Galileo’s death. In it he says that Galileo showed, by “repeated experiments made from the height of the Leaning Tower of Pisa in the presence of other professors and all the students”, that weights of the same material fall at the same speed, whatever their size.

That is the only source. Nobody else who was in Pisa between 1589 and 1592, when Galileo taught there, mentions it. Galileo wrote a great deal about falling and never once mentions the tower. The same Viviani is also the only source for the story of Galileo timing a swinging lamp in Pisa cathedral with his pulse, and the lamp that hangs there now was put up after Galileo had left.

What Galileo actually wrote

Galileo did write about dropping two balls. He says he tested a cannonball against a musket ball and that they “did not quite fall together”: the heavy one landed a little ahead. He was honest about it. The air holds the small ball back slightly, as Chapter 4 explains, so a real drop never gives the perfect single thud the legend wants.

His real weapon was not a drop at all but an argument, and it is one of the best in physics. Suppose, with Aristotle, that heavier things fall faster. Now tie a light ball to a heavy one with a string and drop the pair. The light ball, being slower, should hold the heavy one back, so the pair should fall more slowly than the heavy ball alone. But the pair is heavier than the heavy ball alone, so it should fall faster. Both cannot be true. So the rule must be wrong, and the only way out is that all bodies fall alike. He did not need a tower for that; he needed a quiet room.

Most historians today think the tower drop was a thought experiment, or at most a private test. One serious scholar, Stillman Drake, thought it did happen, as a show for students, roughly as Viviani says. Either way, the old man telling the story to his young assistant may have remembered a demonstration that never quite took place.

Even the legend would have been messy

In the 1980s a historian, Thomas Settle, repeated the drop with real balls and found something odd: the lighter ball tended to pull ahead at the start. His explanation was that the hand holding the heavier ball tires and lets go a fraction later. A drop from the tower, done in front of a crowd, would have been a muddle of early releases and air resistance. Legends are tidier than experiments.

What really happened

In 1586, three years before Galileo arrived in Pisa, two men climbed about thirty feet up the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft, in the Netherlands. Simon Stevin, a mathematician, and his friend Jan Cornets de Groot dropped two lead balls, one ten times heavier than the other, onto a wooden board. “They fall together at the same time on the ground,” Stevin wrote, and “this proves that Aristotle is wrong.” He published it the same year. The Delft drop has its own page in this book, under Stevin’s name, because it is the one that is documented.

How to weigh a story

You can test a historical story the way a physicist tests a claim: ask where it comes from. Who first told it? When? Were they there? Does the person it is about mention it themselves? The tower scores badly on every question: one teller, writing after the hero’s death, who was not there, about a man who never mentioned it. Newton’s apple scores better, since Newton told the story himself, though sixty years late. Stevin’s drop scores best of all: he did it, wrote it down, and printed it within the year.

Careful

“Galileo proved that heavy and light things fall together by dropping them off the Leaning Tower.”

The documented drop is Stevin’s, at Delft, in 1586. Galileo’s own test, by his own account, did not come out clean, and his real contribution was the argument with the tied balls and the ramps you meet in Chapter 1, which slowed falling down enough to measure it.

In Chapter 4, Section 4.1, you do the drop yourself with two coins and a steel thali, and find out what the air does to a feather.

1940

Galloping Gertie and Tubby the dog

F. B. Farquharson, Leonard Coatsworth, Leon Moisseiff

The Tacoma Narrows, Washington State, 7 November 1940

The bridge was four months old. It had opened on 1 July 1940 across a narrow arm of the sea near Tacoma, with a main span of 2,800 feet, about 850 metres, the third-longest in the world. It was also unusually slim. Its designer, Leon Moisseiff, had stiffened the two-lane deck, only 12 metres wide, with solid steel girders 2.4 metres deep instead of the much deeper open framework first proposed, and the result was elegant and light.

It was also lively. From the first weeks, in quite mild winds, the deck rose and fell in slow waves, several feet high, every four or five seconds. The workers who built it called it Galloping Gertie. People drove across for the ride. Engineers tied it down with cables, which snapped, and fitted dampers, which failed. A professor of civil engineering from the University of Washington, F. B. Farquharson, was hired to study the motion and find a cure, and his wind-tunnel tests on a model finished on 2 November.

The morning

On 7 November a steady wind of about 42 miles an hour, 68 km/h, was blowing down the Narrows. It was not a storm, and it was not gusting. At about a quarter to ten the deck began its usual rise and fall. Then it did something new. It began to twist, one side of the roadway lifting while the other dropped, about twelve times a minute, once every five seconds, and the twisting grew.

Leonard Coatsworth, an editor at the local newspaper, was driving across towards Tacoma with his daughter’s dog in the back seat. Tubby was a cocker spaniel who had lost a leg and was partly paralysed. Halfway across, the heaving became too much to drive through. Coatsworth got out and was thrown to the road. He tried to reach Tubby, who was far too frightened to leave the car, and in the end crawled on hands and knees to the shore.

Others tried. The last to try was Farquharson himself, who had come that morning with cameras to film the motion he had been studying. He walked out along the twisting deck to the car, keeping to the middle, where the twist moved least. Tubby, terrified, bit him. Farquharson made his way back. A few minutes later, at about eleven o’clock, the main span tore loose and fell into the water, which was more than a hundred feet deep, and Coatsworth’s car and Tubby went with it. Neither was ever found. Tubby was the only life lost that day. A frightened animal bites the hand that reaches for it; nobody blamed him. “What appals me most,” Coatsworth wrote afterwards, “is that within a few hours I must tell my daughter that her dog is dead.”

Two men from a camera shop in Tacoma filmed the whole collapse on colour film. Most copies you will see run about half again too fast, because the film was shot at a slower frame rate than it is usually played, so the real twisting was even more stately than it looks.

What it was not

Nearly every physics textbook, and some you may own, says the bridge was destroyed by resonance: gusts of wind arriving in time with the bridge’s natural rhythm, like a parent pushing a swing. The wind that day was not gusting. Two engineers, Billah and Scanlan, showed in 1991 that the textbook story does not work, and the course notes this book is built on are blunt about it. This book does not repeat it.

What it was

What happened is called flutter, and it is the same thing that makes a flag flap in a steady breeze. The deck twisted slightly. A twisted deck meets the wind at an angle, and the wind then pushes on it differently: harder on the side that has lifted. That changed push twists the deck further. The larger twist changes the push again. Each twist feeds the next, and the bridge makes its own rhythm out of a wind that has none. Engineers call it self-excitation, or negative damping: instead of the air soaking up the motion as it normally would, the air was feeding it. Resonance needs a push that keeps time. Flutter needs only a steady wind and a deck that is too slim and too flexible to resist the first small twist.

The sunken deck lies where it fell and is now an artificial reef, listed as a historic place. A new bridge opened on the same piers in 1950, deeper and stiffer, and every long bridge since has been tested in a wind tunnel for flutter before it is built. The collapse that cost one dog’s life is the reason bridge engineers study the wind at all.

Careful

“The wind just happened to match the bridge’s rhythm.”

There was no rhythm in the wind to match. A steady wind and a flexible deck are enough: the deck’s own twisting changes the push on it, and the push grows the twist. Watch a flag in a steady breeze. The breeze is not flapping. The flag is.

A flag in your hand

Hold a strip of paper about 3 cm wide and 30 cm long by one end in front of a fan, lying along the airflow. The air is steady. The paper flaps. Try a strip of stiff card: it holds still. Flexibility is what lets the first small bend change the push and feed the next, and that is Galloping Gertie in miniature.

Chapter 9, Section 9.2, sets Tacoma beside the Millennium Bridge in London, which also swayed and also was not resonance, and shows you what a push that keeps time really does.

1831 to 1899

The quote Faraday never said

Michael Faraday, William Gladstone, W. E. H. Lecky

London, 1899

Here is the story. The politician William Gladstone, the most powerful man in Britain, is shown round Michael Faraday’s laboratory. Faraday explains his latest discovery. Gladstone listens, frowns, and asks the question politicians ask: “But, after all, what use is it?” And Faraday replies: “Why, sir, there is every probability that you will soon be able to tax it.”

It is a perfect story. The scientist is witty, the politician is dull, and electricity did indeed turn out to be useful, and taxable. It is in textbooks, on posters and in speeches. And it almost certainly never happened.

Following the trail

A good test of any quotation is to ask where it was first written down. This one first appears in 1899, in a book called Democracy and Liberty by the historian W. E. H. Lecky, who says he had it from “an intimate friend of Faraday”. Faraday had died in 1867. So the earliest record is a second-hand memory, written down thirty-two years after the man was dead, of a conversation nobody dated.

It gets thinner. Lecky’s version does not say what the discovery was; “electricity” was added by later tellers, in 1918 and again in 1977, when the tidier wording “One day, sir, you may tax it” appeared. Nothing like it is in Faraday’s own letters or notebooks, or in anything written by the people who knew him. Gladstone became prime minister in 1868, the year after Faraday died, so the grand version is impossible; he had earlier been Chancellor of the Exchequer, the minister in charge of taxes, so a meeting is possible. Possible is not evidence. The fact-checkers who have looked call it almost certainly invented.

Its twin is the same. “What use is a new-born baby?”, which Faraday is supposed to have said when asked the same question, has no source from his lifetime either. One widely used textbook has Queen Victoria asking the question; that version is unverified too.

What did happen

The true story needs no quip. On 3 and 4 September 1821, at the Royal Institution in London, Faraday made a wire hang in a dish of mercury beside a magnet and, with a current flowing, watched the wire go round and round the magnet by itself. That was the first electric motor. Ten years later, on 29 August 1831, he wound two coils of wire on an iron ring, connected one to a battery, and saw the needle of a meter on the other coil jump at the moment he closed the switch, and jump the other way when he opened it. That is electromagnetic induction, and that ring is the ancestor of every generator and every transformer in the world. The machines that make Mumbai’s electricity, in Chapter 13, are Faraday’s ring and spinning wire grown very large. The use of it was never in doubt. The tax came later.

Three questions

You can run the same test on any story in this book, and you should. Ask: who first wrote it down? How long after the event? Were they there?

  • Faraday’s tax: written down in 1899, thirty-two years after his death, by someone who was not there. Legend.
  • Galileo on the Leaning Tower of Pisa: written down in 1654 by his assistant Viviani, twelve years after Galileo’s death, not there. Legend, told on its own page.
  • Hertz saying his radio waves were “of no use whatsoever”: no source from his time at all. The story goes.
  • Newton’s apple: told by Newton himself, to a friend who wrote it down in 1726, sixty years after the event. True in outline, polished in the telling.
  • Franklin’s kite: written up by a friend fifteen years later; the only witness was Franklin’s son. Historians disagree.
  • Stevin’s drop at Delft: done by Stevin, written by Stevin, printed by Stevin in 1586, the same year. Documented.

Notice that the best stories cluster at the top of the list and the best evidence at the bottom. That is not an accident. A story that is sharpened each time it is told gets better and less true, and the ones that survive are the ones that were sharpened most.

Careful

“It’s in the textbook, so it must be true.”

Textbooks copy each other, and a quotation can travel through fifty of them without anyone going back to the start. The chain always ends somewhere. When it ends thirty years late with an unnamed friend, you have a story, not a fact, and the honest thing is to say so, which is what this book does.

In Chapter 13, Sections 13.4 and 13.5, you build Faraday’s motor and see his ring at work, which is a better monument than a quotation he never gave.

1841 to 1907

Chased out of Bombay by the trams

Nanabhoy Moos, Charles Chambers

Colaba, Bombay, 1904

At the southern tip of Bombay, past the docks, stood an observatory that had been watching one thing since 1841: the direction and strength of the Earth’s magnetism. From 1846 someone read its instruments every hour, day and night. From 1872 the reading was done by light, a beam reflected from a mirror on the magnet tracing a line on photographic paper, so that every twitch of the needle was recorded. Charles Chambers, the superintendent, published Bombay’s magnetic results in the Royal Society’s journal. His successor, Nanabhoy Moos, the first Indian to direct the observatory, would gather the whole record, 1846 to 1905, into two enormous volumes, and find in it that the needle’s disturbances follow the spots on the Sun.

The record showed things nobody could have seen any other way. The compass in Bombay had been pointing 57 minutes of arc east of true north in 1880, and by 1904 the drift had brought it to 10 minutes; today it points almost exactly true north. Storms on the Sun shook the needle. Sixty years of hourly readings from one spot is one of the longest such records in the world, and it was about to be ruined by public transport.

The problem with trams

Bombay had horse trams from 1874, and the tram company wanted to run them on electricity. An electric tram draws a large steady current from an overhead wire and sends it back through the rails and the ground. Chapter 13 tells you what Ørsted found in 1820: a current makes a magnetic field, in circles around the wire. A tram line is a wire the length of a city.

How much would a tram disturb the needle? No record survives of the planned tram currents, so take a guess of 500 amperes flowing along a line 200 metres from the observatory. The field of a long straight current is B = μ₀I ÷ (2πr), with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ in SI units.
B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 500) ÷ (2π × 200) = 5 × 10⁻⁷ tesla, which is 500 nanotesla.
The sideways part of the Earth’s field in Mumbai is about 38,400 nanotesla. So each passing tram would swing the needle by about 1.3 per cent of the whole field. The changes the observatory existed to track, the daily wobble and the slow drift, are far smaller than that. Every tram, every few minutes, all day: the record would have drowned.

Moos understood what was coming and helped to find the answer, which was not to fight the trams but to get out of their way. A new observatory was built at Alibag, about thirty kilometres south across the harbour, far from any wire. It was running by 1904. For two years, 1904 to 1906, both observatories recorded at once, side by side, so that the two records could be matched and the sixty-year series continued without a break. Then Colaba’s magnetic recording stopped. On 7 May 1907, at half past five in the afternoon, the first electric tram ran from the Municipal Office to Crawford Market. The date varies a little between sources, but the order of events does not: the magnets left first.

Alibag is still recording. The Earth’s field there today is about 43,400 nanotesla, dipping 27° into the ground, and the station is one of the reference points by which the whole planet’s magnetism is mapped.

The lesson of the sensitive instrument

Notice what kind of problem this was. The trams were not going to break anything. They were simply going to add a disturbance, small by any ordinary standard, that was large compared with the signal. It is the same problem Cavendish solved with his shed and his holes in the wall, and that Faraday solved with his foil box: when your instrument is sensitive enough to be interesting, the world around it becomes noise. You can shield, or you can move. Bombay moved.

Careful

“A compass just points north, so a magnetic observatory must be a very boring place.”

It does not point exactly north, and it does not point the same way from year to year, and it twitches when the Sun erupts. Those changes are the whole point. In Bombay the needle drifted by nearly a degree in a quarter of a century, and a great storm on the Sun can swing it by far more in an hour. The observatory tracked the changes; a tram would have buried them.

Make your own tram

The free phyphox app turns your phone into a magnetometer. Open it, lay the phone on a wooden table and read the total field: in Mumbai expect roughly 40 to 45 microtesla, which is 40,000 to 45,000 nanotesla, though phone sensors are rough. Now bring a steel spoon, then a running fan, then a charging cable with a current in it, slowly towards the phone and watch the number change. Every one of them is a tram, as far as the needle is concerned.

Chapter 13 opens with the Earth as a magnet in Section 13.2, and the chapter’s case file, The trams and the magnetometer, lets you work out for yourself how far away the trams had to be.

2000 to 2021

The bridge that walked

the engineers of Arup, Igor Belykh

The Millennium Bridge, London, 10 June 2000

The new footbridge across the Thames was meant to look like a blade of light: 325 metres long, only four metres wide, designed by the engineers Arup with the architects Foster + Partners and the sculptor Anthony Caro, and opened, a month late, on 10 June 2000. About ninety thousand people crossed it that day, as many as two thousand at a time.

And as the crowds packed on, it began to sway. Not up and down but from side to side, the deck moving as much as seven centimetres each way. People stopped and grabbed the handrails. The sway did not die down while the crowd stayed. Two days later, on 12 June, the bridge was closed, and Londoners had already given it the name that stuck: the Wobbly Bridge.

The first explanation

Arup’s engineers worked out what had happened and published it the next year. Walking is not only a push forwards. Each step also pushes the ground a little to one side, then the other, as your weight shifts from foot to foot. On solid ground the sideways pushes of a crowd point every which way and cancel. But a deck that sways even slightly changes how people walk. To keep their balance they adjust their steps to the movement, and that adjustment times their pushes with the sway. The pushes stop cancelling and start adding. More sway, more people adjusting, more push. The engineers called it synchronous lateral excitation; the plain description is a feedback loop, and it has nothing to do with anyone marching. Nobody was in step when they walked on. The sway came first and the steps followed.

That makes it different from the old rule about soldiers, who are ordered to break step on a bridge because hundreds of boots landing together are a push that keeps time, and a push that keeps time at the bridge’s own rhythm is resonance, the subject of Chapter 9. The Millennium Bridge supplied its own timing.

The cure

The cure was friction, of a controlled kind. Between May 2001 and January 2002 the engineers fitted 37 fluid-filled dampers, which work like the piston in a door-closer, and 52 tuned mass dampers, weights on springs that swing against the deck’s motion and soak it up. The job cost £5 million. The bridge reopened on 22 February 2002, and the sway was gone. In the language of Chapter 9: more damping, lower peak. A loop that feeds a little energy in with every step cannot grow if the dampers take that energy out faster.

The second explanation

That might have been the end of it, but in 2021 a group of mathematicians led by Igor Belykh published a different account in the journal Nature Communications, and its title gives it away: the instability can emerge “without synchronisation”. Their argument is that you do not need people to fall into step at all. Each walker, simply keeping balance on a surface that moves, adjusts their steps in a way that on average feeds a little energy into the sway, whether or not anyone else is doing the same. Engineers call that negative damping: a walker is a damper working backwards. Add enough walkers and the energy they feed in beats the energy the bridge can lose on its own, and the sway grows. The falling-into-step that everyone saw on the film, they say, was a result of the sway, not its cause. Their formula predicts a critical crowd size, and the group has suggested the Millennium Bridge could carry about 164 people steadily and that one more tipped it.

Which account is right is still argued, and you should know that honestly. Both agree about the cure, because both are about energy: walkers put it in, dampers take it out, and the bridge stands or sways depending on which wins.

Careful

“The crowd marched in step and set up a resonance, like soldiers on a bridge.”

Nobody marched. Ninety thousand people walking at their own pace do not share a rhythm. The sway came first, and either the sway pulled their steps into time with it or, in the newer account, each walker fed it without any timing at all. Resonance needs a push that keeps time from outside; this bridge made its own.

Chapter 9, Section 9.2, puts the Wobbly Bridge next to a far more dramatic one, the Tacoma Narrows bridge of 1940, which is also usually explained wrongly, and shows you what the two really have in common.

1673

Why there is no force flinging you out

Christiaan Huygens, Isaac Newton

Paris, 1673

Whirl a stone on a string and the string goes taut and tugs at your hand. Something, it seems, is pulling the stone outward, and the faster you whirl, the harder it pulls. In 1673 the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens published a book on pendulum clocks, the Horologium Oscillatorium, and in it he set out his rules for exactly that tug. He had worked them out years earlier, in 1659, in a manuscript called De vi centrifuga, and the word is his: centrifugal, fleeing the centre. His rules were right. The tug grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed makes it four times as big, and it shrinks as the circle gets wider.

Eleven years after Huygens’ book, Isaac Newton sent Edmond Halley a manuscript in which he named a force too, and pointed it the other way: centripetal, seeking the centre. Both men had the same mathematics. The difference is which way the arrow points, and that difference is the whole of this story.

Step 1: Going round is accelerating

A stone whirled at a steady speed is not moving steadily. Its speed is constant, but its velocity, which includes direction, changes every instant: north, then east, then south. In Chapter 1 you learned that any change of velocity is an acceleration, so the stone is accelerating the whole way round, even at constant speed. Which way? Draw the velocity arrow at one moment and again a moment later, and the change between them points towards the centre of the circle. The acceleration of anything moving in a circle points inward, and its size is v²/r: the speed squared, divided by the radius. That is Huygens’ rule, and it is why a car taking a bend at 100 km/h needs four times the grip it needs at 50.

Step 2: Something real must pull inward

An acceleration needs a force, pointing the same way: inward. For the stone it is the string’s tension. For a car on a bend it is friction from the road on the tyres. For the Moon going round the Earth it is gravity. Whatever real force happens to point at the centre is doing the job, and Newton’s name for the job is centripetal force. It is a role, not a new kind of force: a centripetal force is always a tension or a friction or a gravity or the push of a wall, and it never gets a separate arrow of its own on a diagram.

But the string really is taut, and it really does tug your hand outward. What pulls on it? The stone does. This is the third law: the string pulls the stone inward, so the stone pulls the string outward, equally hard. There is an outward force in the picture, and it is real. It acts on the string, not on the stone. Nothing pulls the stone outward. The stone is being pulled in, and that is the only reason it goes round at all.

Step 3: Let go

If the inward force stops, the stone does not fly outward. It goes straight on, along the line it was moving on at that instant, which is the tangent to the circle. In a 1980 study of 47 university students, 30 per cent drew a ball released from a whirling string carrying on along a curve, as if the circle were somehow still in it; the “flies outward” picture is just as common in classrooms. Both are wrong in the same way: once nothing pushes, nothing bends.

Cut a gap in the rim of a paper plate and roll a marble round the inside. It leaves through the gap in a straight line, along the tangent, not outward and not curving. A hammer thrower lets go and the hammer flies off along the tangent; a drop of water on a spinning bicycle wheel leaves along the tangent too.

Step 4: What you feel on a turning bus

Now the feeling that started it all. A bus turns left and you, standing in the aisle, lean to the right as if something had shoved you outward. Watch yourself from the pavement instead. Before the turn you and the bus are moving straight ahead. The bus turns; you, with nothing yet pushing you sideways, carry straight on, exactly as Newton’s first law says. The bus comes round to meet you: its floor drags your feet and its wall or pole presses your shoulder, and those pushes are inward, towards the centre of the bend. From outside, nothing pushed you outward. You went straight while the bus turned under you. The “flung out” feeling is the feeling of not yet having been turned.

Step 5: The honest note about rotating frames

Huygens was not simply wrong. If you insist on describing the world from inside the turning bus, treating the bus as if it stood still, then Newton’s laws stop working unless you add a made-up outward force on everything, and that is what Huygens’ centrifugal force is. Physicists call it fictitious: no object exerts it, and it appears only because the frame you are measuring in is turning. Engineers use it every day as a bookkeeping device, and it is fine if you know what you are doing. In this book we stand on the pavement, where every force has an object that exerts it, and from the pavement the centrifugal force does not exist.

One place the turning of the frame is big enough to measure is the Earth itself. The ground you stand on is going round the Earth’s axis once a day, so a weighing scale at the equator reads very slightly less than it would if the Earth stood still: the correction is about 0.034 m/s², a third of one per cent of g. At Mumbai’s latitude it is about 0.032 m/s². That is centrifugal bookkeeping doing real work.

Water in a swinging bucket (the radius is a guess).
Swing a bucket of water in a vertical circle of radius 0.8 m. At the top the bucket is upside down, and the water stays in if the bucket is moving fast enough to need an inward, which here means downward, acceleration of at least g. The condition is v²/r ≥ g, so v ≥ √(9.8 × 0.8) = 2.8 m/s: one full swing every 2π × 0.8 ÷ 2.8 = 1.8 s, or faster.
Swing it at 5 m/s and the inward acceleration is 5² ÷ 0.8 = 31 m/s², about 3.2 g. The bottom of the bucket has to push the water inward with three times its weight. Nothing is holding the water in; the bucket is pulling it round.

Careful

“When I let go of the whirling ball, it flies outward.”

It flies along the tangent: straight on, in the direction it was moving at that instant. Outward would mean away from the centre along the radius, and nothing pushes it that way. Watch the marble leave the plate, or the drops leave a spinning wheel.

Careful

“Centrifugal force throws me against the door when the car turns.”

Nothing throws you. You keep moving straight while the car turns, and the door comes round and meets you; then the door pushes you inward and you turn with the car. Every real force on you points towards the centre of the bend. The outward “force” is a way of describing the ride from inside the car, and it has no object exerting it.

At school

Your IGCSE syllabus describes circular motion as motion in a circular path due to a force perpendicular to the motion. The word “centrifugal” never appears in it. In an exam, name the real inward force: tension, friction, gravity or the push of a surface.

The plate with a gap

Cut a gap about the width of your thumb in the rim of a paper plate. Put the plate on a smooth floor and set a marble rolling round the inside, fast enough to hug the rim. Before it reaches the gap, say out loud which way it will go. It leaves in a straight line along the rim’s direction at the gap. Mark its path with a strip of tape and compare it with the line from the centre of the plate out through the gap.

In Chapter 4 the whirl-and-release figure comes alive, and in Chapter 5 you meet the biggest centripetal force you know: the Earth’s pull on the Moon, bending a straight line into an orbit.

1586 to 1971

The single thud at Delft

Simon Stevin, Jan Cornets de Groot, John Philoponus, Galileo Galilei, David Scott

Delft, 1586

Two men, Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot, have climbed about thirty feet, some nine metres, up the tower of the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft, in the Netherlands, carrying two lead balls, one of them ten times heavier than the other. On the ground below lies a wooden board. They let the two balls go at the same instant and listen. Aristotle, whose physics had ruled for nearly two thousand years, said that heavier things fall faster, in proportion to their weight, so the heavy ball should land while the light one is still a tenth of the way down, and the board should sound twice. It sounds once. One thud.

Stevin, a mathematician, published the result in 1586. Galileo Galilei would not arrive in Pisa, with its leaning tower, for another three years.

Step 1: Aristotle’s prediction

It is worth seeing why Aristotle’s rule was believed for so long: it agrees with what you see. Drop a stone and a feather together and the stone wins easily. Drop a coin and a sheet of paper and the coin wins. Everyday falling really does sort things by weight, and Aristotle made the pattern into a law. Ten times the weight, ten times the speed. The belief has not gone away. When 478 university students in the United States were tested in 1985, 82 per cent believed that what a thing is made of affects how it falls even with the air taken away.

Step 2: Philoponus tries it

Aristotle was not the last word even in the ancient world. In Alexandria in the sixth century, John Philoponus wrote that if you drop two very different weights from the same height, the difference in the time they take is tiny, nothing like the difference in their weights. He had, it seems, tried it. The observation did not catch on, and the rule carried on for another thousand years.

Step 3: Why one thud settles it

The Delft drop in numbers. The height is about 30 feet, which is 9.1 m. A ball dropped from rest falls a height h in a time √(2h ÷ g), with g = 9.8 m/s².
√(2 × 9.1 ÷ 9.8) = 1.37 s. If Stevin and de Groot were right, both balls hit the board 1.37 s after release.
If Aristotle were right, the light ball would fall at a tenth of the speed and take ten times as long: about 13.7 s. It would still be hanging near the top of the drop when the heavy one landed.
Nobody needs a stopwatch to tell one thud from two thuds twelve seconds apart. That is what makes the test decisive: the two predictions are not close.

Step 4: The tower that probably never was

The famous version of this story has Galileo dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. The only source for it is his late-life secretary Viviani, writing long afterwards; Galileo himself never described doing it. Most historians think it was a thought experiment or, at most, a private test. The real drop, with real lead and a real board, happened in Delft, three years before Galileo reached Pisa, and it is Stevin’s thud that this story is named for.

Step 5: Why the feather still loses

So why does a feather lose to a stone, every time? Because of the air. Anything moving through air is pushed backward by it, and the push, called air resistance or drag, grows as the thing speeds up: roughly four times the drag at twice the speed. A falling object has two forces on it: its weight, pulling down and never changing, and drag, pushing up and growing. The moment they are equal, the net force is zero and the speed stops changing. That steady speed is the terminal velocity, or terminal speed, and it is different for different things. A spread-out, light thing like a feather or a flat sheet of paper reaches it almost at once, at a crawl. A dense, compact thing like a lead ball would have to fall a long way before its drag caught up with its weight.

That is why the test is weight against drag, not weight alone. Crumple a sheet of paper into a tight ball and drop it beside a flat sheet of the same paper. Same weight; the ball lands first, because it presents far less to the air. A raindrop about 2 mm across falls at roughly 6.5 m/s and no faster; the biggest drops top out near 10 m/s. A skydiver falling head-down reaches about 350 km/h. In every case the limit is set by the balance of weight and drag. With no air there is no drag, no limit and no sorting by weight. Physicists call falling with nothing but gravity acting free fall, and in free fall everything falls alike.

Step 6: A hammer and a feather on the Moon

Hadley Rille, the Moon, 2 August 1971

The cleanest version of Stevin’s experiment was done where there is no air at all. At the end of the last moonwalk of Apollo 15, the astronaut David Scott held out a geological hammer of 1.32 kg in one hand and a falcon’s feather in the other, about 1.6 m above the ground, and let go of both together, for the television cameras. They landed together. “How about that! Mr Galileo was correct in his findings,” he said.

The Moon pulls about a sixth as hard as the Earth, so the fall was slow: about 1.38 s from 1.6 m, against 0.57 s for the same drop on Earth. But slow for both, and together.

Step 7: Why it is true

Stevin showed that heavy and light fall together. The why took another hundred years and belongs to Newton, and it is one of the neatest cancellations in physics. The Earth pulls a heavier ball harder: ten times the mass, ten times the pull. But a heavier ball is also harder to get moving: ten times the mass, ten times the sluggishness. The two effects are both in proportion to the mass, so they cancel exactly, and every mass speeds up at the same rate. Chapter 3 gives you the second half of that argument and Chapter 5 the first.

Careful

“Heavy and light things always fall together.”

Only when air is out of the way. In air, a tennis ball dropped with a cricket ball lands a little later, because its drag is a bigger share of its weight. The true rule is: with nothing but gravity acting, everything falls alike. Air adds a second force that depends on size and shape, and that is what sorts the feather from the stone.

Careful

“The feather fell slowly on the Moon because there’s no air to hold it up, and there’s hardly any gravity there.”

Air never holds a feather up; on Earth it slows the feather down. On the Moon the feather fell slowly for the same reason the hammer did: the Moon’s pull is about a sixth of the Earth’s. There is gravity on the Moon, which is why both of them fell at all.

One clink

Hold a ₹1 coin and a ₹5 coin side by side at the same height over a steel thali and let go together. Listen for one clink, not two. Then drop a flat sheet of A4 paper beside a sheet crumpled into a tight ball. Then crumple two sheets together into one ball and race it against a single-sheet ball: twice the weight, nearly the same size. Which races are decided by weight, and which by air? Try the coins again from a chair, with an adult steadying it, and listen harder.

In Chapter 4 you drop things for yourself, time a one-metre fall with your phone, and meet the raindrops of the monsoon. Chapter 5 explains why the Earth’s pull is in proportion to mass, and that is where the single thud finally comes from.

530 to 1687

The arrow problem: two thousand years of a wrong idea

Aristotle, John Philoponus, Ibn Sina, Jean Buridan, Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton

Alexandria, about 530

An archer draws a bow and lets go. For a fraction of a second the string pushes the arrow. Then the arrow is on its own, flying across the field with nothing touching it at all. Why does it keep going?

In the sixth century, in Alexandria, a scholar named John Philoponus worried at that question, and he had good reason to. The most respected account of motion in the world, written by Aristotle nearly nine hundred years earlier, said something about it that Philoponus could not believe. Aristotle’s rule was that everything which moves is moved by something. An ox moves the cart; a hand moves the stone; when the mover stops, the moving stops too. The rule fits almost everything you have ever seen, which is why it lasted so long. It fails for the arrow. Nothing is touching the arrow, and it flies on.

Aristotle’s answer was the air. The bowstring, he said, sets the air moving, and the moving air carries the arrow along behind it. Philoponus found that hard to accept, and you can see why with a ball on a table: fan the air behind it as hard as you like with a notebook and it barely stirs. Air is a feeble pusher. Ride a bicycle fast and you feel on your face which way air really pushes on a moving thing: backwards. So Philoponus proposed something different. The bow, he said, puts something into the arrow, a kind of motive power that travels with it and is gradually used up as it flies. The mover was not in the air. It was inside the arrow.

Step 1: Why the idea felt right

Hold on to that picture for a moment and notice how good it is. It explains why a harder shot flies further: more of the something goes in. It explains why every arrow eventually drops: the something runs out. And it matches the feeling in your own arm when you throw a cricket ball. You give the ball the throw, and the throw seems to travel with it.

It matches so well that most people believe it still. In 1985 two physicists, Halloun and Hestenes, gave a careful test to 478 university students in the United States before their first physics course. Sixty-five per cent explained motion with a force carried inside the moving object; after a term of lectures, 44 per cent still did. Forty-seven per cent believed that a thing with no force on it at all slows down anyway. Nearly fifteen hundred years after Philoponus, his idea is the most popular physics on Earth. It is wrong. It is not stupid, and finding exactly where it goes wrong is the point of this story.

Step 2: Bukhara: the idea gets a name

Philoponus wrote in Greek, and his idea went east before it went west. Five hundred years later, in Bukhara, the scholar Ibn Sina discussed it in his great Book of Healing and gave the carried something a name of its own: mayl, an inclination. An arrow in flight had an inclination to keep going, put there by the bow.

Step 3: Paris: Buridan’s recipe

In the fourteenth century the idea reached the University of Paris, probably by way of the Arabic writers rather than from Philoponus directly. Jean Buridan called the something impetus, and he did more than name it. He said how much of it a moving body carries: more if it moves faster, and more if there is more matter in it. A heavy stone and a light one thrown at the same speed carry different amounts of impetus; the same stone thrown faster carries more.

That recipe, speed multiplied by quantity of matter, is exactly the modern recipe for momentum, which you meet in Chapter 3. Buridan had the right two ingredients more than three hundred years before Newton.

Buridan’s recipe with modern numbers (the inputs are rough guesses).
A cricket ball has a mass of about 0.16 kg. Thrown at 25 m/s, which is 90 km/h, its quantity of motion is 0.16 × 25 = 4 kg·m/s.
You, at about 40 kg, shuffling along at 0.1 m/s, carry 40 × 0.1 = 4 kg·m/s. The same.
Buridan would say the ball and you carry equal impetus. Newton would say equal momentum. On the amount, they agree completely.

Step 4: Where it goes wrong

The mistake is in what kind of thing impetus is. Buridan’s impetus is a force stored inside the arrow: a push the arrow owns and spends. Here is the test that catches it, and it is the single most useful habit in this book. For every force you name, name the other object that exerts it. A force is always one object acting on another. The string on the arrow: two objects. The Earth on the arrow: two objects. Now look at the arrow in mid-flight and ask who is exerting “the force of the shot”. The string has gone. The archer is standing fifty metres behind. Nobody is left to do the pushing, so there is no such force. Only two things can act on the flying arrow at all: the air it moves through and the Earth beneath it.

And neither of those two pushes the arrow forward. The air pushes backward, as your face on the bicycle told you. The Earth pulls downward. Both are busy changing the arrow’s motion: the air slowing it, the Earth bending its path into the familiar arc. Take them away, by firing the arrow in empty space, and it would fly straight for ever at the speed it left the string. The arrow needs nothing inside it to keep going. It needs something outside it to stop.

Step 5: What Galileo changed

The man who turned the question round was Galileo Galilei. Instead of asking what keeps a moving thing moving, he asked what stops it, and found that the answer was always something he could name: a floor, a slope, the air. Reduce the rubbing and the stopping takes longer; remove it, in a thought experiment, and the stopping never comes. That is the subject of the story The ball that never stops, and of Chapter 2.

Isaac Newton made it the first of his laws of motion in 1687, and he dealt with the arrow in a sentence: a projectile keeps moving except in so far as the air slows it and gravity pulls it down, and the planets, which meet almost no air, keep going for ages. He also kept the good half of Buridan’s idea. He defined a body’s “quantity of motion” as its velocity and its quantity of matter taken together, which is Buridan’s recipe, and today we call it momentum. What a moving thing carries is motion. A force is the only thing that can change it, and a force is never carried; it is always exerted, by something you can point to.

Careful

“All right, there’s no force inside. But a moving thing still loses its motion slowly by itself, even with nothing touching it.”

Nothing has ever been seen to do that. Every slowing you have ever watched had a cause you could name: the floor under the book, the cloth under the ice cube, the air around the ball. Newton’s own evidence was the planets, which meet almost nothing and have not slowed down. Nearly half of the students in the 1985 study believed in motion that fades on its own. When something slows, look for the force. It is always there.

The puff test

Put a ping-pong ball, or a tight ball of paper, on a smooth table. Try to move it Aristotle’s way: fan the air behind it hard with a notebook, without touching it. Now flick it with a finger and watch it roll. Which did more, the air or the touch? Then throw the paper ball gently across the room and, while it is in the air, name every force on it and the object that exerts each one. If you want to name “the force of the throw”, find the object that is exerting it right now.

In Chapter 2 you follow Galileo’s ramps to the law that replaced two thousand years of impetus. In Chapter 3 Buridan’s two ingredients come back under their modern name, and in Chapter 5 you meet an arrow that never comes down: the Moon.

1604 to 1687

The ball that never stops

Galileo Galilei, René Descartes, Isaac Newton

Padua, about 1604

Galileo Galilei could not time a falling ball. A ball dropped from head height is on the floor in less than half a second, far too quick for any clock he had. So in Padua he slowed falling down. He let balls roll down long, gently sloping ramps, where the same kind of motion takes several seconds, and measured that instead. You met those ramps in Chapter 1.

Later, in the books he wrote as an old man, he described an experiment that he could only do in his head. Set two ramps facing each other, like a letter V, and let a ball roll down one. It rolls up the other and climbs to very nearly the height it started from, falling a little short because of the rubbing. Make the second ramp shallower. The ball has to travel further along it to climb back to its starting height, and it does. Make the ramp shallower still, and the ball rolls further still. Now lay the second ramp perfectly flat. The ball can never climb back to its starting height, however far it rolls. So, Galileo reasoned, it never stops.

Step 1: Follow the trend to its end

Look at what kind of argument that is. Galileo never watched a ball roll for ever; no one can. He watched a trend. Every time he made the ramp shallower the ball went further, and the only thing spoiling the pattern was friction. Reasoning about where a trend points once you remove the thing that spoils it is a thought experiment, and it is only trustworthy when every step has been checked against real ramps first.

You can walk the same trend on a floor. Slide a steel katori across a rough floor and it stops quickly. Dust the floor with talcum powder and it slides further. Oil the floor and it slides further still. Each change reduces the rubbing, and each time the stopping takes longer. Follow the trend to its end: take the rubbing away entirely, and the stopping takes for ever. An air-hockey table comes close: with the fan on, a cushion of air lifts the puck clear of the table and it glides from end to end at very nearly constant speed.

Step 2: A rule in two halves

In 1644 the French philosopher René Descartes wrote the result down as a law of nature in his Principles of Philosophy: a body left to itself keeps moving at the same speed and in a straight line. Read that sentence slowly, because there are two claims in it. The direction does not change. The speed does not change either. People find the first half much easier to believe than the second. When Halloun and Hestenes tested 478 university students in 1985, 84 per cent agreed that a body with no force on it moves in a straight line, but only 30 per cent agreed that its speed stays the same. Half a law is a very common thing to believe.

In 1687 Isaac Newton made the whole law the first of his three laws of motion, in the book known as the Principia. In today’s words: every body keeps its state of rest, or of steady motion in a straight line, unless forces acting on it compel it to change that state. Galileo had seen it first, with his ramps, and Newton never said so. Notice two things about the wording. A body at rest is covered as well as a moving one: rest is just the steady speed that happens to be zero. And the law is exact. A body left alone does not “tend” to keep moving, as if it might wear out eventually. It keeps its velocity exactly, speed and direction both, for as long as the total force on it is zero.

Step 3: What inertia is, and what it is not

The behaviour the law describes has a name: inertia, the tendency of a thing to stay at rest or to keep moving in a straight line at a steady speed. Every object has it, parked or moving. How much it has is measured by its mass, the quantity of matter in it. Try to shove a basketball and it goes; shove a boulder the same way and it barely moves. A kilogram of kurmura and a kilogram of steel bolts have the same mass and the same inertia, though one fills a bag and the other fits in your fist. Mass is the same on Earth, in orbit and on the Moon. It counts stuff; it is not a pull.

Now the trap. People say “the katori kept sliding because of its inertia”, as if inertia were a push that keeps things going. Swap the word for a made-up one: “the katori kept sliding because of its movability”. The sentence says exactly as much, which is nothing. Inertia is not a force. It is the name for the fact that motion continues until a force changes it. The explanation of why the katori kept sliding is that nothing had stopped it yet: the floor’s friction was small, so it took a while. Name the forces, or their absence. Never let the word do the explaining.

Step 4: The lurch

Now the question this law answers best. A local train is slowing into a station, and everyone standing lurches towards the front. What pushed them? Watch from the platform first. Before the brakes, every passenger is moving at the train’s speed. Then the brakes grip, and the train slows. What slows the passengers? Only what touches them. The floor touches their feet, and the floor is part of the train, so friction drags their feet to a slower speed. Nothing is touching their heads and shoulders. Those parts keep the speed the train had a moment ago, exactly as Galileo’s ball would, and from the platform you watch a whole compartment of people tilt forward.
