Now step inside and feel it. From in here it genuinely feels as if something shoves you forward, and if you shut your eyes you would swear to it. Physicists call that feeling a fictitious force: inside anything that is speeding up, slowing down or turning, everything seems to be pushed the other way. Apply the test from the story of the arrow. What object is doing the pushing? There is none. The feeling is real; the force is not. It is the first law seen from inside a carriage that is changing its velocity while your body carries on with its own.

How far ahead does your head get? (The train numbers are guesses; measure your own.)
A local train at 60 km/h is moving at 16.7 m/s. Suppose it brakes to a stop in 20 s. It loses 16.7 ÷ 20 = 0.83 m/s of speed every second.
Your feet, gripped by the floor, slow with the train. If nothing slowed your head at all, after one second it would be ½ × 0.83 × 1² = 0.42 m ahead of where the floor has carried your feet. After two seconds, 1.7 m.
Your head is not free, of course. Your legs and back pull it along, and that pull is the lurch you feel. Grab the pole and your arm does the pulling instead.

Careful

“A moving thing keeps moving, but it slowly runs down on its own.”

The law has no “slowly runs down” in it. Every real thing stops because a real force stops it: friction from the floor, the drag of the air. The test is not to watch for a ball that rolls for ever, which is impossible, but to watch the stopping fade exactly as the friction fades. Rough floor, talc, oil, air cushion: each step confirms it. Remove the last of the friction and you remove the last of the stopping.

The tray that stops

Put a small toy car, or a ₹5 coin standing on its edge, in the middle of a flat tray or a hardback book. Hold it level, walk across the room at a steady pace, then stop sharply. The toy carries on towards the front of the tray; the coin topples forward. Nothing pushed them. The tray stopped and they did not. Now walk, and start sharply instead of stopping: they slide backwards, towards you, which is the same thing as being pressed into your seat when a plane takes off. Clear the floor first.

In Chapter 2 you put friction itself on the scales and find out what kind of force it is. Chapter 3 asks the next question: a force changes motion, but by how much? And in Chapter 5 the Moon turns out to be a body that would go in a straight line, bent every second into a circle by the Earth’s pull.

1963

Rockets from a church

Vikram Sarabhai, Anna Mani, Isaac Newton

Thumba, Kerala, 21 November 1963

On the coast of Kerala, beside a fishing village called Thumba, stood the church of St Mary Magdalene. In 1963 it became the first building of India’s space programme. The church was the control room and the place where the rockets were put together, with the rockets laid out about where the altar had been. The story goes that parts arrived by bicycle and by bullock cart. On 21 November 1963 a small American-made research rocket, a Nike-Apache, rose from beside the church: India’s first rocket launch.

The scientist who organised it was Vikram Sarabhai. The weather instruments on the site were Anna Mani’s: that same year she built the meteorological tower at Thumba for Sarabhai, as part of her life’s work of giving India weather instruments of its own.

A rocket beside a church raises an obvious question. A car pushes on the road. A swimmer pushes on the water. What does a rocket push on, once it is high above Thumba in thinning air, and later in space, where there is nothing at all?

Step 1: The quantity of motion

Start with the quantity Newton called the “quantity of motion” and we call momentum: a body’s mass multiplied by its velocity. A 0.16 kg cricket ball at 25 m/s has 0.16 × 25 = 4 kg·m/s of it. Two things about momentum matter here. First, it has a direction, the direction of the velocity, so momentum to the left and momentum to the right can add up to nothing. Second, it belongs to the moving thing. In the story of the arrow you saw that a moving thing carries no force; what it carries is momentum, and only a force can change it. A big force, or a small force acting for a long time, changes it a lot.

Step 2: Push, and you are pushed

Now bring in the third law. When two things push on each other, the forces are equal and opposite and last for exactly the same time. So the momentum one gains, the other loses, in equal measure. Add the two together before and after, and the total has not changed. That is the conservation of momentum: for a group of objects that nothing outside is pushing on, the total momentum stays the same, whatever they do to each other inside the group.

The catch is in “nothing outside is pushing on”. A single cricket ball’s momentum changes all the time, because the bat and the Earth and the air push on it. Take the ball, the bat, the batter and the Earth together, and the total is constant. Momentum never appears or disappears; it only moves between things, and if you have lost track of some, you have drawn the boundary of your group too small.

Throwing a bag on a skateboard (the inputs are round guesses).
You stand on a skateboard, at rest; you and the board together have a mass of 40 kg. You throw a 4 kg school bag forward at 5 m/s.
The bag’s momentum: 4 × 5 = 20 kg·m/s, forward.
Before the throw the total was zero, and nothing outside pushed, so the total is still zero. Your momentum must be 20 kg·m/s backward: 40 × v = 20, so v = 0.5 m/s. You roll gently backward.
Every jump you make does the same to the Earth. Leaving the ground at 2 m/s with a mass of 40 kg, you give the Earth 80 kg·m/s the other way. Its mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, so it recoils at 80 ÷ (5.97 × 10²⁴) = 1.3 × 10⁻²³ m/s. The Earth jumps when you do; it just does not jump far.

Step 3: A rocket is a machine for throwing

That is the whole secret. A rocket pushes on nothing outside itself. It carries its own load of stuff to throw, the hot gas made by burning its fuel, and it throws that gas backward out of its tail as fast as it can. The rocket pushes the gas backward; the gas, by the third law, pushes the rocket forward. The rocket gains forward momentum exactly as fast as the gas gains backward momentum. Nothing else is needed. Not air, not ground, not a launch pad. A rocket works better in empty space than at Thumba, because air only gets in the way of the gas coming out.

The gas is light and the rocket is heavy, so the gas must leave very fast for the rocket to gain much: small mass times big speed balancing big mass times small speed, just as the school bag balanced you. That is why rocket exhaust comes out in a roaring jet rather than a gentle puff. And because the rocket is throwing away part of itself, it gets lighter as it climbs, and the same push moves what is left more and more easily.

Sixty years after Thumba, on 23 August 2023, the lander of Chandrayaan-3 came down over the Moon’s south polar region with its engines pointing at the ground, throwing gas downward to slow its fall, and touched down at 18:04 Indian time. The Moon has no air for an engine to push against. It did not need any. The gas pushed the lander, and the lander settled onto the dust at the spot later named Shiv Shakti Point.

Step 4: The balloon rocket

You have a rocket in the house. Blow up a balloon and let go without tying it. The air rushes out one way and the balloon shoots off the other. The common explanation is that the escaping air hits the room and bounces the balloon along; that is Aristotle’s old mistake in a new costume. The balloon’s stretched rubber squeezes the air out backward, and the air pushes the balloon forward as it leaves. The air that has already left is beside the point. It is the air on its way out, pushing on the balloon as it goes, that does the work.

Careful

“The rocket pushes against the air, or against the launch pad, to lift off.”

It pushes against its own exhaust, and against nothing else. If it needed air, it would stop working at the top of the atmosphere, and it does not; it works better there. If it needed the pad, it could not steer or speed up once airborne, and it can. The thing being pushed on is the gas, which the rocket brought with it.

A rocket on a string

Thread a long piece of string through a drinking straw and tie the string tight across a room, between two chairs, with the straw free to slide. Blow up a balloon, pinch its neck shut, and tape the balloon to the straw with the neck pointing along the string. Let go. Watch which way the air goes and which way the balloon goes. Then try a smaller balloon, or the same balloon blown up less: less gas to throw, less momentum gained. Predict before each run how far it will get.

In Chapter 3 you meet momentum properly, with carts that collide on a track, and the chapter ends back at Thumba. In Chapter 5 you follow Chandrayaan-3’s long, looping road to the Moon, every loop of it driven by the same throwing-away.

1687

Every push has a partner

Isaac Newton, Edmond Halley

London, 1687

In the summer of 1687 a book in Latin came off a London press, paid for out of the pocket of the astronomer Edmond Halley, because the Royal Society had spent its money on a lavish history of fishes that did not sell. The book was Isaac Newton’s Principia. Near its front stand three laws of motion, and the third is the one that people have found hardest ever since; the physics course at MIT still calls it the most subtle of the three. Newton gave two everyday examples. “If you press a stone with your finger, the finger is also pressed by the stone.” And if a horse pulls a stone along by a rope, the horse, he wrote, “will be equally drawn back towards the stone”: the stretched rope pulls the horse backward exactly as hard as it pulls the stone forward.

Read that again, because it says something strange. The horse is strong and the stone is dead weight, yet the rope pulls each of them with the same force. The law puts it generally: whenever one body pushes or pulls on another, the second pushes or pulls back on the first, equally hard and in the opposite direction. Always. At the same instant. For every force in the universe there is a partner force.

Step 1: One interaction, two forces

The cleanest way to hold the law in your head is this: a force is never a thing that one object has. It is an interaction between two objects, and like a handshake it has two ends. When your hand pushes a door, the door pushes your hand; you can feel it in your palm. When the Earth pulls you down, you pull the Earth up. The two forces of a pair are always the same size, always opposite in direction, and always act on different objects: one on the door, one on your hand. That last point matters more than any other. Because the two forces act on different things, they never cancel each other out. The door moves because of the force on the door; your hand feels the force on your hand.

Which of the two you call the action and which the reaction is up to you. Nothing happens first. The stone does not wait for the finger to press before it presses back; both forces exist together, and vanish together.

Step 2: The marble and the train

Here is the test MIT puts to its students. A marble hits a moving train. At the instant of impact, which feels the bigger force, the marble or the train? Nearly everyone says the marble, because the marble is smashed and the train is not. Wrong: the forces are equal. What differs is the effect. The same force gives a marble an enormous change in velocity and gives a train a change too small to measure, because the train has millions of times the marble’s mass. Equal forces; wildly unequal accelerations. When a truck and a car collide, the same thing is true: the forces on the two are equal, and the car is wrecked because it is lighter and weaker, not because it was pushed harder. In a study of about 900 university students in Pittsburgh, 73 per cent said the truck pushes harder before their physics course, and 39 per cent still said so after it.

Same force, different effect (the masses are round guesses).
A car of 1,000 kg and a loaded truck of 10,000 kg push on each other with equal forces during a collision.
Chapter 3 shows that the same force changes velocity in inverse proportion to mass. The truck has ten times the mass, so its velocity changes one-tenth as much as the car’s.
Now the extreme case. You stand on the floor. The Earth pulls you down with your weight, about 392 N if your mass is 40 kg, and you pull the Earth up with 392 N. The Earth’s mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, so its acceleration towards you is 392 ÷ (5.97 × 10²⁴) = 6.6 × 10⁻²³ m/s². The force is there. The effect is invisible.

Step 3: Prove it with two luggage scales

You can measure the law in your hallway. Hook two hanging luggage scales together, the kind families use for airline bags. You pull one handle and an adult pulls the other, as hard as either of you likes. Both scales read the same, to within about a tenth of a kilogram, however much harder one of you “pulls”. Hook one scale to a door handle instead and pull the other: the two still agree. A luggage scale reads in kilograms, but it is measuring a force; a reading of 10 kg means a pull of about 98 N, and the door handle is pulling back with 98 N too.

Step 4: Which pairs are not pairs

The commonest slip, found in plenty of textbooks, is to pick the wrong partner. Stand still on the floor. The Earth pulls you down (your weight) and the floor pushes you up. Those two forces are equal and opposite, and they are not a third-law pair, because both of them act on the same object: you. They balance, which is why you are not accelerating, but balancing is a different thing from partnering. Your weight’s partner is you pulling the Earth up. The floor’s push has its partner in you pushing the floor down. Write pairs out by name, always with two objects: “the Earth on Kym, Kym on the Earth”; “the floor on Kym’s shoe, Kym’s shoe on the floor”. If a sentence has only one object in it, it is not describing a pair.

Step 5: Getting about by pushing the world

Once you see pairs everywhere, you see how anything moves at all. When you walk, your foot pushes the floor backward, and the floor pushes your foot forward: friction, pointing the way you want to go. A swimmer pushes the wall backward and the wall sends her down the pool. A car’s tyres push the road backward. A helicopter pushes air downward and the air pushes it up. A rocket throws hot gas out of its tail and the gas pushes the rocket the other way, which is why rockets work in empty space, where there is nothing else to push on. That last example has a story of its own, Rockets from a church.

Careful

“The truck hits the car harder than the car hits the truck.”

It does not. The force of the truck on the car and the force of the car on the truck are one interaction seen from its two ends, and they are equal at every instant. The car comes off worse because the same force produces a bigger change in velocity in a lighter body, and because a car’s body crumples more easily than a truck’s. “Harder” belongs to the damage, not to the force.

At school

Many school books word the law as “to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction”, which is close to Newton’s own wording. The two words can mislead: there is no delay, and “reaction” does not mean a reply. In an exam answer, name both objects and both forces, and say which object each force acts on.

Two scales, one pull

Borrow two luggage scales. Hook them together and pull against a friend or a parent; read both. Now one of you pulls gently and the other pulls as hard as possible: read again. Hook one scale to a sturdy door handle and pull the other. Then sit on a chair with wheels on a smooth floor, push flat-handed against a wall, and notice which way you go and what pushed you.

In Chapter 3 the law meets the chapter’s big question, a mosquito on a windscreen, and the next section turns pairs of forces into the idea of momentum, which is what lets a rocket climb. In Chapter 5 the same law says that while the Earth pulls the Moon, the Moon pulls back on the Earth with exactly the same force.

250 BCE to 1586

Galileo and the crown

Archimedes, Vitruvius, Galileo Galilei

Syracuse, Sicily, about 250 BCE

Here is the story as it is usually told. The king of Syracuse has given a goldsmith a lump of gold to make into a crown. The crown comes back weighing exactly what the gold weighed, but the king suspects the smith has kept some of the gold and made up the weight with silver. He asks Archimedes to find out without damaging the crown. Archimedes is stumped until, lowering himself into a full bath, he sees the water slop over the side, realises that a body pushes aside its own volume of water, and runs home through the streets shouting Eureka, “I have found it”, having forgotten to dress.

It is a wonderful story and almost certainly not true. Nobody wrote it down until the Roman author Vitruvius, about two centuries after Archimedes. And in 1586 a 22-year-old Galileo Galilei worked out why it could not have been done that way.

Florence, 1586

Galileo’s little essay, La Bilancetta, “The Little Balance”, makes a simple point. Vitruvius has Archimedes measuring the water that the crown pushes out of a brim-full vessel, and comparing it with the overflow from pure gold and pure silver. But the difference between the overflow from a crown of pure gold and from one adulterated with silver is small, a spoonful or so of water, and water clinging to the vessel and to the crown would swamp the measurement. Nobody could have decided a king’s case that way. Galileo proposed a balance instead: weigh the crown in air, then weigh it hanging in water, and let the water do the measuring. To see why that works, you need the thing Archimedes really did discover.

Step 1: What water does to anything inside it

Chapter 6 shows that pressure in water grows with depth. Hold a closed tin under water and the water pushes on every face of it, but it pushes on the bottom face, which is deeper, harder than on the top face. The sideways pushes on opposite faces cancel. The up-and-down pushes do not: the push up on the bottom beats the push down on the top. Every object in a fluid feels this net upward push, whether it floats, sinks or hangs. This is buoyancy; the push is called the buoyant force, and some books call it upthrust.

The buoyant force on a 10 cm cube, from the pressures alone.
Water pressure grows by 1,000 × 9.8 × 0.1 = 980 newtons per square metre for every 10 cm of depth, whatever depth you start at.
The cube’s bottom face is 10 cm deeper than its top, so the water pushes up on the bottom with 980 N/m² more pressure than it pushes down on the top. Each face is 0.01 m², so the extra push is 980 × 0.01 = 9.8 N upward.
9.8 N is the weight of exactly 1 kg of water, which is one litre, which is the volume of the cube. The water pushes up on the cube with the weight of the water the cube has pushed aside.

Step 2: Archimedes’ principle

The last line of that calculation is Archimedes’ real discovery, and it is true for any shape, not just a cube. Here is the argument that shows why. Picture the object gone, and its space filled with water instead. That water would just sit there, floating in the rest of the water, neither rising nor sinking; so the surrounding water must be holding it up with a push exactly equal to its weight. Now put the object back. The surrounding water has not changed, so it pushes on the object exactly as it pushed on the water: upward, with the weight of the water displaced. That is Archimedes’ principle: the buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it pushes aside.

Everything about floating follows. If the object weighs less than the water it displaces, the buoyant force wins and it rises; if more, it sinks; if the same, it hangs. And since an object displaces its own volume when fully under, “weighs less than the same volume of water” is the same as “is less dense than water”. Density, mass divided by volume, decides. Water is 1,000 kg per cubic metre, which is 1 gram per cubic centimetre. Wood at about 0.7 floats; steel at 7.8 sinks; ice at 0.92 floats with about 92 per cent of itself under the surface.

Step 3: Galileo’s balance

Now Galileo’s method. Weigh an object in air. Then weigh it hanging on a thread, fully under water. It weighs less, and the loss is the buoyant force: the weight of the water it displaces. From the loss you know the volume of water displaced, which is the object’s own volume, and from mass and volume you have the density, with no overflow to catch. A worked example from a textbook: a coin weighs 8.630 g in air and 7.800 g under water. The loss, 0.830 g, is the mass of 0.830 cm³ of water, so the coin’s volume is 0.830 cm³ and its density is 8.630 ÷ 0.830 = 10.4 g/cm³. Gold is 19.3. This coin is not gold; it is about the density of silver. A balance can decide a king’s case. A puddle on the floor cannot.

Step 4: Why a steel ship floats

Steel is 7.8 times as dense as water, so a lump of it sinks. A ship of 50,000 tonnes floats because a ship is not a lump. To float, it must displace 50,000 tonnes of water: in the Arabian Sea, whose water is slightly denser than fresh water, about 49,000 cubic metres of it. The hull is shaped to push aside that much sea, and most of what fills the hull’s volume is air, cargo and empty rooms, not steel. The ship’s average density, steel and air together, is less than the sea’s, so it floats. Load it and it sinks lower, displacing more; sail it into a fresh-water river and it sinks lower still, because each cubic metre of fresh water weighs a little less. A ball of atta dough sinks in a bucket; press the same dough into a bowl shape and it floats. Nothing about the dough has changed except how much water it pushes aside.

Step 5: The egg

Put an egg in a glass of tap water and it sinks: an egg is a little denser than water. Now stir in salt, a spoonful at a time. Nothing about the egg changes. The water changes: dissolved salt makes each cubic centimetre of it heavier, and once the salt water is denser than the egg, the egg lifts off the bottom and floats. It takes several spoons. Try the same idea the other way round with an orange: the whole orange floats, because its peel is full of tiny air pockets, and the peeled orange, denser without them, sinks.

Careful

“Heavy things sink and light things float.”

A 50,000-tonne ship floats and a ₹5 coin sinks. Weight is the wrong thing to compare. Compare the object’s density, its mass for its volume, with the density of the liquid: lower floats, higher sinks. “Heavy for its size” is the phrase to use, and it is the only one that gets the ship and the coin both right.

At school

Your IGCSE syllabus covers density, ρ = m/V. It does not use the word “upthrust”, though many school books do; this book says buoyant force, which is the same thing. Whichever word you use, say what causes it: the pressure of the fluid, greater on the bottom of the object than on the top.

Floaters and sinkers

Put an egg in a tall glass of tap water: it sinks. Add salt a teaspoon at a time, stirring until each spoonful dissolves, and count the spoons until the egg lifts. Several are needed; stop when it floats. Put a whole orange in a bowl of water, then the same orange peeled. Then make a boat: a sheet of aluminium foil rolled into a tight ball sinks; the same sheet shaped into a dish floats, and will carry ₹1 coins as cargo. Count how many it takes to sink it, then reshape the foil and try to carry more.

In Chapter 6 you meet the pressures that make all this happen, and the chapter ends with the case of the egg that changed its mind.

1643 to 1654

We live at the bottom of an ocean of air

Evangelista Torricelli, Blaise Pascal, Florin Périer, Otto von Guericke

Florence, 1643

In the 1640s everyone who built pumps knew an annoying fact, and nobody could explain it. A pump will lift water out of a well, but only to a height of about ten metres. Make the pipe longer and the water simply stops rising, as if ten metres were the end of its rope.

In Florence, Evangelista Torricelli tried the problem with a heavier liquid. He filled a tube with mercury, turned it upside down into a dish of mercury and opened the end. The mercury ran down the tube, but not all the way. It stopped when the column stood about 76 centimetres above the mercury in the dish, and above it, at the top of the tube, was a space with nothing in it. In a letter dated 11 June 1644, Torricelli wrote the sentence this story is named for: Noi viviamo sommersi nel fondo d’un pelago d’aria. We live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air.

Step 1: What holds the mercury up

The first thought almost everyone has is that the empty space at the top is sucking the mercury up. Torricelli’s thought was the opposite, and it is the heart of the matter. Empty space has nothing in it, so it has nothing to pull with. What there is plenty of is air, pressing on the open surface of the mercury in the dish. We live at the bottom of a deep sea of air, and like water at the bottom of a sea, the air at the bottom is under pressure from all the air above it. That atmospheric pressure pushes down on the dish and so pushes mercury up the tube, and it keeps pushing until the weight of the column in the tube balances it. Then it stops. The height of the column is a measure of how hard the air is pushing: Torricelli had invented the barometer.

Step 2: Weighing the air

Now the pump makes sense. Mercury is 13.6 times as dense as water, so the air that can hold up 76 cm of mercury can hold up 13.6 × 0.76 = 10.3 m of water, and no more. A pump does not pull water up a pipe. It takes air out of the top of the pipe, and the air pressing on the well pushes the water up, until the column weighs as much as the air can hold. Ten metres is the end of the air’s rope, not the water’s.

You can also weigh the air. The pressure at sea level, about 101,000 newtons on every square metre, means that the column of air standing on a one-centimetre square, all the way to the top of the atmosphere, weighs about 10 newtons: it has a mass of about a kilogram. On a square metre that comes to about ten tonnes. Ten tonnes of air stands on every square metre of Marine Drive, and on every square metre of you. You are not crushed because the air pushes on every surface in every direction, up and sideways as well as down, and because the air and fluids inside your body push outward just as hard. Air pressure only hurts when it is unbalanced, which is the whole lesson of Step 4.

Step 3: Up the mountain

Puy de Dôme, 19 September 1648

If the air is an ocean with weight, then on a mountain there should be less of it above you, and the barometer should read lower. In France, Blaise Pascal wanted the test done and was too ill to climb, so on 19 September 1648 his brother-in-law Florin Périer carried a mercury tube up the Puy de Dôme, a mountain near Clermont. Périer did something that every good experiment since has copied: he left a second, identical tube at the bottom, in Clermont, with a priest watching it all day. On the summit the mercury stood about three inches, some 8 cm, lower than it had at the bottom. Back in Clermont, the tube that stayed behind had not moved all day. So the drop was not the weather and not the time of day. It was the mountain.

How much air did Périer climb above? Eight centimetres of mercury is a pressure of 13,600 × 9.8 × 0.08 ≈ 10,700 newtons per square metre.
Sea-level pressure is about 101,300, so the barometer had fallen by 10,700 ÷ 101,300 ≈ 10.5 per cent. Roughly a tenth of the ocean of air was below Périer’s feet.

Step 4: The horses

Regensburg, 1654

Otto von Guericke had built a pump that could take the air out of a vessel. In Regensburg in 1654, or a little later (the accounts disagree), he fitted two copper hemispheres together, pumped the air out of the inside, and hitched teams of horses to the two halves. The horses could not pull them apart. How many horses depends on who is telling the story: a letter of 1657 says twelve, most popular accounts say sixteen, and one says thirty. Say “teams of horses” and you are safe.

Nothing inside the Magdeburg hemispheres was holding them together, because there was almost nothing inside. The air outside was pushing in, on every square centimetre of copper, with nothing inside to push back. If the hemispheres were half a metre across (a round guess; the real size is not in this book’s sources), the area the air pushes on is about 0.2 m², and 0.2 × 101,000 ≈ 20,000 newtons, the weight of about two tonnes, holds the halves together. Let the air back in through a valve and the two halves come apart with no effort at all.

Step 5: Nothing sucks

Every one of these stories looks, at first, like something pulling: the empty space pulling mercury up the tube, the pump pulling water up the pipe, the empty hemispheres pulling each other shut, your mouth pulling a drink up a straw. In every case the truth is a push from the side with more air. A vacuum is a space with nothing, or almost nothing, in it, and nothing cannot pull. When you drink through a straw you lower the air pressure inside your mouth, and the ordinary air pressing on the surface of your drink pushes the drink up to fill the gap. Even a perfect vacuum in your mouth could lift water only 10.3 m; nobody drinks through a three-storey straw. Fill a glass to the brim, lay a card on it, turn it over above the sink and the card stays: the air pushes up on a card 10 cm square with about 1,000 newtons, the weight of a hundred kilograms, against a few newtons of water. Suction is not a force. It is the name people give to a push they cannot see.

Careful

“The straw sucks the drink up into my mouth.”

You cannot pull on a liquid with empty space. What you do is remove some air from your mouth, so that the air pushing on the drink in the glass is pushing harder than the air left in your mouth. The drink moves from the harder push towards the softer one. Nothing pulls; the room’s air does the pushing, down on the glass and up the straw.

At school

The word “suction” does not appear in your IGCSE syllabus. In an exam, explain that the air pressure outside is bigger and pushes. The syllabus does have Δp = ρgΔh: that is Torricelli’s column, with a deeper liquid giving a bigger pressure.

The card and the straw

Over the sink: fill a glass to the brim with water, lay a stiff, wet postcard flat on top so that it seals, hold the card in place with your palm and turn the glass upside down. Take your hand away. The card stays. Then dip a straw in a glass of water, put a fingertip over the top, and lift it out: the water stays in the straw until you lift your finger and let air in at the top. Name the pusher each time.

In Chapter 6 you weigh the air for yourself, follow pressure down into the sea, where it grows with every metre of depth, and find that the same growth with depth is what holds a ship up.

2023

The slow road to the Moon

ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 team

Sriharikota, 14 July 2023

At 14:35 on 14 July 2023 an LVM3 rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at Sriharikota carrying Chandrayaan-3. The spacecraft weighed about 3.9 tonnes: a propulsion module of 2,148 kg to do the travelling, and a lander of 1,752 kg, the Vikram lander, with a 26 kg rover called Pragyan folded inside it.

It did not fly to the Moon. Nothing does, directly. The rocket put it into a long thin loop around Earth, and then for three weeks the spacecraft went round and round, each loop a little bigger than the last, before it let go of Earth at all. The slow road is the physics of Chapter 5 made visible, so it is worth walking down it step by step.

Step 1: the parking orbit

The rocket’s job ended a few minutes after launch, with the spacecraft in an orbit that ISRO had planned as about 170 km above Earth at its lowest point and about 36,500 km at its highest. That shape is an ellipse, Kepler’s shape, with Earth at one focus; the low point is the perigee and the high point the apogee. Once there, no engine was running. The spacecraft was coasting, falling around Earth exactly as the Moon does, swinging fast through perigee and slow through apogee.

Step 2: loops that grow

Then came the firings, each one as the spacecraft swept through perigee. ISRO called them “Earth-bound perigee firings”. The engine burned for a while, the spacecraft gained speed along its path, and the engine stopped. Nothing visible happened at once; the spacecraft was still at perigee, still a couple of hundred kilometres up. The effect appeared half an orbit later. With more speed at the low point it coasted out further before gravity turned it round, so the apogee rose while the perigee hardly moved.

ISRO’s public updates record the orbit after each firing:

15 July, after the first firing: 173 × 41,762 km.
17 July, after the second: 226 × 41,603 km.
22 July, after the fourth: 233 × 71,351 km. (The update list skips the third firing and gives no orbit for a further one on 25 July.)
Kepler’s third law says a bigger orbit takes longer. Taking ISRO’s figures as heights above the surface, one lap took about 12.5 hours after the first firing and about 23.9 hours after the fourth.
At perigee of that fourth orbit the spacecraft was moving at about 10.6 km/s; at apogee, 71,000 km out, at about 0.9 km/s. Kepler’s second law in action: fast when near, slow when far.

Why loops rather than a straight shot? ISRO’s pages say what was done, not why, and this book will not guess for them. What the physics tells you is what each burn does: a short push at the fastest point of an orbit buys a big rise in its far point, and between pushes the spacecraft rides for free on gravity alone.

Step 3: letting go of Earth

On 1 August the engine fired once more at perigee, and this time the apogee leapt out to about 369,000 km: a loop that would reach the Moon’s distance. ISRO called the manoeuvre trans-lunar injection. For four days the spacecraft climbed, slowing all the way as Earth’s pull drew on it, towards a Moon that was moving along its own orbit to meet it.

Step 4: the brake behind the Moon

Here is the step most people get backwards. To be caught by the Moon, a spacecraft must slow down. Arriving from Earth, it is moving too fast for the Moon’s weak pull to hold; left alone it would not be captured. So on 5 August, at 19:12, as it passed its closest to the Moon, Chandrayaan-3 fired its engine against its own motion for 1,835 seconds, about half an hour. The Moon’s gravity closed round it, and it was in a lunar orbit, 164 km at its nearest and 18,074 km at its farthest, taking about 28 hours a lap. ISRO’s press release says the orbit was “as intended”.

The loops now shrank instead of growing: 170 × 4,313 km on 6 August, 174 × 1,437 km on 9 August, 151 × 179 km on 14 August and 153 × 163 km on 16 August, a near-circle about two hours round. On 17 August the lander separated from the propulsion module, which stayed behind in lunar orbit. By 20 August the lander was in a 25 × 134 km orbit, skimming within 25 km of the surface at its lowest.

Step 5: 18:04 on 23 August

The powered descent began on the afternoon of 23 August 2023, and at 18:04 Indian time Vikram touched down softly near 69.4° S. On 26 August the spot was named Shiv Shakti Point. Forty days had passed since launch, and eighteen since the brake behind the Moon.

The next day Pragyan rolled down its ramp. Over the following days it drove about 101 metres across the surface, and its laser instrument, which fires at a patch of soil and reads the colours in the flash, confirmed sulphur in the ground near the pole. A day on the Moon lasts about fourteen Earth days, with a night as long again, and the mission had been planned for one lunar day. On 4 September the lander and rover were put into sleep mode; on 22 September ISRO tried to re-establish contact, and that is where its public updates end.

Chandrayaan-3 had a predecessor. Chandrayaan-1 orbited the Moon in 2008 and 2009 carrying, among other instruments, NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper, which found the signature of water and hydroxyl in the lunar soil, announced on 24 September 2009. ISRO has also said that one of its own instruments on that mission saw water earlier; that claim is disputed.

Careful

“The engine fires to push the spacecraft outwards, away from Earth.”

Every one of the Earth-bound firings pushed it forwards along its path, at perigee, adding speed. The orbit stretched outward half a lap later, because a faster spacecraft coasts further before gravity turns it round. It is Newton’s cannon again: fire the ball faster and the loop gets longer.

Careful

“Once it was in orbit round the Moon it had basically landed.”

Eighteen days and a string of further manoeuvres separate the brake of 5 August from the touchdown of 23 August: the orbit had to be shrunk and rounded, the lander separated, and the final descent flown on its own engines. Getting into orbit is the easy half.

In Chapter 5 the Sky explorer’s mission tab plots every one of these ISRO orbits to scale, and Chapter 3 is where you learned how a rocket’s push changes its speed in the first place.

499

Aryabhata's boat

Aryabhata, Léon Foucault

Kusumapura (Patna), 499 CE

In the year 499, in Kusumapura, near today’s Patna, a young astronomer named Aryabhata finished a short book of mathematics and astronomy. He was about twenty-three. The book is called the Aryabhatiya after him, and scholars still argue about its exact date; some put it nearer 510. One of its claims was so far ahead of its time that people went on arguing against it for a thousand years.

The stars, he wrote, only seem to move. Just as a person in a moving boat sees the trees on the bank slide backwards, the stars seem to drift westward across the sky each night because the Earth turns beneath them.

Step 1: the boat

Think about the boat first, because it is the whole argument. Sit in a boat moving steadily down a river and look at the trees on the bank. They glide backwards past you. Nothing is happening to the trees. The motion is yours, and your eye has handed it to the shore.

Aryabhata’s point was that the night sky is the bank. The stars rise in the east, wheel overhead and set in the west because the ground under your feet is turning the other way, towards the east, carrying you with it.

Step 2: you cannot tell by looking

Here is why the argument lasted a thousand years. Watch the stars rise and set, as carefully as you like, and you cannot tell which of two things is happening: a huge sky turning around a still Earth once a day, or a still sky with a small Earth turning inside it. The two pictures predict exactly the same view. Seeing is not enough. You need an experiment that only one of the two pictures can pass.

Aryabhata chose the turning Earth. Most astronomers came round to the same view only in the 1600s, and the experiment that settled it did not arrive until 1851.

Step 3: why you don’t feel it

If Earth turns once a day, Mumbai is moving fast. Work it out: Mumbai’s circle of latitude is about 37,800 km round, and the city travels the whole of it in 24 hours.

Distance Mumbai travels in a day: 2 × π × 6,371 km × cos(19.08°) ≈ 37,800 km.
Speed: 37,800 km ÷ 24 h ≈ 1,580 km/h, which is about 440 metres every second.

Nobody feels it. That is not because the number is wrong but because of what you learned in Chapter 2: you never feel steady motion, only changes in it. On a local train at full speed you can pour a drink; it is the braking that throws everyone forward. Earth’s spin is the steadiest motion there is, and the only “change” in it is the gentle bending of your path round the axis once a day. That bending takes a pull of about 0.03 m/s², a third of one per cent of gravity. No bathroom scale in Mumbai is sensitive enough to notice it.

Step 4: shadows, not demons

Aryabhata made a second claim in the same book, and it was just as bold. An eclipse of the Moon, he said, is the Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon; an eclipse of the Sun is the Moon’s shadow falling on the Earth. The stories of his time blamed a demon that swallowed the Sun and the Moon. Aryabhata replaced the demon with geometry, and the geometry is the one we still use. The Moon-phases story works through it.

Step 5: the proof, 1,352 years later

The experiment that only a turning Earth can pass is a pendulum. In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a heavy bob, about 28 kg, from a wire about 67 m long under the dome of the Panthéon in Paris and set it swinging. A pendulum keeps swinging in the same plane; nothing about a swinging weight can make it turn. Yet over the hours the line of its swing drifted slowly round the floor. The pendulum was not turning. The floor was, and Paris with it. The newspapers asked their readers, “Have you seen the Earth turn?” That story has its own page in this book.

Two cautions, because websites exaggerate Aryabhata. He did not put the Sun at the centre of the universe, whatever you may read. And the suspiciously exact “accuracy” percentages quoted for his astronomy online have no good source behind them. What he did say was narrower and still remarkable: the ground is moving, and the sky is not.

Careful

“If the ground were really moving at 1,500 km/h we’d feel it, or be flung off.”

You feel changes in motion, never motion itself; that was Chapter 2’s whole point. Earth’s turn is perfectly steady, and the bending it gives your path is about a third of one per cent of gravity. Gravity wins by a factor of three hundred, and nobody is going anywhere.

Careful

“The Sun goes round us. I can see it move across the sky.”

You can see that the Sun and the ground change their angle to each other. That is all seeing can tell you. The trees seem to move past the boat too. The pendulum, not the eye, decided which one is turning.

The creeping shadow

On a sunny morning stand a pencil upright in a lump of clay, or push it through a bottle cap, on a balcony or windowsill that gets sun for a couple of hours. Every fifteen minutes, mark where the tip of its shadow falls. The marks creep along in a line. The Sun crosses the sky at fifteen degrees an hour, so in two hours it has moved thirty degrees, and your pencil’s shadow has swung round to show it. Then ask Aryabhata’s question: what moved, the Sun or the floor? Never look directly at the Sun.

In Chapter 14 the turning Earth gives you day and night, and in Chapter 2 you already met the reason you never feel it.

1666 to 1687

The apple and the Moon

Isaac Newton, Edmond Halley

Woolsthorpe, Lincolnshire, 1666

In 1666 Isaac Newton was twenty-three and living at his mother’s farmhouse in Woolsthorpe, a village in the English county of Lincolnshire. Cambridge, where he was a student, had closed because of plague, and he had a great deal of time to think. There was an apple tree in the garden. There still is.

Sixty years later, as an old man, he told a friend called William Stukeley that his thinking about gravity had been “occasion’d by the fall of an apple, as he sat in contemplative mood”. That is the whole of the evidence: one memory, told six decades after the event. The apple did not hit him on the head. That detail was added by other people, and a librarian at the Royal Society has called the finished story “an 18th-century sound bite”. So treat the apple as the story goes, not as a fact.

The question behind it is real, though, and it is one of the best questions anyone has ever asked. An apple falls. The Moon, hanging in the same sky, does not. Why not?

Newton’s answer was that it does.

Step 1: the Moon is falling

Think back to Chapter 2. A thing left alone keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed. The Moon does not move in a straight line; it goes round us in a near-circle, month after month. So something must be bending its path towards Earth, all the time. Whatever that something is, it pulls the Moon towards us, and a pull towards us is exactly what makes an apple fall.

Why, then, does the Moon not land on us? Because it is also moving sideways, fast: about 1 km every second. In each second it falls a little towards Earth, but it also moves a long way along, so it ends up at the same height, a little further round. It falls around Earth instead of into it. Chapter 5 and the story of Newton’s cannon make that idea do real work; here we only need the first half of it. The Moon is falling.

Step 2: how far does it fall?

Here is the sum Newton did, with today’s numbers. From the size of the Moon’s orbit and the time it takes, you can work out how much its path bends. In one second, the Moon ends up 1.36 mm below the straight line it would have followed with no pull at all. One millimetre and a bit, in a second. That is a gentle fall.

Now wait a minute instead of a second. Falls grow with the square of the time, so in sixty seconds the Moon drops 60 × 60 = 3,600 times as far: about 4.9 metres below its straight line.

An apple dropped from your hand falls 4.9 metres in its first second.

So the Moon, in a minute, falls what an apple falls in a second. Earth pulls on each kilogram of the Moon 3,600 times more weakly than it pulls on each kilogram of apple.

Step 3: sixty times further, 3,600 times weaker

Now the second number. How far away is the Moon? About 384,000 km from Earth’s centre, while the apple is 6,371 km from Earth’s centre, down at the surface. Divide: the Moon is about 60 times further from Earth’s centre than the apple is.

Sixty times further. Three thousand six hundred times weaker. And 60 × 60 = 3,600.

That is the pattern Newton saw, and it is called the inverse square law: double the distance and the pull drops to a quarter; triple it and the pull drops to a ninth; sixty times the distance and the pull drops to one part in 3,600. “Inverse” because the pull goes down as the distance goes up; “square” because it is the distance squared that matters.

Newton’s check, in modern numbers.
Pull on an apple at the surface: 9.8 m/s² (every kilogram gains 9.8 m/s of speed each second it falls).
Predicted pull at the Moon, 60 times further away: 9.8 ÷ 60² = 9.8 ÷ 3,600 = 0.0027 m/s².
Pull actually needed to bend the Moon’s path into its orbit (from its distance and its 27.3-day month): 0.0027 m/s².
They match. Newton himself found that his two numbers agreed, in his words, “pretty nearly”. With today’s figures the leftover difference is under 1%, and it comes from the Moon’s slightly oval orbit and from Earth moving too.

Why a square, and not just “weaker with distance”? Picture a torch. Its light spreads out as it travels. At twice the distance the same light covers a patch twice as wide and twice as tall, so four times the area, and each bit of the wall gets a quarter as much. Gravity is not light, but it spreads out through space in the same way: the same influence, shared over a bigger and bigger sphere. The sphere’s area grows with the square of its radius, and that is where the square comes from.

Step 4: the same rule for everything

Newton did not stop at Earth and the Moon. He proposed that every lump of matter pulls on every other lump, with a force that grows with both masses and shrinks with the square of the distance between them. That is universal gravitation, and “universal” is the daring word. The same pull that drops a mango on Marine Drive holds the Moon in its month, holds Earth in its year around the Sun, and, in Chapter 5, steers Chandrayaan-3.

Two things about this rule surprise people.

First, it works both ways. Earth pulls the Moon, and the Moon pulls Earth back with exactly the same force. That is the third law from Chapter 3. The effects differ only because the masses differ: the Moon swings round a big loop, while Earth wobbles round a small one. In fact both of them circle a shared balance point that lies about 1,700 km below Earth’s surface.

Second, the pull is tiny between ordinary things. Two 1 kg bags of sugar a metre apart attract each other with about 0.000 000 000 07 newtons, far too little to feel, which is why the kitchen does not slide together. It took until 1798 for Henry Cavendish to measure a pull that small, inside a shed at Clapham, and so weigh the whole Earth.

Step 5: Halley’s question

In August 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley visited Newton in Cambridge with a question. Suppose the Sun pulls a planet with a force that weakens with the square of the distance. What path would the planet follow?

An ellipse, said Newton: the very shape Kepler had found from Tycho’s measurements of Mars seventy-five years earlier. He had worked it out already. He could not find the paper.

Halley pressed him to write it all down properly. The result, three years later, was the Principia of 1687, the book that joined the falling apple and the orbiting Moon under one rule, and that Halley ended up paying to print himself.

Careful

“There’s no gravity in space. That’s why the Moon doesn’t fall down.”

Eight out of ten thirteen-year-olds believe something like this. But the Moon is falling, 1.36 mm every second, and the only thing that can be pulling it is Earth’s gravity, reaching across 384,000 km of empty space. It is weak out there, one part in 3,600 of the pull at the ground, but weak is not nothing. Weak is exactly what keeps the Moon in its month.

Careful

“So the Moon gets 1.36 mm closer to Earth every second.”

No. It falls 1.36 mm below the straight line it would otherwise follow. Because it is also moving sideways at about 1 km/s, that straight line was carrying it away from Earth, and the fall just cancels the drift. Its distance from Earth stays almost the same, month after month.

The torch and the wall

Take a phone torch into a dark room and shine it at a wall from one metre away. Mark the edges of the bright patch with your fingers, or stick two bits of tape. Now step back to two metres. The patch is about twice as wide and twice as tall, so it covers about four times the area, and it looks dimmer, because the same light is shared out over four times as much wall. Three metres gives nine times the area. That spreading, one over the distance squared, is the same pattern gravity follows.

In Chapter 5 you will do Newton’s sum yourself, with the real numbers, and then see why the astronauts on the space station float even though gravity up there is still at 89% strength. The answer, as with the Moon, is that they are falling too.

1576 to 1609

Eight minutes of arc

Tycho Brahe, Johannes Kepler

Hven, 1576

In 1576 the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe began building an observatory called Uraniborg on Hven, a small island in the strait between Denmark and Sweden. There were no telescopes yet; Galileo would not point one at the sky for another thirty-three years. Tycho measured positions with great sighting instruments and his own eyes, and he did it night after night for about twenty years: the Sun, the Moon, and above all the planet Mars.

What made Tycho different was not the instruments. It was his refusal to stop. Astronomers before him had taken a few good measurements and fitted a theory to them. Tycho measured everything, over and over, and his positions disagreed with the published tables of where the planets ought to be.

Prague, 1600

In February 1600 a young German mathematician called Johannes Kepler arrived in Prague to work with Tycho, who had moved there. The two did not have long together. Tycho died in October 1601, and Kepler ended up with the measurements, twenty years of them. (You may read that Tycho was poisoned. That is speculation; his remains were examined in 2010 and the result settled nothing.)

Kepler set out to find the true path of Mars.

Step 1: everyone knew it was a circle

Astronomers had always drawn the planets’ paths as circles, or as circles carried round on other circles. A circle was the perfect shape and the heavens were supposed to be perfect. Nobody seriously asked whether the shape was right; they asked how to arrange the circles.

Kepler began the same way. He built the best circular orbit for Mars that he could, with every allowance the old methods permitted, and compared it with Tycho’s positions.

Step 2: eight minutes of arc

The best circle missed. At some points Mars was eight minutes of arc away from where the circle said it should be.

How big is that? Astronomers measure positions in the sky as angles. A full turn is 360 degrees, and each degree is 60 minutes of arc. The full Moon is about 31 minutes of arc across. Eight minutes is about a quarter of the Moon’s width.

Full Moon’s width: 0.52 degrees = 0.52 × 60 = 31 minutes of arc.
Kepler’s gap: 8 minutes of arc.
8 ÷ 31 = 0.26, about a quarter of a Moon’s width.

That is a small gap. Earlier astronomers would have lived with it, because measurements before Tycho were not good enough to argue with. But Kepler knew how carefully Tycho had worked, and he made a decision that is the whole story: he trusted the measurements more than he trusted the circle. If Tycho’s Mars would not sit on a circle, then Mars did not move on a circle.

Step 3: the shape that fitted

After years of calculation Kepler found the shape. It is an ellipse: the curve you get with two pins, a loop of string and a pencil. Push two pins into a board, loop the string loosely round both, pull it tight with the pencil and draw. Wherever the pencil goes, its distance to one pin plus its distance to the other adds up to the same total, the length of the string. The two pin positions are the ellipse’s foci, a word Kepler himself gave them.

For a planet, the Sun sits at one focus. The other focus is empty space.

Here is the part most drawings get wrong. Mars’s orbit is only very slightly oval. Its nearest distance to the Sun is 0.83 of its farthest, and drawn to scale the orbit looks like a circle with the Sun placed a little off centre, by about 9% of the orbit’s radius. That off-centre Sun, not any visible squashing, is what Tycho’s eight minutes had been pointing at. Kepler was lucky in his planet, too. Of the planets known then, only Mercury’s orbit is more oval than Mars’s; had he started with Venus or Earth, whose orbits are far rounder, Tycho’s data would never have revealed the shape.

Step 4: three laws

Kepler published the ellipse in 1609, in a book called Astronomia Nova, the New Astronomy, together with a second discovery. A planet does not move at a steady speed. It hurries when it is near the Sun and dawdles when it is far away, in such a way that a line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Ten years later, in 1619, he added a third rule linking a planet’s year to its distance: the square of the time it takes to go round is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. Together these are Kepler’s laws.

The third law, with Mars. Measure distances in Earth–Sun distances (1 for Earth) and times in years. Then (years)² = (distance)³.
Mars takes 1.88 years to go round. So 1.88² = 3.53 = distance³, and the distance is the cube root of 3.53, about 1.52.
Mars is about 1.52 times as far from the Sun as Earth is: 1.52 × 150 million km ≈ 228 million km. Kepler could find that from a calendar and arithmetic, with no measuring tape to the planet.

Step 5: how, but not why

Kepler’s laws describe. They tell you what the planets do, to the limit of Tycho’s eyes, and they say nothing about why. The why arrived seventy-five years later, when Edmond Halley asked Isaac Newton what path a body would take under a pull that weakens with the square of the distance, and Newton answered: an ellipse. The gravity story tells that part. Kepler’s ellipses are the measurements that Newton’s law had to explain, and did.

Careful

“Planets go round the Sun in long squashed ovals.”

Only in diagrams, which exaggerate so that you can see the shape. Mars’s orbit is a circle to the eye, and Earth’s is rounder still. The real signature of an ellipse is not squashing; it is the Sun sitting off centre, at a focus.

Careful

“The Sun is at the centre of the ellipse.”

It is not. It sits at one of the two foci, the pins. The centre of the ellipse is empty, and so is the other focus. For Mars the Sun is about 9% of the orbit’s radius away from the centre.

Draw Mars

Push two drawing pins into the flap of a cardboard box, 2 cm apart. Make a loop of thread about 22 cm round, hook it over both pins, pull it tight with a pencil and draw all the way round, keeping the thread taut. You have drawn Mars’s orbit to scale: an ellipse so round that its far ends are only about half a millimetre short of a circle. Now move the pins 8 cm apart, keep the same loop, and draw again; that is the squashed shape the textbook pictures show. Finally put both pins in the same hole, and the ellipse becomes a circle.

In Chapter 5 you will meet the ellipse again as the path every satellite and planet must follow, and you will see why Newton’s inverse-square pull allows no other shape.

Any month

The orange and the lamp

Mumbai, any clear evening

Just after sunset, low in the west, a thin curve of light hangs over the sea: a new crescent Moon. A week later it is a half-disc high in the evening sky. A week after that a full Moon rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west. Then it shrinks again, rising later each night, until it is gone and the cycle starts over.

Ask people what the dark part of the crescent is and about four in ten will say it is the Earth’s shadow. It is a sensible guess. It is also wrong, and finding out why teaches you more about the Moon than any list of phase names.

Step 1: half lit, always

The Moon makes no light of its own. It is a ball of rock in sunlight, and like any ball in sunlight one half of it is lit and the other half is dark. That is true every hour of every day. The Moon is never more or less than half lit. What changes is how much of the lit half is turned towards you.

Step 2: the orange and the lamp

You can see the whole cycle in a minute. Take an orange into a dark room with one lamp on. Hold the orange at arm’s length. Now turn slowly on the spot, keeping the orange in front of you.

When you face the lamp, the orange is between you and the light and you see its dark side: that is new Moon. Turn a quarter of the way round and you see one half lit, one half dark: first quarter. Turn until the lamp is behind you and the orange is fully lit: full Moon. Keep turning and the lit part shrinks back through a half and a thin curve to nothing. At every moment half the orange is lit; you simply see it from a different angle. Your head stood for the Earth, and not once did its shadow touch the orange.

That is all the phases of the Moon are: one lit half, viewed from different angles as the Moon goes round the Earth once a month. A phase thinner than a half is a crescent; fatter than a half is gibbous; the Moon is waxing while the lit part grows and waning while it shrinks.

Step 3: why it is not Earth’s shadow

Two facts kill the shadow idea. First, Earth’s shadow points directly away from the Sun, like your own shadow on a sunny afternoon. At first quarter the Moon stands a right angle away from the Sun in the sky, nowhere near where the shadow points. A thin crescent is even closer to the Sun’s side of the sky, which is why you see it in the west just after sunset. The dark part of the crescent is simply the Moon’s own night side, turned towards you.

Second, when Earth’s shadow does fall on the Moon, we have a name for it: a lunar eclipse. It can happen only at full Moon, when the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, and even then it happens only now and then. If phases were Earth’s shadow, the full Moon would be the dark one, not the bright one.

Step 4: the month

The Moon goes once round the Earth relative to the stars in 27.3 days, but the cycle of phases takes a little longer, 29.5 days, because in that time Earth has moved some way round the Sun and the Moon needs a couple of extra days to catch up with the new direction of the sunlight.

Each day the Moon moves 360° ÷ 29.5 ≈ 12° further round the sky relative to the Sun.
Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so it takes 24 × 60 × 12 ÷ 360 ≈ 49 extra minutes to bring the Moon back over the horizon.
That is why the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day, and why the full Moon, which sits opposite the Sun, rises at sunset and stands highest at midnight. The first-quarter Moon rises around noon.

Step 5: eclipses, and why they are rare

An eclipse is a shadow, which is exactly what Aryabhata said in the year 499. A solar eclipse is the Moon’s shadow falling on Earth; it can happen only at new Moon, when the Moon is between us and the Sun. A lunar eclipse is Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon, at full Moon.

So why isn’t there an eclipse every month, at every new and full Moon? Because the Moon’s orbit is tilted by about 5° compared with Earth’s orbit round the Sun. Most months, at new Moon, the Moon passes a little above or below the Sun in the sky and its shadow misses Earth; at full Moon it passes above or below Earth’s shadow. The tilt sounds small, but at the Moon’s distance it lifts the Moon as much as 34,000 km off the line, and Earth is only 6,371 km in radius. The shadow misses by a long way. Only twice a year, when the line where the two orbits cross points towards the Sun, do new and full Moons line up well enough for eclipses, and those few weeks are called eclipse seasons.

One more coincidence makes solar eclipses so dramatic. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost the same size in our sky, about half a degree each. The Moon can just cover the Sun. During a lunar eclipse the Moon does not go black but a deep coppery red, because some sunlight bends through Earth’s atmosphere into the shadow, the same bending that makes sunsets orange in Chapter 11.

One warning that is not optional. Never look at the Sun, eclipse or no eclipse: not with your eyes, not through sunglasses, not through anything dark. Even a brief look can damage your eyes. The safe way to watch a partial solar eclipse is a pinhole: a 1 mm hole in a card, with the Sun’s image projected onto a second card held behind it.

Careful

“The dark part of the Moon is the Earth’s shadow.”

Earth’s shadow points straight away from the Sun. A crescent Moon is on the Sun’s side of the sky; the shadow is nowhere near it. The dark part is the Moon’s own night. Earth’s shadow does reach the Moon now and then, and that is a lunar eclipse, which happens only at full Moon.

Careful

“The far side of the Moon is the dark side.”

The Moon keeps the same face towards Earth, so there is a far side we never see from here. But it is lit for half of every month, like every other part of the Moon: at new Moon the far side is in full sunlight. There is a far side. There is no permanently dark side.

The orange and the lamp

Find a dark room with a single lamp, or a phone torch propped on a shelf. Stand about two metres from it, hold an orange at arm’s length a little above your head so that your own shadow does not fall on it, and turn slowly on the spot. Watch the lit part of the orange: new, crescent, half, gibbous, full, and back again. Stop at first quarter and check where the lamp is: a right angle away from the orange, exactly as the real first-quarter Moon is a right angle from the Sun.

Chapter 14 puts this on the screen in the Sky explorer, where you can drag the Moon round its orbit and tilt the orbit to see when eclipses can happen; and Chapter 10 is where shadows and straight-line light began.

1687

Falling around the Earth

Isaac Newton

Cambridge, 1687

In 1687 Isaac Newton published the Principia, the book in which the fall of an apple and the orbit of the Moon became one rule. A second account of the same ideas, The System of the World, was printed in 1731, four years after his death, and it contains a drawing that has been copied into physics books ever since: a mountain, impossibly tall, with a cannon on top.

Nobody has ever fired that cannon. It is a thought experiment, and it is still the clearest explanation of an orbit anyone has given.

Step 1: the cannon on the mountain

Put the mountain so high that there is no air up there to slow anything down, and fire the cannon exactly sideways. After the ball leaves the barrel only one thing acts on it: gravity, pulling it down. The ball curves towards the ground and lands some way off.

Fire harder. The ball travels further before it lands. Harder again, and further again. Now notice something about the ground. Earth is round, so as the ball travels, the ground beneath it curves away. A slow ball reaches the ground long before that matters. But a fast enough ball falls towards the ground at exactly the rate the ground curves away beneath it. It falls, and keeps falling, and never gets any nearer the surface. It goes all the way round and arrives back at the mountain from behind. That is an orbit: a fall that keeps missing.

At Earth’s surface the speed that does this is about 7.9 km every second; call it 8 km/s. Fire faster than that and the ball swings out into a longer loop, an ellipse, coming back round to the mountain each time. Fire at about 11 km/s and it never comes back at all: it has escaped.

How fast is 8 km/s?
The Bandra–Worli Sea Link is 5.6 km long.
At 7.9 km/s the cannonball would cross the whole bridge in 5.6 ÷ 7.9 = 0.7 seconds.

Step 2: nothing holds a satellite up

The cannonball shows what every satellite is doing. Nothing holds it up. No engine pushes it along. Once it is above the air there is nothing to slow it, so it keeps its sideways speed, and gravity keeps bending its path round. It is falling, continuously, and continuously missing. The hard part of space travel is not staying up; it is reaching that sideways speed in the first place.

The International Space Station, the ISS, is a cannonball of this kind: about 400 km above the ground, moving at about 7.7 km/s, once round Earth every 92 minutes or so, which is fifteen or sixteen sunrises a day. Even at 400 km there is a whisper of air, which is why very low orbits slowly decay; but that is friction’s doing, not gravity’s.

One more thing the cannon tells you: the ball’s mass never came into it. A heavy ball and a light ball fired at the same speed follow the same path, just as the two coins in Chapter 4 landed together. Every satellite at the same height goes at the same speed, whether it is a one-kilogram cube or the 420-tonne station.

Step 3: why the astronauts float

Here is the puzzle the whole of Chapter 5 is built around. Gravity at the height of the station is not zero. Work it out: the station is 6,371 + 400 = 6,771 km from Earth’s centre, against 6,371 km for you.

Pull at the station compared with the ground = (6,371 ÷ 6,771)² = 0.885.
Gravity up there is about 89% as strong as in your kitchen.

So why do the astronauts float?

Think about a lift whose cable has snapped. The lift falls; you fall with it; the floor drops away from under your feet at exactly the rate you fall, so it stops pressing on them. Let go of a pen and it hangs beside you, because it is falling too. For as long as the fall lasts, you float. Gravity has not gone anywhere. Gravity is doing the pulling.

The station is a lift whose cable has snapped, except that it is moving sideways at 7.7 km/s, so it falls around Earth and the fall never ends. Everyone and everything inside is falling together. Nothing presses on anyone’s feet. And the press of the floor on your feet is the thing you actually feel as weight: take it away and you feel weightless, with gravity at 89% all the while.

At school

At school, weight means the gravitational force on a mass. In that language an astronaut on the ISS still has weight, about 89% of her weight on the ground. What she has lost is the feeling of it, because nothing is holding her up. Say “feels weightless” and you are right in both languages.

Step 4: your phone can feel it

The free phyphox app reads your phone’s motion sensor. Open “Acceleration (with g)” and lay the phone on a table: it reads about 9.8 m/s². That is not gravity it is sensing; it is the table pushing up. Now hold the phone over a pillow and let go. During the fall the reading drops to about zero. For a third of a second your phone is exactly where the astronauts are: falling, with nothing pushing on it, weightless with gravity at full strength.

Careful

“There’s no gravity up there. That’s why they float.”

Then what bends the station’s path into a circle fifteen or sixteen times a day? Gravity at 400 km is 89% of ground strength. The astronauts float because they and the station are falling together, not because the pull has stopped. The lift with the snapped cable is the honest picture.

Careful

“Satellites stay up because they’re above the air.”

Being above the air only stops them slowing down. What keeps them up is sideways speed: about 7.7 km/s at 400 km, enough to keep missing the ground. Take that speed away and a satellite would fall straight down like a dropped stone, air or no air.

The weightless phone

Install phyphox and open “Acceleration (with g)”. Put the phone flat on a table and read about 9.8 m/s². Now hold it about 40 cm above a soft pillow or a folded blanket, start recording, and let it drop. Look at the graph: the reading falls to almost zero for about a third of a second, then jumps as the pillow catches it. That dip is free fall, the same thing an astronaut feels all day. Keep the drop small and the landing soft.

In Chapter 5 Newton’s cannon comes alive on the screen and you can fire it yourself. In Chapter 4 you met a dropped coin and a flicked coin landing at the same moment; a satellite is the flicked coin, flicked hard enough to miss the whole world.

1758 to 1846

The planet found with a pen

Edmond Halley, Nicole-Reine Lepaute, Alexis Clairaut, Jérôme Lalande, Johann Georg Palitzsch, Urbain Le Verrier, Johann Galle

Near Dresden, Christmas night, 1758

On the night of 25 December 1758 a farmer called Johann Georg Palitzsch, who studied the sky in his spare time from his fields near Dresden, saw a faint comet. He was the first person on Earth to see it. Astronomers across Europe had been searching for it for months, because this comet had an appointment.

Edmond Halley, the friend who had badgered Newton into writing the Principia, had worked out that a comet seen before would come back on a long orbit, and had said it would return in 1758. By then Halley had been dead for sixteen years. The comet kept the appointment all the same, and it has been Halley’s comet ever since.

Step 1: three people and a mountain of arithmetic

Halley’s prediction was not quite enough on its own, because a comet does not feel only the Sun. On its way out and back it passes the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn, and each of them tugs at it, speeding it up or slowing it down a little. Those tugs shift the date of its return. Newton’s law tells you exactly how big each tug is at each moment, but there is no neat formula for adding them all up over decades. The only way is to calculate the path step by small step.

In Paris, three people did that: the mathematician Alexis Clairaut, the astronomer Jérôme Lalande, and Nicole-Reine Lepaute, who did a great share of the calculating. Over months of work they predicted that the comet would pass closest to the Sun around the middle of April 1759. Palitzsch saw it on Christmas night, three and a half months before that closest pass, as it came in.

A comet’s path is a very long ellipse, far longer than any planet’s. It spends most of its time crawling through the cold far reaches of its orbit, then rushes through its closest pass to the Sun in a few weeks. Every nudge along the way shifts when that rush arrives.

Step 2: a nudge is a message

Now the idea. Each small tug of one body on another, pulling an orbit off the plain ellipse that Kepler would have drawn, is called a perturbation. The Paris team used perturbations in the obvious direction: they knew where Jupiter and Saturn were, so they could work out how the comet would be nudged. But you can run the arithmetic backwards. If something is being nudged and you can measure the nudge, you can work out where the nudger must be. A pull is a message about the thing that is doing the pulling.

That reversal is what found a planet.

Berlin, 23 September 1846

The planet Uranus was drifting off course. Year after year it strayed from the positions that the tables, worked out from Newton’s law, said it should occupy. In Paris, Urbain Le Verrier took the drift as a message. He supposed that an unseen planet beyond Uranus was tugging it, and he calculated where that planet would have to be to produce exactly the drift observed. Then he wrote the position in a letter and posted it to Johann Galle at the Berlin observatory.

The letter arrived on 23 September 1846. That same night Galle and his assistant Heinrich d’Arrest pointed their telescope where the letter said, and there, within about one degree of Le Verrier’s position, was a planet nobody had ever knowingly seen. It was named Neptune.

How close is one degree? The full Moon is about half a degree across.
Le Verrier’s pen had put Neptune within about two Moon-widths of where it really was, in a sky that measures 360 degrees all the way round.

Two footnotes belong to the story. In England, John Couch Adams had made a similar calculation, but his position was about 12° out, some two dozen Moon-widths, and it played no part in the discovery. And James Challis had actually seen Neptune twice while searching, and had not recognised it as a planet. Seeing is not the same as knowing what you have seen.

Step 3: why it mattered

Newton’s law had been built to explain the apple and the Moon, and then the planets already known. Here it reached past everything it had been made for: it took a wobble in one planet and said there is another one, there, look. That is the strongest test a law of nature can pass, a prediction of something nobody has seen, and it is why Neptune is called the first planet discovered by mathematics.

It is also a warning against overconfidence. The law is simple; the sky is not. With two bodies, the Sun and one planet, Newton’s law gives a perfect ellipse. Add a third and there is no exact answer at all, only step-by-step arithmetic that Lepaute and her colleagues did by hand for months and that computers now do in seconds. The Moon’s own motion, pulled by both Earth and Sun, kept the best mathematicians of the 1700s busy for the whole century.

Careful

“Newton’s law predicts the sky perfectly.”

It predicts the sky very well, which is different. Every extra body adds tugs that can only be followed step by step; that is why the Paris team needed months for one comet, and why Uranus’s tables went wrong in the first place: they left out a planet nobody knew about.

Careful

“Halley discovered Halley’s comet.”

He never saw its 1758 return; he had died in 1742. What he did was recognise that a comet seen before would come back, and say when. The comet carries his name because he predicted it, not because he found it. A farmer near Dresden found it.

In Chapter 5 the comet comes back as the chapter’s closing puzzle, and the small tugs that found Neptune are at work on every orbit in that chapter, Chandrayaan-3’s included.

1987

Harvard graduates and the seasons

Twenty-three Harvard graduates and professors

Harvard, 1987

In 1987 a film crew went to Harvard University on graduation day and asked the new graduates, and some of their professors, a question a child might ask: why is it hotter in summer than in winter? The film is called A Private Universe, and by the usual count twenty-one of the twenty-three people they asked got it wrong. Most gave the same wrong answer, the one most people give: in summer the Earth is closer to the Sun.

The film is famous because the people in it were not ignorant. They had just finished degrees at one of the hardest universities in the world. They had a wrong idea that felt obviously right, and nobody had ever made them check it. Let’s check it.

Step 1: the distance idea cannot be right

Earth’s path around the Sun is very nearly a circle, but not quite, so its distance from the Sun does change through the year. Here is the first problem for the distance idea: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, at about 147.1 million km. That point is called perihelion. It is farthest, at aphelion, about 152.1 million km, in early July. January is Mumbai’s coolest month and the depth of winter across the northern half of the world. If closeness made summer, January would be summer.

Here is the second problem. When it is summer in Mumbai it is winter in Australia, and they are the same distance from the Sun; it is one planet. Distance cannot give two halves of the world opposite seasons at the same moment.

How much does the distance matter at all?
Farthest ÷ nearest = 152.1 ÷ 147.1 = 1.034, so Earth is 3.4% farther away in July than in January.
Sunlight weakens with the square of the distance (the same pattern as in the gravity story), so the Sun’s light is 1.034² = 1.07 times stronger in January: about 7% more, and it arrives in the coolest month. Whatever makes seasons, it is not this.

Step 2: the tilt

The real cause is a tilt. Earth spins round an axis, the line through the North and South Poles, and that axis is not upright with respect to its orbit. It leans over by 23.4°, and, this is the important part, it leans the same way in space all year round, pointing at the same distant stars. Astronomers call it the axial tilt.

So as Earth goes round the Sun there is a time of year when the northern half leans towards the Sun (June) and a time when it leans away (December). In between, at the two equinox points in March and September, neither half leans towards the Sun, and day and night are each about twelve hours long everywhere on Earth. The June and December extremes are the solstices.

The tilt does two things to the sunlight, and both matter.

Step 3: the slanting torch

Shine a torch straight down at the floor and you get a small bright patch. Tilt the torch and the same light spreads over a longer, dimmer patch. Every square centimetre in the slanted patch gets less light, because the same light has been shared over more floor.

The Sun is the torch. In June the noon Sun stands very high over Mumbai, so its light falls almost straight down. In December it is much lower and its light arrives at a slant, spread over more ground, so each square metre of Mumbai is warmed less.

Mumbai’s noon Sun. Mumbai is at latitude 19.1° N. At the June solstice the Sun stands overhead at latitude 23.4° N; at the December solstice at 23.4° S; at the equinoxes over the equator.
June: the Sun is 23.4 − 19.1 = 4.3° north of overhead, so it stands 90 − 4.3 = 85.7° high. Almost straight up.
Equinoxes: 90 − 19.1 = 70.9° high.
December: 90 − (19.1 + 23.4) = 47.5° high.
The light landing on each square metre of flat ground goes with the sine of the Sun’s height: sin 85.7° ÷ sin 47.5° = 1.35. Noon light is about 35% stronger in June than in December, before the clouds have their say.

Step 4: longer days

The second effect is time. When your half of Earth leans towards the Sun it spends more of each turn in the sunlit half, so the days are longer and the Sun has more hours to warm the ground. In Mumbai the longest day, in June, is about 13.2 hours from sunrise to sunset, and the shortest, in December, about 10.9 hours: a swing of about 2.3 hours.
