Far from the equator the swing is enormous, and near the poles the Sun does not set at all in midsummer. Mumbai’s swing is mild, which is one reason Mumbai’s year feels so different from Europe’s.

Step 5: Mumbai’s year

Mumbai lies inside the tropics, the band of the Earth where the Sun can pass directly overhead. Twice a year, once in May on its way north and once in July on its way back, the noon Sun stands exactly overhead and a straight pole casts no shadow at all. Between those two dates the noon Sun is in the northern half of the sky, which surprises people who have learned that the Sun is “always in the south”.

Near the equator, astronomers say, the seasons are the wet one and the dry one; sunlight hardly changes. Mumbai is not on the equator, but its year is marked more by the monsoon, which normally arrives around 11 June, than by any swing in temperature. One more subtlety: the warmest weeks of a year come some time after the solstice, not on it, because land, sea and air take weeks to heat up.

Careful

“It’s summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun.”

Earth is closest in January. Australia has summer in December at the same distance as Mumbai’s winter. The distance changes the Sun’s light by about 7%, in the wrong direction. The tilt changes the height of the noon Sun over Mumbai from 47° to 86°, and the day from 10.9 to 13.2 hours. That is the cause.

Careful

“All right, it’s the tilt: the half that leans towards the Sun is a bit closer to it, so it’s hotter.”

The lean brings the northern half nearer the Sun by at most a few thousand kilometres, out of 150 million. That is a change of a few thousandths of one per cent: nothing. The tilt matters because it changes the angle the light arrives at and the hours it shines for, not the distance.

At school

The IGCSE syllabus says that Earth orbits the Sun once in about 365 days, and uses the orbit to explain why the seasons repeat each year. That is right about the repeating. The reason seasons happen at all is the tilt.

Count the squares

You need a phone torch and a sheet of squared paper in a dim room. Hold the torch 20 cm above the paper, pointing straight down, and count roughly how many squares the bright patch covers. Now keep the torch at the same height but tilt it to about 45°, so the light falls on the paper at a slant. Count again. The same light is spread over many more squares, and each square is dimmer. That is what December’s noon Sun does to Mumbai.

In Chapter 14 this becomes the Sky explorer: drag the date and watch the noon Sun climb over Mumbai. In Chapter 5 you will see why Earth’s orbit, like Mars’s, is so nearly a circle that the 3.4% hardly shows.

2024

A spacecraft that never stops watching the Sun

ISRO's Aditya-L1 team

Between the Earth and the Sun, 6 January 2024

On 6 January 2024, about 1.5 million km from Earth in the direction of the Sun, an Indian spacecraft called Aditya-L1 fired its engines and settled into an orbit around a point in empty space. Not around a planet, not around a moon: around a point, with nothing there. ISRO calls the path a halo orbit, and one loop of it takes about 178 days.

The point has a name, L1, the first Lagrange point, and to understand why anyone would park a spacecraft there you need two ideas you have already met: Kepler’s third law, and the adding-up of pulls.

Step 1: the problem

Aditya-L1 is a Sun-watcher, built for an uninterrupted view, day and night, year after year. From the ground that is impossible: night, clouds and the whole blurring atmosphere get in the way. From a low orbit round Earth it is not much better, because for part of every lap the Earth itself is between the spacecraft and the Sun. What you want is a spot that stays on the sunward side of Earth, out of Earth’s shadow, for ever. The obvious idea is to put the spacecraft a little nearer the Sun than Earth and let it travel round the Sun alongside us.

Step 2: the catch

Kepler’s third law says that cannot work, at first glance. A body orbiting the Sun on a smaller circle takes less time to go round. Put a spacecraft 1.5 million km sunward of Earth, give it an ordinary orbit of its own, and it would lap the Sun in about 360 days instead of 365. It would gain five and a half days on Earth every year, drift steadily ahead, and within a few decades be on the far side of the Sun.

Period of a free orbit at Earth’s distance from the Sun: 365.3 days.
Period of a free orbit 1.5 million km closer in, with Earth’s pull switched off: about 359.8 days.
Difference: about 5.5 days a year. Half a lap is 183 days, so the spacecraft would be on the far side of the Sun after 183 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 33 years.

Step 3: Earth’s pull fixes it

Now switch Earth’s pull back on. From that spot, Earth lies directly away from the Sun, so Earth pulls the spacecraft away from the Sun, in exactly the opposite direction to the Sun’s pull. Earth’s pull there is small, about 3% of the Sun’s, but it subtracts. The spacecraft feels a little less inward pull than the Sun alone would give it.

And a little less inward pull is exactly what a slower orbit needs. To go round in 365 days rather than 360 at that radius, the spacecraft must be pulled inward slightly less hard than a free body would be. Earth’s backward tug provides precisely that reduction at one particular distance. There, and only there along the line, the combined pull matches a one-year lap, and the spacecraft goes round the Sun in step with Earth, staying on the sunward side for ever. That spot is L1.

Where the pulls combine in this way: about 1.5 million km from Earth, which is 1% of the way to the Sun, or about four times the Moon’s distance.
Notice what L1 is not. It is not where the Sun’s pull and Earth’s pull are equal; that point is only about 260,000 km from Earth, inside the Moon’s orbit, and a spacecraft there would not keep pace with anything. At L1 the Sun’s pull is about thirty times Earth’s. L1 is where the two pulls combine to give exactly a one-year orbit.

Step 4: a halo, not a parking spot

Nothing sits still at L1. Aditya-L1 travels in a wide loop around the point, the halo orbit, completing one loop in about 178 days, roughly six months, while the whole arrangement, Earth, L1 and spacecraft, goes round the Sun once a year. From the spacecraft the Sun is always in view, and Earth and the Moon are always behind it, never blocking the light.

Step 5: what it is for

From that vantage point Aditya-L1 watches the Sun’s outer layers and the stream of particles the Sun blows past Earth, continuously, without the gaps that any telescope on the ground must suffer. Chapter 15 is where the Sun itself is explained: what keeps it shining, and why a fire could never have lasted this long.

Careful

“Aditya-L1 is parked at L1, where gravity cancels out, so it just stays there.”

Gravity does not cancel at L1; the Sun’s pull there is about thirty times Earth’s. The two pulls combine to the exact value a one-year orbit needs. And the spacecraft does not sit on the point; it loops round it every 178 days.

Careful

“A spacecraft nearer the Sun than Earth must go round faster than Earth.”

On its own, yes: that is Kepler’s third law. At L1 it is not on its own. Earth’s backward tug takes away just enough of the Sun’s pull to let it dawdle round in a full year, keeping pace with us.

In Chapter 15 you will meet the Sun that Aditya-L1 watches, and Kepler’s third law from Chapter 5 is the reason L1 has to be exactly where it is.

1687

Why Haji Ali goes under the sea

Isaac Newton

Haji Ali, Mumbai, any morning

The dargah of Haji Ali stands on a rock in the sea off Worli, joined to the shore by a narrow causeway. Twice a day the sea rises until the causeway disappears under it, and twice a day it falls and the path reappears and people walk out. If you went every day you would notice something: the times shift. Each high tide comes about fifty minutes later than it did the day before. So does each low tide.

Fifty minutes a day is a number you have met before. It is how much later the Moon rises each day. The tides are keeping time with the Moon. The person who first explained why was Isaac Newton, in 1687, in the same book that explained the Moon’s orbit, and he did it with the same pull.

Step 1: the Moon does not lift the water

The usual picture is that the Moon pulls the sea up towards itself, like a magnet lifting iron filings. That picture is wrong, and the first reason is simple: the Moon’s pull on a bucket of water here is about three millionths of Earth’s pull on it. Nothing is being lifted. Whatever the Moon does to the sea, it does by nudging, not hoisting.

Step 2: the pull is not the same everywhere

Here is the real idea. Earth is 12,742 km across. Its near side is nearer the Moon than its centre is, and its far side is further away. Gravity weakens with distance, so the Moon pulls each kilogram on the near side a little harder than it pulls Earth as a whole, and each kilogram on the far side a little less.

The Moon’s pull per kilogram, worked out from its mass and distance:
on the side of Earth facing the Moon: 3.43 × 10⁻⁵ m/s²
at Earth’s centre: 3.32 × 10⁻⁵ m/s²
on the far side: 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ m/s²
The near side is pulled about 3% harder than the centre, the far side about 3% less. Those differences are the tide-raising forces, and each is about one ten-millionth of Earth’s own gravity.

The whole Earth, land and sea together, responds to the pull at its centre; that is the pull that keeps it circling with the Moon round their shared balance point. The water on the near side gets a little more than that, so it is drawn a little ahead, towards the Moon. The water on the far side gets a little less, so it lags a little behind, away from the Moon. Two sides, two small leftover nudges, pointing in opposite directions.

Step 3: two heaps of water

A nudge of one ten-millionth of gravity cannot lift anything. But it acts sideways as well as outward, and it acts for hours on water that is free to move. Over those hours the water flows, slowly, over Earth’s surface, piling up into two low, wide heaps: one under the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. The heaps are not water being lifted or stretched; they are water that has flowed in from the sides.

Earth turns underneath those two heaps once a day. A place like Mumbai is carried through the first heap, then through a low in between, then through the second heap, then another low: two high tides and two low tides a day.

Why fifty minutes late? While Earth turns once, the Moon moves on about 12° along its orbit, and Earth has to turn for another fifty minutes to bring Mumbai back under it. So the Moon’s day, and the tide’s, is 24 hours 50 minutes, and the two highs come about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.

Step 4: the Sun joins in

The Sun pulls on Earth too, far harder than the Moon does; but it is so far away that its pull is almost the same on both sides of Earth, and tides come from differences. Worked out from the masses and distances, the Sun’s tide-raising effect is about 46% of the Moon’s: real, but less than half.

At new Moon and at full Moon the Sun, Earth and Moon lie in a line, so the Sun’s two heaps sit on top of the Moon’s two heaps and the tides run higher than usual. These are spring tides, and the name has nothing to do with the season: the water “springs up”. A week later, at the quarter Moons, the Sun is at a right angle to the Moon, its heaps sit in the Moon’s hollows, and the tides are tamer: neap tides. Spring tides return roughly every fifteen days, twice a month.

Step 5: the real sea, and Mumbai

If Earth were covered in one smooth ocean, the heaps would be under a metre high. The real sea sits in basins with coasts, shallows and channels; water sloshes against land, rubs on the seabed, is pushed by wind and swung by Earth’s turning. So the simple two-heap picture gives you the rhythm of the tides but not their size or their exact timing at any one place. For those, every port publishes a tide table worked out from years of measurement. At Mumbai the two highs of a day are usually of unequal height, and high water does not arrive at the moment the Moon is overhead but some hours after.

For heights in metres and the times at Haji Ali, read a published table: the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) and the Survey of India both issue them. Do not take a number from a news report or a website that gives no source; this book doesn’t.

Two more things the tides do, slowly. The friction of all that moving water is braking Earth’s spin, lengthening the day by about two thousandths of a second each century. And the Moon is drifting away from us by about 3.8 cm a year, a distance measured by bouncing laser beams off mirrors that the Apollo astronauts left on its surface.

Careful

“The Moon pulls the water up towards itself.”

The Moon’s pull on the sea is about three millionths of Earth’s. It lifts nothing. What raises a tide is the difference between the Moon’s pull on the near side, the centre and the far side of Earth, acting sideways for hours on water that is free to flow. Hence two heaps, not one, and hence a high tide on the side facing away from the Moon as well.

Careful

“High tide is when the Moon is overhead.”

The simple picture says so; the real sea runs late. Water takes time to flow into the heaps, coasts get in the way, and basins slosh to their own rhythms, so at any port high water lags the Moon by hours. The Moon sets the beat; the local coastline sets the delay. That is why tide tables exist.

A month of tides

Ask an adult to help you find an official tide table for Mumbai (INCOIS or the Survey of India). Each day for a month, write down the time of the morning high tide and, from your own eyes or a calendar, the Moon’s phase. Two things will show up: the high tide creeping later by about fifty minutes a day, and the highest highs clustering around new and full Moon. If you go to see the causeway, watch from the shore with an adult, and never walk out onto it when the tide is coming in.

In Chapter 14 the Sky explorer shows the two heaps turning with the Moon, and Chapter 5 is where the pull that raises them was first understood.

1798

Boiling water with a blunt drill

Count Rumford (Benjamin Thompson)

The arsenal at Munich, 1798

In the workshops of the Munich arsenal, cannon were made from solid brass. A rough casting was clamped in place, a steel borer was pressed against it, and horses walking in a circle turned the barrel against the borer for hours, cutting out the bore. The man in charge was Count Rumford, an American-born soldier and inventor who had risen high in the service of the ruler of Bavaria. He had noticed something that everyone in the workshop knew and nobody thought about: the brass got very hot. Hour after hour, as long as the horses walked, the metal and the brass shavings came out hot enough to hurt.

Rumford did think about it, and it worried him, because of what the best science of the day said heat was.

Step 1: the fluid called caloric

The leading theory in 1798 said that heat was a substance. Chemists called it caloric: an invisible, weightless fluid that lived inside every object and flowed from hotter things to colder ones, the way water flows downhill. It was a good theory, as wrong theories go. It explained why a hot spoon warms the tea and not the other way round. It explained why things swell when heated: the caloric pushed their particles apart. It gave chemists a tidy picture in which heat could be poured, stored and measured, and a body held a fixed amount of it.

In that picture, friction warmed the brass by squeezing caloric out of it, as you might squeeze water from a sponge. And a sponge, squeezed hard enough and long enough, runs dry.

Step 2: the blunt borer

Rumford arranged a test. He took a brass barrel, fixed a blunt steel borer against it so that it would scrape and rub rather than cut, and enclosed the end of the barrel in a wooden box filled with cold water. Then he set the horses walking. No fire was anywhere near. The only thing happening to the brass was that it was being rubbed.

The water in the box warmed. It kept warming. In his report to the Royal Society, published in 1798, he recorded the moment with some satisfaction: at two hours and thirty minutes, the water boiled.

Then he asked the question that mattered. The brass had been rubbed for hours and had given out enough heat to boil a box of water. Did it show any sign of running dry? It did not. As long as the horses kept walking, the heat kept coming, and there was no reason to think it would ever stop. A sponge that never runs dry is not holding a fixed amount of water. A lump of brass that gives out heat for as long as you rub it is not holding a fixed amount of caloric.

How much energy did the water take?
Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C takes 4186 J.
From a cool 20 °C to boiling at 100 °C is a rise of 80 °C.
So each kilogram of water in the box needed 80 × 4186 ≈ 335,000 J, about a third of a megajoule, and the horses supplied every joule of it by walking in a circle.

Step 3: what the horses were really supplying

Whatever the water was getting, it was coming from the horses. The horses pushed the barrel round against the borer; the borer resisted; something was being done against that resistance, continuously, for two and a half hours. In the language of the chapters ahead, the horses were doing work, and the work was turning into warmth in the brass and then in the water.

Rumford’s own guess was that heat was a kind of motion rather than a fluid. He could not say what was moving. Nobody could, for another fifty years, until Joule in Manchester measured exactly how much work made how much warming, and until physicists accepted that matter is made of particles that are never still.

Step 4: what an object actually has

Here is the modern answer, which is what caloric was reaching for and missing. Every object is made of particles that jiggle, spin and vibrate. The total energy of all that motion is the object’s internal energy, also called its thermal energy. Warm an object and its particles jiggle faster: its internal energy rises. Rub it, hammer it, stir it, and the same thing happens, because pushing on the particles speeds them up too. Afterwards there is no way to tell which route the energy took. A kilogram of water warmed by a flame and a kilogram warmed by a paddle wheel are identical.

So the brass in Munich did not contain heat. It contained internal energy, and the horses kept adding more. The word heat survives, but physicists now use it for one thing only: energy on the move from a hotter object to a colder one, because of the difference in their temperatures. Heat is a transfer, like a payment, and you cannot store a payment. You can only store what it buys.

Careful

“The brass had heat inside it, and the drill squeezed the heat out.”

Nothing was squeezed out, because heat is not a thing an object holds. The brass held internal energy, the motion of its particles. Rubbing added more, for as long as the rubbing went on, and the extra energy flowed as heat into the colder water. If the brass had really held a fixed stock of heat, it would have run dry long before the water boiled.

Step 5: why caloric lasted so long

It is easy to laugh at caloric. Do not. It fitted most of what people could see, and it took a very odd experiment to catch it out, because almost nothing in ordinary life rubs for two and a half hours without stopping. Rumford’s result sat uncomfortably beside the fluid theory for decades, and the theory was only abandoned when Joule’s careful numbers and the particle picture of matter arrived together. Being wrong for a good reason, and then letting go when the evidence turns, is what science looks like from the inside.

Rumford’s test in ten seconds

Rub a pencil eraser hard against a desk for ten seconds, then touch it to your lip. It is warm. Nothing hot touched it. Your arm did work against friction, and the work became internal energy in the rubber. Rub for twenty seconds and it is warmer still. There is no sign of the eraser running out of heat, for exactly the reason Rumford’s brass did not.

In Chapter 8 you will meet the two words that replaced caloric, internal energy and heat, and see why a steel thali that feels cold in the morning is at exactly the same temperature as the wooden board beside it. In Chapter 7 you will meet the unit named after the man who finished what Rumford started: the joule.

1840 to 1847

The number that never changes

Julius Robert Mayer, James Prescott Joule, William Thomson, Richard Feynman

Batavia, Java, 1840

A Dutch ship lay in the harbour at Batavia, the port that is now Jakarta, and its young German doctor was bleeding sailors. Bleeding was still ordinary medicine in 1840, and Julius Robert Mayer had done it many times at home. But here, in the heat of the tropics, something was different. The blood he drew from the sailors’ veins was a bright red, far brighter than the dark venous blood he knew from Europe.

The story Mayer told afterwards, as far as it can be reconstructed, runs like this. Blood is bright red when it is rich in oxygen. Venous blood is normally dark because the body has used the oxygen to burn food and keep itself warm. In a hot climate the body needs far less warming, so it burns less, and the blood comes back to the heart still bright. That led Mayer to a much larger thought. The body’s warmth, the food it burns, and the work its muscles do must all be forms of one thing, swapped one for another, with nothing created and nothing destroyed.

He wrote it up in 1842. Almost nobody read it. He was a doctor, not a professor, and his paper was not the kind of thing physicists read. Recognition came in the 1860s, when the idea he had reached by a strange road was already becoming the centre of physics.

Step 1: a quantity that can be measured

Manchester, 1840s

At about the same time, in Manchester, the son of a brewer was measuring the same idea. James Joule let heavy weights fall on strings. The strings turned a paddle wheel sitting in a tub of water, and the paddle churned the water. Then he read a thermometer in the tub. The water was warmer. Not by much, but by a measurable amount, and the amount was always the same for the same fall.

That is the key: falling and warming were exchangeable at a fixed rate, like two currencies. So much falling bought so much warming, every time. In today’s units, warming one kilogram of water by one degree takes 4186 joules, which is the same energy as a 10 kg weight falling about 43 m. The warming from one fall in a laboratory is tiny, and Joule’s thermometers had to be very good. They were.

How far must a 10 kg weight fall to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C?
Energy needed: 4186 J.
Energy from the fall: mass × 9.8 × height = 10 × 9.8 × h.
So h = 4186 ÷ 98 = about 43 m. Joule needed many smaller falls, and a thermometer that could read hundredths of a degree.

Step 2: the honeymoon

Chamonix, 1847

In the summer of 1847 Joule married Amelia Grimes and went to the Alps. Near Mont Blanc the couple met William Thomson, a young Scottish physicist who would later become Lord Kelvin and who had just heard Joule speak at a meeting in Oxford. The meeting is true, and the two men became lifelong allies.

The story goes further. Thomson, it is said, found Joule carrying a long thermometer, intending to measure whether the water at the bottom of a waterfall was warmer than at the top, since the falling water’s energy had to go somewhere. It is a lovely story. Treat it as a legend: it surfaced about thirty-five years later, and no measurement was ever reported. What is real is the idea behind it, which Joule had already tested with his paddle: when something falls and stops, the energy of its fall does not vanish. It turns up as warmth.

Step 3: the blocks

The physicist Richard Feynman, a century later, gave a picture for this idea that is worth retelling in our own words.

A child has a set of wooden blocks, say twenty of them, and every night a parent counts them. Twenty, always twenty. One night there are only seventeen. The parent looks around and finds three under the sofa. Another night, eighteen, and the window is open: two are in the garden. Then one night nineteen, and none to be found anywhere, but the child’s toy box is locked. So the parent weighs the box. It is heavier than an empty box by exactly the weight of one block. Another night the bathwater is murky and nobody can see into it, but the water level stands a little higher than usual: by just the volume of two blocks.

After a while the parent stops needing to see the blocks at all. The rule has become: the number is always twenty, and if you cannot see them, work out where they are hiding. Count the ones in view, add the weight of the box, add the rise of the bathwater, and the total is twenty, every single night.

Energy is the number of blocks. It cannot be seen directly. It is a number you calculate: so much for a thing’s speed, so much for its height above the ground, so much for the stretch in a spring, so much for the jiggling of its particles. Add up the lot, and the total never changes. That is the law of conservation of energy. When the total seems to have dropped, physicists do not shrug. They look for the locked box.

Step 4: stores and transfers

School gives these hiding places a name: energy stores. A raised ball and the Earth together hold energy in a gravitational store. A moving ball holds energy in a kinetic store. Food and petrol hold it in a chemical store. A hot object holds it in a thermal store, the jiggling of its particles. When energy moves from one store to another, by a push, by an electric current, by heating, or by a wave such as light or sound, that is an energy transfer. Joule’s experiment, in those words: the gravitational store of the weight and the Earth drops, and the thermal store of the water rises by the same amount.

Step 5: where it goes

Here is the part people most often get wrong. Drop a ball and it bounces lower each time, then stops. It is tempting to say its energy has been used up. It has not. At each bounce the ball and the floor are squashed and warmed, and a click of sound spreads out into the room. The energy is all still there, as slightly faster jiggling in the floor, the ball and the air. It has spread out so thinly that it can never be gathered back into the ball. It is not destroyed; it is scattered, and scattered energy is less useful.

If you time the clicks of a bouncing ball with a phone, you can see this. Suppose one bounce lasts 0.60 s from click to click and the next 0.50 s. The height of a bounce goes with the square of its time, so the second bounce reached (0.50 ÷ 0.60)², which is about 69%, of the first one’s height. About 31% of the ball’s energy had moved into warmth and sound in one bounce.

Careful

“The ball stops bouncing because its energy ran out.”

Energy never runs out; it moves. At every bounce some of the ball’s energy becomes warmth in the ball and the floor, and a little becomes sound. After a dozen bounces all of it has spread into the room as slightly faster jiggling of particles. The total is unchanged. What has changed is that it is now spread so thinly that it cannot be gathered up to lift the ball again.

Warm hands

Rub your palms together hard for twenty seconds. They are warm. Nothing hot touched them. Your muscles did work against the friction between your hands, and that work became warmth in your skin, exactly as Joule’s falling weights became warmth in his water. Now hold your palms still, pressed together just as hard, for twenty seconds. No warming. Pressing is not work; moving against a force is.

Mayer saw it in blood, Joule in a thermometer, and neither used the word energy in the way we do now. The word came into its modern meaning over the following decades, as physicists realised that the same number kept its total through every change they could devise. In Chapter 7 you will do that bookkeeping yourself, and find out why your electricity bill says “units consumed” when nothing has been consumed at all. In Chapter 8 you will see what the thermal store really is, and why the energy that goes into it is so hard to get back.

1824

Waterfalls of heat

Sadi Carnot, Lazare Carnot

Paris, 1824

In 1824 a young engineer named Sadi Carnot paid a Paris printer to run off six hundred copies of a booklet, 118 pages long, about the engines that were changing the world. Across the Channel, British steam engines were pumping water out of mines and driving mills. They burned coal and did work. Carnot asked a question nobody had asked clearly: for a given amount of burning, how much work can an engine possibly do? Could a cleverer design go on getting more and more, without limit?

Almost nobody bought the booklet. It was a decade before other engineers and physicists picked it up, and when they did, it became the foundation of the science of heat and work.

Step 1: a picture borrowed from water

Carnot’s father, Lazare, had studied water engines: the mill wheels that turned when a stream fell over them. A water wheel does work because water falls from a higher level to a lower one, and the work it can do depends on how much water falls and how far. The son, as historians summarise his thinking, saw a heat engine the same way. Heat flows from something hot, the boiler, to something cold, the air or the river outside, and on the way down some of it can be made to do work, as falling water turns a wheel. The words are the historians’; the picture is his.

Step 2: the water has to arrive at the bottom

The picture has a consequence that is easy to miss. The water that turns a mill wheel does not vanish into the wheel. It arrives at the bottom, every drop of it, and flows away. If the heat in an engine is like falling water, then the heat must arrive at the cold side too. An engine cannot turn all of its heat into work. There must always be a cold place for some of the energy to go.

This is exactly what you see at a power station. The great cooling towers are not a fault in the design. They are the bottom of the waterfall, where the energy that did not become electricity is handed to the air.

Step 3: how far the heat falls

Carnot’s conclusion, in today’s words, was that the most work an engine can possibly get from a given flow of heat depends on how far the heat falls: on how hot the hot side is and how cold the cold side is. It does not depend on what the engine is made of or what fluid runs round inside it. A bigger temperature difference allows more work; a small one allows very little. That is a limit no cleverness can beat, and it was the first such limit anyone had found.

Step 4: a number for how good

The word for how much of the input becomes useful output is efficiency: useful energy out, divided by energy in. A steam engine of the kind Carnot knew manages about 17%. A petrol engine manages about 30%, a diesel about 35%, a coal-fired power station about 42%. An electric motor, which is not a heat engine at all and has no waterfall inside it, manages about 98%. These are representative figures; real machines vary.

A steam engine, for every 100 J the fire gives
Useful work out: 17 J.
Handed to the cold side as warmth in the air and water: 100 − 17 = 83 J.
Efficiency: 17 ÷ 100 = 17%.
For a coal power station at 42%: 42 J become electricity, 58 J warm the surroundings.

Step 5: nothing is destroyed

Read the 83 J carefully. They are not destroyed; energy never is. They are still energy, now spread out as slightly faster jiggling in the air and the river, so thinly that no engine could gather them up again. That is the second great fact about energy, standing beside the first. The first says the total never changes. The second says that whenever energy is turned into a useful form, some of it always ends up spread out as warmth. Carnot found the second fact before anyone had properly stated the first.

Careful

“An engine that is 17% efficient destroys the other 83% of the energy.”

It destroys nothing. The 83 J leave as warmth in the surroundings: the hot exhaust, the warm river, the steam from the cooling tower. The total is still 100 J. What has changed is that 83 J are now spread so thinly through the air that they can never again be made to turn a wheel. Efficiency measures how much stayed useful, not how much survived.

The bottom of the waterfall

Hold your hand near the back of the fridge, or beside the vent of a laptop that has been working hard, or over a running mixer-grinder just after it stops. Each is warm. Every machine that does useful work hands some energy to its surroundings as warmth, and in a working machine there is no way round it. Count the warm machines in your flat: each one is a small cooling tower.

In Chapter 7 the efficiency of the coal station that lights Mumbai is worked through, and the bookkeeping shows where every joule goes. In Chapter 8 you will see what the “cold side” really receives, and why energy that has spread out as warmth is so hard to get back.

1761

The ice that would not warm up

Joseph Black

Glasgow, 1761

Joseph Black lectured on chemistry at Glasgow, and in 1761 he showed his students something that everyone had seen and nobody had thought about. Take a bowl of ice that has just begun to melt, stand a thermometer in it, and leave it in a warm room. The ice melts, slowly, for hours. Warmth is plainly flowing in from the room, because the ice is turning to water. And the thermometer does not move. It sits at the melting point, 0 °C in our units, until the last sliver of ice is gone, and only then does it begin to climb.

Black never properly published what he made of this; it survives in the notes of his lectures. His argument was simple and strong. If melting ice took only a little heat, the first warm day of spring would turn every snowfield into a flood within the hour. Instead the snow lingers for weeks, melting a little each day. Melting, he concluded, must swallow a great deal of heat without showing any of it on a thermometer. He called that heat latent, which means hidden.

Step 1: a thermometer does not measure heat

Temperature is how fast the particles of a thing are jiggling, on average. Heat is energy flowing from something warmer to something cooler. Most of the time the two go together: pour energy into a pan of water and the particles jiggle faster, so the thermometer rises. Melting is the great exception, and it shows that temperature and heat are different things. Energy can go in while the temperature stands still.

Step 2: where the energy goes

In ice, the water particles are locked into a pattern, each held in place by its attraction to its neighbours. To become liquid, they have to be pulled loose from that pattern. That takes energy, and the energy goes into loosening the grips, not into making the particles move faster. So the thermometer, which reads only the speed of the jiggling, sees nothing happen. The energy is still there, stored in the new, looser arrangement. That stored energy is the latent heat.

The same thing happens again, on a far larger scale, at the boiling point. To turn liquid water into vapour, the particles must be pulled completely clear of one another, and that costs much more.

Step 3: how much

Melting one kilogram of ice at 0 °C takes about 334 kJ. That is as much energy as it would take to warm the same kilogram of water from 0 °C all the way to about 80 °C. Boiling one kilogram of water at 100 °C takes about 2256 kJ, nearly seven times as much as melting it. Put the two together with the ordinary warming in between, and you get the heating curve for a kilogram of ice taken from the freezer to steam.

One kilogram, from −20 °C ice to steam
Warming the ice to 0 °C: about 42 kJ.
Melting it, at a steady 0 °C: 334 kJ.
Warming the water from 0 to 100 °C: about 419 kJ.
Boiling it, at a steady 100 °C: 2256 kJ.
Total: about 3050 kJ, and three-quarters of it went into the two flat stretches.

The flat stretches are why ice is such a good way to keep a drink cold. Three small ice cubes, 6 g each, dropped into a 250 g glass of soda at 20 °C, bring it down to about 13 °C, and nearly all of that cooling comes from the melting, not from the ice being cold to begin with.

Step 4: it comes back out

Hidden heat is not gone. When water freezes, the 334 kJ per kilogram come back out as warmth; when vapour condenses, the 2256 kJ come back. We think of condensation as a cold thing, because we see it on cold glasses, but it warms whatever it forms on: the drops on the outside of a glass of iced water are handing energy to the glass and speeding up the melting inside. Fruit growers in cold places spray their orchards with water before a frosty night, because as the water freezes on the fruit it gives out latent heat and keeps the fruit near 0 °C instead of letting it drop below.

Step 5: the sweat on your arm

Evaporation at skin temperature costs even more than boiling: about 2430 kJ for every kilogram of sweat, nearly 8% more than at 100 °C. That is the hidden heat your body spends to cool you, and it is the whole working of the matka on the kitchen counter. Black’s ice and a Mumbai summer are one piece of physics.

Careful

“The heat disappears while the ice melts, and comes from nowhere when the water freezes.”

Nothing disappears. The energy that melts the ice is stored in the loosened arrangement of the liquid’s particles, and it is paid back, every joule of it, when they lock into a pattern again. A thermometer cannot see it, because it only reads how fast the particles move, not how they are arranged.

Watch the thermometer refuse

Fill a steel tumbler with ice cubes and a little water, stir, and read a kitchen thermometer every minute. It stays at 0 °C while the ice shrinks: for ten minutes, twenty, as long as any ice is left, even though the warm room is pouring energy in the whole time. Note the minute the last sliver vanishes. From then on the reading climbs steadily. You have just repeated Black’s lecture.

Chapter 8 draws this heating curve and uses it for the matka and for sweat. In The Invisible World, the chemistry book next door, Chapter 3 looks at the same melting and boiling from the particles’ side, and asks what the attractions between them are made of.

every summer

Why the matka works in May

A kitchen in Mumbai, May

On the kitchen counter stands a matka, a round pot of unglazed clay, and in the heat of May the water inside it is cool. Not fridge-cold, but cool enough that a glass of it is a relief. Nobody plugged it in. Nobody put ice in it. The pot simply stands there, slightly damp on the outside, and does its work.

Then the monsoon arrives. The same pot, the same water, the same counter, and the water is barely cooler than the tap. People say the matka has “stopped working”. It has not stopped doing anything. The air around it has changed, and the matka’s trick depends on the air.

Step 1: the fastest leave

The particles in a glass of water are not all moving at the same speed. Most jiggle at some middling pace; a few are much faster. At the surface, the fastest ones occasionally move quickly enough to break away from their neighbours and escape into the air as vapour. That is evaporation, and it needs no boiling. It happens at any temperature, from a puddle after the rain to the sweat on your arm.

Here is the part that matters. The particles that leave are the fast ones. So the average speed of those left behind falls, and a falling average speed is a falling temperature. Evaporation cools whatever is left behind. The amount is large: each gram that escapes from warm water carries off about 2.4 kJ, which is as much energy as it would take to warm that gram by nearly six hundred degrees if it could stay liquid. This is evaporative cooling, and it is the only part of the matka’s trick that is about the pot.

Step 2: a pot that leaks on purpose

Fired clay is full of tiny pores. Water seeps through them from the inside to the outer surface, where it evaporates, and every gram that leaves takes its 2.4 kJ from the water that is left. A glazed pot of the same clay cannot sweat and cools nothing.

How much water must a matka sweat?
To cool 10 litres (10 kg) of water by 10 °C, the water must give up 10 × 4186 × 10 = 418,600 J.
Each gram evaporated carries away about 2430 J.
So about 418,600 ÷ 2430 ≈ 170 g must seep out and evaporate: a little less than a cupful, over the day.

Your body runs the same system. A resting person gives out about 120 W of warmth, and to carry that away by sweating alone you would need to evaporate about 3 g of sweat every minute. On a dry day you hardly notice it happening, because the sweat is gone as soon as it forms. On a humid day it stays on your skin, and that is the clue to the whole puzzle.

Step 3: damp air pushes back

Evaporation is not one-way traffic. While fast particles leave the water, some of the vapour particles already in the air come back and rejoin it. At any given temperature, the air just above a water surface can only have so much vapour in it before the two flows balance: as many particles returning as leaving. Beyond that point, no more water evaporates, however long you wait.

How close the air is to that balance point is its relative humidity. At 50%, the air has half the vapour it could have at that temperature, and evaporation runs briskly. At 100%, there is no net evaporation at all. People say the air “holds” water like a sponge, and that is a handy way to talk, but nothing is holding anything. It is a balance between particles leaving and particles returning.

On a Mumbai afternoon in May the humidity is typically around 65%. In July it is typically around 81%, and the air is already close to the balance point. The matka’s water can still seep to the surface; it just cannot leave fast enough to do much cooling.

Step 4: the floor

So an evaporating surface cools, and damp air slows the cooling. Where does it stop? It stops when the thin layer of air right next to the wet surface has cooled and dampened to its own balance point. The temperature of the surface at that moment is the wet-bulb temperature, named for the way it is measured: a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in wet cloth and fanned. No wet cloth, no sweating skin and no matka can go below it. It is the floor.

The floor depends on both the air temperature and the humidity, and it can be calculated. Here are three afternoons.

Three afternoons, three floors
Mumbai, May: air 34.3 °C, humidity 65%. Floor: 28.7 °C. The most a matka can cool is 34.3 − 28.7 = 5.6 °C.
Mumbai, July: air 29.4 °C, humidity 81%. Floor: 26.7 °C. The most it can cool is 2.7 °C.
A dry inland town: air 38 °C, humidity 20%. Floor: 21.3 °C. The most it can cool is 16.7 °C.

So May gives the matka about twice the room that July does, and even May is poor beside a dry town. A real pot never quite reaches its floor, because energy also leaks in from the warm room through the clay. Measured matkas drop their water by anywhere between 5 and 15 °C depending on the air; one measurement in humid Kolkata managed 7 °C.

Step 5: why the fan helps, and what it cannot do

Stand a wet-wrapped tumbler in front of a fan and it cools faster. Not because the fan’s air is cold: it is at the room’s temperature. The fan sweeps away the damp layer next to the cloth and brings drier air in to take its place, so evaporation keeps going. A fan on dry skin in a 30 °C room cannot take you below 30 °C. Moving air alone never cools anything below its own temperature. Evaporation can, and that difference is the whole secret of the matka.

Careful

“The fan makes the air colder, so I feel cool.”

The air from the fan is at exactly the room’s temperature. What the fan does is carry away the damp air next to your skin so that your sweat evaporates faster, and it is the evaporation that cools you, to a floor set by the humidity. Switch the fan off, the damp layer builds up again, evaporation slows, and the cooling fades.

Measure the floor yourself

Take a kitchen thermometer and wrap a scrap of cotton cloth, soaked in water, around its tip. Hold it in front of a fan and watch the reading fall, then settle. That lowest steady reading is the wet-bulb temperature of the air in your kitchen. Now read a dry thermometer beside it. The gap between the two is a measure of how dry the air is, and it is the most any matka in that room can hope to cool its water. Do it once in May and once in July and write both pairs of numbers down.

In Chapter 8 the matka returns as the case at the end of the chapter, and the question “May or July?” is answered with these numbers. The energy that each gram of vapour carries away is the same hidden heat that Joseph Black found in melting ice; Section 8.5 explains why changing from liquid to vapour costs so much.

1686 to 2021

The wind that turns around

Edmond Halley, Anna Mani, Sulochana Gadgil

London, 1686

In 1686 Edmond Halley, the astronomer who a year later would pay to print Newton’s Principia, turned his attention from the sky to the wind. Over the Indian Ocean, sailors knew, the wind blows from the sea towards the land for half the year and from the land towards the sea for the other half, and the half when it blows in from the sea brings the rain. The monsoon fed half the world, and nobody could say what drove it. Halley proposed an answer that is still the one most books give. To understand it, start with something you can feel on Marine Drive any afternoon.

Step 1: the breeze you can feel

In the late afternoon in Mumbai a cool wind comes in off the Arabian Sea. It comes because land and sea do not warm equally in the same sunshine. Warming a kilogram of water by one degree takes about 4186 J; warming a kilogram of dry sand by one degree takes only about 800 J. For the same sunshine, the sand warms about five times as much. By midday the ground is hot and the sea is barely changed.

Step 2: why warm air goes up

The air sitting over the hot ground warms, and warm air expands, so a cubic metre of it is lighter than a cubic metre of the cooler air around it. The cooler, denser air pushes the warm air upwards, exactly as water pushes a floating orange up to the surface in Chapter 6. Warm air does not rise by itself; it is pushed up by denser air. Cooler air from over the sea flows in along the ground to take its place, warms in turn, and is pushed up too. High up, the air drifts back out to sea and sinks. The result is a loop, a convection current, and the moving fluid carries energy with it. That carrying of energy by a moving fluid is convection.

The flow along the ground, from sea to land, is the sea breeze. At night the land cools faster than the sea, the loop turns the other way, and a gentle wind blows out to sea: the land breeze.

Step 3: Halley’s leap

Halley’s idea was to make the picture bigger. Take the whole of Asia as the land and the whole Indian Ocean as the sea, and let the year stand in for the day. Through the summer the land heats up more than the ocean, the air over the land is pushed upwards, and moist air flows in off the sea for months, not hours, bringing the rain with it. In winter the land cools faster than the ocean, and the whole system turns round: dry air flows out from the land to the sea. The monsoon, in Halley’s picture, is a sea breeze the size of a continent, and the wind turns around twice a year for the same reason it turns around twice a day at Marine Drive.

It is a beautiful idea, and for three hundred years it was the explanation.

Step 4: measuring it

An idea about the wind cannot be tested without instruments to measure the wind, the rain, the temperature and the sunshine, in thousands of places, year after year. In India the person who made that possible was Anna Mani. She trained in meteorological instruments in London and joined the India Meteorological Department in 1948. She standardised the drawings for about a hundred of them so that India could make its own, set up a network of stations measuring the Sun’s radiation for the International Geophysical Year of 1957–58, began measuring ozone in 1960, built the meteorological tower at Thumba for Vikram Sarabhai’s rocket launches in 1963, and retired as a Deputy Director General in 1976. When the Department announces that the monsoon has reached Mumbai, around 11 June in a normal year, it is reading instruments that follow her drawings.

Step 5: the challenge

Bengaluru, 2021

Numbers are what allow a beautiful idea to be tested, and tested it was. In 2021 Sulochana Gadgil and her colleagues argued that Halley’s giant sea breeze fails several tests when it is compared with what the instruments actually record. In their picture, the monsoon rains are better understood as the seasonal movement of a band of rain that circles the Earth near the equator. In the northern summer that band shifts north and sits over India; in winter it moves south again. The land-versus-sea heating is still there, but it is no longer the main character.

The argument is not finished, and this book will not pretend it is. Nobody disputes the sea breeze on Marine Drive. What is disputed is whether the monsoon is a giant one. You are reading this in the middle of an unsettled scientific question, which is the ordinary condition of science: an idea that fitted for centuries, numbers that fit less well than people thought, and a better idea being argued over right now.

Careful

“Warm air rises because heat rises.”

Heat does not rise; it is not a thing that can rise. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, and the denser air pushes it up, just as water pushes up anything less dense than itself. Take away the surrounding cooler air and warm air would go nowhere. The orange floating in Chapter 6 and the sea breeze on Marine Drive are the same physics.

Land and sea on a windowsill

Fill two identical steel tumblers, one with dry sand or soil and one with water, to the same depth, and stand them side by side in direct sunshine for an hour. Read a kitchen thermometer pushed into each. The sand will be far warmer. Then move both into the shade and read them every ten minutes: the sand cools fast, the water slowly. You have just made the land and the sea, and the reason the breeze turns around at night.

In Chapter 8 the matka and the monsoon share a section, because both are about what water and air do with energy. Halley you have met already, in Chapter 5, predicting the return of a comet he would not live to see. The monsoon was the one prediction of his that the instruments have not yet confirmed.

1722 to 1740

mv or mv²?

Willem 's Gravesande, Émilie du Châtelet, Gottfried Leibniz, René Descartes

Leiden, 1722

A cannonball in flight can do things a cannonball at rest cannot. It can knock down a wall, dent a shield, stop a charging horse. So a moving thing must carry something, and in the early 1700s the cleverest people in Europe were quarrelling about how to measure it.

One side followed René Descartes. Multiply the mass by the speed, they said: twice the speed, twice the “quantity of motion”. The other side followed Gottfried Leibniz. Multiply the mass by the speed squared, they said: twice the speed, four times as much. Leibniz’s followers called their quantity vis viva, living force. Both sides used the word “force” for what they were measuring, which made the argument harder, because today that word means a push or a pull, and neither mv nor mv² is a push.

At Leiden, in the Netherlands, Willem ‘s Gravesande decided to ask the clay.

Step 1: the dent test

He took brass balls and dropped them into a tray of soft clay. A ball hits the clay, the clay pushes back, and the ball stops after sinking in some distance. That distance, the depth of the dent, is what he measured.

Why the dent? Because it measures how much pushing it takes to stop the ball. The clay resists with a roughly steady force all the way down, so a dent twice as deep means the clay had to push for twice the distance. If a moving body “carries” something, a fair measure of it is how much work it takes to bring it to rest.

Step 2: making a ball arrive twice as fast

You cannot throw a ball at an exact speed, but you can drop it, and a dropped ball’s speed depends only on the height it falls from. The catch is that doubling the height does not double the speed. To arrive twice as fast, a ball must fall from four times the height, because the speed of a falling object grows with the square root of the drop (Chapter 1 explains why).

Two drops, one twice as fast as the other (our heights, not his)
From 25 cm: speed at the clay = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.25) = 2.2 m/s.
From 1 m, four times the height: √(2 × 9.8 × 1.0) = 4.4 m/s. Twice the speed.

Step 3: what the clay said

The ball arriving twice as fast made a dent about four times as deep. Not twice. Four times. A ball arriving three times as fast would make a dent about nine times as deep. The dent followed the square of the speed.

So, if the thing a moving body carries is measured by the pushing needed to stop it, that thing goes as mv², Leibniz’s way, not mv. ‘s Gravesande had started out on the other side of the argument, and the clay changed his mind.

Careful

“The deeper dent is the energy. The second ball had exactly four times as much.”

Roughly four times. The dent is a fair measure only because the clay pushes back with a roughly steady force as the ball sinks. Real clay (and real flour, if you try this at home) stiffens as it is squashed, so the ratio comes out near four, not exactly four. Say “about four times, as the square law predicts”, never “exactly”.

Step 4: a book in a château

Cirey, 1740

Eighteen years later, in a château in eastern France, Émilie du Châtelet published her Institutions de physique, a book meant to lay out the foundations of physics for her son. She came down firmly on Leibniz’s side, and ‘s Gravesande’s dents were among her evidence. People sometimes say she “proved” that the true measure is mv². She did not, and she did not claim to. She argued the case, clearly and with experiments behind her, in a quarrel that had already run for half a century.

The quarrel took most of another century to settle, and it settled in an unexpected way: both sides had been right.

Step 5: both were right

Mass times speed, mv, is real. Physicists now call it momentum, and it is the quantity that stays fixed when two things collide, as you will see in Chapter 3. Mass times speed squared is also real. With a half in front of it, ½mv², it is the kinetic energy, the energy a thing has because it is moving, and it is the quantity that tells you how much work it takes to stop something, or how much work it took to get it going. (The half appears when you work out the pushing it takes to bring a body up to speed; Chapter 7 shows where it comes from.)

The two quantities answer different questions. How long must a force act to stop the ball? That is set by its momentum. How far must the force push? That is set by its kinetic energy. The clay answered the second question, and the second question is the one that goes as the square.

A car at 50 km/h and the same car at 100 km/h
Momentum, mv: twice as much at 100 km/h.
Kinetic energy, ½mv²: 2² = 4 times as much at 100 km/h.
If the brakes push with the same force both times, the stopping distance is four times as long. The brakes are doing the clay’s job.

A marble in the atta

Pour atta or maida into a tray to a depth of a few centimetres and smooth the top. Drop a marble into it from 25 cm, then push a toothpick into the crater and mark the depth. Smooth the flour again and drop the same marble from 1 m, four times the height, so that it arrives twice as fast. Measure again. You should get a crater roughly four times as deep, not exactly four times, for the reason in the warning above. If you have a bigger marble, drop it from 25 cm and compare: double the mass, and the dent only doubles.

The word vis viva has gone, and nobody now calls either quantity a force. But every time an engineer works out how fast a car can safely take a bend, or how much energy a cricket ball delivers to a bat, she is using the quantity that ‘s Gravesande read off the clay: mass times speed squared. In Chapter 3 you will meet mv under its own name, momentum, with a law all of its own. In Chapter 7, ½mv² joins the family of energies, and you will see why doubling your speed on a bicycle costs you four times the braking.

1869 to 1871

Why the sky is blue and the sunset orange

John Tyndall, Lord Rayleigh

Marine Drive, Mumbai, any clear evening

Stand on the sea wall at Marine Drive a little before sunset and look west, out over the Arabian Sea. The Sun is orange and getting redder as it sinks. The sky near it is yellow and orange too. But look straight up, and the sky overhead is still blue, and behind you, over the city, it is blue as well. One Sun, one sky, one lot of air, and three colours at once. After the Sun has gone the blue drains slowly away and the sky goes dark.

A common guess is that the sky is blue because it reflects the sea, which does not explain the orange, or why the sky is blue over a desert. The real answer came in two steps, beginning in London.

London, 1869

John Tyndall, lecturing at the Royal Institution, filled a long glass tube with air and a little vapour and shone a strong beam of light down it. As a fine haze of tiny particles formed inside, something happened that anyone could see. Looked at from the side, the beam glowed sky blue. Looked at end-on, through the whole length of the tube, the lamp behind it had turned orange, like a setting Sun. A tube of air and a lamp had made a sky and a sunset on a bench. Tyndall noticed one thing more, which we will come back to: the blue light coming out of the side of the tube was polarised.

Two years later a young English physicist, John William Strutt, better known by his title as Lord Rayleigh, worked out the mathematics of what Tyndall had seen: how much light a particle far smaller than a wavelength sends sideways, and how strongly that depends on the colour. The rule he found carries his name, and it turned out to need no haze at all. Much later he showed that the molecules of the air are enough on their own.

Step 1: what scattering is

Light is a travelling shake of electric and magnetic influence (you will meet those influences properly in Chapter 13). When light passes an air molecule, it shakes the molecule’s electrons back and forth. A shaking electric charge sends out light of its own, in all directions, like a tiny antenna. So each molecule takes a very small share of the sunlight passing it and re-sends it sideways. That is scattering: not a bounce, but a catch and a re-broadcast.

Step 2: blue scatters more

How much a tiny antenna re-sends depends strongly on how fast it is shaken, and so on the colour of the light. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red, which means more shakes per second. For scatterers far smaller than the wavelength, the share of light scattered goes as one over the wavelength multiplied by itself four times. This is Rayleigh scattering, and the fourth power is what makes the numbers dramatic.

Blue against red. Blue light has a wavelength of about 450 nm, red about 700 nm.
Scattering goes as 1 ÷ λ⁴, so the ratio is (700 ÷ 450)⁴ = 1.56⁴ = 5.9.
Air scatters blue light about six times as strongly as red.

Notice what the sum does not say. It does not say that only blue is scattered. Every colour is scattered; blue simply gets scattered about six times more than red, and the colours in between fall in between.

Step 3: the blue sky

Look anywhere in the sky except at the Sun itself. What reaches your eye from that direction is light that was travelling somewhere else, until an air molecule between you and empty space caught it and re-sent it towards you. The sky is sunlight, re-sent sideways by the air, and because the air re-sends blue six times more readily than red, the re-sent light is blue. Take the air away and there is nothing to do the re-sending: on the Moon, which has no air, the sky is black at noon with the Sun blazing in it.

Step 4: the orange sunset

The same rule, run the other way. At noon the sunlight that reaches you has crossed the thickness of the atmosphere more or less straight down, and lost only a little blue on the way. At sunset the Sun’s light comes to you along a slanting path through the air that is far longer: roughly six times as much air when the Sun is 10° above the horizon, and about eleven times as much at 5° (these are rough figures, from treating the air as a flat layer). Along that long path most of the blue is scattered out of the direct beam, sent sideways to light up other people’s skies. What arrives straight from the Sun is what is left: yellow, then orange, then red. The Sun has not cooled. Its light has been sieved by the air it crossed, and the blue was the part that fell through the sieve.

So the two colours have one cause. The blue over your head is the blue that was taken out of someone else’s sunset, and the orange in front of you is sunlight with its blue taken out and sent to someone else’s sky. Marine Drive, facing west over open sea, is one of the best places in the city to watch both at once.

Step 5: Tyndall’s extra clue

Now the word from the tube. Light shakes across its direction of travel, the way a wave on a rope shakes up and down while it runs along the rope. Ordinary sunlight is a jumble of shakes in every sideways direction. Light whose shake has one definite direction is polarised light, and the property is called polarisation.

Scattering sorts shakes. An electron can only re-send light in the directions it is not shaking along, so light scattered off at right angles to the sunbeam comes away shaking mostly in one direction. That is why Tyndall’s blue glow was polarised, and why the blue sky is too, most strongly about 90° away from the Sun. You can check it. Polarised sunglasses pass shakes in one direction only. Look at a patch of blue sky well away from the Sun through them and slowly rotate the glasses: the patch darkens and brightens. It will not go black, because light that has been scattered twice or more arrives with its shakes jumbled again. Test the glasses first on a phone or laptop screen, which gives out polarised light: if the screen darkens as you turn the lenses, the lenses are polarised. If nothing changes, they are only tinted, and the sky will not perform for them.

Careful

“The sky is blue because it reflects the sea.”

The sea has nothing to do with it. The sky is just as blue over Rajasthan and in the middle of Russia, and it is blue over the Arabian Sea at noon when the sea beneath it is grey with monsoon cloud. The air does it, catching sunlight and re-sending the blue. What makes the sea blue is a question of its own, and a scientist from Calcutta answered it from the deck of a ship.

The sky in a glass

Fill a clear glass with water, add a few drops of milk and stir, and in a darkened room shine a torch through it from one side. Look at the glass from the side and the beam has a bluish tinge; look through the glass towards the torch and the torch looks orange. Too milky and everything goes white, so start with very little milk and add a drop at a time. This is a model of the sky rather than a copy of it: the specks of fat in milk are much bigger than air molecules, so the imitation is rough, but the sorting of blue from orange is the same.

In Chapter 11 the sky and the sunset are Section 11.3, and Section 11.4 takes the sunglasses to the sea wall, where the question of why the sea is blue turns out to have a different answer.

1842 to 1845

Horn players on a train

Christian Doppler, Christophorus Buys Ballot

Prague, 25 May 1842

Christian Doppler, thirty-eight years old, stood up before a handful of members of the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences and read them a paper with a bold idea in it. Waves of any kind, he argued, should arrive at a different rate if their source is moving towards you or away from you. Towards you, they arrive more often, so a sound should seem higher. Away from you, less often, so lower.

For his best example he pointed at the sky. Double stars, pairs of stars circling each other, often show different colours, and Doppler thought their motion towards and away from us had tinted them. That example was wrong. Stars get their colours mostly from how hot they are, and a star’s speed is far too small a fraction of the speed of light to shift its colour visibly. But the idea was right, and three years later somebody found a way to test it, with sound instead of starlight.

Step 1: a train of squeezes

Sound in air is a train of squeezes. A horn squeezes the air beside it, the squeeze shoves the next bit of air, and so on outward, and each squeeze travels at the speed of sound: about 349 metres a second in Mumbai’s warm air (30 °C), a little less when it is cooler. A horn that makes 300 squeezes a second sends them out one after another, and if the horn is standing still they spread out evenly spaced all round it, like rings on a pond.

Step 2: the horn moves

Now let the horn move. Each squeeze still spreads out from the place where it was made, at the same speed as before; the air does not care how the horn is moving. But by the time the horn makes its next squeeze, it has moved on. So the squeezes ahead of the horn are made closer together, and the squeezes behind it are made farther apart. Their speed through the air is fixed; their spacing has changed; so the rate at which they arrive has changed too. Ahead of the horn they arrive more often, and you hear a higher note. Behind it they arrive less often, and you hear a lower one. This change in the note you hear, caused by motion, is the Doppler effect.

Utrecht, 1845

Testing this needed something that could carry a steady note at speed, and in 1845 there was exactly one such thing: a railway. Christophorus Buys Ballot, a Dutch scientist, put horn players on an open wagon on the line between Utrecht and Maarssen, and had them hold one note while a locomotive pulled the wagon past musicians standing beside the track, people with perfect pitch who could name a note on hearing it. As the wagon came towards them, the note they heard was higher than the one being played. As it passed and drew away, it dropped below. Doppler was right, at least for sound.

Many textbooks say Doppler ran this experiment himself. He did not. It was Buys Ballot’s, three years after Doppler’s paper.

Step 3: how much does the note change?

A horn at 150 Hz, sound at 340 m/s, the horn coming towards you at 35 m/s (a fast car).
Coming: the squeezes are packed into a shorter distance, so more arrive each second:
150 × 340 ÷ (340 − 35) = 167 Hz.
Going: 150 × 340 ÷ (340 + 35) = 136 Hz.
The rise (+17 Hz) is a little bigger than the fall (−14 Hz). The effect is not symmetrical.

Now a Mumbai local. Suppose its horn sounds at 300 Hz and it passes you at 80 km/h, which is 22 m/s, through warm air where sound travels at 349 m/s. (Both numbers are guesses; the sum is what matters.) Coming towards you the horn sounds at 320 Hz; going away, 282 Hz. The ratio is about 1.14, which on a piano is a drop of a little more than one whole tone as the train passes.

Step 4: what the driver hears

The driver hears the horn’s true note, because the driver moves with it: each squeeze reaches the cab with the same spacing it was made with. Only motion between the source and the listener matters, which is why two passengers chatting on a moving train hear each other perfectly normally.

And the change is not a smooth slide. While the train is still far down the track, almost all of its motion is towards you, so the note sits steadily high. It drops quickly in the second or two as the train passes, then sits steadily low. If you have ever heard a passing horn as “neeeee-yowwww”, that quick drop in the middle is the Doppler effect happening.

The same thing happens to light, as Doppler guessed, only the shifts are tiny unless the source is moving at a good fraction of the speed of light. Nothing on Earth does. Whole galaxies do, and in Chapter 15 the colour shift of their light, towards the red, tells us that they are moving away from us. Doppler’s stars were the wrong example and the right idea.

Careful

“As the train comes closer the horn gets louder, so of course it sounds higher.”

Louder and higher are different things. The horn does get louder as it nears you, because its sound has spread over a smaller area by the time it reaches you. The note rises for a different reason: the squeezes arrive more often. A horn standing still gets louder as you walk towards it and does not change its note at all.

The passing horn

From a balcony or an open window, listen to a motorbike or an ambulance coming along the road and going away again. Hum the note you hear while it is approaching, then the note after it has passed, and check the two hums against a tuner app on a phone. The second will be lower. Then listen to one that is parked and revving: louder or quieter as it likes, but the same note. Please do not do this on a railway platform; the local train’s horn is loud and the platform edge is no place for an experiment.

In Chapter 9 the moving whistle is Section 9.7, with a live figure that lets you drive the horn yourself. In Chapter 15, Section 15.7, the same idea applied to light stretches across the whole universe.

1803 to 1819

The spot that shouldn't exist

Thomas Young, Augustin Fresnel, Siméon Poisson, François Arago

London, 24 November 1803

Thomas Young, thirty years old, let a narrow sunbeam into a darkened room. Into the beam he held a thin card, about a thirtieth of an inch wide (less than a millimetre), edge-on, so that the light passed on both sides of it. On the wall behind, inside the card’s shadow, where it should have been darkest, he saw fine stripes: bright, dark, bright, dark. The light that had passed on the two sides of the card was meeting behind it, and where it met it was adding up in some places and cancelling in others.

That was a large claim to hang on a few stripes, because a century earlier Isaac Newton had argued that light is a stream of tiny particles, and Newton’s word still carried enormous weight. Two streams of particles cannot cancel each other. Two waves can. If you have seen pictures of this experiment with light going through two narrow slits, that is a later tidy-up for textbooks; the thing Young did was hold a card in a sunbeam.

Step 1: the thing only a wave can do

Drop two stones into still water and watch where the two sets of ripples cross. Where a crest from one meets a crest from the other, the water lifts twice as high. Where a crest meets a trough, they cancel and the water lies flat. The pattern of doubled and flattened places is interference, and nothing but a wave can make it. Throw two balls at a wall and you get two thumps, never silence.

So if light shows interference, light is a wave. That single idea, that light travels as waves and does what waves do, is the wave theory of light, and the stripes in the shadow were its first direct evidence.

Step 2: Young’s card

Behind the card, light from its two edges overlaps. On the line straight behind the middle of the card, the two paths are equal, so the waves arrive in step, crest with crest, and that line is bright. Move a little to one side and one path is longer than the other. When it is longer by half a wavelength, a crest arrives with a trough and the two cancel: dark. Longer by a whole wavelength, and crests meet crests again: bright. So the shadow fills with stripes, one for every extra half-wavelength of path difference.

Light’s wavelength is tiny, about 400 to 700 nanometres, which is some 1,800 waves to the millimetre for green light. That is why nobody had noticed before. In the textbook version, with two slits half a millimetre apart and a wall one metre away, the bright stripes come about a millimetre apart; Young’s card gave stripes of a similar size. You need a small bright source, a dark room and patience, and Young had all three. From the spacing of the stripes, the wavelength of the light can be worked out.

Step 3: round the corner

The stripes raise a question. If light goes in straight lines, how did any of it get into the shadow at all? The answer is an idea from Christiaan Huygens, who did the arithmetic for the speed of light: every point on a wave’s crest acts as a small new source of waves spreading out in all directions. Behind a wide opening the little waves add up to a wave going straight on, which is why light seems to travel in straight lines. At an edge they spill round the corner. This bending of waves round edges is diffraction, and how far a wave bends depends on its wavelength. Sound waves are centimetres to metres long, so sound bends freely round the corner of a building and you hear traffic you cannot see. Light’s waves are a thousandth of a millimetre, so light bends by amounts you never notice, until you hold something less than a millimetre wide in a sunbeam.

Paris, 1818

The decisive scene came fifteen years later. The French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for the best account of diffraction, and a young engineer, Augustin Fresnel, submitted a complete wave theory of light, with the mathematics to go with it. On the jury sat Siméon Poisson, a formidable mathematician and a particle man. Poisson worked through Fresnel’s equations looking for a flaw, and found what he took to be a fatal one. Take a small round disc, light it with a single point of light, and look at its shadow. Fresnel’s theory, Poisson showed, predicts a bright spot right at the centre of the shadow, where the shadow ought to be darkest of all. Absurd, said Poisson. The theory must be wrong.

François Arago set the experiment up and looked. There was the spot: a point of light in the middle of the shadow, exactly where the wave theory said it should be. Fresnel won the prize in 1819. Poisson was never convinced, and the spot is now called both the Poisson spot and the Arago spot, which is a fair reward for an honest wrong prediction and an honest look. It later turned out that Maraldi had seen the spot decades earlier without anyone grasping what it meant.

Step 4: why the spot is there

Picture the disc with its rim, and the point on the wall exactly behind its centre. Every point on the rim is the same distance from that one point, because the disc is round. So the little waves that spill round the rim all travel the same distance to reach the centre of the shadow, and they arrive in step, crest with crest, and add up: a bright spot. Move away from the centre and the distances from the different parts of the rim no longer match, so the waves mostly cancel and the shadow is dark, as shadows should be. Poisson’s “absurd” spot is nothing but the roundness of the disc, read through Huygens’s little waves.

The same adding and cancelling paints a soap bubble. Light reflected from the outer surface of the thin film meets light reflected from the inner surface, and for each thickness of film some colours add up and others cancel, so the colours swirl as the film thins. Just before the bubble pops, the top goes black: the film there is so thin that the two reflections cancel for every colour at once.

Careful

“So Newton was simply wrong. Light is a wave, not particles.”

Hold that thought loosely. These experiments show that light spreads and interferes exactly as a wave does, and that is true. In Chapter 15 you will meet experiments showing that light also arrives in packets, one at a time, which is not what a simple wave does. Both are true, and physicists learned to keep both.

Waves you can see

Blow soap bubbles in sunlight and watch the colours swirl, then watch one bubble closely until it pops: the top goes dark first. Tilt an old CD or DVD under a lamp and look at the rainbow on it. That rainbow is not a prism’s sorting but diffraction at the thousands of fine tracks on the disc, which act as thousands of tiny edges, all spilling light round themselves in step. After rain, look for the rainbow colours in a thin film of oil on the road: the same adding and cancelling as the bubble.

In Chapter 11 Young’s card and Arago’s spot are Section 11.5. The packets arrive in Chapter 15, Section 15.1, where the argument Poisson lost turns out to have had something in it after all.

1666 to 1672

Newton's dark room

Isaac Newton

Cambridge, 1666

In the beginning of 1666, by his own account, Isaac Newton bought a triangular glass prism “to try therewith the celebrated phœnomena of Colours”, as he put it in the old spelling. Everyone knew what a prism did. Hold it in sunlight and a patch of rainbow colours appears on the wall. The usual explanation was that pure white light had been stained on its way through the glass, the way clear water is coloured by passing through a tea bag.

Newton set up to look properly. “Having darkened my chamber, and made a small hole in my window-shuts” to let in a thin beam of sunlight, he placed the prism in the beam so that the light fell on the wall across the room. He expected a round patch of colour, because the hole was round and the beam that came through it was round, and the known rules of bending said a round beam should bend as a whole and stay round. Instead the patch was an oblong: 13¼ inches long and 2⅝ wide, about five times longer than it was broad, red at one end and violet at the other. The beam had not just been bent. It had been fanned out, and some of the light was bending more than the rest.

Step 1: two ideas and a test

There were two ways to explain the oblong. The first: the glass stains the light, adding colours as it goes, and somehow stretches it too. The second: the colours were in the sunlight all along, mixed together to look white, and each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the prism sorts them out. The first idea was the one everyone believed. The second was Newton’s.

How do you decide between them? Newton saw that the two ideas predict different things for a second prism. If glass stains light, then taking one colour out of the fan and sending it through a second prism should stain it again and change it. If glass only sorts, a single colour has nothing left to be sorted: it should bend, and come out the same colour it went in.

Step 2: the experimentum crucis

“I took two boards,” he wrote, “and placed one of them close behind the Prisme at the window.” The board had a small hole, so that only one colour of the fan passed through it. Further on stood a second board with a hole, and behind that a second prism. He turned the first prism a little to send each colour in turn through the holes.

The red came out of the second prism red, bent but otherwise unchanged. The blue came out blue, bent more than the red had been. No new colours appeared anywhere. He called it his experimentum crucis, the decisive experiment, and his conclusion in the letter is the whole of the matter in one sentence: “Light it self is a Heterogeneous mixture of differently refrangible Rays.” Refrangible was his word for how much a ray bends. White light is not pure. It is every colour at once, and a prism adds nothing to it. It sorts.

Step 3: why glass sorts

Light slows down when it enters glass or water, and slowing at a slant swings the beam round, which is why it bends.
