What Newton found is that the slowing is not quite the same for every colour: violet slows a little more than red, so it bends a little more. The spreading of colours that comes from bending them by different amounts is dispersion.

The differences are tiny. Water slows red light by a factor of 1.331 and violet by 1.342. Send a beam into water at 45° and the red continues at 32.09°, the violet at 31.80°: three-tenths of a degree apart. Glass does a little better, which is why Newton used it, and across a long room a small difference in angle grows into a wide band of colour on the far wall. That is also why a rainbow needs a whole sky of raindrops and a dark cloud behind it to show up at all.

Step 4: a rainbow is a million prisms

Sunlight enters a raindrop, is bent and sorted at the surface, bounces off the inside of the back of the drop, and is bent and sorted again on the way out, so the colours come back towards the Sun’s side of the sky. That is why you only ever see a rainbow with the Sun behind you. Each drop sends one colour to your eye, and millions of drops at slightly different heights send you the whole band. The band is continuous; “seven colours” is a habit of naming, not a fact about the light.

Newton was not the first to study rainbows with care. Some three and a half centuries before him, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi and Theodoric of Freiberg, working separately, filled glass spheres with water to make giant raindrops and traced the light through them, building on the work of Ibn al-Haytham. Nobody before Newton, though, had shown that white light was a mixture.

Step 5: the letter and the quarrel

Newton wrote all this up in a letter dated from Cambridge on 6 February 1672, which was read to the Royal Society in London and printed. Then the arguing began. Other natural philosophers, Robert Hooke the loudest among them, disputed what the colours meant and what light was made of, and Newton came to dislike the quarrelling so much that he held back his full book on light for more than thirty years. The experiment itself was never seriously in doubt. Anyone with two prisms and a sunny day could repeat it, and they did.

Careful

“The prism puts the colours into the light.”

Then a second prism would put in more, and it does not. A single colour sent through a second prism comes out the same colour, only bent. The colours were already in the sunlight, travelling together; the prism separates them because each bends by a slightly different amount. White light is a mixture that looks like nothing at all.

A prism from the kitchen

On a sunny morning, stand a plain glass of water on a windowsill where the Sun shines through it, and look on the floor or the wall on the far side for a small band of colour, red at one edge and violet at the other. A round glass bends light the way a prism does. For a rainbow of your own, go out on the balcony with the Sun behind you and spray a fine mist from a plant sprayer: look into the mist, away from the Sun. A CD’s rainbow looks similar but is made a different way, by diffraction at the fine tracks on its surface, which is a story of its own.

In Chapter 11 the prism opens Section 11.1 and the question of what white light is, and Section 11.2 asks what a banana does with that mixture when it lands. The bending itself, and why slowing makes light swing round, is Section 10.4.

1921 to 1930

The colour of the sea

C. V. Raman, K. S. Krishnan

The Mediterranean Sea, September 1921

The liner Narkunda is steaming east, bound for Bombay, and a physicist from Calcutta is standing at the rail looking at the sea through a small crystal. C. V. Raman is thirty-two and on his way home to India, and the Mediterranean around him is a deep, dark blue.

He knows the standard explanation. Lord Rayleigh, the English physicist who had explained why the sky is blue, had said that the sea is blue because it reflects the sky. Raman has a way to test that, right here at the rail. The crystal in his hand is a Nicol prism, a piece of mineral cut so that it lets through only light that is shaking in one direction, a polarising filter. Light reflected from the surface of water shakes mostly in one direction, so a Nicol prism held at the right angle can block the reflected sky almost completely. He turns the prism until the reflected sky is gone. If Rayleigh is right, the blue should go with it.

The sea is still blue. With the reflection removed, the colour remains, so it must be coming from inside the water. Raman writes it up on board, a short letter to the journal Nature called “The Colour of the Sea”, and when the Narkunda docks at Bombay he posts it.

Step 1: how a crystal can delete a reflection

Light is a sideways shake. When a beam meets a water surface at a slant, the little that bounces off is mostly shaking parallel to the surface, side to side. At one particular slant, 53° from the vertical for water, which means looking down at the sea about 37° below the horizon, the reflected light is shaking side to side and nothing else. A filter set to pass only up-and-down shaking blocks it entirely.

What such a filter does not block is the light that comes up from inside the water. That light has been scattered about inside and shakes every which way, so the filter takes half of it and lets the rest through. Hold the filter right, then, and the reflected sky vanishes while the water’s own light stays. The surface, by the way, reflects very little in the first place: of sunlight falling straight down onto calm water, only about 2 in every 100 parts bounce back. The rest goes in. Whatever the sea does with that light is what the sea’s colour is made of.

Step 2: what the water does with the light

Raman’s explanation was that the water does what the air does. Sunlight enters the sea, its molecules scatter a share of it, blue most of all, and some of that scattered light comes back up to your eye. The sea’s blue and the sky’s blue are cousins, both made by scattering; one is not a reflection of the other. His test did not say everything there is to say about the colour of the sea. It settled one thing: the blue is the water’s own, and a question that had been argued about could now be argued with evidence.

It also set Raman thinking about scattering, and he went on thinking about it for seven years.

Calcutta, February 1928

At the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, Raman and his students had spent those years studying how liquids scatter light. By 1928 he had a young colleague, K. S. Krishnan, twenty-nine years old, and in February the two of them found something that nobody expected.

Shine light of one colour into a liquid, and look at the light scattered sideways. Almost all of it comes out the same colour it went in; that is the ordinary scattering of the sky and the sea. But a small fraction of it comes out a different colour, shifted a little, and the size of the shift depends on the liquid. Krishnan’s diary records the work day by day from 5 February. On 9 February Raman said the discovery should be called the “Raman–Krishnan effect”. On 28 February they announced it, and the diary breaks off in mid-sentence after that day. The world’s books call it the Raman effect, but Krishnan’s name belongs in the story, and Raman himself put it there first.

In 1930 Raman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics “for his work on the scattering of light and for the discovery of the effect named after him”. In India, 28 February is now National Science Day.

Step 3: why a changed colour matters

Ordinary scattering is a catch and a re-send: the molecule shakes with the light and re-broadcasts the same colour. In the Raman effect something is exchanged. The light hands a little of its energy to the molecule and sets it vibrating, and light with a little less energy is a little redder; now and then an already-vibrating molecule hands energy back, and the light comes out a little bluer. (Why light’s energy and its colour go together is a question for Chapter 15.) Each kind of molecule vibrates in its own ways, so each gives its own set of shifts. Measure the shifted colours, and you can tell what the liquid is made of without touching it. The sea had led Raman to a fingerprint for molecules.

Careful

“Raman discovered why the sky is blue.”

That was ordinary scattering, which keeps the colour, and Rayleigh had explained it fifty years before. Raman showed that the sea’s blue is its own, and then found the rare scattering that changes colour. And “the light scattered by a liquid changes colour” is wrong too: almost all of it keeps its colour, and only a tiny fraction shifts. The smallness of the fraction is why the discovery took seven years and a careful laboratory, and why nobody can see it at home.

Raman’s test at the sea wall

Borrow a pair of polarised sunglasses and first check them on a phone or laptop screen: if the screen darkens as you slowly turn the lenses, they are polarised. (If nothing changes, they are only tinted and will not work.) Then, with an adult, go to Marine Drive on a bright day, look at the sea about a third of the way down from the horizon to your feet, and tilt your head slowly from one shoulder to the other. The glare on the water brightens and dims as you tilt. The sea’s blue stays. You have just repeated Raman’s experiment, with sunglasses instead of a crystal.

In Chapter 11 the Narkunda is Section 11.4 and the colour that changed is Section 11.6, which opens the ladder of light from radio waves to gamma rays. Why a shift in colour means a shift in energy waits for Chapter 15.

984 to 1621

The coin that rises

Ibn Sahl, Willebrord Snell

Your kitchen, this afternoon

Drop a coin into an empty steel tumbler and look at it from above. Now pour in water, slowly, and keep looking. The coin seems to rise. The bottom of the tumbler looks nearer than it did, and the coin with it, though neither has moved a millimetre. Stand a pencil in a glass half full of water and look from the side: the pencil appears bent, or broken, exactly at the waterline.

Nothing has happened to the coin or the pencil. Something has happened to the light on its way from them to you. It has changed direction where it left the water, and your eye, which assumes light arrives in straight lines, has been fooled about where it came from.

The rule for how much light bends at a surface was written down in 984 by Ibn Sahl, and found again about six centuries later by Willebrord Snell in Leiden, around 1621, so that it carries Snell’s name. Neither of them could say why light bends. That came later, and it is the simplest part of the story.

Step 1: light bends because it slows

Light travels more slowly in water than in air: three-quarters as fast, 2.25 hundred million metres a second instead of 3.00. Now picture a beam meeting the water at a slant. The side of the beam that reaches the water first slows down first, while the other side is still moving at full speed in the air. The fast side swings round the slow side, the way a lawnmower swings when one wheel runs off the path onto thick grass, and the whole beam turns towards the perpendicular to the surface. Leaving the water, the reverse happens: the side that reaches the air first speeds up first, and the beam turns away from the perpendicular. A beam that meets the surface head-on slows down but has no reason to turn, so it goes straight.

This change of direction at a boundary is refraction, and light that has done it has been refracted. The cause is the change of speed. Not weight, not density, not any pull from the water: speed.

How much a material slows light is its refractive index, the speed of light in empty space divided by the speed in the material. Water’s is 1.333, ordinary glass about 1.52, diamond 2.42. A bigger index means more slowing and more bending, which is why a diamond flashes and a glass of water only bends things a little.

Step 2: the rule

The rule Ibn Sahl and Snell found, Snell’s law, fixes the angles. For light passing from air into water, a beam arriving at 45° to the perpendicular continues at 32°; one arriving at 30° continues at 22°. At school you will meet it as a rule about sines, and it works for any wave that changes speed at a boundary: ripples running from deep water into shallow, sound passing from warm air into cold, light passing from air into glass.

Step 3: the coin

Light from the coin heads up to the surface at a slant and bends away from the perpendicular as it leaves the water. Your eye catches that bent ray and traces it straight back, as eyes do, to a point above and nearer than the coin. Every ray from the coin is bent the same way, so the whole coin appears to have risen. The coin has not moved. Its image has.

How much does it rise? Looking straight down, the water’s depth appears divided by its refractive index.
A coin under 10 cm of water: 10 ÷ 1.333 = 7.5 cm. It looks 2.5 cm nearer than it is.
Under 8 cm of water: 8 ÷ 1.333 = 6.0 cm.
Looking in at a slant, it looks shallower still.

This is why a pond always looks shallower than it is, and why people who dive into unfamiliar water can hurt themselves on a bottom that looked further away. It is also why your legs look short when you stand in a swimming pool: the light from your feet bends on its way out, and your eye traces it back to feet that are not there.

Step 4: a curve makes a lens

At a flat surface every part of a beam bends by the same amount, so the beam stays a beam. Curve the surface, and different parts of the beam meet it at different slants and bend by different amounts. Shape the curve right, bulging outwards like a lentil, and all the rays of a parallel beam can be brought together at one point, the focus. A piece of glass or water shaped to do this is a lens, and lenses are what the rest of this story is about.

A magnifying glass is a lens. Hold one in sunlight and it gathers the whole beam that falls on it into a point so bright and hot it can scorch paper, which is why you must never let a lens focus sunlight anywhere near an eye. Every part of the lens helps to form its image: cover half the lens and you still see the whole image, only dimmer. A drop of water bulges too. Put a drop on a sheet of clear plastic laid over newsprint and look through it: the letters beneath are magnified. You have made a lens out of water.

Step 5: the two lenses in your head

Your eye is a lens system, and it forms a real, upside-down image on the retina at the back, like the pinhole camera’s picture on its screen but far brighter. The surprising part is which piece does the work. Most of the bending happens at the cornea, the clear front of the eye, because air to cornea is the biggest change of speed on the way in; the cornea does about two-thirds of the job. The lens inside, behind the pupil, does the fine tuning. Muscles around it make it fatter to focus on near things and let it flatten for far ones, and for a young eye the nearest comfortable point is about 25 cm away.

Open your eyes underwater and everything blurs. The cornea’s index is 1.38, and water’s is 1.33, so the change of speed at the cornea nearly vanishes and two-thirds of the eye’s bending goes missing. A swimming mask puts a layer of air back in front of the eye and the bending returns. Glasses work on the same principle. A short-sighted eye bends light too strongly, so its glasses bend it slightly outwards first; a long-sighted eye bends too weakly, so its glasses add a little bending. Glasses change the light on its way in. They do not change the eye.

Careful

“The water pulls the light towards it, and that is why it bends.”

Nothing pulls. Light slows down in water, and when a slanting beam slows on one side before the other it swings round. Leaving the water it speeds up and swings the other way. If it were a pull, light leaving water would bend the same way as light entering it, and it bends the opposite way.

The coin, the pencil and a drop

Put a coin in a steel tumbler and look at it from above as you pour in water: watch it seem to rise. Stand a pencil in a glass half full of water and look from the side, then from above, then from below the waterline, and notice where it looks bent and where it looks whole. For the lens, lay a piece of clear plastic (the lid of a food box works) over a page of small print, put one drop of water on it, and read through the drop. Then flatten the drop with a fingertip and read again: a flatter drop magnifies less. The curve is the lens.

In Chapter 10, Section 10.4 is the bending and the disappearing coin, and Section 10.5 is lenses and the eye. In Chapter 11 the bending turns out to be slightly different for each colour, which is what a prism is for.

about 1583

Pushing a swing

Galileo Galilei, Vincenzo Viviani

Pisa, about 1583

The story goes like this. Galileo Galilei, nineteen years old and a student at the university, is sitting through a long service in the cathedral at Pisa. A lamp hanging from the ceiling on a chain has been left swinging, and Galileo watches it. The swings slowly die down, from wide arcs to small ones, and yet, as far as he can tell, each swing takes the same time as the one before. He has no watch, so he times the lamp against his own pulse. Wide swing or narrow swing: the same number of heartbeats.

It is a good story, and you should know that it is a legend. It comes from one source only, Vincenzo Viviani, who was Galileo’s assistant in the last years of Galileo’s life and wrote it down long afterwards, without a date. Galileo never told it himself. The lamp that hangs in the cathedral today was put up after Galileo had left Pisa.

Here is the true part. Galileo really did study swinging weights, and the rule he found is where this story starts. From there we go to a child on a swing, a singer and a wine glass, and two bridges that moved when they should not have.

Step 1: every swing has its own rhythm

Tie a key to a metre of thread, pull it a little to one side and let go. It swings across and back, and one complete swing, out and home again, takes about two seconds. A weight swinging like this is a pendulum, and any motion that repeats itself in this way, back and forth about a resting place, is an oscillation.

Now change things and watch what happens to the two seconds. Pull the key further to one side before you let go: it travels further, but each swing still takes about two seconds, because it moves faster. Tie on a heavier key: still two seconds. The mass does not matter at all. Only one thing changes the time, and that is the length of the thread. A thread four times as long swings twice as slowly; a thread a quarter as long swings twice as fast.

So a pendulum has a rhythm of its own, fixed by its length. Physicists count it as swings per second and call it the natural frequency: the rate at which a thing oscillates when nothing is pushing it and nothing is holding it back. A pendulum has one. So does a playground swing, a guitar string, a wine glass, a tall building and a bridge. Anything that can wobble has a rhythm it wobbles at when left alone.

One honest footnote to the legend. “Wide swings take the same time as narrow ones” is nearly true. For small swings the time hardly changes at all. For big swings it grows a little: a swing out to 60° from the vertical takes about 7% longer than a tiny one. A pulse could never have noticed; a phone stopwatch can.

Step 2: pushing in time

Watch a parent pushing a small child on a swing. The swing has its own rhythm. If its chains are 2.5 m long, one swing out and back takes about 3.2 s. The parent does not shove. They give a small push each time the seat comes back to them, and the swings grow, and grow, until the child is flying.

Why does a small push do so much? Each push adds a little energy of motion to the swing. If the pushes come at the swing’s own rhythm, every push lands just as the seat is moving away from the pusher, so every push speeds it up. The small additions add up, swing after swing.

Now try pushing at the wrong rhythm, say twice a second. Some pushes land while the seat is moving away and speed it up; others land while it is moving towards you and slow it down. The pushes cancel each other out and the swing never gets going. Push far too slowly and the seat just follows your hand.

Driving a thing at its own natural frequency, so that small pushes add up into a large motion, is resonance. That is the whole idea. Everything else in this story is the same idea in different clothes.

How often should the parent push? Suppose the swing’s chains are 2.5 m long (a guess for a park swing).
Time for one swing: T = 2π√(L ÷ g) = 2π × √(2.5 ÷ 9.8) = 3.2 s.
So: one push every 3.2 s, each time the seat returns. Pushes every 1.6 s, or every 6.4 s, land at the wrong moment half the time and fight each other.

Step 3: a wine glass and a singer

Wet a finger and rub it slowly round the rim of a wine glass, and the glass sings a clear note. Your finger slips and catches, slips and catches, hundreds of times a second, and each catch is a tiny push. The glass answers at its own natural frequency; that one note is the sound of the glass resonating.

This is also how a singer can break a glass, and the trick is not loudness alone. The singer has to find the glass’s own note and hold it, so that each ripple of sound arriving at the glass pushes it the way it is already moving. A loud wrong note leaves the glass unharmed; the right note, held steadily, can shake it until it shatters. (Not one to try at home: it takes a loudspeaker.)

How large the motion grows depends on friction. A swing with very little friction keeps adding up pushes for a long time before the losses catch up, so its peak is tall and narrow, and you must hit the rhythm almost exactly. More friction drains the energy faster, so the peak is lower and broader, and the rhythm matters less.

Step 4: two bridges

Soldiers crossing a bridge are ordered to break step. Hundreds of boots landing together at a steady rhythm are hundreds of small pushes in time, and if that rhythm happens to match the bridge’s own, the pushes add up.

Something like that happened in London on 10 June 2000, when the Millennium Bridge, a new footbridge over the Thames, opened to crowds. The deck began to sway from side to side. People adjusted their steps to keep their balance, fell into step with the sway without meaning to, and their footfalls pushed it further. The bridge closed two days later and reopened in 2002 with dampers fitted: devices that drain away the energy of the sway faster than walkers can add it. More friction, lower peak.

The most famous bridge collapse of all is usually told as resonance, and it was not. In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge, in the state of Washington, twisted itself to pieces in a steady wind, and the film is shown in physics classes everywhere with the explanation that gusts of wind happened to arrive in time with the bridge’s natural rhythm. The wind that day was not gusting. The deck twisted a little; the twist changed the way the steady wind pushed on it; the changed push twisted it further. Each twist fed the next, with no rhythm from outside at all. Engineers call that flutter, and it is the same thing that makes a flag flap in a steady breeze. Resonance needs a push that keeps time. Flutter makes its own.

Careful

“Resonance turns a small push into a huge force. It must be making energy from nothing.”

It makes nothing. Each push adds a little energy of motion, and resonance only arranges the pushes so that they add up instead of cancelling. The energy in the child’s enormous swing is the sum of all the parent’s small pushes, less what friction has taken away. Stop pushing and the swing dies down.

Find the rhythm

Tie a key or a nut to about half a metre of thread and hold the top end between finger and thumb. Move your hand gently from side to side, a centimetre or two, at different rhythms. Most rhythms do almost nothing: the key jiggles, or just follows your hand. One rhythm, about once every 1.4 s for a half-metre thread, builds a big steady swing out of the same tiny hand movements. Now lengthen the thread to a metre and find the rhythm again. It should be about once every 2 s. Longer thread, slower rhythm.

In Chapter 9 the pendulum is the first thing you meet that oscillates (Section 9.1), and resonance returns in Section 9.2, where the two bridges get a closer look, and again in Section 9.6, where a drumhead rings at its own set of natural frequencies.

about 1011 to 1021

Light comes in

Ibn al-Haytham, Euclid, Ptolemy

Cairo, about 1011

The story goes that Ibn al-Haytham came to Cairo with a promise he could not keep, a scheme to tame the floods of the Nile for the Caliph al-Hakim, and that when it failed he pretended to be mad to escape the Caliph’s anger, and was shut up in his house for years with nothing to do but think. Historians doubt that story. What nobody doubts is the book he wrote in Cairo in the years around 1011 to 1021, the Book of Optics, and the question at the heart of it: how do we see?

The old answer came from Euclid and, later, Ptolemy, two of the greatest names in Greek science. The eye, they said, does the seeing by sending something out: rays that leave the eye, travel to the object and feel it, rather as a stick feels the ground. The idea is called extramission, “sending out”, and before you smile at it, know that most people still believe it. When students were asked to draw how a person sees a balloon, 86 in every 100 drew arrows going from the eye to the balloon. Among adults asked directly, 69 in 100 said that something leaves the eye. Even for a lit bulb, a third of adults said so. It feels right. You look at things, and looking feels like an action, something you do to the world.

Ibn al-Haytham argued the other way: nothing leaves the eye, and light comes in. He gave reasons. Look at the Sun or a very bright lamp and your eyes hurt; if the eye were the one sending out rays, why should a brighter object hurt it more? And every point of a lit object, he said, sends out light of its own in every direction, so light from every point of it can reach your eye. Then he did what the Greeks had not done. He tested his ideas with experiments, including one in a dark room.

Step 1: the dark room, first version

Try his question yourself tonight. Go into a windowless bathroom, shut the door, switch off the light, and wait a full minute for your eyes to adjust. Now hold your hand in front of your face. Can you see it?

If your eyes sent out rays, there is no reason you should not. Your hand is right there, and your eyes are working perfectly. But you see nothing at all. The waiting matters, because it rules out the excuse “my eyes just needed time”. With no light in the room, time does not help. Your eyes are collectors, not torches, and there is nothing to collect.

Step 2: the chain

So here is the chain that seeing needs. A source makes light: the Sun, a lamp, a screen. The light travels to your hand. Your hand is not a mirror; its rough surface sends the light off in every direction, which is why everyone in the room can see your hand from wherever they happen to be standing. A tiny share of that scattered light enters your eye. Three links, and the light moves towards the eye at every step: from the source, off the hand, into the eye. Break any link and you see nothing. In the dark bathroom the first link is missing.

Your eye can work with astonishingly little. It copes with brightness from the faintest light it can detect up to ten thousand million times brighter. That is why “a bit of light from somewhere” is nearly always enough, and why a truly dark room is such a rare experience that the bathroom test surprises people.

Step 3: the dark room, second version

Ibn al-Haytham’s second use of a dark room is still famous, and still works. Make a room completely dark except for one small hole in the shutter, and look at the wall opposite the hole. The sunlit scene outside appears on it: dim, in colour, moving, and upside down. People in the street walk along the wall with their feet in the air. The Latin name for such a room, camera obscura, means “dark chamber”, and it is where the word camera comes from.

Why upside down? Because light travels in straight lines. Light from the top of a tree outside passes straight through the hole and keeps going straight, so it lands low on the wall. Light from the bottom of the tree lands high. Every point outside sends light through the hole to exactly one point on the wall, and the picture is the scene turned over. The hole must be small. A big hole lets light from one point outside land in many places on the wall, and the picture blurs into a glow.

This is a strong argument against rays from the eye, because the picture forms whether anyone is looking or not. A wall does not look at anything. Light is arriving there, through the hole, in straight lines, and making the picture by itself. A shoebox with a pinhole in one end, a pinhole camera, does exactly the same, and you can build one this afternoon.

How big is the picture? Suppose a doorway 2 m tall stands 5 m from the pinhole of a shoebox camera 30 cm deep. Light from the top and the bottom of the doorway crosses at the hole and spreads out again inside the box. The two triangles, outside and inside, have the same shape, so
image height ÷ 0.30 m = 2 m ÷ 5 m, and the image is 2 × 0.30 ÷ 5 = 0.12 m: a 12 cm doorway, upside down.

Careful

“My eyes need light to work, the way a torch needs batteries.”

That puts light inside the eye’s job. Light is not fuel for the eye; it is the thing the eye collects. Light has to travel from an object into your eye, and if nothing is sending light your way, the best eyes in the world see nothing. Every arrow in a drawing of seeing should end at the eye.

A camera obscura from a shoebox

Cut a window about the size of a playing card in one end of a shoebox and tape tracing paper, or thin white paper, over it as a screen. Cover the other end with kitchen foil and prick one small hole in the middle of the foil with a pin. Put the lid on. In a dim room, point the pinhole end at a bright window and look at the paper screen: the window appears on it, upside down, with the room’s ceiling at the bottom. Try pricking a second, bigger hole with a pencil point: brighter, and blurred. Never point the camera at the Sun, and never look at the Sun through the hole. For the chain’s first link, fill a plant sprayer with water, darken the room, and shine a torch across it while you spray a fine mist. The beam appears only where droplets are sending light into your eye, and vanishes where the air is clear.

In Chapter 10 the dark bathroom opens Section 10.1 and the pinhole camera is Section 10.2. The idea that nothing leaves the eye comes back in Chapter 11, where a banana under red light turns out to be a question about what arrives, not about what the banana is.

1676 to 1849

Ten minutes late

Ole Rømer, Christiaan Huygens, Hippolyte Fizeau

Paris, September 1676

Jupiter has moons, and one of them, Io, slips into Jupiter’s shadow on a schedule as regular as a clock. At the new observatory in Paris, Ole Rømer had been timing these eclipses for months, and the schedule would not hold. While the Earth, on its own orbit round the Sun, was moving away from Jupiter, each eclipse came a little later than the last one had predicted. While the Earth was moving back towards Jupiter, they came early.

Nothing was wrong with Io. Rømer saw what the drift meant. The light that showed him each eclipse had to travel from Jupiter to his telescope, and when the Earth was farther away it had farther to travel, so it arrived later. Light was not instant. It took time, and the drifting schedule was that time showing itself. In September 1676 he announced that the eclipse due that November would come about ten minutes later than the tables said. It did.

Step 1: a time, not a speed

People today say Rømer measured the speed of light. He did not, and the honest version is better. He never stated a speed. In a letter the following year he put his result as a time: about 22 minutes, he reckoned, for light to cross the full width of the Earth’s orbit, from one side of the Sun to the other. His friend Christiaan Huygens did the arithmetic that turned the time into a speed, and his answer came out well short of the truth, because Rømer’s 22 minutes was too long. The real figure is about 16.6 minutes. But it was the first number anyone had, and it was enormous. Galileo, a generation earlier, had concluded only that light was extremely fast, perhaps instantaneous. Now it had a size.

Step 2: how fast is that?

Today the speed of light in empty space is known exactly: 299,792,458 metres every second. Exactly, because since 1983 nobody measures it any more; the metre itself is defined from it, as the distance light covers in a certain tiny fraction of a second. In round numbers, light goes nearly 300,000 kilometres in one second, which would take it round the Earth seven and a half times.

At that speed, distances turn into times. Light from the Moon takes 1.3 seconds to reach you. Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes and 19 seconds, so the sunshine on your arm left the Sun before you started reading this page. Light crossing the whole width of the Earth’s orbit, Rømer’s distance, takes 16.6 minutes, and that is the delay he saw in Io’s timetable.

How old is sunlight? The Sun is 149,597,870,700 m away (an exact value, fixed by astronomers).
Time = distance ÷ speed = 149,597,870,700 ÷ 299,792,458 = 499 s.
499 s = 8 min 19 s. Across the Earth’s orbit, twice that: 998 s, or 16.6 min.

Step 3: a cogwheel across Paris

For a hundred and seventy years the speed of light was known only from the sky. Measuring it on the ground meant timing something that crossed a city in a hundred-thousandth of a second, and no clock could do that. In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau found a way to make a wheel do it instead.

Paris, 1849

He set a lamp behind a spinning cogwheel with 720 teeth on a hill at Suresnes, on the edge of Paris, and a mirror on Montmartre, about 8.6 km away. Light flashed out through a gap between two teeth, crossed to the mirror, and came back to the wheel. If the wheel turned slowly, the returning light came back through the same gap and he saw the mirror glow. Spin the wheel faster, and there comes a speed at which, in the time the light took to go there and back, the wheel has turned by exactly half a tooth, so the returning flash meets a tooth and is blocked. The mirror goes dark. The wheel’s spin was his clock. The round trip is about 17 km, and the mirror first goes dark at about twelve turns a second, which makes each flash’s journey about sixty millionths of a second. From that Fizeau got about 315,000 km/s, around 5% too high, which for a cogwheel and a lamp is remarkable.

After him, Léon Foucault did it with a spinning mirror in 1862 and came within 0.6%, and Albert Michelson kept refining the method until 1926. Then the measuring stopped, for the reason in Step 2: in 1983 the value was fixed by definition, and the metre was redefined to fit it.

Careful

“Lightning comes before thunder, so that proves light is incredibly fast.”

It proves only that light is faster than sound. The flash and the bang leave the lightning together; the bang arrives seconds later because sound crawls along at about a third of a kilometre a second. The flash also takes time, about three millionths of a second for each kilometre, and that is far too short for you to notice. “Too fast to notice” is not the same as “instant”. Rømer’s whole discovery was the difference between the two.

Count the storm

During a monsoon storm, stay indoors by a window and watch for a flash. The moment you see it, count seconds, and stop at the thunder. Sound travels about 349 metres a second in warm air, so every three seconds of counting is roughly one kilometre between you and the lightning. Fifteen seconds is about five kilometres. If the count shrinks from one flash to the next, the storm is coming nearer. The light’s own delay over five kilometres is seventeen millionths of a second, which is why you can treat the flash as the moment it happened.

In Chapter 10 the speed of light is Section 10.6, where the Moon’s radio delay and the age of sunlight come back. In Chapter 13, Section 13.6, James Clerk Maxwell works out from electricity and magnetism how fast a certain kind of wave must travel, and gets Fizeau’s number.

about 1589 to 1920

How a tabla sings

Vincenzo Galilei, C. V. Raman, Sivakali Kumar

Florence, about 1589

Vincenzo Galilei was a musician, a player of the lute, with a scientist’s habit of checking things. He also had a son in his twenties called Galileo.

The thing Vincenzo checked was two thousand years old. The story goes that Pythagoras, walking past a blacksmith’s, heard the hammers ringing out notes in harmony, weighed the hammers, and found that their weights stood in simple ratios, two to one for the octave. From that, so the story says, came the laws of harmony. It is a legend. It was first written down by Nicomachus about six hundred years after Pythagoras lived, and the physics in it is wrong: the weight of a hammer does not set its note.

Vincenzo tested the string version of the idea. Everyone knew that a string half as long sounds an octave higher. The legend’s logic says that a string pulled twice as tight should do the same. So Vincenzo hung weights from strings to stretch them, and listened. Twice the weight did not give an octave. Four times the weight did. There was a simple ratio in it, but it was the square of the one in the story, and only an experiment could have found that.

That one measurement is the first true thing in this story. The rest is about why a string sings a note at all, why a drum usually does not, and how drum-makers in India made one that does.

Step 1: what pitch is

Pluck a string and it vibrates, swinging back and forth too fast to see. The air beside it is shoved back and forth at the same rate, and that is what reaches your ear. The number of vibrations each second is the frequency; what you hear is pitch. Fast vibration, high note; slow vibration, low note. Human ears hear from about 20 vibrations a second up to about 20,000.

Pull a string tighter and it vibrates faster, so its note rises. That is what Vincenzo’s weights were doing, and it is what a tabla player does when tuning: the head is tightened or slackened until the note is right.

Step 2: a string’s ladder of notes

A string fixed at both ends cannot vibrate in just any way. Its ends are held still, so the simplest pattern is the whole string swinging as one hump, out and back. That gives the lowest note the string can make, its fundamental. But the string can also swing in two halves, with the middle point still and the two halves moving opposite ways; or in three thirds; or four quarters. Each pattern has its own frequency, and because a half is half as long as the whole, the halves vibrate exactly twice as fast; the thirds three times as fast; the quarters four times.

When you pluck a string you set off many of these patterns at once, so the string sounds its fundamental and a stack of higher notes with it. The higher notes are called overtones. Overtones that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental (two times, three times, four times, and so on) are called harmonics. For an ideal string every overtone is a harmonic: the rungs of its ladder sit at 1, 2, 3, 4 times the lowest note, evenly spaced.

Your ear does something clever with a ladder like that. It hears the whole stack as one note, the fundamental, with a particular colour. How strong each rung is sets the colour, and that is why a violin and a piano playing the same note sound nothing alike.

Now Vincenzo’s result makes sense. A wiggle travels along a tighter string faster, and the speed grows with the square root of the pull. To double every frequency on the ladder you must double the speed, and to double the speed you need four times the pull. Four times the weight: an octave.

A string’s ladder. If the whole-string hump vibrates 100 times a second:
halves → 200 Hz · thirds → 300 Hz · quarters → 400 Hz · fifths → 500 Hz.
Every rung is a whole-number multiple, so the ear hears one note at 100 Hz, coloured by the rest.

Step 3: why a drum thuds

A drumhead is a skin held still all round its rim, and it too can only vibrate in certain patterns: one hump in the middle; two halves rocking like a seesaw; a ring moving opposite to the centre; quarters; and so on. The catch is in the frequencies. Work them out for a perfectly even, flat drumhead and the ladder comes out at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30 and 2.65 times the lowest note. Not one of those is a whole number. The rungs are out of tune with one another, so the ear cannot gather them into a single note, and what you hear is a thud with a vague sense of height. That is most drums, from an upturned bucket to a bass drum.

A plain drumhead’s ladder. If its lowest pattern vibrates 100 times a second, the next ones are at about
159 Hz, 214 Hz, 230 Hz and 265 Hz.
No whole numbers. Played together they clash, and the ear gives up on finding a note.

Calcutta, 1920

Strike a tabla and you get something different: a clear, singing note you could hum back. In January 1920 C. V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar published a short paper in Nature on why. Most drums, they showed, give overtones that are out of tune, just as the arithmetic says. The tabla and the mridangam give overtones that are harmonic, in whole-number steps like a string’s. The reason is the black patch.

Look at a tabla’s head. In the middle is a dark disc, the syahi, a patch that loads the centre of the skin and makes it heavier than the rest. Loading the middle changes the rhythms of the different patterns, most of all the ones that move the middle most, and the patch is made to just the size and weight that pull the out-of-tune rungs onto whole numbers. The drum-makers found this by ear, generations before anyone could write down why it worked. Raman and Kumar wrote it down.

Careful

“Hit the tabla harder and the note goes up.”

Harder gives a bigger vibration, and a bigger vibration is louder, not higher. Pitch is set by how fast the head vibrates, and that depends on how tight it is and how big it is, which a harder blow does not change. Loudness and pitch are separate knobs. Turning one does not turn the other.

Notes from a bottle, and a string cut in half

Blow gently across the top of an empty glass bottle until it toots. Pour in some water and blow again: the note is higher, because the column of air that vibrates is shorter. More water, higher still. If there is a guitar or any stringed instrument at home, try this too: pluck a string, then pluck it again while touching it very lightly at its exact middle with a fingertip. The note jumps an octave higher and sounds thinner. Your finger has held the middle still, so the string can only vibrate in halves, and you are hearing the second rung of its ladder on its own.

In Chapter 9, Section 9.5 separates loud from high, and Section 9.6 builds the ladder of harmonics rung by rung and lets you hear the difference between a string’s ladder and a drum’s. Raman returns in Chapter 11, on the deck of a ship, asking why the sea is blue.

1895 to 1897

Invisible waves in Calcutta

Jagadish Chandra Bose, Lord Rayleigh, Guglielmo Marconi

Calcutta, 1895

In 1895 Jagadish Chandra Bose, a physics teacher at Presidency College in Calcutta, gave a public demonstration of something nobody in the room could see. On one side stood his transmitter, a spark that set electric charge surging back and forth tens of thousands of millions of times a second. Twenty-three metres away, about seventy-five feet, beyond two intervening walls, stood a receiver. When the spark fired, the receiver rang a bell and set off a small charge of gunpowder. Nothing visible had crossed the room. The story goes that the Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, Sir Alexander Mackenzie, presided; accounts written later disagree about the date and about how many walls there were, so hold those details loosely. The experiment itself is not in doubt.

Hertz, in Karlsruhe eight years earlier, had made Maxwell’s waves with wavelengths of metres. Bose went the other way. His waves were between 2.5 centimetres and 5 millimetres long, which made them, in modern language, microwaves, and at the short end millimetre waves. He chose that range partly for a practical reason: his laboratory at Presidency College was small, and short waves can be steered and focused in a small space. To do the steering he built, from scratch, almost every part of the kit: a spark transmitter, lenses of dielectric material to focus the waves, a polariser, horn-shaped antennas to gather them, a grating to split them, and a receiver, the coherer, that could tell when a wave had arrived.

London, January 1897

In January 1897 Bose lectured on his waves at the Royal Institution in London, at the invitation of Lord Rayleigh. It was the same lecture hall where Faraday had shown his motor and his iron ring. Bose was thirty-eight. In December 1901, on a hill in Newfoundland, Marconi reported hearing three faint dots, the letter S, sent from Cornwall across the Atlantic by waves of the same family; sceptics have argued ever since about whether he heard a signal or static. Bose was not in that race, and it is worth being exact about why. In 1901 a patent application for his crystal detector was filed in the United States, not by him but on his behalf by his friends Sara Bull and Sister Nivedita; it was granted in 1904 as US patent 755,840. Bose did not pursue it commercially, and it lapsed. The often-repeated line that he refused to patent anything is too simple; what is true is that he did not try to make money from the work.

In 2012 the IEEE placed a plaque in the main building of Presidency College, naming his experiments of 1894 to 1896 a Milestone in the history of electrical engineering.

Step 1: what a five-millimetre wave is

An electromagnetic wave is a ripple of electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light, 300,000 kilometres a second. Its wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next; its frequency is how many crests pass each second. Multiply them and you always get the speed of light, so a shorter wave swings faster.

How fast do Bose’s waves swing?
frequency = speed ÷ wavelength = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s ÷ 0.005 m = 6.0 × 10¹⁰ per second.
Sixty thousand million swings a second: 60 gigahertz.
A metre-long radio wave swings 300 million times a second, two hundred times more slowly.

Step 2: why short waves behave like light

The shorter a wave, the more it behaves like a ray of light: it can be focused by a lens, bent, split, blocked by a polariser, and aimed. Metre-long waves spread round corners and wash over whole buildings. Bose’s millimetre waves could be shaped with lenses and horns small enough for a bench, which is exactly why he could do optics with them: reflection, refraction, polarisation, all with waves the eye cannot see. Those same waves pass through walls that stop visible light, which is how they reached the bell. Whether a wall is “transparent” depends on the wave, not on the wall.

Step 3: how the bell rang

The receiver had to turn an arriving wave into something that could ring a bell. Bose’s coherer did that: a device whose electrical contact changed when the waves hit it, so that a current from an ordinary battery could suddenly flow and work the bell. The waves themselves carried almost no energy. They carried a signal, and the battery supplied the push. Every radio receiver since has worked on the same division of labour: a faint wave is detected, and local power does the rest.

Step 4: the same waves today

The physics has not changed since 1895. A wave five millimetres long still swings sixty thousand million times a second, still focuses through a lens, still passes through a wall, and the slice of the ladder from centimetres down to millimetres is now crowded with the signals that carry modern life about.

Careful

“Bose invented radio.”

The documented record is narrower and more interesting. He made and detected millimetre waves in 1894 to 1896, built the first instruments for handling them, and showed them in Calcutta and London before Marconi’s Atlantic signal. Hertz made the waves first; Marconi built the long-distance business. Bose’s contribution was the short-wave optics, and it was far ahead of its time.

Careful

“Walls stop waves.”

Walls stop some waves. Visible light does not get through brick; Bose’s millimetre waves did. What a material blocks depends on the wavelength, which is also why a phone works indoors but a torch does not shine through a door.

In Chapter 13 Bose’s bell is the last scene of the electromagnetism story, and the ladder of light is laid out rung by rung. Chapter 15 asks what these waves are made of, and finds an answer that would have surprised him.

1827

What goes round

Georg Simon Ohm

Berlin, 1827

In 1827 a mathematics teacher on leave from a school in Cologne published a book in Berlin with a forbidding title: Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet, “The galvanic circuit, treated mathematically”. His name was Georg Simon Ohm. Since hearing of Ørsted’s discovery in 1820 he had been experimenting in his school’s well-equipped physics laboratory, and in 1826 he had published two papers that treated the flow of electricity through a wire the way Fourier had treated the flow of heat through a bar. The book put it all together. Inside it is the rule now written into every physics syllabus: the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it.

The book was received, in one historian’s words, with little enthusiasm. The older German physicists were not convinced that a mathematical approach was the right one, and Ohm’s writing did not help: he never quite said which form of his law was the fundamental one. He had hoped the book would win him a university post. Instead he resigned from the Cologne school in March 1828 and took temporary teaching work in Berlin. The post he accepted in Nuremberg in 1833 carried the title of professor, but it was not a university chair.

Recognition came from abroad, and slowly. In 1841, fourteen years after the book, the Royal Society in London gave him its Copley Medal. In 1852, two years before he died, the University of Munich made him its professor of physics. The unit of resistance carries his name.

To see what his rule says, and why it matters, you need the whole loop first.

Step 1: a loop, not a pipe

A battery has two terminals. Join them with a continuous path of conductor, a wire, a bulb, a wire back, and charge flows round the whole path. Break the path anywhere and it stops. That is all an electric circuit is: a complete, closed loop. One wire from the battery to the bulb is never enough, and the reason is not that the bulb needs a “return pipe” for used-up electricity. The reason is that the battery’s chemistry only runs when the loop is complete; the reaction inside it will not take place without one.

Textbooks like to compare a circuit with water in a pipe, and the comparison helps up to a point. Here is where it stops. The wire is solid metal that is already full of electrons free to move. Nothing pours into it from the battery. Cut a wire and nothing spills out.

Step 2: the rope

Picture instead a long loop of rope passing through the hands of a circle of people. One of them is the battery: she hauls the rope steadily along. Another is the bulb: he grips it, the rope rubs through his fingers, and his hands get warm. Everyone else lets the rope slide. Notice three things. The rope moves everywhere at once: the moment the battery pulls, the far side of the loop moves too. No rope is used up: exactly as much comes back into her hands as leaves them. And the warmth appears only where the rope is gripped. (The rope is this book’s own picture, not a measurement. Like every model it stops somewhere, and it stops at telling you what the rope is made of.)

Measure the current in a real loop and that is what you find: the same current at every point, including inside the battery. The current neither speeds up in the wires nor slows down in the bulb; if it did, charge would pile up somewhere, and it does not. What the bulb takes is energy, delivered where the charge is squeezed through. Energy is what gets used up. Current is what goes round.

Step 3: push and resistance

The battery’s job is to push. Its voltage is the push per coulomb of charge: a 1.5 V cell gives each coulomb 1.5 joules of energy to spend on the way round. Resistance is how much a component opposes the flow: a long thin wire opposes more than a short thick one. Ohm found that, for a given conductor at an ordinary temperature, doubling the push doubles the current. Written out:

V = I × R (voltage = current × resistance)

A car headlamp carries 2.50 A when 12.0 V is across it. What is its resistance?
R = V ÷ I = 12.0 ÷ 2.50 = 4.8 Ω.
Halve the voltage to 6.0 V and, if the resistance stays at 4.8 Ω, the current halves to 1.25 A.

It is an empirical rule, found by measuring, and it holds for most materials at common temperatures. It fails for some. A lamp filament’s resistance rises as it heats, so the line bends. An LED hardly passes any current until the push reaches about 2 volts, and then passes a great deal. A battery sets the push, roughly, not the current; the current depends on what you connect.

Step 4: slow drift, fast signal

Flick a switch and the light comes on at once, so the electrons must race round the loop. They do not. In a copper wire half a millimetre thick carrying 15 mA to an LED, the electrons drift along at about 6 millionths of a metre per second: two days to crawl one metre. (Each electron also jiggles about at high speed in random directions, but the jiggling averages to nothing.) What travels fast is the push itself, a change in the electric field that runs along the already-full wire at roughly 10⁸ m/s, a million million times faster than the drift. Every electron in the loop starts moving almost at once, but each one only creeps. The rope moves everywhere at once; no single fibre travels far.

Step 5: one after another, or side by side

Put two bulbs in one loop, one after the other, and you have a series circuit: the same current passes through both, their resistances add, the current falls, and both glow dimmer, the first no brighter than the second. Join them side by side instead, each with both its ends on the battery, and you have a parallel circuit: each gets the full push, and the currents through them add. Your flat is wired in parallel. Every light and fan sits on its own branch, so when one bulb’s filament breaks, only that branch opens and the rest stay lit.

One last convention. Circuit diagrams draw the current flowing from the battery’s + terminal round to its −. That direction, conventional current, was agreed before anyone knew about electrons. In a metal wire the electrons move the other way. Both arrows are correct, as long as you say which one you mean.

Careful

“The bulb uses up the current, so less comes back to the battery.”

The same current flows out of the bulb as into it, and the same current flows through the battery. Nothing is lost on the way round. What the bulb uses is energy: the battery gives each coulomb a push, and the bulb turns that energy into light and heat.

Careful

“A battery always gives the same current.”

A battery gives roughly the same push. The current depends on what you connect: more bulbs in series, less current; more in parallel, more. A tired battery pushes less, and sags more under a heavy load.

A current you can count

Fill a drinking straw with dried chana or peas until it is full. Push one more in at one end: one falls out of the other end at once, though no single pea has travelled the length of the straw. Push peas in steadily for thirty seconds, count how many fall out, and divide by thirty. That is your pea current, in peas per second. Electrons in a wire behave a little like this, with one difference the straw cannot show: they push each other along by electric repulsion, not by bumping.

In Chapter 12 you will build this loop yourself, with two AA cells, an LED and a resistor, and find out why a white LED can stay dark on three volts while a red one shines.

1600

The little Earth

William Gilbert, Giambattista della Porta

London, 1600

Sailors in 1600 trusted their compass needles with their lives, and nobody could say why the needle pointed north. One thing many of them did believe was that garlic ruins a compass. William Gilbert, writing his book De Magnete in London, had heard that one and called it “fable and falsehood”. He could afford to be blunt: the Italian scholar Giambattista della Porta had already breathed garlic all over a lodestone and found it worked exactly as before.

For the pointing itself, Gilbert did something cleverer than arguing. He had a lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock, ground into a sphere and called it a terrella: a little Earth. Then he moved a small magnetised needle over its surface and watched which way it tilted.

Over the terrella’s “equator” the needle lay level. Moved towards either “pole”, it tilted, one end dipping more and more steeply towards the stone. Sailors already knew that compass needles do the same on the real Earth: level near the equator, dipping as a ship sails towards the north. The little Earth copied the big one. So the big one, Gilbert concluded, is behaving like a giant version of his stone: the Earth itself is a magnet. No magic mountain at the top of the world, no garlic.

He also noticed, in the same book, that the amber kind of attraction (the story Rubbing doesn’t make charge is about it) and the magnet’s pull are different things. The magnet grabs iron and ignores paper; rubbed amber lifts paper and ignores iron. Four hundred years later that distinction still holds.

Step 1: what a compass is

Hang a bar magnet from a thread so that it can turn freely and it swings round until one end points roughly north. That end is called the magnet’s north pole, and that is all a compass is: a small magnet free to turn. The name is a trap, though. Unlike poles attract, so if the north pole of your needle is pulled towards the far north, whatever is up there must be a south magnetic pole. It is: the magnetic pole near Earth’s geographic North Pole is, as a magnet, a south pole. Confusion arises because people call it “the north magnetic pole”, meaning the one in the north.

Step 2: the field

Lay a compass anywhere near a magnet and its needle settles in a definite direction. Move it a little and the direction changes a little. Join up those directions and you have drawn the magnet’s field lines: the direction a compass’s north end points at every place. Near a bar magnet the lines run out of its north end, round, and back into its south end, and continue through the magnet to make closed loops. Where the lines crowd together the field is strong; where they spread out it is weak.

Two facts about poles matter here. They always come in pairs: cut a magnet in half and you get two complete magnets, each with a north and a south, never a lone north. And a field line is a drawing of directions, not a track that anything travels along.

Step 3: the Earth’s field in Mumbai

The Earth’s field has a size and a direction at every place, and the direction is not along the ground. In Mumbai, according to the World Magnetic Model that navigation systems use, the field points almost exactly at true north (within a fraction of a degree) and dips about 28° downwards into the ground. Its total strength is about 43.6 microtesla, about 87% of the round “5 × 10⁻⁵ tesla” that textbooks quote for the Earth as a whole. Of that, the horizontal part, the part a compass needle can follow, is about 38 microtesla. At the old Alibag observatory down the coast the dip is 27°. Gilbert could not measure any of this; he could only see the dip. He had the shape right.

A phone’s magnetometer (the free phyphox app shows it) will give you a rough version of these numbers, something like 40 to 45 microtesla in total. Phone sensors are uncalibrated and easily thrown by nearby steel, so treat the reading as a sketch, not a measurement.

Step 4: what we are not telling you

Gilbert thought the Earth was a magnet all the way through, like his stone. It is not that simple, and the sources this book is built from do not explain what really makes the Earth’s field, so this story will not pretend to. The honest sentence is: the Earth acts like a huge magnet, with its magnetic south pole in the far north. What makes it act that way belongs to a later book.

Careful

“The Earth’s North Pole is a magnet’s north pole.”

As a magnet, the pole in the north is a south pole. That is why the north end of every compass needle is pulled towards it: unlike poles attract. “Magnetic north” means the place a compass points to, not the kind of pole that sits there.

Careful

“A compass needle points along the ground towards the north.”

The field it is following dips into the ground, by about 28° in Mumbai. A compass needle is pivoted so that it can only turn in the flat, so it shows you the horizontal part of the field and hides the dip. Gilbert’s needle, free to tilt, showed both.

A compass on a leaf

Stroke a steel sewing needle about twenty times with a fridge magnet, always in the same direction, lifting the magnet clear between strokes. Lay the needle gently on a small leaf floating in a bowl of water, away from anything made of steel, and wait. It turns and settles pointing north–south. Turn the leaf and let go: it comes back. Handle the needle with care.

Mumbai has its own chapter in this story. From 1841 an observatory at Colaba measured the Earth’s field, hourly from 1846, and did so for sixty years, until the city’s new electric trams threatened to swamp the readings and the instruments were moved down the coast to Alibag. That tale is told in Chased out of Bombay by the trams. In Chapter 13 you will float the needle, read the phone’s magnetometer, and then meet the surprise Gilbert never saw: a current in a wire can move a compass too.

1821 to 1831

Magnets make electricity

Michael Faraday, Joseph Henry

Royal Institution, London, 3 September 1821

In September 1821, a year after Ørsted’s needle twitched in Copenhagen, Michael Faraday set up a small dish of mercury at the Royal Institution in London, stood a magnet in it, and dipped a wire into the mercury so that it hung free. When he sent a current through the wire, the wire began to circle round the magnet, and kept circling for as long as the current flowed. On 3 and 4 September 1821 he had built the first electric motor. (Mercury is poisonous. Nobody repeats this version today, and neither will you.)

A current near a magnet feels a push. Faraday had turned that push into movement. The question that kept him busy for the next ten years ran the other way. If a current can make a magnet move, can a magnet make a current?

Royal Institution, London, 29 August 1831

On 29 August 1831 he wound two separate coils of wire onto opposite sides of an iron ring. One coil he connected to a battery through a switch. The other he connected only to a small compass needle, which would swing if any current passed. There was no electrical connection between the two coils at all.

He closed the switch. The needle jumped, and then settled back to rest, though the current in the first coil was still flowing steadily. He opened the switch. The needle jumped again, the other way, and settled. For as long as the current was simply on, nothing happened; the needle moved only at the moments of change. In the same year, across the Atlantic, Joseph Henry found the same thing independently.

Step 1: the motor effect

Start with 1821. A wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force, at right angles to both the current and the field. Make the wire a loop and the forces on its two sides push opposite ways, so the loop turns. Add a trick to reverse the current every half turn, so that the push always carries it onwards, and you have an electric motor: a device that turns electrical energy into movement. Every fan in your flat, every mixer, every local train, is a loop of wire being pushed round by a magnetic field.

Step 2: induction, which only happens when something changes

Now 1831. Push a bar magnet into a coil of wire connected to a sensitive meter and the meter flicks. Hold the magnet still inside the coil and the meter reads zero. Pull it out and the meter flicks the other way. Push it in faster and the flick is bigger. A magnet sitting beside a wire does nothing at all; a changing magnetic field through a coil pushes the coil’s electrons along, and that push appears in the wire as a voltage. This is electromagnetic induction. It does not matter how the change happens: move the magnet, move the coil, switch a nearby current on or off, or turn the coil so that the field passes through it at a different angle. Any change in how much field threads the coil induces a voltage.

The direction has a rule too. The induced current always acts against the change that made it. Push a magnet’s north end towards a coil and the coil’s current makes the coil a north pole facing it, pushing back; pull the magnet away and the coil’s current reverses to tug it back. Experiments at MIT drop a magnet towards a cold copper ring and watch it slow in mid-air, braked by the current it induces.

Step 3: the generator

Turn a coil steadily between the poles of a magnet. As it turns, the field through it rises, falls, reverses, rises again, and so a voltage appears in the coil that swings back and forth with every turn. That is a generator, and it is built almost exactly like a motor, run backwards: a motor takes current and gives movement; a generator takes movement and gives current. The electricity it gives is alternating, because the coil is turning.

A generator does not make energy. The work done turning the coil is what comes out as electrical energy, no more. So every power station needs something to turn the coil: falling water, steam from boiling water, or wind.

Why Mumbai’s mains is 50 hertz.
Mumbai’s supply is alternating current at 50 cycles per second. That is the generators’ coils reversing their voltage 100 times a second, 50 times one way and 50 the other, all across the grid in step.

Some of Mumbai’s electricity comes from exactly this. In the Western Ghats east of the city, in Raigad district, water from a lake at Thokerwadi falls down a steep slope through a pipe to the Bhivpuri power station, built between 1916 and 1922, and spins its turbines. All of its output, about 300 million units a year, is sent to Mumbai. With its two sister stations at Khopoli and Bhira it also forms the city’s “islanding” system: the backup that keeps Mumbai lit when the wider grid fails. Power stations everywhere else do the same job with steam or wind turning the coil.

Step 4: the transformer, which Faraday also built

Faraday’s ring was the first transformer. A changing current in one coil induces a voltage in another, and if the second coil has more turns than the first, the induced voltage is higher; fewer turns, lower. That is how electricity travels. Power stations step the voltage up to anywhere between 120,000 and 700,000 volts for the long lines, because for the same power a higher voltage means a smaller current, and the heat wasted in the wires grows with the square of the current. Ten times the voltage, one hundredth of the loss. Substations near your home step it back down to about 230 volts.

A transformer works only on changing current. Feed it a steady direct current and the second coil gives nothing, exactly as Faraday’s needle gave nothing while his switch stayed closed.

Careful

“A magnet near a wire makes electricity.”

Only a changing field does. Move the magnet, or change the current, and a push appears in the wire. Hold everything still and there is nothing, however strong the magnet.

Careful

“Generators make energy.”

They convert it. Something has to turn the coil, and the electrical energy that comes out is the work that went in, minus losses. The dam, the boiler and the wind are where the energy really comes from.

A magnet that falls slowly

Ask an adult for a strong magnet (the kind sold as a neodymium disc) and a length of copper or aluminium pipe from a hardware shop, wider than the magnet. Drop a steel nut down the pipe: it clatters out at once. Drop the magnet: it drifts down, visibly slower, braked by the currents its moving field induces in the pipe. Nothing in this is electrical, but strong magnets pinch fingers, wipe cards and must be kept away from small children.

In Chapter 13 you will push a magnet into a coil and watch a meter, then follow the electricity from the Ghats to your flat; Chapter 12 explains why that 230 volts must never be part of any experiment.

1862 to 1888

Light is electromagnetic

James Clerk Maxwell, Heinrich Hertz, Hippolyte Fizeau

London, 1862

In a paper published in parts across 1861 and 1862, James Clerk Maxwell did a piece of arithmetic that still startles people. He had been building a theory of how electric and magnetic fields behave, borrowing Faraday’s lines of force and giving them equations. The theory predicted that a disturbance in the fields should travel as a wave, and it gave the wave’s speed in terms of two numbers from the electrical laboratory, measured by Weber and Kohlrausch with coils and charged jars. Maxwell put the numbers in. Out came 310,740 kilometres per second.

Thirteen years earlier Hippolyte Fizeau had measured the speed of light across Paris with a spinning cogwheel and got 314,858 kilometres per second. The two figures differed by about one per cent. Nothing about light had gone into Maxwell’s equations; only electricity and magnetism. He wrote: “we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.” In 1865 he set the whole theory out again, cleaned up, in A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field. Light, the thing people had been splitting with prisms since Newton, was an electromagnetic wave.

One word in his sentence did not survive. Maxwell pictured the waves rippling through a “medium” filling space. Later physics dropped the medium: the waves need nothing to travel through, and cross empty space between the Sun and us at the same speed. Everything else in the inference stood.

Step 1: four rules in words

Maxwell’s equations gather up what Ørsted, Ampère, Coulomb, Gauss and Faraday had found. In words, without the mathematics, they say four things. Electric field lines start and end on charges. Magnetic field lines have no ends; they always close into loops. A changing magnetic field makes an electric field, which is Faraday’s induction. And a magnetic field is made by moving charges, or, the piece Maxwell added himself, by a changing electric field.

That last clause is the hinge. A changing electric field makes a magnetic field; a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Each change creates the other, and the pair can run away together across space with nothing left behind to hold them. That is an electromagnetic wave: electric and magnetic fields swinging at right angles to each other and to the direction they travel, each one regenerating the other as they go.

Step 2: how to make one

Charges that sit still make no waves, and neither does a steady current in a wire. To launch a wave you must shake a charge: accelerate it, back and forth. Every jerk sends a ripple of changing field outwards at the speed

c = 1 ⁄ √(μ₀ ε₀) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s

where μ₀ and ε₀ are the two laboratory constants Maxwell used. Put in the modern values and you get 299,860 kilometres per second. The speed of light is not a fact about light. It is a fact about electricity and magnetism.

Step 3: Hertz makes them

Karlsruhe, 1887

Maxwell died in 1879 without seeing his waves. In Karlsruhe, from 1887, Heinrich Hertz made them. He let a spark jump across a gap in a tuned circuit, so that charge surged back and forth very fast, and across the room a second loop of wire with its own tiny gap began to spark in sympathy: the wave had crossed the room and shaken the charges in the receiver. He went on to show that the waves travel at the speed of light, and that they reflect, refract and interfere exactly as light does, only with wavelengths enormously longer than light’s.

The story goes that a student asked Hertz what use his discovery was, and that he replied it was of no use whatsoever. It is a good story, and it may even be true, but no record of the exchange exists from Hertz’s lifetime; the earliest source anyone has traced is an article from 2013. Within fifteen years of his experiments, as the story Invisible waves in Calcutta tells, people were ringing bells through walls and sending signals across the Atlantic with Hertz’s waves. We call them radio waves.

Step 4: the ladder of light

Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same thing: electromagnetic waves, differing only in how fast the fields swing, and so in how long each wave is. Laid out in order they make the electromagnetic spectrum, a ladder whose rungs run from waves thousands of kilometres long to waves smaller than an atom’s nucleus.

Visible light runs from about 400 nanometres (violet) to 750 nanometres (red); as a frequency, that is 400 to 750 million million swings per second. A typical TV remote talks to the television with infrared at about 940 nanometres, just too long for your eye, though not for a phone camera. J. C. Bose’s waves in Calcutta were 5 millimetres long, 60 thousand million swings per second. The radio telescope at Khodad, near Pune, collects waves about a metre long. And the alternating current in your flat’s wiring, swinging 50 times a second, corresponds to a wavelength of about 6,000 kilometres. Same wave, same speed, one ladder.

Careful

“Radio waves are made by an electric current.”

Not a steady one. A steady current makes a steady magnetic field and no wave at all. You have to shake the charge: accelerate it back and forth, as the spark did in Hertz’s gap and as the electrons do in a transmitter’s antenna. Waves come from charges that are accelerating.

Careful

“Light needs something to travel through, like sound needs air.”

Maxwell thought so too, which is why his sentence says “medium”. It turned out that the fields carry themselves: a changing electric field makes the magnetic one and vice versa, and empty space is enough. Sunlight crosses 150 million kilometres of nothing on the way to Marine Drive.

In Chapter 13 this story closes the circle that began with Ørsted’s needle: electricity, magnetism and light turn out to be one subject. Chapter 11 is about the rung of the ladder your eye can see, and in Chapter 15 the waves spring one more surprise, by arriving in packets.

1820

The needle that twitched

Hans Christian Ørsted, François Arago, André-Marie Ampère

Copenhagen, 21 April 1820

On 21 April 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted was giving a lecture in Copenhagen with a battery and a wire on the bench, and a compass lying nearby. When he connected the wire so that a current flowed, the compass needle twitched. It moved so slightly that the audience did not notice. Ørsted did.

Over the following weeks he tried it again and again. A wire carrying a current, laid over a compass, pushed the needle aside. Reverse the current, and the needle swung the other way. Take the current away, and it settled back to north as if nothing had happened. In July he published what he had found, in four pages of Latin, and sent them to scientists across Europe.

Why did a twitch matter so much? For two hundred years, since Gilbert kept them apart in De Magnete, electricity and magnetism had been two separate subjects. Rubbed amber lifted paper; lodestones lifted iron; neither did anything to the other. Now a current, which is charge in motion, had moved a magnet. The two subjects were one.

Paris, September 1820

The four pages reached Paris at the end of the summer. On 4 September François Arago told the Académie des Sciences about the experiment, and on 11 September he repeated it in front of the members. One of them was André-Marie Ampère. A week later, on 18 September, Ampère presented his first work on what he named electrodynamics, and in that week he had already made the leap that turned the discovery inside out. If a current acts like a magnet, he proposed, then perhaps every magnet is a bundle of currents: the magnetism of a lodestone or a compass needle is itself caused by electric currents circulating inside it. He also gave a rule, pictured as a little man lying along the wire, for working out which way a nearby needle must turn. Two centuries later that is still, in essence, how physics sees it.

Step 1: moving charge, not charge

A charged balloon does nothing to a compass. You can hold a rubbed comb against a compass case all afternoon and the needle will not stir. Let the charge move, as a current in a wire, and the needle turns. That is the first half of electromagnetism in one sentence: magnetism comes from charges that are moving.

Step 2: the shape of the field around a wire

Map the field around a long straight wire with a compass and you find circles. The field lines loop round the wire, with no beginning and no end, and a needle anywhere on a circle points along it. Point the thumb of your right hand along the current and your curled fingers show the way the field goes; reverse the current and the circles run the other way, which is why Ørsted’s needle swung the other way.

The field is weaker farther from the wire. Its strength is B = μ₀I/(2πr): double the distance, half the field.

How far would a compass turn under a wire carrying 1 A?
At 1 cm from a wire carrying 1 A the field is 20 microtesla.
Mumbai’s own horizontal field is about 38 microtesla, pointing north.
If the wire runs north–south over the compass, the two fields are at right angles, and the needle settles at an angle of tan⁻¹(20 ÷ 38) ≈ 27° from north.
Ørsted’s batteries gave small currents, which is why his needle only twitched.

Step 3: from a wire to a magnet

Wind the wire into a coil and the circles around each turn add up. Sprinkle iron filings around a current-carrying coil and you get the same two-ended pattern you get around a bar magnet: a north end, a south end, loops between. Slide an iron bar inside and the field is far stronger, because the iron’s own tiny magnets line up with it. That is an electromagnet, and it is a magnet only while the current flows. Switch off, and the pull mostly vanishes; reverse the current, and north and south swap.

Ampère’s leap closes the circle. Why is a fridge magnet a magnet, with no battery attached? Because its electrons behave like tiny magnets, and in some materials they line up. Physicists sometimes draw this as electrons spinning or orbiting like little loops of current. Both pictures are crude, and the people who draw them say so; the true account is quantum, and comes later. But the one-line summary holds: every magnetic field, including the Earth’s and the fridge magnet’s, comes from moving charge.
