Step 4: a test that fools almost everyone

Lay two wires side by side and send currents along both in the same direction. Do they push apart, as two like charges would, or pull together? They pull together. Currents in the same direction attract; currents in opposite directions repel. “Likes repel” is a rule for charges, not for currents, and it is one of the first things Ampère worked out.

Careful

“Electricity and magnetism are the same thing.”

Not quite. A charge sitting still has no magnetic effect on a compass. A moving charge does. The honest sentence is: magnetism comes from charges that are moving, and, as Chapter 13 will show, a changing magnetic field pushes charges in turn.

Careful

“Field lines are something that streams out of the wire.”

They are a drawing. Each line records the direction a compass would point at that spot. Nothing flows along them, and no particle rides them like a rail.

Ørsted at your kitchen table

Ask an adult to help. Lay a phone with its compass app open, or a small pocket compass, flat on the table, and find north. Hold a piece of insulated copper wire, with its ends bared, so that it runs north–south about a centimetre above the compass. Touch the ends to the two terminals of an AA cell for a moment and watch the needle swing; swap the ends and it swings the other way. Touch for a second at a time only: the wire is a short circuit across the cell and gets hot. Never use mains electricity for this, or for anything.

Ørsted had shown that a current moves a magnet. The obvious next question, whether a magnet can be made to move charge and drive a current, took eleven more years and another man at a bench in London. In Chapter 13 you will meet both: first the wire over the compass, then Faraday’s spinning wire and his iron ring.

1600 to 1752

Rubbing doesn't make charge

William Gilbert, Benjamin Franklin

London, 1600

In 1600 a book came out in London with a long Latin title that everyone shortens to De Magnete, “On the Magnet”. Its author, William Gilbert, had spent years testing the stories people told about magnets, and about amber. Amber was the puzzle. Rub a piece of it on cloth and it picks up chaff and scraps, as people had known since ancient Greece. Was that the same pull as a magnet’s?

Gilbert built a tool to find out: a light metal needle balanced on a point, which he called a versorium, so that it would swing towards anything that pulled on it. Then he rubbed every substance he could lay hands on. Some swung the needle as amber did; many did not. The Greek word for amber is elektron, so he called the substances that behaved like amber electricus, amber-like. Our words “electric” and “electricity” grow out of that one adjective.

He also noticed what the magnet did not do. A lodestone pulls on iron, rubbed or not, and ignores almost everything else. Rubbed amber pulls on nearly anything light: paper, leaves, even a trickle of water. Two different things were going on. Gilbert kept them apart, and so will this book.

Step 1: nothing is made, something is moved

Every atom holds two kinds of electric charge: protons, with a positive charge, in its nucleus, and electrons, with a negative charge, around it. A neutral object has equal amounts of each, which is why it pulls on nothing. Now press two different materials together. One of them holds its electrons more tightly than the other, and when the two part, it keeps a few extra. Rubbing is a way of pressing the surfaces together more closely, over and over, so that more electrons cross.

Count the charge before and after and the total is the same. The balloon has gained electrons and is negative; your hair has lost exactly that many, and the positive charge left behind is exactly as large. Charge is never created or destroyed; it is only transferred from one body to another. That is the whole of this story’s title. Rubbing doesn’t make charge. It separates charge that was already there.

In solids it is always the electrons that move. Nothing positive travels onto the hair; the positive charge is simply what remains when electrons leave.

Step 2: two kinds, and who named them

Philadelphia, 1752

Like charges push each other apart; unlike charges pull together. Which kind to call positive and which negative was a free choice, and Benjamin Franklin made it: glass rubbed with silk, he said, is positive. We still use his convention. Since it is electrons that leave the glass, the electron ended up carrying the minus sign.

Franklin is also the man in the story about the kite: a kite flown into a thunderstorm, a key on the string, a spark from the key, and so proof that lightning is the same stuff as the spark from rubbed glass. The story goes that he did it in June 1752. Perhaps he did. But no account of it survives in Franklin’s own handwriting; the first full description was written by Joseph Priestley fifteen years later, and the only witness was Franklin’s son. Historians still disagree about whether it happened at all. What is certain is the idea, which was right. Lightning is an enormous version of the carpet spark: in one bolt about 10²⁰ electrons can move in two thousandths of a second, a current of 8,000 amperes.

Step 3: where charge can go

In some materials, metals above all, some electrons are free to wander from atom to atom, so charge placed on one spot spreads through the whole object at once. These are conductors. In others, such as rubber, glass, plastic and dry air, the electrons stay with their atoms, and charge placed on one spot stays there. These are insulators. A balloon is an insulator, which is why the charge you rub onto one side stays on that side and can hold the balloon against a wall for an hour.

Clinging to a neutral wall needs one more idea. The wall has no net charge, but it is full of charges. Bring a negative balloon close and the electrons in the wall’s surface are nudged slightly away while the positive nuclei stay put; the surface nearest the balloon is left slightly positive, and the balloon is pulled towards it. This shuffling inside a neutral object is called polarisation. It is why a rubbed comb bends a thin stream of tap water, and why a charged balloon lifts scraps of paper that carry no charge at all.

Step 4: how much charge is that?

Charge is measured in coulombs, and one coulomb is a great deal: about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Everyday static is a tiny imbalance on an otherwise neutral object. When an ink-jet printer puts −1 × 10⁻¹⁰ coulombs on a single drop of ink, that is about 600 million extra electrons, which sounds like a lot until you count the atoms in the drop: there is one extra electron for every ten million atoms.

Careful

“Rubbing makes electricity.”

It moves it. The balloon and the cloth start neutral and end with equal and opposite charges, because electrons crossed from one to the other. Nothing new came into existence.

Careful

“Static is a different kind of electricity from the kind in wires.”

Same charge, same electrons. On the balloon the extra electrons sit still, because it is an insulator and they have nowhere to go. In a wire they drift. “Static” means sitting still, nothing more.

Why the trick fails in July

Try the balloon on a dry January evening in Mumbai and it clings and crackles. Try it in the monsoon and almost nothing happens. The sources this book trusts say only this much for certain: in damp air the extra charge leaks away faster, so the effect is weaker. How moist air carries the charge off is not something we can tell you from a source we have checked, so we leave it there. You can measure the difference yourself: the same balloon, the same hair, July and then January.

Two strips of tape

Take two pieces of sticky tape about 4 cm long. Stick both to a table, side by side, then peel them off quickly and hold them near each other. They push apart: both lost electrons to the table in the same way, so both carry the same kind of charge. Now stick one strip on top of the other, peel the pair off the table together, and then peel them apart. Hold them near each other again. This time they pull together: one strip took electrons from the other. Best on a dry day.

In Chapter 12 the charge stops sitting still. The same electrons, drifting round a closed loop of wire, are what we call a current, and the first question there is what, if anything, gets used up.

1929

The stretching universe

Edwin Hubble, Milton Humason, Vesto Slipher

Mount Wilson, California, 1929

Through the 1920s Edwin Hubble, at the Mount Wilson Observatory in California, did two things to galaxy after galaxy. He measured how far away each one was, using Henrietta Leavitt’s blinking Cepheids as his measuring tape. And, with his colleague Milton Humason, he measured the speed at which each was moving towards or away from us, using a trick that Vesto Slipher had been using since 1912. Slipher had already found something odd: nearly every spiral galaxy he looked at was rushing away, some at up to 1,800 kilometres a second.

In 1929 Hubble put the two measurements side by side, and in 1931 he and Humason extended the result to fainter galaxies. The pattern was plain. The farther away a galaxy was, the faster it was receding, and in proportion: twice as far, twice as fast. Written as a rule, now called Hubble’s law, the speed v is the distance d multiplied by a constant:

v = H × d

Measurements since have converged on H close to 22 kilometres per second for every million light-years of distance. A galaxy 100 million light-years away is receding at about 2,200 kilometres a second.

Step 1: how you measure a galaxy’s speed

The trick is in the light. Every element leaves its fingerprint of lines in a spectrum, as the story What the stars are made of explains, and the lines sit at exactly known colours. In the light of a receding galaxy, every line has moved towards the red end, to a longer wavelength than it has in a laboratory. That shift is called redshift, and the faster the galaxy recedes, the bigger it is. The first picture to reach for is the Doppler effect you can hear from a passing train horn: the pitch drops as the source moves away. For a nearby galaxy that picture works well enough. Keep reading, because for the universe as a whole there is a better one.

Step 2: ants on a ruler

Picture a rubber ruler with ants standing on it at the 2 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm and 12 cm marks. You are the ant at 2 cm. In one minute the ruler is stretched to twice its length, so every mark moves to double its number: your three neighbours are now at 8, 14 and 24 cm, and you are at 4.

Measure from where you stand. The ant that was 2 cm away is now 4 cm away: it moved 2 cm in the minute. The one that was 5 cm away is now 10 cm away: it moved 5 cm. The one that was 10 cm away moved 10 cm. Speed in proportion to distance, exactly Hubble’s law. Now be the ant at 7 cm instead and do the sums again: the ants that were 5, 3 and 5 cm away moved 5, 3 and 5 cm. Every ant sees every other ant receding at a speed proportional to its distance, and every ant could claim to be the one standing still. None of them is at the centre, and none of them walked anywhere. The stretching of the ruler moved them apart.

Step 3: what stretches and what does not

That is the better picture of the universe. The galaxies are not flying apart through space like shrapnel; the space between them is growing, and they are carried along, passive participants in the expansion. Inside a galaxy, gravity holds the stars together, so the galaxy itself does not grow, just as the raisins in a rising loaf stay the same size while the dough between them swells. You, Mumbai and the Milky Way are not stretching.

Light is. A wave of light setting out from a distant galaxy travels for millions of years through space that is stretching as it goes, and the wave is stretched with it. By the time it arrives, every wavelength is longer than when it left: redshifted. For nearby galaxies this gives the same answer as the Doppler picture; for the farthest ones only the stretching picture gives the right one. Astronomers describe the amount by the fraction a wavelength has grown, written z.

Step 4: running it backwards

If everything is moving apart now, everything was closer together before. Run the stretching backwards, far enough, and all the matter we can see was packed together at enormous density and temperature. That beginning is called the Big Bang, and it is the most misdrawn event in physics. It was not an explosion at a spot in space, with galaxies flying out of it into emptiness. It happened everywhere at once, because everywhere was what was being stretched. There is no location you can visit where the stretching of space began. Every point, including the one you are sitting on, was once in the thick of it.

How long ago? Divide a distance by the speed and you get a time, so one over Hubble’s constant is a rough age for the universe, and it comes out at about 13.6 billion years. The careful figure, allowing for the stretching having slowed and then sped up over its history, is 13.8 billion years, give or take about a hundred million.

At school

Your IGCSE syllabus says that distant galaxies are “receding” and that redshift “supports the Big Bang Theory”, and it may say that all the matter in the universe was once “present at a single point”. A careful way to picture it is space stretching between the galaxies, with the whole of space once squeezed far closer together, everywhere. The syllabus also writes Hubble’s law as H₀ = v/d; the 22 kilometres per second per million light-years above is about 72 kilometres per second per megaparsec in the units it uses.

Careful

“The Big Bang was an explosion in space, and we can point to where it happened.”

There is no such place. The stretching began everywhere at once, and every galaxy, ours included, sees all the others receding. The ruler had no centre either.

Careful

“Everything is moving away from us, so we must be at the centre.”

Every ant on the ruler thought the same, and each was equally right and equally wrong. Speed in proportion to distance is exactly the pattern that looks the same from everywhere.

A universe on a balloon

Draw a dozen dots on a balloon with a marker, and one short wavy line. Blow it up slowly. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and the dots farthest apart separate fastest, while each dot itself stays small. The wavy line stretches as the rubber does: that is the redshift. Pick any dot and call it home; the view is the same from all of them. The balloon has a centre, inside it, where there is no rubber at all; the universe does not have even that.

In Chapter 15 this is the last section of the book, where Leavitt’s tape, Saha’s thermometer and Hubble’s redshifts come together to ask how old everything is. The Doppler effect you start from is in the story Horn players on a train.

1905 to 1924

Light in packets

Albert Einstein, Satyendra Nath Bose

Bern, 1905

In 1905 Albert Einstein was twenty-six and worked in the patent office in Bern, examining other people’s inventions. That year he sent four papers to the journal Annalen der Physik. One was about the jiggling of pollen grains in water, one about space and time, one about the formula E = mc². The first of the four, received on 18 March and printed on 9 June, was about light, and it said something that most physicists found harder to accept than relativity. Light, it proposed, is not delivered smoothly. It arrives in packets.

When the Nobel committee finally gave Einstein the Physics prize for 1921, the citation named this work, on what is called the photoelectric effect, as the one specific discovery it was rewarding. It did not mention relativity.

Step 1: the puzzle

Shine light on a clean metal surface in a vacuum and, for some lights and some metals, electrons jump out of the metal. That is the photoelectric effect, and by 1905 careful measurements had shown four things about it that nobody could explain. First, for each metal there is a threshold: light below a certain frequency, that is, light that is too red, knocks out no electrons at all, however bright you make it. Second, light above the threshold knocks electrons out instantly, even when it is dim. Third, brighter light knocks out more electrons. Fourth, brighter light does not make them any faster; only bluer light does that.

If light were a smooth wave, a bright red lamp should pour energy into the metal until electrons boiled out of it. It does not happen. You can bathe the metal in red light all day and nothing emerges, then touch it with a faint violet glimmer and electrons fly.

Step 2: Einstein’s packets

Einstein’s answer was that light is delivered in packets, now called photons, and the energy of each packet depends only on the light’s frequency:

E = h f (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds)

An electron takes the whole of one packet or nothing. To escape the metal it must pay an entry fee, the metal’s binding energy, and keep the change as speed. So if one packet is worth less than the fee, no electron leaves, and piling up more packets does not help, because each electron is only ever handed one. That is the threshold. A packet worth more than the fee frees an electron at once, with the difference as kinetic energy. Brighter light means more packets, so more electrons, each with the same energy as before. Bluer light means bigger packets, so faster electrons. All four puzzles in one sentence.

Violet light of wavelength 420 nm falls on calcium, whose binding energy is 2.71 eV.
Each violet packet carries 2.95 eV. The electron pays 2.71 eV to leave and keeps 0.24 eV.
A TV remote’s infrared, wavelength 940 nm, falls on the same calcium.
Each packet carries 1.32 eV, less than the 2.71 eV fee. No electron leaves, however bright the remote.

Step 3: so is light a wave or not?

It still travels like one. Light still spreads, bends round edges and makes interference fringes, as Young’s card showed in 1803, and nothing in Einstein’s paper undid that. What changed is how it delivers its energy: in packets, one at a time. Both are true at once, and the honest summary is simply that light travels like a wave and lands like a particle. If that sits uncomfortably, you are in good company; physicists took years to make peace with it.

The packets are so small that ordinary light seems smooth. A 100-watt bulb that puts a tenth of its power into yellow light sends out about 3 × 10¹⁹ packets every second. Nobody sees a flicker. The quantum shows itself only where one packet meets one electron.

Step 4: a letter from Dacca

Dacca, 4 June 1924

On 4 June 1924 a physics teacher at the University of Dacca, Satyendra Nath Bose, posted a letter to Einstein in Berlin. It began “Respected Sir”. He had written a short paper about how to count packets of light, had sent it to the Philosophical Magazine in London, and had heard nothing back. He did not, he said, know enough German to have it published in a German journal himself; would Einstein read it, and, if he thought it worth anything, arrange for it to appear?

Einstein read it, translated it into German himself, sent Bose a postcard on 2 July saying so, and had it printed in August with a note of his own attached. Bose’s way of counting turned out to describe not only light but a whole class of particles, which are now called bosons in his honour. A teacher in Dacca, with no answer from London, had put his name permanently into the vocabulary of physics.

Careful

“Light is a particle, not a wave.”

It is neither word on its own. Light travels like a wave and delivers its energy in packets. Drop either half and you will get the wrong answer to some experiment.

Careful

“Brighter light knocks out faster electrons.”

Brighter light knocks out more electrons, each with the same energy as before. Only a higher frequency, bluer light, makes them faster. Below the threshold frequency, no brightness at all is enough.

Careful

“The phone camera is seeing heat from the remote.”

It is seeing light: near-infrared from a small LED in the remote, at a wavelength of about 940 nanometres, just beyond red. That is not the same as the warmth you feel from a hot cup, and the remote is not warm.

See the invisible

Point a TV remote at your phone’s camera in a dim room and press a button while watching the screen. The remote’s bulb, dark to your eye, flashes on the screen: the camera’s sensor can see infrared at 940 nm that your eye cannot. If one camera shows nothing, try the other. Each flash is a stream of packets of about 1.3 eV, too small to free an electron from a metal and completely harmless.

In Chapter 15 the packets explain why ultraviolet burns and radio does not, and the same chapter follows a second letter-writer from Bengal, Meghnad Saha, out to the stars. Chapter 11 is the wave half of the story.

1896

Radiation is not catching

Henri Becquerel

A hospital in Mumbai, any afternoon

A girl of twelve has a chest X-ray. It takes a fraction of a second; a machine clicks, and she goes home. On the way out she wonders: is she radioactive now? If she hugs her little brother, will some of it rub off on him? Should she keep away from the dog?

Asked questions like these, between 63 and 75 per cent of students in three separate studies said yes: things that have been near radiation become radioactive. The answer is no. The reason is worth more than the answer, because it tells you what radiation is.

Step 1: what the word means

“Radiation” means energy travelling outwards from a source. It is a wide word. The light from this page is radiation. So is the warmth from a cup of chai on your hands, the invisible flash from a TV remote that a phone camera can see, the radio waves that carry a cricket commentary, and the X-rays that made the picture of the girl’s lungs. All of these are electromagnetic waves on the same ladder, from radio at the bottom to gamma rays at the top; the story Light is electromagnetic lays the ladder out. And light arrives in packets, as Light in packets explains, so a beam of radiation is a stream of packets, each carrying an amount of energy that depends on where it sits on the ladder.

Step 2: what makes some of it dangerous

Each packet of visible light carries between about 1.6 and 3.3 electron-volts of energy. The electrons that hold a molecule together are bound by about 10 electron-volts, and knocking an electron clean out of an atom, ionising it, takes anywhere from 10 to 1,000. So a visible packet cannot do it, and neither can infrared or radio, however many packets arrive: each electron only ever meets one packet at a time. Those lower rungs can harm you only by heating, through enormous numbers of packets acting together, which is what a microwave oven does to food.

Ultraviolet packets, X-rays and gamma rays carry more energy per packet than a molecule’s bonds can withstand. They can break molecules and ionise atoms, which is why they are called ionising radiation, and why sunburn, X-ray shielding and radiation safety are all about the top of the ladder and not the bottom.

Paris, 1896

The top of the ladder has a second source besides hot things and X-ray tubes. In 1896 Henri Becquerel in Paris found that a lump of uranium ore, left on photographic plates wrapped in black paper, darkened them through the wrapping. Something was coming out of the uranium itself, with no sunlight and no electricity involved. The atoms’ nuclei were unstable, and as each one rearranged itself it threw out a packet or a particle carrying around a million electron-volts, a hundred thousand times what an ordinary chemical change releases. A substance that does this is radioactive, and the behaviour is radioactivity. Three kinds of emission turned up: alpha particles, which are stopped soonest; beta particles, which travel farther; and gamma rays, which go farthest of all.

Step 3: being hit is not the same as carrying

Here is the heart of it. When an X-ray or a gamma ray passes through you, it may break a few molecules on the way, and then it is gone. It does not stay in you, and it does not make your atoms unstable. X-rays, gamma rays and electron beams induce no nuclear reactions in what they pass through, which is why food irradiated with them to kill bacteria is not radioactive afterwards. The United States’ public-health agency, the CDC, puts it plainly: a person exposed to radiation is not necessarily contaminated with radioactive material. When a person has an X-ray, he or she is exposed to radiation but is not contaminated.

Contamination is a different thing. It means radioactive material, dust or liquid whose own nuclei are unstable, on your skin, hair or clothes, or breathed in or swallowed. That material keeps emitting wherever it is, and it can be carried from place to place, washed off, or passed on. The X-rayed girl has been exposed; she carries nothing, so she can hug anyone she likes. A worker who gets radioactive dust on his sleeve is contaminated; the dust is the problem, and taking off the sleeve removes most of it.

One honest footnote. “Radiation never makes anything radioactive” is also too simple. Neutrons, which come from some nuclear reactions, can make the nuclei they hit unstable. That is precisely why neutrons are not used to irradiate food, and why the true rule is about which kind of radiation, not about radiation in general.

Step 4: how long it lasts

An unstable nucleus does not decay on a timetable. For any one nucleus the moment is random. But take a large number of them and the pattern is exact: in a fixed time, called the half-life, half of them will have decayed, whichever half that turns out to be. Wait another half-life and half the remainder go, and so on. After ten half-lives, about one part in a thousand is left.

Half-lives span an absurd range, from less than 10⁻²³ seconds to more than 10¹⁶ years. Carbon-14’s is 5,730 years, which makes it a clock for things that were alive within the last fifty thousand years or so. Caesium-137’s is 30.2 years. Uranium-238’s is 4.5 billion years, about the age of the Sun, which is why there is still plenty of it in the rocks.

Step 5: the background you live in

You are being hit by ionising radiation now. Cosmic rays from space give the average person about 0.4 millisievert a year; the rocks and soil add more, up to ten times more in some places than others; the food you eat contains traces of radioactive atoms, so, in the words of one textbook, we are all a little radioactive. A twelve-hour flight to London adds about 0.02 to 0.03 millisievert, roughly three weeks’ worth of the average cosmic dose, because the air above you is thinner. Airline crew pick up about 2 millisievert a year. None of this makes anyone radioactive. What matters is the dose: how much ionising energy was deposited, and in how much of you.

Careful

“Anything that has been near radiation becomes radioactive.”

Being hit by X-rays, gamma rays or light leaves nothing behind in you. Only radioactive material, on you or inside you, makes you a source, and that is contamination, not exposure. The one exception, neutrons, is the reason the rule is stated carefully.

Careful

“All radiation is dangerous.”

Radio waves and visible light are radiation too. What matters is the energy per packet, which decides whether it can break molecules, and then the dose. A phone camera watching a TV remote is watching radiation, and it is completely harmless.

A half-life you can toss

Take 32 coins. Toss them all, remove every one that lands heads, and count what is left; write the number down. Toss the survivors, remove the heads again, and repeat until none remain. Each round is one half-life: about 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0, with wobbles, because for any one coin the result is chance while for many the halving is steady. That is exactly how a lump of radioactive material behaves, with years in place of tosses.

In Chapter 15 the ladder, the packets and the nucleus come together, and this is the section that defuses the X-ray scare for good. The nucleus itself, and what Becquerel’s uranium was doing, is told from the chemistry side in The Invisible World, Chapter 1.

1930 to 1935

The limit worked out at sea

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, Arthur Eddington

Bombay, 1930

In 1930 Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, nineteen years old, boarded the SS Pilsna at Bombay to sail to England. He had been born in Lahore in 1910, had finished college at nineteen, had a scholarship to Cambridge, and had an uncle, C. V. Raman, who was about to win the Nobel Prize. The voyage was long. He spent it on a calculation.

The question was what happens to a star like the Sun when its fuel runs out. Astronomers already knew the answer in outline: it shrinks into a white dwarf, a star’s worth of mass squeezed into something far smaller, held up by a new kind of pressure that comes from electrons refusing to be crowded. Chandrasekhar added one ingredient the existing theory had left out. In a star squeezed that hard, the electrons move at speeds close to that of light, and Einstein’s relativity changes how they push back. When he put that in, the theory did something unexpected. Above a certain mass, the pressure could not win. A star heavier than the limit could not become a white dwarf at all. His first figure for the limit was 0.91 times the Sun’s mass; with better values for the star’s make-up it became about 1.4, which is the number used today. He kept refining the work through his years at Cambridge.

London, January 1935

In January 1935 he was invited to present the result at a meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society in London. Arthur Eddington, famous across the world for the 1919 eclipse expedition that had confirmed Einstein, spoke immediately after him, with a paper attacking the whole idea. “I think there should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way!” he said. Chandrasekhar was not allowed to reply from the floor. He wrote instead to the physicists who understood relativity and quantum theory, found that they agreed with him, and published his rebuttal. Eddington never accepted it. Chandrasekhar later said that his old hero, for all his insight, “has always operated with preconceived ideas”. The Nobel Prize in Physics came to Chandrasekhar in 1983, fifty-three years after the voyage.

Step 1: what holds a star up

A star is a ball of gas pulled inwards by its own gravity. What stops it collapsing is the heat from fusion in its core, which keeps the gas pushing outwards. For as long as the fuel lasts, the two balance. When the core runs out of hydrogen, and later of whatever it fused next, the push weakens and gravity begins to win. The core contracts.

Step 2: electrons that refuse to be crowded

Squeeze matter hard enough and a rule of quantum physics takes over: no two electrons can be in the same place at the same time doing the same thing. Pack them closer and they are forced into faster and faster motion, and that motion is a pressure, called degeneracy pressure. It has nothing to do with electrons repelling each other because they are both negative; it is a different and far stronger effect. A white dwarf is a dead star held up by nothing but this refusal: the mass of a star, no longer making any heat, kept from collapsing by crowded electrons.

Step 3: the strange rule and the limit

White dwarfs break a rule that everything else in daily life obeys. Add mass to one and it gets smaller. Gravity squeezes harder, the electrons are packed tighter, and the star shrinks. Follow the models upwards and the shrinking runs away: at about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass the calculated radius drops to zero. That is the mathematics’ way of saying that no white dwarf can exist above that mass; even the force of degenerate electrons cannot stop the collapse of a star with more mass than this. The mass at which a star can still end its life as a white dwarf, about 1.4 Suns, is the Chandrasekhar limit.

The Sun, at exactly one solar mass, is safely below the limit, and will end as a white dwarf. So will many stars born much heavier, because stars shed a great deal of mass in their old age before the core settles.

Step 4: what happens above the limit

When the core of a very massive star passes the limit, degenerate electrons can no longer hold it, and it shrinks rapidly. The collapse does not stop until the core is as dense as an atomic nucleus, at which point the electrons have been crushed into the protons to make neutrons, and the neutrons, obeying the same quantum rule, push back far harder than the electrons could. What remains is a neutron star: about a Sun’s mass of matter in a ball less than twenty kilometres across. The outer layers of the star, at least five Suns’ worth, are blasted into space in the explosion we call a supernova.

Neutrons have a limit too, perhaps about three times the Sun’s mass; nobody knows the number exactly. A core heavier than that cannot be stopped by anything, and keeps collapsing into the state of ultimate compaction: a black hole. Every one of these endings follows from the calculation a teenager began on a ship from Bombay.

Careful

“At 1.4 Suns a white dwarf really shrinks to a point.”

The zero in the model is a signpost, not a description. It says the white dwarf solution stops existing there; what actually happens is that the star collapses into something else, a neutron star or a black hole.

Careful

“The electrons hold the star up because negative charges repel.”

Electrical repulsion is there, but it is not what does the work. Degeneracy pressure comes from the quantum rule that electrons cannot share the same state, and it is much stronger than their electrical push.

Careful

“He worked it all out on the ship.”

He began it there, and it is a fine beginning. The limit as we know it took years of further work at Cambridge, a correction to his own first number, and a long fight to be heard.

In Chapter 15 the limit is the last stop on the tour of a star’s life, from the fusion that lights it to the three ways it can end; it is also where Mumbai’s own physicist in the story turns out to have been right all along.

1912

A measuring tape to the stars

Henrietta Leavitt, Friedrich Bessel

Harvard, 1912

In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt was one of the women employed at Harvard College Observatory as “computers”: people who measured and catalogued the stars on photographic plates, at a third or a quarter of what the observatory paid men. Her plates showed the Small Magellanic Cloud, a smudge of stars visible from the southern hemisphere, photographed night after night. Some of the stars in it were variable: they brightened and faded, over and over, each on its own steady rhythm of days or weeks. Stars of this kind are called Cepheids, after the first one found, in the constellation Cepheus.

Leavitt measured twenty-five of them, and saw a pattern. The brighter a Cepheid appeared, the longer it took to go through one cycle of brightening and fading. The slow blinkers were always the bright ones.

The key to why that mattered is where the stars were. All of them sat in the same small cloud, which meant all of them were at about the same distance from Earth. For stars at the same distance, looking brighter means being brighter. So Leavitt had found a rule about the stars themselves: a Cepheid’s rhythm tells you its true brightness. She could not turn that into distances herself, because in 1912 nobody knew how far away the Cloud was. Others calibrated her rule later, using Cepheids closer to home. A reanalysis published in 2025 found that her original relation holds up.

Step 1: the jump of a thumb

Hold your thumb up at arm’s length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps against the wall behind it. Bring it closer and the jump grows; hold it farther away and the jump shrinks. That jump is parallax, and it is the oldest way of measuring a distance you cannot walk. Surveyors do it with a baseline and two angles; your eyes do it with the few centimetres between them. For a thumb at arm’s length the jump is about six degrees.

Step 2: a baseline the size of the Earth’s orbit

For stars, the two “eyes” are the Earth in January and the Earth in July, on opposite sides of its orbit, 300 million kilometres apart. Photograph a nearby star against the distant ones six months apart and it has shifted. Astronomers call half that total shift the star’s parallax, so that it corresponds to a baseline of one Earth–Sun distance, and that is the number to remember when you read a table.

The shifts are tiny. The unit astronomers invented for them is the parsec: the distance at which the parallax is one arcsecond, one 3,600th of a degree. A star one parsec away is 206,265 times as far as the Sun, which is 3.26 light-years.

How small is one arcsecond?
A ₹1 coin is 22 mm across. Seen from 4.5 km away it would look one arcsecond wide:
0.022 m × 206,265 ≈ 4,540 m.
That is a coin held up at the far end of the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, seen from the near end.
The nearest star, Proxima Centauri, 4.25 light-years away, has a parallax of 0.77 arcsecond: smaller than that coin.

Friedrich Bessel made the first trustworthy measurement of a star’s parallax in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni. The space telescope Gaia now measures the parallaxes of nearly a billion stars to a few millionths of an arcsecond. Even so, parallax runs out: for stars in other galaxies the shifts are far too small to measure, and that is most of the universe.

Step 3: a light-year is a distance

The light-year sounds like a time and is not. It is how far light travels in a year: about 9.5 million million kilometres. The Sun’s light takes 8.3 minutes to reach Mumbai, so the Sun is 8.3 light-minutes away. Proxima’s light takes 4.25 years, so when you look at it you see it as it was 4.25 years ago. A light-year is 9.5 × 10¹² km, and one parsec is 3.26 of them.

Step 4: the measuring tape

Here is where Leavitt’s rule becomes a tape. Find a Cepheid anywhere, time its blinking, and her rule tells you how bright it truly is. Measure how bright it looks, and the gap between true and apparent brightness tells you how far away it must be, because light spreads out and dims with distance in a known way. The farther the star, the dimmer it appears for its rhythm. A Cepheid in another galaxy is a lamp of known wattage seen across the void.

Within twenty years Edwin Hubble had used Cepheids to measure the distances to other galaxies, and found something in those distances that nobody expected: the story The stretching universe is what he found.

Careful

“A light-year is a length of time.”

It is a distance: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million kilometres. When astronomers say a galaxy is a million light-years away, they mean its light is a million years old when it arrives, and that is a consequence, not the definition.

Careful

“Leavitt measured the distances to the stars.”

She found the rule, that slower-blinking Cepheids are truly brighter, and she could prove it because her stars were all at one distance. Turning the rule into distances needed a calibration she did not have. Others supplied it; the tape was hers.

Parallax on a rooftop

Ask an adult to come up to the terrace with you. Stand at one end and line up a nearby water tank with something far away, a tower or a tree on the horizon. Walk to the other end of the terrace and look again: the tank has jumped against the far background. Pace the length of the terrace, and the farther the tank, the smaller the jump. That is Bessel’s measurement, with your terrace as the Earth’s orbit.

In Chapter 15 the tape is laid out from the Moon to the nearest stars and then, with Leavitt’s Cepheids, to the galaxies, where its last reading changes what the whole universe is doing.

1920 to 1929

What the stars are made of

Meghnad Saha, Cecilia Payne, Henry Norris Russell

Calcutta, 1919

In 1919 Meghnad Saha was a young lecturer at the University College of Science in Calcutta, a few years out of Presidency College, and he had a puzzle in front of him that astronomers had been staring at for sixty years. Split a star’s light with a prism and you get a rainbow crossed by dark lines, a stellar spectrum. The lines are the fingerprints of elements. But different stars show different fingerprints: some are crowded with hydrogen lines, some have almost none and show lines of other elements instead. The obvious reading was that different stars are made of different stuff.

Saha thought the difference was temperature, and he worked out exactly how. In a very hot gas, collisions knock electrons clean off their atoms, a process called ionisation, and an ionised atom absorbs a completely different set of lines from a whole one, or none at all in visible light. Saha wrote an equation, now the Saha equation, that gives the fraction of atoms ionised at any temperature and pressure. With it, a star’s spectrum stopped being a list of ingredients and became a thermometer. He left for Europe in September 1919 to finish the work; in London Alfred Fowler at Imperial College helped him revise the papers, and the first of them, “On Ionization in the Solar Chromosphere”, appeared in the Philosophical Magazine in 1920.

Step 1: the fingerprint

Light from a hot, dense body is a smooth rainbow. Pass it through a cooler gas and the gas’s atoms swallow light at a few exact colours, leaving dark lines; heat a thin gas on its own and it glows at exactly those same colours, as bright lines. In 1815 Joseph von Fraunhofer counted about 600 dark lines in sunlight. In 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff matched one set of them to sodium, the first element identified in the Sun. Helium was found in the Sun’s spectrum before anyone found it on Earth.

Step 2: the wrong idea, taken seriously

So a star’s lines tell you what it is made of. Half true, and the false half misled astronomers for decades. Hydrogen is the most abundant element in nearly every star, yet its lines are faint or missing in the very hottest stars and in the very coolest. Saha’s equation says why. In the hottest stars, hydrogen is almost entirely ionised, its single electron stripped away, and an ionised hydrogen atom, a bare proton, has no lines to show. In the coolest stars the electrons sit on the lowest rung of hydrogen’s energy ladder, and from there the jumps that make visible-light lines cannot happen. Only in stars of middling temperature, where plenty of atoms are whole and plenty of electrons sit one rung up, do the famous hydrogen lines show strongly.

The same logic runs for every element. Which lines show depends on which atoms are whole, which are ionised, and where their electrons sit, and all of that is set by temperature. The letters astronomers use to sort stars, O B A F G K M, worked out at Harvard by Annie Jump Cannon, are a sequence of falling temperature, not a list of recipes.

Step 3: Cecilia Payne reads the recipe

Harvard, 1925

In 1925 Cecilia Payne, a young Englishwoman finishing a doctorate at Harvard, did what Saha’s equation made possible. If temperature explains which lines appear, you can correct for temperature and work backwards to how much of each element is really there. She did it for star after star. The answer was that stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, with everything else, the oxygen, silicon and iron that make up the Earth’s crust, present only in traces.

Everyone expected the Sun to be made of much the same stuff as the Earth. Henry Norris Russell, one of the most influential astronomers in America, told her the result was “clearly impossible”. Her thesis was printed with the hydrogen and helium figures labelled “spurious”. Within a few years the evidence had piled up, Russell himself reached the same conclusion in 1929, and the result became the foundation of how stars are understood. The astronomer Otto Struve later called it “the most brilliant PhD thesis ever written in astronomy”.

Step 4: the recipe

By mass, the Sun is about 73 per cent hydrogen and 25 per cent helium. Everything else, every other element in the periodic table together, makes up the remaining 2 per cent. The Earth’s crust, by contrast, is mostly oxygen, silicon and aluminium. The Sun is not a bigger Earth that happens to be hot; it is made of different stuff, and so are nearly all the stars.

It is not fire, either. At those temperatures the gas is ionised, a mixture of free electrons and bare nuclei, which physicists call a plasma. A star is a ball of plasma held together by its own gravity and lit from inside, as the story A fire that has lasted four and a half billion years explains, by fusion in its core.

Careful

“Stars with different spectra are made of different things.”

Mostly they are made of the same things, in nearly the same proportions. Their lines differ because their temperatures differ, which changes which atoms are ionised and where their electrons sit. That is Saha’s point, and it is why Payne could read the recipe at all.

Careful

“Payne was ignored and proved right only decades later.”

She was doubted, and told to call her result spurious, which was wrong of her elders. But the confirmation came within a few years, not decades, and Russell published the same conclusion in 1929.

A spectroscope from a CD

Hold an old CD or DVD at a slant so that it reflects a street lamp into your eye, and tilt it until the light spreads into a rainbow. A yellow sodium street lamp gives a few sharp coloured bands; a white LED gives a smooth rainbow. The sharp bands are the lamp’s fingerprint, the same idea Fraunhofer and Kirchhoff used on the Sun. Never try this with the Sun itself, directly or in a reflection.

In Chapter 15 you will meet the fingerprints again and ask what the Sun’s 73 per cent hydrogen is for; Chapter 11 is where the prism first splits white light into the rainbow these lines are drawn on.

1938

A fire that has lasted four and a half billion years

Lise Meitner, Otto Frisch, Otto Hahn

Kungälv, Sweden, Christmas 1938

Lise Meitner spent Christmas 1938 in Kungälv, a small town on the west coast of Sweden. That summer she had fled Berlin, where she had worked for thirty years, because the Nazi laws had reached her; she was sixty, with no laboratory and almost no money. Her nephew Otto Frisch, also a physicist and also in exile, came to visit, and she showed him a letter from her old colleague Otto Hahn.

Hahn’s letter made no sense. He and Fritz Strassmann had been firing neutrons at uranium, the heaviest natural element, and had found barium in the results. Barium is barely more than half as heavy as uranium. Tapping a nucleus with a single neutron and getting something half its size was like tapping a boulder and watching it fall cleanly into two rocks.

They went out walking in the snow to think about it. The story goes that Frisch was on skis and Meitner on foot, and that they sat down on a tree trunk to work with pencil and paper; those details come from Frisch’s memoir years later, so hold them loosely. What they worked out is not in doubt. Picture the uranium nucleus as a wobbling drop of liquid. An extra neutron sets it wobbling harder, it stretches into a waist, and the electrical repulsion between its two positively charged ends tears it in two. Barium could be one of the pieces. Then Meitner did the sum that mattered. The two pieces together should weigh slightly less than the uranium nucleus had. By Einstein’s rule, E = mc², that lost mass had to appear as energy, and it came to about 200 million electron-volts for every nucleus that split, roughly forty million times what a single molecule gives up in burning. They published it in Nature in February 1939. Frisch borrowed a word from biology and called the process fission: the splitting of a nucleus.

It is the nucleus that splits. Not an atom’s bonds, not the atom itself: the tiny core, a hundred-thousandth of the atom’s width.

Step 1: why the Sun cannot be burning

The Sun pours out about 4 × 10²⁶ joules every second, and the Earth’s rocks say it has done so for a very long time: there was liquid water here nearly four billion years ago, and the Sun is about four and a half billion years old. No fire can do that. A Sun made of coal, burning at its present rate, would be used up in a few thousand years, and nothing like solid coal could even survive at the Sun’s temperature. The nineteenth century’s best alternative, that the Sun shines by slowly shrinking under its own gravity, lasts longer, but only about a hundred million years. The rocks said four billion. Something else had to be going on, and nobody knew what until mass turned out to be a form of energy.

Step 2: mass is energy

Einstein’s 1905 equation says that a mass m is worth an energy mc², where c is the speed of light. Because c² is so enormous, nine times ten to the sixteen, a very little mass is worth a very great deal of energy. In the Sun’s core, four hydrogen nuclei combine, in steps, into one helium nucleus. That joining is nuclear fusion, and the helium weighs 0.71 per cent less than the four hydrogens did. The difference leaves as energy.

How much energy does one kilogram of hydrogen give when it fuses into helium?
0.0071 kg of it turns into energy.
E = 0.0071 × (3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 6.4 × 10¹⁴ J.
That is enough to run a 10-watt LED bulb for about two million years.

Step 3: why it needs the centre of a star

Hydrogen nuclei are protons, and protons repel each other. To fuse, two of them must get close enough for the nuclear force to grab, which means they must be moving fast enough to overcome the push. That takes a temperature above about 12 million kelvin. The Sun’s centre is at about 15 million kelvin, so fusion happens there, in the core, and nowhere near the surface. The surface, at a few thousand degrees, is merely glowing with the energy that has worked its way out.

Step 4: the Sun’s budget

Each second the Sun converts about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium. Of that, about 4 million tonnes becomes energy, which is exactly the 4 × 10²⁶ joules we see arriving. Four million tonnes a second sounds like a frightening rate of loss until you set it against the Sun’s mass, which is about two thousand million million million million tonnes. Over its whole four and a half billion years, the Sun has converted about three parts in ten thousand of its mass into energy. Most of its protons have not yet taken part in a single fusion.

The energy made in the core does not reach us quickly. It staggers outwards as light, absorbed and re-emitted countless times, for somewhere between a hundred thousand and a million years before it escapes the surface and then takes eight minutes to reach Mumbai. The ghostly particles called neutrinos made in the same reactions do not stagger; they leave the Sun in about two seconds. Since January 2024, India’s Aditya-L1 spacecraft has watched the Sun from a point about 1.5 million kilometres sunward of the Earth, looping around that point once every 178 days.

Step 5: fission and fusion, the same bookkeeping

Meitner’s split uranium and the Sun’s fusing hydrogen look like opposites: one breaks a heavy nucleus in two, the other joins light nuclei into one. They release energy for the same reason. In both, the pieces at the end weigh less than the pieces at the start, and the missing mass leaves as energy, exactly as E = mc² says. Which way a nucleus “goes” depends on its size: very heavy nuclei give up energy by splitting, very light ones by joining.

Careful

“The Sun is burning.”

Burning is chemistry: atoms rearranging, with the Sun’s whole supply used up in a few thousand years. The Sun is fusing: nuclei joining, at its centre, and a nucleus rearranging releases hundreds of thousands of times the energy of any chemical change. Say “shining”, or “fusing”, and keep “burning” for the kitchen.

Careful

“E = mc² destroys mass.”

Nothing is destroyed. The total energy, counting mass as one of its forms, is exactly the same before and after; it has changed form, from mass into light and motion. Think of it as bookkeeping with a very large exchange rate.

Careful

“E = mc² is only about bombs.”

The Sun has been running on it for four and a half billion years, and every bit of warmth on your arm at Marine Drive is mass that left the Sun eight minutes ago as light. The equation is about where sunlight comes from.

Chapter 15 takes this story from the X-ray room to the centre of the Sun, and that is where its big question is answered. Lise Meitner’s own life, from the basement laboratory in Berlin to the tree trunk in the snow, is told in The Invisible World, the chemistry book next door.

thinking tool

Guess like a physicist

Enrico Fermi

A kitchen in Mumbai, a July afternoon

The rain has not stopped since breakfast, and the news says 100 mm has fallen on the city since morning. How much water is that, over the whole of Mumbai? Nobody has measured it. Nobody could. And yet in two minutes, with nothing but a pencil, you can have a number you could defend to a room full of engineers.

Physicists do this so often that it has a name. A rough, reasoned answer to a question nobody can measure directly is a Fermi problem, after Enrico Fermi, who was famous for working out surprising numbers on the back of an envelope. The skill is called estimation, and it is a chain, not a guess.

Step 1: break it into pieces you can defend

You do not know the rain on Mumbai. You do know, from a map, that the city is a long strip about 40 km long and about 15 km wide. You know the rain lay 100 mm deep, which is 0.1 m. Each of those is a number you could argue for. An estimate is built from pieces like these, and choosing them is most of the skill.

Step 2: find the relationship

Volume is area times depth. Mass is volume times the mass of a cubic metre of water, which is 1,000 kg.

Rain on Mumbai
Area: 40 km × 15 km = 600 km² = 6 × 10⁸ m².
Volume: 6 × 10⁸ m² × 0.1 m = 6 × 10⁷ m³.
Mass: 6 × 10⁷ m³ × 1,000 kg/m³ = 6 × 10¹⁰ kg, about 60 million tonnes.

Step 3: check the units

Kilometres had to become metres before they met the depth in metres. Then m² × m gave m³, a volume, and m³ × kg/m³ gave kg, a mass. If the units had come out as m² or kg/m, something was wrong. Units that disagree always mean a mistake. Units that agree do not prove you right, but they catch most of the slips.

Step 4: find the weakest link

An estimate is only as good as its shakiest input. The city’s area is good to perhaps 20%. The rain is far shakier: 100 mm was one gauge’s reading, and rain over a city is patchy. If the true average was 50 mm, the answer halves. So the depth is the number worth improving, and you can improve it yourself with a straight-sided jar on the balcony.

The same lesson, the other way round: estimate the mass of all the oceans using an average depth of 1 km, and the answer comes out roughly ten times too small, because the real average depth is nearer 3.7 km. Everything else in that chain was fine. One weak input swallowed the whole answer.

Step 5: write only the digits you have earned

Fermi’s own favourite example was: how many piano tuners work in Chicago? About 3 million people, perhaps 5 to a home, perhaps one home in ten with a piano: about 60,000 pianos. A tuner might manage about 750 a year, so the city needs about 80 tuners. Fermi called that “about a hundred”, and about a hundred is right.

Notice the wording. Never “60,300,000 tonnes” or “exactly 80 tuners”. Inputs that are good to 20% cannot give an answer good to the nearest tonne. One significant figure, sometimes two, is all an estimate has earned. Often what matters is only the power of ten, the order of magnitude: is it thousands of tonnes, millions, or billions? For a question like that, an answer within a factor of ten either way counts as close enough.

Careful

“An answer with more digits is a better answer.”

The opposite. The weakest input sets how many digits the answer can have, and writing more pretends to a precision you do not possess. “About 60 million tonnes” is honest. “60,300,000 tonnes” is a small lie dressed up as care.

How many breaths have you taken?

Count your breaths for one minute while sitting still. Say you get 15. Then build the chain: 15 a minute × 60 minutes × 24 hours ≈ 22,000 a day; × 365 ≈ 8 million a year; × 12 years ≈ 100 million, or 10⁸, breaths so far. Now find the weakest link: is 15 right when you are asleep, or running? Measure it once more after climbing the stairs, and see how much the final answer moves.

In Chapter 0 this habit gets a section of its own, and the rain on Mumbai gets a figure. From then on it runs underneath every chapter: before any experiment, ask what you expect, roughly. If the measurement comes out a thousand times off your estimate, one of them is wrong, and you will want to know which.

thinking tool

Reading a motion graph

A corridor in a Mumbai flat, this afternoon

Stick a strip of masking tape on the floor every metre along the corridor, eight of them. A friend stands at the end with a phone stopwatch and calls out the seconds. You walk: steadily for four metres, then stop for two seconds, then walk faster for the last four metres. The whole thing takes eight seconds. Now turn that walk into a picture.

Step 1: walk it, write it

Every time your friend calls a second, note which tape you are nearest. You get a short table: at 0 s you were at 0 m, at 4 s at 4 m, at 6 s still at 4 m, at 8 s at 8 m. That table is the motion. Everything else is a way of looking at it.

Step 2: plot it

Time goes along the bottom, always. Distance walked goes up the side. Mark the four points and join them. You have a distance–time graph, and its shape already tells the story: a line sloping up, then a flat stretch, then a line sloping up more steeply.

Step 3: read the slope

The slope of a line (at school it is called the gradient) is how much it rises for each step along. On this graph, rising means metres and stepping along means seconds, so the slope is metres per second: a speed. Steeper means faster. Flat means stopped.

Reading the three slopes
First stretch: rose 4 m in 4 s, so the speed was 4 ÷ 4 = 1 m/s.
Flat stretch: rose 0 m in 2 s, so the speed was 0.
Last stretch: rose 4 m in 2 s, so the speed was 4 ÷ 2 = 2 m/s.

A straight line means a steady speed. A line that curves means the speed is changing. When Galileo rolled balls down a ramp (Chapter 1) the distance grew with the square of the time, and his graph would bend upward, steeper and steeper, because the ball kept getting faster. On a curved graph, the speed at any instant is the slope of the straight line that just touches the curve there.

Step 4: the other graph

Now plot the speeds you just read, against time. One metre per second for four seconds, zero for two, two for two. This is a velocity–time graph, and it looks like a set of steps. Its trick is the opposite of the first graph’s. There the slope gave you speed. Here the area under the line gives you distance, because a speed in metres per second, multiplied by a time in seconds, is a distance in metres.

Reading the areas
First step: 1 m/s × 4 s = 4 m.
Flat at zero: 0 m.
Last step: 2 m/s × 2 s = 4 m.
Total: 8 m, which is exactly where the top graph ended.

Step 5: three traps

The graph is not a map. The horizontal axis is time, so a line that curves does not mean you turned a corner; the corridor is dead straight. Keep saying “time” to yourself as you read along the bottom.

Two lines crossing mean two walkers at the same place at the same time. They do not mean the same speed. More than a third of students say they do, and it is an easy slip, because the lines look as if they meet “as equals”. The speeds are the slopes, and at a crossing the slopes are usually different.

Walking back is where distance and position part company. Distance walked only ever adds up, so a distance–time graph never comes down. A graph of your position along the corridor does come down when you turn round, with a downhill slope, as the walk in Chapter 1’s figure shows. Check which kind of graph you are reading before you read it.

Careful

“The line on the graph curves, so the path must have curved.”

The bottom axis is time, not distance across the floor. A curve means the speed was changing; a straight line means it was steady. Someone walking in a perfectly straight corridor but speeding up draws a curved line. Someone walking round a bend at a steady pace draws a straight one.

Draw your own

Lay out tape marks every metre in a corridor or along a compound wall, and have a friend call the seconds from a phone stopwatch. Walk the pattern above and plot it on squared paper. Then walk a new pattern without telling your friend what it will be, plot it, and see whether they can read your walk back from the graph alone: where you stopped, where you hurried. Finally, start as slowly as you can and speed up smoothly: watch the line bend.

Chapter 1 uses these two graphs for the local train, for Galileo’s ramps, and for a ball thrown straight up, where the velocity–time graph is a straight line that passes through zero at the very top. In Chapter 4 the same two graphs describe a falling cricket ball.

thinking tool

Powers of ten

Juhu beach, Mumbai, any evening

Pick up one grain of sand. It is about a millimetre across: a thousandth of a metre. You are about a metre and a half tall. The Earth under your feet is about ten million metres across. The Sun is about a hundred billion metres away, and the Milky Way, faint overhead if the lights would let you see it, is about a thousand billion billion metres from side to side. Go the other way: a wave of light is about a millionth of a metre long, an atom of hydrogen a ten-billionth, and the proton at its centre a thousandth of that again.

Numbers like these cannot be held in the head as a string of zeros. Physicists hold them as steps, and each step is a ten.

Step 1: 10³

Ten multiplied by itself three times is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000, and it is written 10³. The little raised number counts the tens. So 10⁶ is a million, a one followed by six zeros, and 10² is a hundred. These are the powers of ten.

They have one lovely property. To multiply two of them, you add the little numbers: 10³ × 10³ = 10⁶, because a thousand thousands is a million. That is why the prefixes you already know are powers of ten: kilo means ×10³, so a kilometre is 10³ metres.

Step 2: 10⁻³

A minus sign on the little number means divide instead of multiply. 10⁻³ is 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001, a thousandth: the sand grain, in metres. Milli means ×10⁻³; centi ×10⁻²; micro ×10⁻⁶; nano ×10⁻⁹. And 10⁰, no tens at all, is simply 1: you, roughly, in metres.

Step 3: writing a big number small

The mass of the Earth is about 5,970,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg. Nobody can read that, and nobody can check it. Written as 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg it is easy to read and easy to check: the power of ten says what scale you are on, and the number in front gives the detail. This way of writing, a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, is called scientific notation; at school you may meet it as standard form. It works for small numbers too: an electron’s mass is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

A day and a year, in standard form
A day: 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400 s = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.
A year: about 365 days, so about 3.16 × 10⁷ s.
The powers tell you at once that a year is between a hundred and a thousand times a day (365 lies between 10² and 10³).

Step 4: the zoom

Here is the step most people get wrong. Ten times bigger, and then ten times bigger again, is not twenty times bigger. It is a hundred times. Each step multiplies. Three steps is a thousand times, six steps a million. From a grain of sand to you is three steps. From a hydrogen atom to the Sun is nineteen. “Too small to see” is not one size: a bacterium and an electron are both invisible, and in mass they are fifteen steps of ten apart, more steps than separate you from the Sun.

Step 5: a ruler made of tens

The ladder in the figure is drawn so that each step of ×10 has the same width. A ruler like that is a logarithmic scale, and it is the only kind of ruler that can fit a proton and a galaxy on one page. Ordinary rulers add: each centimetre is one more. This one multiplies: each mark is ten times the last. It has one odd property: it never reaches zero, because below any mark there is always another, a tenth of it, and another below that, for ever. The scale for earthquakes works this way, and so does the decibel scale for loudness that you will meet in Chapter 9, where every 10 decibels is a sound ten times as intense.

Careful

“10⁶ is twice as big as 10³, because 6 is twice 3.”

It is a thousand times as big. The little numbers are counts of tens, and three more tens means multiplying by ten three more times. A million is a thousand thousands, not two thousands.

A page you cannot measure

A single page of a notebook is too thin for a ruler. So measure a hundred of them pressed flat: about a centimetre, say, which is 10⁻² m. One page is then 10⁻² ÷ 10² = 10⁻⁴ m, a tenth of a millimetre. Now work out how many pages, stacked, would reach the top of your head: your height in metres divided by 10⁻⁴. For 1.5 m that is 15,000 pages, or 1.5 × 10⁴. Check it against the number of pages in a notebook and the thickness of the notebook.

Chapter 0 opens the Powers of Ten explorer, where you can climb this ladder with your thumb. You will need it in Chapter 15 most of all, where the distances to the stars are written in powers of ten because there is no other way to write them.

thinking tool

Twice as far, four times as weak

A dark room in Mumbai, with a torch

Switch off the lights, stand a metre from a wall and shine a torch at it. There is a bright patch. Step back to two metres. The patch is bigger and dimmer. How much bigger, and how much dimmer? The answer to that small question turns out to be the answer to how gravity weakens with distance, how sound fades across a room, and why the Sun does not roast the Earth. Physics is full of questions of the form “if I double this, what happens to that?”, and the answers come in only a few shapes.

Step 1: double it, double it

The simplest shape: double one thing and the other doubles too. A 1 kg bag of atta weighs 9.8 N; a 2 kg bag weighs 19.6 N. Walk at a steady pace for twice the time and you cover twice the distance. One quantity is proportional to the other, and the relationship is called proportionality. On a graph it is a straight line through the origin: nothing in, nothing out.

Step 2: double it, four times

The next shape is the square law: double the input and the output goes up four times, because 2 × 2 = 4. Triple it and the output goes up nine times. You have met it already if you read the story of ‘s Gravesande’s clay: a ball moving twice as fast has four times the energy of motion, and makes a dent four times as deep. Galileo’s balls on their ramp obeyed a square law too: the distance rolled in 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds went 1 : 4 : 9 : 16, so the gaps between the seconds went 1, 3, 5, 7. And a wave with twice the height carries four times the energy, which is why a big wave does far more than twice the damage of a small one.

Step 3: double it, halve it

Some pairs go the other way. Push a trolley with the same force and double its load: the acceleration halves. Share the same cake among twice as many people: each slice halves. The output is proportional to one over the input. Double, and you get a half.

Step 4: double it, a quarter

Now the torch. At one metre, the beam lights a patch one square wide. At two metres, the beam has spread sideways to twice the width and twice the height, so it lights four squares. The torch is sending out the same light, so each square now gets a quarter of what the single square got. At three metres, nine squares, each a ninth as bright. Twice as far, four times as weak: a square law turned upside down, the inverse square.

The torch
At 1 m: 1 × 1 = 1 square, full brightness.
At 2 m: 2 × 2 = 4 squares, each ¼ as bright.
At 3 m: 3 × 3 = 9 squares, each ⅑ as bright.
The same light, spread over an area that grows with the square of the distance.

Anything that spreads out evenly from a point follows this law, because the surface it spreads over grows as the square of the distance. Sound does: twice as far from a speaker, a quarter of the intensity, because the same sound power is spread over a sphere four times the area. Gravity does, and that was Newton’s great check in Chapter 5. The Moon is about 60 Earth-radii away, so Earth’s pull on it should be 1 ÷ 60², or 1 ÷ 3600, of the pull at the surface: 9.8 ÷ 3600 ≈ 0.0027 m/s², and that is exactly the acceleration the Moon needs to stay on its orbit.

Step 5: the doubling test

To find which shape a pair of quantities follows, do one experiment: double the input and see what the output does. Doubles: proportional. Four times: square law. Halves: inverse. A quarter: inverse square. One doubling tells you the shape; a second doubling, to four times, confirms it. This test runs underneath every “law” in the book.

Careful

“Twice as far from the torch means half as bright.”

A quarter. The beam spreads in two directions at once, across and up, so the patch grows in area as the square of the distance, and the same light has to cover four times the area. Half is the answer for things that spread along a line, like paint from a brush; light, sound and gravity spread in all directions.

The torch on the wall

In a dark room, shine a torch straight at a wall from exactly 1 m and mark the edges of the bright patch with two bits of tape. Step back to exactly 2 m and mark again. Measure both widths: the second should be about twice the first, so the patch has four times the area. The torch has not changed; the same light is spread four times thinner. If you have a phone with a light-meter app, hold it at the wall each time and see whether the reading drops to about a quarter.

Chapter 1 meets the square law on Galileo’s ramp, Chapter 5 uses the inverse square to weigh the Moon’s fall, Chapter 7 finds energy of motion growing with the square of speed, and Chapter 9 finds the loudness of sound fading as the inverse square. Four chapters, one shape.

thinking tool

Measuring anything

Sèvres, near Paris, 20 May 2019

On 20 May 2019 the last of the world’s measuring units that still depended on a physical object, the kilogram, was redefined in terms of a constant of nature, and every one of the seven base units of the international system came to rest on something that cannot drift or tarnish. The tale of the metal cylinder it replaced is told elsewhere in this book. This is about the system itself, and about why three of its units turn up on a bill that arrives at your flat every month.

Step 1: why units at all

“The pitch is 20” means nothing. “The pitch is 20 metres” means something, and “20 yards” means something slightly different. A measurement is always a number times a unit, and the unit is what lets two people in two cities agree. You cannot add quantities with different units: 10 km plus 5 kg is nonsense, and even 10 km plus 20 m has to be made into one unit before it can be added.

The system almost every country uses is the SI, from its French name, Système international. It rests on seven base units: the metre, the kilogram, the second, the ampere, the kelvin, the mole and the candela. For everything in the first half of this book you need only the first three.

Step 2: building new units from old ones

Every other unit in mechanics is a combination of the metre, the kilogram and the second. Speed is metres per second. Acceleration is metres per second each second, m/s². Some combinations come up so often that they are given names, and the names honour the people who did the work.

The newton is the force that gives one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared. So a one-kilogram bag of atta, which falls at 9.8 m/s² when you drop it, weighs about 9.8 newtons.

The joule is one newton pushed through one metre. Lifting that bag of atta by about 10 cm takes about one joule. It is the unit of energy, of every kind: of movement, of height, of heat, of food.

The watt is one joule every second: the unit of how fast energy moves. A 60 W bulb moves 60 J every second from the mains into light and warmth, and only about 5 of those watts come out as light; the rest warms the room.

Step 3: converting

Prefixes are powers of ten: kilo means a thousand, so a kilowatt is 1,000 W. And multiplying a power by a time gives an energy, because joules per second, times seconds, is joules.

The unit on the bill
1 kilowatt for 1 hour = 1,000 J/s × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 MJ.
That is one kilowatt-hour, and when your electricity bill says “units consumed”, one unit means one kilowatt-hour.
A 10 W LED bulb burning for 100 hours: 10 × 100 = 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh, one unit.
A 500 W mixer-grinder running for 2 hours: 500 × 2 = 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh, the same unit. (Read the labels on yours; those wattages are typical, not certain.)

Step 4: comparing

Once everything is in joules, odd things can be compared. One kilowatt-hour is about 860 kilocalories, the “calories” printed on food packets. A person eating 2,000 kcal a day is running on about 2.3 kWh a day, roughly the energy that lights a flat for an evening. A 30 kcal biscuit holds about 35 Wh, enough to run a 10 W LED for three and a half hours. And a labourer working steadily at about 100 W needs ten hours to deliver one kilowatt-hour. One unit on the bill is a full working day of human effort.

Careful

“A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power. Or is it watts per hour?”

Neither. A watt is already “per second”: it is a joule every second, a rate. Multiply a rate by a time and you get back to an amount, so a kilowatt-hour is an energy, 3.6 million joules. “Watts per hour” is not a unit of anything useful. Bills count energy; the appliance label gives power; the hours you run it join the two.

Step 5: units as a check

Carry the units through every calculation. Area times depth gives m² × m = m³, a volume; a volume times kg/m³ gives kg, a mass. If you set out to find an energy and the units come out as kg or m/s, you have made a mistake somewhere, and the units found it before you did.

Read the labels

Find the wattage printed on the mixer-grinder, the fridge, an LED bulb and a phone charger. Then find the “units consumed” on last month’s electricity bill. Work out how many hours of each appliance one unit buys: 1,000 Wh divided by the wattage. Finally, read the kilocalories on a biscuit packet and convert one biscuit to watt-hours (multiply by 4,184 J, divide by 3,600). How many biscuits is one unit on the bill?

Chapter 0 introduces the SI and the measuring habit. Chapter 7 does the bill properly, and shows why “units consumed” is a slightly misleading phrase, since nothing has been consumed: 3.6 million joules per unit have been delivered to your flat and have become light, motion, sound and warmth.

thinking tool

Arrows that add

A school ground in Mumbai, sports day

Seven children, one rope, and the rope is not moving. Four pull one way and three the other, all of them straining, heels dug in. A lot is happening to that rope. And yet, as far as its motion is concerned, the total of all that pulling is exactly nothing. To see why, you need one idea: some quantities point.

Step 1: amounts and arrows

Your mass is 40 kg; the room is 30 °C; the market is 5 km away. Each is just an amount; none of them points anywhere. Quantities like these are scalars.

Now suppose you cycle 3 km west and then 2 km east. The distance you covered is 5 km, a scalar. But where you ended up is 1 km west of where you started, and “west” is part of the answer. A quantity with an amount and a direction is a vector. Your change of position is a vector. So is your velocity, which is your speed together with the direction you are going. So is every push and pull.

Step 2: draw them

A vector is drawn as an arrow. Its length shows the amount, to some scale, and it points the way the quantity points. A 100 N pull to the left is an arrow 5 cm long pointing left, say; a 50 N pull to the right is an arrow 2.5 cm long pointing right. Forces are drawn from the point where they act.

Step 3: adding along a line

Back to the rope. Suppose the four on the left pull with 120, 100, 90 and 80 newtons, and the three on the right with 150, 130 and 110. Arrows along one line are easy to add: total the ones pointing one way, total the ones pointing the other, and subtract.

The tug of war
Left: 120 + 100 + 90 + 80 = 390 N.
Right: 150 + 130 + 110 = 390 N.
Net force on the rope: 390 − 390 = 0 N.

The leftover, after all the cancelling, is the net force on the rope. At school it is called the resultant force, or the unbalanced force; the three names mean the same thing. Here it is zero, so the rope’s motion does not change. The children are not doing nothing: the rope is stretched tight and every arm aches. But nothing about its motion changes until the two totals differ. If one child on the left let go, the net force would be 80 N to the right, and the rope would start to move that way.

Step 4: adding at an angle

Now the arrows do not lie along one line. A boat is rowed straight across a river at 3 m/s, while the current carries everything downstream at 4 m/s. How fast is the boat really moving, and which way?

The rule is head to tail: draw the first arrow, then start the second where the first one ends. The answer, the resultant, is the arrow from the very start to the very end.

The boat
Across: 3 m/s. Downstream, from the tip of that arrow: 4 m/s.
The two make a right angle, so the resultant is the long side of a 3–4–5 triangle: 5 m/s, pointing about 37° from the bank.
If the river is 60 m wide, crossing takes 60 ÷ 3 = 20 s, and in those 20 s the current carries the boat 4 × 20 = 80 m downstream.

The same rule works inside a moving train. A train at 80 km/h passes the platform at about 22 m/s; walk forward at 1.4 m/s and you pass it at about 23.6 m/s, because the two arrows point the same way and add. Walk towards the back and they subtract.

Step 5: why 5 + 5 is not always 10

Two 5 N pulls in the same direction add to 10 N. Two 5 N pulls in opposite directions add to 0. Two 5 N pulls at right angles add to about 7 N, the diagonal of a square with sides of 5. Vectors only add like ordinary numbers when they lie along one line. Everywhere else, you draw.

Careful

“Two forces of 5 N make 10 N. Numbers add.”

Only if they point the same way. Opposite, they make 0 N; at right angles, about 7 N. A vector is an amount and a direction, and the direction changes the sum. Off a line, lay the arrows head to tail and measure; never just add the numbers.

Two strings and a book

Tie two strings to a book lying on a smooth table. Pull both gently with the same effort at right angles to each other: the book slides off along the diagonal between them, the resultant. Pull both the same way and it goes that way, faster. Pull in opposite directions with equal effort and it goes nowhere, like the rope on sports day. Now pull one string a little harder than the other and watch the diagonal swing towards it.

Chapter 1 uses vectors for velocity, and the train walk comes from there. Chapter 3 opens with adding forces, where the net force is the whole story of whether anything changes its motion. And in Chapter 4 a ball thrown sideways has its motion split into two arrows, across and down, that behave as if they had never met.

The adventure in time
