The ideas in this book were not found in the order a textbook teaches them. Here they are in the order they actually happened: two and a half thousand years of people asking how things move, and why.

  1. The ancient world
  2. 499
    Aryabhata’s boat

    A 23-year-old in Kusumapura wrote that the stars only seem to move, the way the riverbank seems to slide past a moving boat, and that eclipses are shadows, not demons.

  3. 499 CE
    The boy who put the sky in a boat

    At twenty-three in Kusumapura, Aryabhata compared the turning Earth to a boat on a river and replaced the eclipse demon with geometry.

  4. The Middle Ages
  5. 530 to 1687
    The arrow problem: two thousand years of a wrong idea

    Why an arrow keeps flying after it leaves the bow puzzled thinkers from Alexandria to Paris, and the answer they settled on is the one most people still believe today.

  6. 628 CE
    Zero, negative numbers, and the nature of heavy things

    In 628 CE Brahmagupta gave arithmetic its rules for zero and negative numbers, and described heavy bodies falling because it is the Earth’s nature to attract them.

  7. about 1011 to 1021
    Light comes in

    For centuries the best thinkers said the eye sends out rays to feel the world. A scholar in Cairo argued that light comes in, and backed it with a dark room and a small hole.

  8. about 1015
    The man in the dark room

    Working in Cairo a thousand years ago, Ibn al-Haytham used dark rooms, small holes, and plain evidence from our own eyes to show that light travels into the eye, not out of it.

  9. about 1150
    A hundredth part of the circumference

    From the observatory at Ujjain in 1150, Bhaskara II explained why a huge spherical Earth looks flat under our feet and why people on the far side of the globe do not fall off.

  10. about 1583
    Pushing a swing

    A legend about a swinging lamp, the true thing Galileo found in swinging weights, and why a small push at the right moment builds a huge swing while a big push at the wrong moment does nothing.

  11. 1586 to 1971
    The single thud at Delft

    Two lead balls, a church tower in Delft and a single thud, three years before Galileo reached Pisa; then a hammer and a feather on the Moon finished the argument.

  12. 250 BCE to 1586
    Galileo and the crown

    The “Eureka” bath is a legend, and a 22-year-old Galileo explained why it could not have worked; what Archimedes really found is why a steel ship floats and an egg sinks.

  13. 1586
    The single thud at Delft

    Three years before Galileo went to Pisa, the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin dropped two lead balls of tenfold different weight in Delft and heard a single thud on a wooden board.

  14. 1586 to 1654
    The drop that probably never happened

    The most famous experiment in physics has one witness, who wrote it down twelve years after Galileo died, and Galileo himself never mentioned it; the real drop happened in Delft.

  15. The 1600s
  16. 1600
    The little Earth

    By grinding a lodestone into a ball and watching a needle tilt over it, William Gilbert worked out that the Earth itself is a magnet, and that garlic has nothing to do with compasses.

  17. 1600 to 1752
    Rubbing doesn’t make charge

    A rubbed balloon clings to a wall because electrons moved from one material to the other; nothing was created, and the man who first sorted out which substances do this gave electricity its name.

  18. 1586 to 1638
    The man who slowed down falling

    From his father’s lute strings in Florence to inclined ramps in Padua and the moons of Jupiter, Galileo turned physics into an art of measurement.

  19. 1576 to 1609
    Eight minutes of arc

    Twenty years of naked-eye measurements on a Danish island, and a stubborn gap a quarter of the Moon’s width, turned the planets’ circles into ellipses.

  20. 984 to 1621
    The coin that rises

    Why a coin under water looks nearer than it is, why light bends when it changes speed, and how a curved bit of water or glass becomes a lens, including the two in your head.

  21. 1604 to 1687
    The ball that never stops

    Galileo imagined a ramp that never climbs, Descartes wrote the rule down, and Newton made it his first law: a moving thing keeps its velocity until a force changes it.

  22. 1643 to 1654
    We live at the bottom of an ocean of air

    A pump that stopped at ten metres, a tube of mercury in Florence, a barometer carried up a mountain and two copper bowls that horses could not pull apart: how people discovered that air has weight.

  23. 1666 to 1687
    The apple and the Moon

    A young man at a farmhouse wondered whether the pull that drops an apple reaches all the way to the Moon, and worked out that it does, exactly 3,600 times weaker.

  24. 1666 to 1672
    Newton’s dark room

    A small hole in a shutter, a glass prism, and a coloured patch that was the wrong shape: how Newton showed that white light is a mixture and that a prism only sorts it.

  25. 1673
    Why there is no force flinging you out

    Huygens worked out the pull on a stone whirled on a string, Newton named the inward force, and the outward shove you feel on a turning bus is your own body carrying straight on.

  26. 1676 to 1849
    Ten minutes late

    An astronomer in Paris noticed Jupiter’s moon running late and realised he was watching light take its time; a spinning cogwheel across Paris later put a number on it.

  27. 1686 to 2021
    The wind that turns around

    Edmond Halley explained the monsoon as a sea breeze the size of a continent. Three centuries later, Indian scientists argue that the picture fails, and the question is still open.

  28. 1684 to 1758
    The man who bet on a comet he would never see

    Edmond Halley charted the southern stars at twenty, paid to print Newton’s Principia, drew the first map of the monsoon winds, and predicted the return of a comet after his death.

  29. 1684 to 1687
    The book that nearly sank the Principia

    The Royal Society spent its money on an expensive book about fish, so the most important physics book ever written was paid for by an astronomer, who was then paid his salary in fish books.

  30. 1687
    Falling around the Earth

    Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain so high that its ball never came down, and in doing so explained why astronauts float while gravity still pulls on them at nearly full strength.

  31. 1666 to 1687
    The apple, the prism, and the falling Moon

    Sent home to Lincolnshire during the plague of 1665, Isaac Newton split sunlight with two prisms and asked whether the pull that drops an apple reaches all the way to the Moon.

  32. 1687
    Every push has a partner

    Newton’s third law in his own examples, a finger on a stone and a horse on a rope, and why a truck and a car in a collision feel exactly the same force.

  33. 1687
    Why Haji Ali goes under the sea

    Twice a day the causeway to Haji Ali drowns and reappears, about fifty minutes later each day; the Moon’s pull, slightly different from one side of the Earth to the other, is the reason.

  34. The 1700s
  35. 1737 to 2009
    Galileo’s fingers

    Ninety-five years after Galileo died, his body was moved to a grand tomb and admirers took parts of it as souvenirs; two fingers and a tooth went missing in 1905 and turned up at an auction in 2009.

  36. 1740 to 1749
    Four times the dent in the clay

    Barred from Paris universities and the Royal Academy as a woman, Émilie du Châtelet turned a country château into a laboratory, backed mv² in the debate over moving force, and translated Newton’s Principia into French.

  37. 1722 to 1740
    mv or mv²?

    Brass balls dropped into soft clay helped settle a long quarrel about what a moving body carries, and the answer turned out to be a square.

  38. 1761
    The ice that would not warm up

    A Glasgow professor heated melting ice and watched the thermometer refuse to move. The warmth was going somewhere, and finding where changed what heat meant.

  39. 1798
    Boiling water with a blunt drill

    The best theory of heat in 1798 said it was an invisible fluid stored inside things. A cannon-maker in Munich showed that the fluid never ran out.

  40. 1798
    Weighing the world through a hole in the wall

    A shy, silent millionaire shut himself out of his own experiment, watched two lead balls through a telescope poked through a wall, and weighed the Earth.

  41. The 1800s
  42. 1803 to 1819
    The spot that shouldn’t exist

    A thin card in a sunbeam, a prize jury’s “absurd” prediction and a bright dot in the middle of a shadow: how light was shown to be a wave, and how a sceptic’s own argument settled it.

  43. 1820
    The needle that twitched

    During a lecture in Copenhagen a compass needle moved so slightly that the audience missed it; within five months Ampère in Paris had turned the twitch into a theory of what magnetism is.

  44. 1824
    Waterfalls of heat

    A young French engineer paid to print six hundred copies of a booklet asking how good a steam engine could possibly be. Almost nobody read it, and it founded a science.

  45. 1827
    What goes round

    A schoolteacher from Cologne measured how much current a given push drives through a wire, was ignored for fourteen years, and left us the rule that every loop of wire in your flat obeys.

  46. 1821 to 1831
    Magnets make electricity

    Ten years after he made a wire spin round a magnet, Faraday wound two coils on an iron ring and saw a needle jump only at the moment he switched on: the trick behind every power station, including the ones that light Mumbai.

  47. 1812 to 1836
    The bookbinder’s apprentice and the invisible lines

    A blacksmith’s son who left school at thirteen bound three hundred pages of lecture notes to win a laboratory job, then built the first electric motor, the first transformer, and the concept of a field.

  48. 1836
    The man in the foil box

    Faraday built a cube twelve feet across, covered it in metal foil, charged the outside until sparks flew, and sat inside with his most sensitive instrument, finding nothing at all.

  49. 1842 to 1845
    Horn players on a train

    Doppler’s idea was right and his favourite example was wrong; three years later a Dutch scientist tested it the only way he could, with horn players on an open railway wagon.

  50. 1758 to 1846
    The planet found with a pen

    A comet that came back when three people’s arithmetic said it would, and a planet nobody had knowingly seen that a letter from Paris told Berlin exactly where to look for.

  51. 1840 to 1847
    The number that never changes

    A ship’s doctor puzzled by the colour of blood, a brewer’s son with a paddle wheel, and the one number in physics that is never destroyed.

  52. 1849
    A cogwheel across Paris

    A young man who had given up medicine spun a toothed wheel fast enough to chop a beam of light, bounced it off a hilltop 8.6 km away, and caught the speed of light on the ground for the first time.

  53. 1851
    Have you seen the Earth turn?

    In 1851 a self-taught Parisian hung a 28-kilogram ball from a 67-metre wire in the Panthéon and let the whole city watch the floor turn under it.

  54. 1862 to 1888
    Light is electromagnetic

    A speed came out of Maxwell’s equations that nobody had put in, and it matched the speed of light measured across Paris; twenty-five years later Hertz made the waves with a spark.

  55. 1869 to 1871
    Why the sky is blue and the sunset orange

    The air itself is the painter: molecules fling blue light sideways about six times more than red, which makes the noon sky blue and the Sun orange as it sets over Marine Drive.

  56. 1895 to 1897
    Invisible waves in Calcutta

    In a cramped college laboratory in Calcutta, J. C. Bose made waves five millimetres long, sent them through two walls to ring a bell, and lectured on them in London before Marconi’s first signal crossed the Atlantic.

  57. 1894 to 1897
    Millimetre waves through the walls of Calcutta

    In a small room at Presidency College in 1895, Jagadish Chandra Bose shrank electromagnetic waves down to five millimetres and sent them through walls to ring a bell.

  58. 1896
    Radiation is not catching

    Most students think a chest X-ray leaves you radioactive. It does not, and the difference between being hit by radiation and carrying radioactive dust is the whole of radiation safety.

  59. 1831 to 1899
    The quote Faraday never said

    “One day, sir, you may tax it” is the best reply in the history of science, and there is no evidence that anyone ever said it; here is how to tell a true story from a good one.

  60. The 1900s
  61. 1841 to 1907
    Chased out of Bombay by the trams

    For sixty years Bombay’s observatory at Colaba recorded the Earth’s magnetism hour by hour, until the city decided to run its trams on electricity and the magnets had to leave town.

  62. 1905 to 1924
    Light in packets

    A patent clerk in Bern explained why a dim violet lamp can knock electrons out of a metal when a blinding red one cannot, and nineteen years later a teacher in Dacca wrote to him with a better way to count the packets.

  63. 1908 to 1912
    The blinking stars in the southern cloud

    Studying glass photographic plates of a southern star cloud, Henrietta Leavitt found that brighter Cepheid stars pulse more slowly, giving astronomy its cosmic measuring tape.

  64. 1912
    A measuring tape to the stars

    A Harvard “computer” noticed that the slow blinkers among the stars of one small cloud were always the bright ones, and gave astronomers a tape that reaches far beyond anything a surveyor’s triangle can measure.

  65. 1919 to 1980
    The eclipse that made Einstein famous, and the argument after

    Two British expeditions photographed stars beside the darkened Sun and found their light bent by twice the old amount; sixty years later historians accused them of throwing away the plates that disagreed.

  66. 1920
    The Thermometer of the Stars

    A physicist from a flood-prone Bengal village combined thermodynamics with Bohr’s atom to turn stellar spectra into a thermometer for the stars.

  67. about 1589 to 1920
    How a tabla sings

    Why a plucked string sounds like a note, why most drums only thud, and how the black patch on a tabla turns the thud into music, as Raman and Kumar showed in 1920.

  68. 1921 to 1930
    The colour of the sea

    On a liner steaming home to Bombay, Raman held a crystal over the rail and found that the sea’s blue is its own; seven years later in Calcutta he and Krishnan found scattered light that changes colour.

  69. 1924
    A Four-Page Letter to Berlin

    When a British journal ignored his four-page derivation of Planck’s law, a reader in physics at Dacca mailed it directly to Albert Einstein.

  70. 1925
    What the Stars Are Made Of

    Using Meghnad Saha’s ionisation formula and Harvard’s glass-plate archive, a twenty-five-year-old doctoral student discovered that the stars are made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium.

  71. 1920 to 1929
    What the stars are made of

    A Calcutta physicist worked out why hot stars hide their hydrogen; a Harvard student used his equation to show that stars are almost nothing but hydrogen, and was told to call her own result spurious.

  72. 1919 to 1930
    Five Weeks in Calcutta

    A civil-service accountant who spent his evenings in a Calcutta laboratory explained the acoustics of the tabla, the blue of the deep ocean, and the molecular scattering of light.

  73. 1929
    The stretching universe

    Every distant galaxy’s light is stretched towards the red, and the farther the galaxy the more it is stretched; the right picture is not galaxies flying apart through space but space itself growing between them.

  74. 1930 to 1983
    The Calculation on the Ship

    On a steamship voyage from Bombay to Venice in 1930, a nineteen-year-old student combined relativity with quantum mechanics and found that heavy white dwarf stars cannot hold themselves up.

  75. 1930 to 1935
    The limit worked out at sea

    A nineteen-year-old on a ship out of Bombay worked out that a dead star heavier than about 1.4 Suns cannot hold itself up; the astronomer who had made Einstein famous called the idea absurd, and the Nobel committee sided with the teenager forty-eight years later.

  76. 1938
    A fire that has lasted four and a half billion years

    No fire could shine for four and a half billion years, and the Sun is not burning at all; the walk in the snow that explained a split nucleus also explains where sunlight comes from.

  77. 1940
    Galloping Gertie and Tubby the dog

    A brand-new suspension bridge twisted itself to pieces in a steady wind, on film, and the only life lost was a frightened cocker spaniel who bit the man trying to save him.

  78. 1939 to 1949
    Star Tracks on Sandakphu

    High on Himalayan ridges between 1939 and 1942, Bibha Chowdhuri and D. M. Bose exposed photographic plates to cosmic rays and measured the mass of subatomic mesons years before particle accelerators could make them.

  79. 1928 to 1945
    The Bargain at Cambridge

    After striking a bargain with his father to finish an engineering degree first, Homi Bhabha worked out how cosmic rays shower through the atmosphere and built India’s school of modern physics in Bombay.

  80. 1948 to 1976
    The Woman Who Measured the Wind

    When newly independent India could not even manufacture a clinical thermometer or rain gauge of its own, Anna Mani drew up the blueprints for nearly a hundred weather instruments and mapped the nation’s wind, sunshine, and ozone.

  81. 1955 to 1998
    The brain in the jars

    When Einstein died, the pathologist on duty kept his brain without permission, and for forty years it travelled America in two jars inside a cider box while scientists looked in it for the secret of genius and did not find one.

  82. 1956
    The Mirror That Cracked

    Over Christmas 1956, Chien-Shiung Wu cooled radioactive cobalt nuclei to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero and proved that the weak nuclear force can tell left from right.

  83. 1963
    Rockets from a church

    India’s first rocket rose from beside a village church in Kerala in 1963, and it climbed by throwing things away: the idea of momentum, and why a rocket needs nothing to push against.

  84. 1963 to 1969
    The schoolboy and the ice cream

    A Tanzanian schoolboy insisted that his hot ice-cream mix had frozen before everyone’s cold one, was laughed at, kept asking, and ended up with an effect named after him that physicists still cannot agree is real.

  85. 1947 to 1971
    The Church on the Magnetic Equator

    Convinced that a poor country needed satellites for monsoon warnings and village classrooms rather than prestige, Vikram Sarabhai launched India’s first sounding rocket from a fishing-village church on the magnetic equator.

  86. 1971
    A hammer, a feather and the Moon

    At the end of the last moonwalk of Apollo 15, an astronaut dropped a hammer and a falcon’s feather for the television cameras, and an argument 385 years old ended in about 1.2 seconds.

  87. 1987
    Harvard graduates and the seasons

    On graduation day, 21 of 23 people in gowns got the seasons wrong; the right answer is a tilt, a slanting torch, and a Mumbai noon Sun that stands north of overhead in June.

  88. 1970 to 1996
    A Hillside and Thirty Wire Dishes

    By matching a half-kilometre radio telescope to the natural slope of a Nilgiri hill and building thirty giant dishes out of light wire mesh near Pune, Govind Swarup made India a leader in low-frequency radio astronomy.

  89. 1997 to 2003
    From Karnal to Orbit

    Growing up watching small aeroplanes climb from the flying club in Karnal, Kalpana Chawla became the first woman in her aeronautical engineering department and flew twice into Earth orbit aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia.

  90. The 2000s
  91. 2000 to 2021
    The bridge that walked

    On its opening day a slim new footbridge across the Thames swayed so much that it closed after two days; twenty years later engineers were still arguing about exactly why.

  92. 1889 to 2019
    The kilogram that changed

    For 130 years the whole world’s kilogram was a small metal cylinder in a vault near Paris; when it began, slowly and inexplicably, to disagree with its own copies, the kilogram was rebuilt on a number of nature instead.

  93. 2023
    The slow road to the Moon

    Forty days from Sriharikota to the Moon’s south polar region in widening loops, a half-hour brake behind the Moon, and a soft landing at 18:04 on 23 August 2023.

  94. 2024
    A spacecraft that never stops watching the Sun

    One and a half million kilometres sunward of Earth there is a spot where the Sun’s pull and Earth’s pull combine so neatly that a spacecraft can keep pace with us for years; India parked a Sun-watcher there in January 2024.

Answers to Check yourself

Try each question before you look. If your answer differs, the reasoning matters more than the words: see whether you used the same idea.

Chapter 0. The physicist’s way of seeing

0.1

A friend says: “The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so the Sun goes round the Earth.” Which part of that sentence is an observation, and which is a model? Can you think of a second model that fits the same observation?

The observation is that the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west; anyone can check it. “The Sun goes round the Earth” is a model built to explain it. A second model that fits just as well is Aryabhata’s from the letter at the front of this book: the Earth turns towards the east, so everything in the sky seems to drift west. One observation cannot choose between the two. You need more observations, and later chapters collect them.

Back to section 0.1

0.2

A friend measures a pencil with an ordinary school ruler and writes down 17.3482 cm. What has gone wrong?

A ruler marked in millimetres lets you read to the nearest millimetre and estimate one more digit: 17.35 cm at best. The 8 and the 2 are invented; the ruler cannot see them. Writing extra digits does not make a measurement better. It makes it dishonest about its uncertainty.

Back to section 0.2

0.3

How many seconds are there in a day? Write the answer in the form “a number times a power of ten”, and say how many steps up the ladder a year is from a day.

24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 86,400 s, which is 8.64 × 10⁴ s. A year is about 365 days, so about 3.16 × 10⁷ s. That is between two and three steps up the ladder, since 365 lies between 100 and 1,000.

Back to section 0.3

0.4

A new tower near your school has 40 storeys. Estimate its height, and say which input you trust least.

A storey is about 3 m (a ceiling a little above your reach, plus the floor between), so 40 × 3 m = 120 m, roughly. The storey height is the weak link: real storeys run from about 2.5 m to 4 m, so the answer could be 100 m or 160 m. Counting the storeys exactly does not help much; measuring one storey would.

Back to section 0.4

Chapter 1. Describing motion

1.1

You walk from your front door to the shop at the corner, 300 m away, and come back. What distance did you cover, and what was your displacement?

Distance 600 m: the whole path, there and back. Displacement zero: you ended where you started, so your position did not change at all.

Back to section 1.1

1.2

Does a car’s odometer measure distance or displacement? Does its speedometer show speed or velocity?

The odometer adds up distance: every kilometre driven counts, whichever way you went, so a round trip still adds to it. The speedometer shows speed, the size of the velocity at that instant, with no direction. If it showed velocity it would need a compass as well.

Back to section 1.2

1.3

A train is moving to the left and comes smoothly to a stop. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the direction of its acceleration, and what is its sign?

The train is slowing, so its acceleration points opposite to its velocity: to the right. With right as positive, that is a positive acceleration, even though the train is slowing down.

Back to section 1.3

1.4

A ball starts from rest and its speed grows by 4 m/s every second. After 2 seconds, is its speed 8 m/s or 16 m/s? How far has it travelled?

Its speed is 8 m/s: it gained 4 m/s in each of two seconds. The 16 belongs to the distance pattern, not the speed. Its distance is ½ × 4 × 2² = 8 m, which you can also get as average speed × time: it averaged 4 m/s over the two seconds, so 4 × 2 = 8 m.

Back to section 1.4

1.5

A ball thrown almost straight up passes a coconut on the way up, misses it, and passes it again on the way down. Ignoring air, how do its speeds compare at the coconut the two times?

They are the same size, in opposite directions. On the way up the ball loses 9.8 m/s of speed every second over the climb from the coconut to the top; on the way down it gains speed at the same rate over the same height, so it arrives back at the coconut with exactly the speed it had there before, now pointing down.

Back to section 1.5

Chapter 2. Why things keep moving

2.1

In Chapter 0 you kept observations and models apart. Sort these three sentences about a katori flicked across the counter: “it slid about 40 cm and stopped”; “it stopped because the push you gave it ran out”; “it stopped because the counter pushed back on it”.

The first is the observation: anyone watching would agree on it. The other two are models, stories about the cause. Both explain the same observation, so the observation alone cannot choose between them. You need a new observation that the two models predict differently, which is what Section 2.3 provides.

Back to section 2.1

2.1

Think of three things you pushed today that stopped after you let go. For each one, name what was touching it while it slowed down.

Whatever you chose (a door, a chair, a cup slid across the table, a ball rolled on the floor), something was touching it as it slowed: the floor, the table, its hinges, and always the air. Each of those is a candidate for the hidden backward push. Nothing you pushed today stopped while touching nothing at all.

Back to section 2.1

2.2

A crumpled paper ball flies across the classroom. While it is in the air, list every force acting on it, and for each force name the object that exerts it.

Two forces. The Earth pulls it downward (gravity), and the air pushes on it, mostly backward against its motion. There is no forward force, because nothing is touching it from behind: your hand stopped acting the moment the ball left it. The ball keeps moving forward because nothing is stopping it, except, slowly, the air.

Back to section 2.2

2.3

You push a box across the floor and let go. It slides on for a moment, slowing down. While it slides, which way does the total force on it point: forward, backward, or nowhere?

Backward. The only horizontal force left is friction from the floor, which pushes against the sliding. That backward force is what makes the velocity shrink. If the total force pointed nowhere, the velocity would not change, and the box would slide on at the same speed.

Back to section 2.3

2.4

In Chapter 1 you threw a ball straight up and watched the very top of its flight, where for an instant it is still. Suppose you toss your keys up on the platform while you wait for the next train. At the top, is any force acting on them? And does Newton’s first law say they should stay there?

The Earth is pulling the keys down the whole time, so a force is acting, and the first law says their velocity must be changing. It is: from upward to downward, through zero. Zero speed for an instant does not mean zero acceleration. If no force acted, the law says the keys would hang at the top for ever. They do not, which is proof enough that a force is there.

Back to section 2.4

2.4

A friend says: “Newton’s first law means that a moving object keeps a constant acceleration unless a force acts on it.” Fix the sentence, and say why the fix matters.

Replace “acceleration” with “velocity”. A body with no net force on it keeps a constant velocity: the same speed in the same direction. Its acceleration is zero. If a body kept a constant non-zero acceleration with no force acting, its velocity would be changing by itself, which is exactly what the law rules out.

Back to section 2.4

2.5

A book rests on a level table and nobody touches it. How much friction acts on the book?

None at all. Friction before sliding takes whatever value is needed to stop the surfaces slipping, up to a limit, and with no sideways push there is nothing to oppose. The old recipe “friction equals the coefficient times the pressing force” gives only the maximum friction can reach before the book slips, not the friction acting at any moment.

Back to section 2.5

Chapter 3. Forces come in pairs

3.1

Two friends push a stalled scooter in the same direction with 200 N and 150 N. Friction and the rough road resist with 350 N. What is the net force on the scooter, and what does it do?

200 + 150 − 350 = 0 N. The net force is zero, so the scooter’s velocity does not change. If it was at rest, it stays at rest, which is why the friends feel they are pushing hard and getting nowhere. One more push of any size would tip the balance and start it moving.

Back to section 3.1

3.2

A trolley and its load have a mass of 60 kg. You push with 80 N, and friction pushes back with 50 N. What is the trolley’s acceleration?

Net force = 80 − 50 = 30 N. Acceleration = 30 N ÷ 60 kg = 0.5 m/s². Only the net force counts; using the 80 N on its own would give the wrong answer.

Back to section 3.2

3.3

When you jump off a low wall, for the moment you are in the air you feel weightless. Has gravity switched off? What has changed?

Gravity has not switched off; it is what brings you down. What has gone is the normal force. On the ground, the floor pushed up on your feet and your body felt that push as “weight”. In the air, nothing supports you, so there is no push to feel, and you are falling freely. Astronauts in orbit feel the same, for the same reason (Chapter 5).

Back to section 3.3

3.4

If every pull your tug-of-war team gives the rope is matched by an equal pull from the rope on your team, how can your team ever win?

Because the pair acts on different objects: the rope’s pull on you is matched by your pull on the rope, and neither of those is the whole story of what happens to you. To see which way your team moves, add up the forces on your team: the rope’s pull one way and the ground’s friction on your feet the other. The team with the better grip gets more friction from the ground than the rope can match, and goes backward, dragging the rope and the other team with it. A tug of war is won through the shoes.

Back to section 3.4

3.5

A spacecraft far from any planet switches off its engines. It keeps going at the same speed. A friend says: “The push from the engines is stored inside it, and it will slow down when that push runs out.” What is wrong with that, and what does the spacecraft actually carry?

Apply Chapter 2’s test: who exerts “the push from the engines” after they are off? Nobody. There is no stored force, and nothing to run out. What the spacecraft carries is momentum, mass times velocity, and momentum changes only when a force acts. With no force, it keeps the same velocity for ever, just as the arrow would in empty space.

Back to section 3.5

3.5

An astronaut is floating in the middle of a space-station module, out of reach of every wall, holding a spanner. She wants to drift to the window. What should she do?

Throw the spanner directly away from the window. Her push on the spanner is matched by the spanner’s push on her, and the total momentum of astronaut plus spanner stays zero: the spanner goes one way with some momentum, and she goes the other way with the same amount. Because her mass is much bigger, she drifts slowly, but she drifts. There is nothing else to push on, so this is the only way.

Back to section 3.5

Chapter 4. Falling

4.1

A friend drops a glass marble and a cricket ball together from a first-floor balcony about 4 m up, and says the ball will land first because it is heavier. What do you say, and how long does the fall take?

They land together, or so close that you cannot tell. Both are dense, so air barely matters over 4 m, and with air out of the way everything accelerates at 9.8 m/s². The time comes from 4 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t = √(8 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.9 s.

Back to section 4.1

4.2

Two skydivers jump in the same spread-eagled position, one much heavier than the other. The heavier one ends up falling faster. Why, if both are pulled towards Earth with the same acceleration at the start?

Both start at 9.8 m/s², but the heavier skydiver has more weight to balance. Drag grows with speed, so she must reach a higher speed before the drag on her matches her larger weight. Her terminal speed is higher.

Back to section 4.2

4.3

Suppose Stevin and de Groot had done their experiment on the Moon, dropping their two lead balls about 9 m onto a board. What would they have heard, and when?

One thud, as at Delft: the balls fall together whatever they weigh, and with no air there is nothing to separate them. They would have waited longer for it, about 3.3 s instead of 1.4 s, because the Moon’s pull is weaker (9 = ½ × 1.67 × t² gives t ≈ 3.3 s).

Back to section 4.3

4.4

“The flicked coin keeps going forward because it carries the push of your finger with it, and when that runs out it falls.” What is wrong with this picture?

This is the impetus idea from Chapter 2. Once the coin has left your finger, nothing pushes it forward. Its sideways speed simply stays, because a force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going. And it starts falling at once, not when something runs out: the Earth’s pull acts from the first instant.

Back to section 4.4

4.4

A ball is thrown horizontally from a balcony and takes 1.2 s to reach the ground. The same ball is then thrown horizontally from the same spot at twice the speed. How long does it take to reach the ground now, and what changes?

Still 1.2 s. The time to fall depends only on the height and on g; the sideways speed does not touch it. What changes is where the ball lands: twice the sideways speed for the same time means it lands twice as far out.

Back to section 4.4

4.5

A racing car goes round a bend at a perfectly steady 120 km/h. Is it accelerating? If so, which way?

Yes. Its speed is steady but its direction is changing, and velocity includes direction, so its velocity is changing: that is an acceleration. It points towards the centre of the bend, where the friction of the road on the tyres is pulling the car.

Back to section 4.5

Chapter 5. Gravity and orbits

5.1

“Nothing is pushing the Moon along its orbit, so it ought to slow down and eventually stop.” What is wrong here?

The Moon needs no push to keep moving; that is the lesson of Chapter 2. A force is needed only to change motion. Earth’s pull does change the Moon’s motion, but sideways: it bends the path into a circle without speeding the Moon up or slowing it down. No force along the orbit is needed, and none acts.

Back to section 5.1

5.1

Suppose Earth kept the same mass but swelled to twice its radius, and you stood on the new surface. By what factor would your weight change?

It would fall to a quarter. Your weight is Earth’s pull on you, and you would be twice as far from Earth’s centre. Twice the distance, under an inverse-square rule, means one quarter of the pull. Your mass would not change at all.

Back to section 5.1

5.2

In Chapter 4 you dropped a cricket ball and a coin. Now an astronaut of 70 kg and a space station of 420 tonnes are both falling round the Earth. Does the heavier one fall faster and pull away from the lighter one?

No. Everything falls alike when nothing but gravity acts, whatever its mass, because a heavier thing is pulled harder and is exactly that much harder to accelerate. The station and the astronaut fall round the Earth together, so neither drifts towards the other. That is why she floats in the middle of the cabin.

Back to section 5.2

5.2

Anna says a satellite in orbit is in free fall. Tom says it cannot be, because its acceleration is not 9.8 m/s². Who is right?

Anna. Free fall means that gravity is the only force acting, and that is true of a satellite. The acceleration is smaller than 9.8 m/s² only because gravity is weaker up there (about 8.7 m/s² at 400 km), not because anything else is acting.

Back to section 5.2

5.3

A distant object goes round the Sun at an average distance of 50 astronomical units, fifty times Earth’s distance. How long is its year?

About 354 Earth years. Kepler’s third law gives P² = 50³ = 125,000, so P = √125,000 ≈ 354 years. The farther out, the slower the journey and the longer the path.

Back to section 5.3

5.4

Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, has a radius of 2.58 × 10⁶ m and a mass of 1.35 × 10²³ kg. What is the acceleration of free fall at its surface?

About 1.35 m/s², a little less than on our Moon. The acceleration at a world’s surface is GM/R²: 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.35 × 10²³ ÷ (2.58 × 10⁶)² ≈ 1.35 m/s². A hammer dropped on Titan would take about 1.5 s to fall 1.6 m.

Back to section 5.4

5.5

Why do astronomers say that Neptune was the first planet discovered through mathematics, when Galle found it with a telescope?

Because the telescope was pointed where the mathematics said to look. Le Verrier calculated Neptune’s position from the way Uranus was being pulled off course, using Newton’s law of gravitation; Galle only had to confirm that something was there. Uranus itself had been seen through a telescope before anyone calculated where to look.

Back to section 5.5

5.6

Once the propulsion module was in its near-circular orbit of about 153 km by 163 km round the Moon, did it need to keep its engine running to stay there?

No. In orbit it was falling freely round the Moon, held in its curve by the Moon’s gravity alone, like Newton’s cannonball or the Moon round the Earth. An engine is needed only to change from one orbit to another. With no air at the Moon to drag on it, it could circle for a very long time with the engine off.

Back to section 5.6

Chapter 6. Pressure, floating and the ocean of air

6.1

A sharp knife slices a tomato with a gentle push. A blunt knife, pushed just as hard, squashes it. Explain the difference using pressure.

The force is the same, but the sharp edge meets the tomato’s skin along a far narrower strip, so the same force is spread over a much smaller area. Force ÷ area is much larger, and the skin gives way. The blunt edge spreads the same force over a wider strip; the pressure is too low to cut, so the tomato squashes instead.

Back to section 6.1

6.2

In Chapter 4 you saw that a hammer and a feather fell together on the Moon, where there is no air. Suppose an astronaut set up Torricelli’s barometer there. Would the mercury be pulled down by gravity, and how tall would the column be?

Gravity on the Moon is real (the hammer fell), so the mercury would be pulled down into the dish like anything else. But with no air there is nothing to press on the mercury in the dish, so nothing pushes any of it up the tube. The column would drain to the level of the dish: a reading of zero. Gravity does not need air, and the barometer measures the air, not gravity.

Back to section 6.2

6.2

Torricelli’s mercury column is about 76 cm tall. How tall would the column be if he had used water instead, and why?

About 10.3 m. The air can only hold up a column whose weight per area matches the air’s pressure. Water is 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so it takes 13.6 times the height to weigh the same: 0.76 m × 13.6 ≈ 10.3 m. That is also why pumps of Torricelli’s day could not lift water more than about 10 m.

Back to section 6.2

6.3

A rubber suction hook sticks to a bathroom tile for weeks and then falls off. What held it up, and what changed when it fell?

Pressing the cup flat pushed most of the air out from under it. The air in the room then pressed the cup against the tile (about 10 N on every square centimetre of the cup) with nothing inside pushing back. It fell when air had slowly leaked in round the rim: once the pressure under the cup matched the room’s, the pushes balanced and only the weak rubber was holding it.

Back to section 6.3

6.4

A river is in flood, and water is seeping under the levee that protects a town. Engineers stack sandbags in a ring round the leak on the town side and let the leak fill the ring. The small puddle inside the ring stops the leak. How can a little water hold back a whole river?

Only depth matters. Water rises inside the ring until its surface is level with the river’s. Then the pressure at the leak from the water in the ring equals the pressure from the river at the same depth, the pushes balance, and the leak stops flowing. The river’s enormous width is irrelevant, exactly as the length of a reservoir is irrelevant to its dam.

Back to section 6.4

6.5

In Chapter 3 you met the idea that a table cannot push up on a book, because it is “just in the way”. Now a 50,000-tonne ship sits on the sea. Is the water pushing up on it? With how much force, and how does water, which has no stiffness at all, manage to push?

The water pushes up on the hull with a force exactly equal to the ship’s weight, otherwise the ship would be sinking or rising. A table pushes by being squashed a tiny bit and springing back. Water pushes by its pressure: the molecules of water keep hitting the hull’s underside, and because pressure grows with depth, the hits on the bottom of the hull add up to more than the hits on anything above. The push is the sum of countless small collisions. It is as real a force as the table’s, and it points up.

Back to section 6.5

6.5

A loaded cargo ship sails from the Arabian Sea up a river into fresh water. Does it float higher or lower in the river?

Lower. To float, the ship must displace its own weight of water. Fresh water is less dense than sea water (1,000 kg/m³ against about 1,025), so the same weight of fresh water takes up more volume. The hull has to sink a little deeper to push that much aside.

Back to section 6.5

Chapter 7. Energy

7.1

A friend says, “Energy is what makes things go.” Try the swap test on that sentence: replace “energy” with a made-up word, and say whether the sentence still sounds like an explanation. What does that tell you?

“Movability is what makes things go” sounds exactly as convincing, and it says nothing at all. So the original sentence was a label, not an explanation. Energy explains things only when you use its formulas: the ball reaches 4.4 m/s at the bottom because the 0.98 J it had as height has become 0.98 J of motion, and ½mv² = 0.98 J gives 4.4 m/s. The numbers do the explaining; the name never does.

Back to section 7.1

7.2

A scooter is going at 20 km/h. The rider speeds up to 60 km/h. By what factor has the scooter’s kinetic energy increased?

Nine times. The speed has tripled, and kinetic energy goes with the square of speed: 3² = 9. Its momentum has only tripled.

Back to section 7.2

7.3

In Chapter 4 a hammer and a feather, dropped together on the Moon, landed together. Back on Earth, in a vacuum tube, a 1 kg ball and a 0.1 kg ball are dropped from 2 m and land together at the same speed. Does the heavier ball arrive with more kinetic energy, the same, or less, and how can that be if their speeds are equal?

Ten times more. Kinetic energy is ½mv²: same v, ten times the m, ten times the energy. There is no contradiction, because the heavier ball also started with ten times the gravitational energy (mgh with ten times the m). Same speed does not mean same energy; it means energy and mass grew in step. Equal falling speeds are a statement about v, and energy is about mv².

Back to section 7.3

7.3

Does the energy that goes into the gravitational store when you carry a 2 kg bag of rice up one floor depend on whether you take the stairs or the lift? On how fast you climb? On how high the floor is?

Only on the height (and on the mass and g): PE = mgh. Stairs, ramp or lift give the same answer for the same floor. Climbing faster changes how quickly the energy is transferred (that is power, Section 7.5), never how much.

Back to section 7.3

7.4

Back in Chapter 2, people said a rolling ball stops because it “runs out of push”. You learned that nothing was pushing it in the first place: friction was slowing it. Now a classmate says the ball stops because it “runs out of energy”. Is that better?

A little, and still wrong. The ball’s own store of kinetic energy does empty. But the energy has not run out of existence; friction moved it, joule for joule, into warmth in the ball, the floor and the air. “Runs out of push” imagined a push that was never there. “Runs out of energy” imagines a destruction that never happens. The honest sentence is: friction spread the ball’s energy into the surroundings as thermal energy, where it can no longer move the ball.

Back to section 7.4

7.4

An old-style bulb is fed 60 W and gives out 5 W of light. What is its efficiency, and where does the other 55 W go?

Efficiency = 5/60 ≈ 0.083, about 8%. The other 55 W goes out as thermal energy: the bulb and the air around it get warm. All 60 W leaves the bulb every second; only 5 W of it leaves as the light you wanted.

Back to section 7.4

7.5

Which transfers more energy in a day: a 2,000 W geyser switched on for 15 minutes, or a 10 W LED bulb left on for 24 hours?

The geyser. 2,000 W × 0.25 h = 500 Wh, half a unit. The LED: 10 W × 24 h = 240 Wh, about a quarter of a unit. The high-power devices that run for long stretches, geysers and air conditioners, decide most bills; a bulb left on matters far less than it feels like it should.

Back to section 7.5

7.6

A coal-fired power station is about 40% efficient. Does that mean 60% of the coal’s energy was destroyed?

No. All of the coal’s chemical energy is accounted for: about 40% left as electrical energy, and about 60% left as thermal energy, warming the air and the cooling water. Conservation holds exactly. Efficiency measures how much came out in the form we wanted, never how much survived.

Back to section 7.6

Chapter 8. Heat and temperature

8.1

Sample A is warmed with a flame until it has gained 10 kJ. Sample B, identical, is stirred hard by a paddle until it has gained 10 kJ. Afterwards, can a thermometer tell you which was which?

No. Both samples have gained 10 kJ of internal energy, and their particles jiggle in the same way. Heating and doing work are two ways of adding energy; once added, the energy carries no label saying how it arrived.

Back to section 8.1

8.2

The bucket of bath water is left overnight and is at room temperature by morning. Its 418,600 J have gone. Were they used up?

No. They spread into the room: into the air, the floor, the walls, and out through the windows. The room is warmer by an amount too small to notice, because the energy is now shared among a far larger crowd of particles. The total is unchanged; it has only spread out, which is the pattern Chapter 7 found everywhere.

Back to section 8.2

8.2

A block needs 25 kJ to warm from 25 °C to 30 °C. How much does it need to go from 45 °C to 50 °C?

The same 25 kJ. The mass, the material and the size of the temperature change (5 °C) are the same, so the energy is the same. It does not matter where on the scale the five degrees sit.

Back to section 8.2

8.3

A cook lifts the steel lid off a boiling pot with a cloth, then picks up the wooden spoon that has been standing in the same pot with bare fingers. Both have been in the same steam. Why does only the lid need a cloth?

Both are hot. The steel lid conducts energy into the cook’s fingers quickly, so the skin heats fast and it hurts. The wooden spoon conducts about a hundred times more slowly: the handle’s surface gives up its energy to the fingers slowly, and the handle is cooler to begin with because the wood could not carry the pot’s energy along its length. The difference is the rate, as it was with the thali.

Back to section 8.3

8.4

A Styrofoam box keeps ice cold for a picnic. Does the box make cold, keep cold in, or slow energy flowing in from outside? One such box, with walls 2.5 cm thick, sitting in 35 °C air, still lets about 3.4 kg of ice melt a day. What would make it lose less?

It slows energy flowing in: Styrofoam conducts at about 0.010, worse than wool, because it is mostly trapped air. The ice melts anyway, because the flow is slowed and never stopped. Thicker walls, a smaller box (less area), or a cooler place to stand it would all cut the flow. Nothing can “keep cold in”, because cold is not a thing.

Back to section 8.4

8.5

Ice at exactly 0 °C is dropped into water at exactly 0 °C in a perfectly insulated box. Does any ice melt, or any water freeze?

Neither, on balance. There is no temperature difference, so no energy flows from one to the other. Melting needs energy to arrive; freezing needs energy to leave. With nothing flowing, the amounts of ice and water stay as they are.

Back to section 8.5

8.6

“Hot air rises because heat rises.” Chapter 6 found a floating orange and a sinking peeled one. Use it to say what really pushes warm air up.

Heat does not rise; it is not a thing that can rise. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, and the denser air pushes it up, just as water pushes up anything less dense than itself. The orange floated for the same reason. Take away the surrounding cooler air and warm air would go nowhere.

Back to section 8.6

8.6

A fan blows air at the room’s own temperature, 30 °C, over your damp skin, and you feel cool. Why, when the air is no cooler than before you switched it on?

Moving air itself cannot cool you below 30 °C. It sweeps away the damp air next to your skin and replaces it with drier air, so your sweat evaporates faster. Each gram that evaporates carries about 2.4 kJ out of your skin, and your skin’s temperature drops below the air’s. Switch off the fan and the damp air builds up again, evaporation slows, and the cooling fades.

Back to section 8.6

Chapter 9. Vibrations, waves and sound

9.1

A pendulum clock keeps perfect time in Mumbai. It is moved to a city where g is very slightly larger. It now runs fast. Should its pendulum be lengthened or shortened to fix it?

Lengthened. Larger g makes the period shorter, so the clock ticks too often and runs fast. A longer pendulum has a longer period, which cancels the change.

Back to section 9.1

9.2

A parent gives a swing one small push every 3.2 s, and after a minute the child is swinging two metres high. Is energy being made from nothing?

No. Each push does a little work and adds a little energy; resonance makes the twenty small contributions add up instead of cancelling. Meanwhile friction and the air drain some away every swing. The swing grows until the drain per swing matches the push per swing.

Back to section 9.2

9.2

Soldiers crossing a bridge are ordered to break step and walk out of rhythm. Why?

Marching in step delivers a push to the bridge at one steady frequency. If that frequency is near the bridge’s natural frequency, the pushes add up and the bridge could swing dangerously. Breaking step scatters the pushes across many rhythms, so they mostly cancel.

Back to section 9.2

9.3

“The swell carries the water along, the way a thrown ball carries its push inside it.” Chapter 2 had something to say about pushes carried inside things. What really travels in the swell?

Nothing carries a push inside it, and the swell carries no water. Each bit of water is pushed by its neighbour, moves round a small loop, and pushes the next; it is the pattern of pushes that moves on, together with the energy. Unlike the ball in Chapter 2, each bit of water is pulled back by its neighbours after every loop.

Back to section 9.3

9.3

Drop a stone into still water. The rings spread out and, as they spread, get lower. Why?

The stone gave the water a fixed amount of energy. As a ring spreads, that energy is shared around a circle whose circumference keeps growing, so each metre of the ring carries less. Energy goes with amplitude squared, so the amplitude falls as the ring grows.

Back to section 9.3

9.4

On Diwali night you see one firework burst and hear its bang at the same instant. Another, further off, bursts in silence, and the bang arrives a moment later. Why?

Light reaches you almost instantly from both (Chapter 10 says how fast). Sound from the near one takes so little time that you cannot notice the gap. Sound from the far one, at about 349 m/s, takes about 2.9 s for every kilometre, so its bang arrives late. Count the seconds between flash and bang and you can tell how far away the firework was.

Back to section 9.4

9.5

A mayor announces that the new trains will add “only 30 dB” to the noise beside the line. Should the residents be reassured?

No. Each 10 dB is ten times the sound energy, so 30 dB is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times. “Only 30 dB” on top of 40 dB is 70 dB, the level of busy traffic.

Back to section 9.5

9.6

Two wind instruments are the same length. One is a pipe open at both ends; the other is closed at one end. Which can play the lower note?

The closed one. Its fundamental fits a quarter of a wavelength into the pipe, so its wavelength is four times the length; the open pipe’s fundamental fits half a wavelength, so its wavelength is only twice the length. The closed pipe’s fundamental is an octave lower, at half the frequency.

Back to section 9.6

9.7

Two cars sound identical horns as they drive towards you, one at 20 m/s and one at 40 m/s. Which horn sounds higher?

The faster one. The faster the source moves towards you, the more each new compression starts ahead of the last, so the more bunched they are and the more often they arrive.

Back to section 9.7

Chapter 10. Light and seeing

10.1

Someone with an oily, shiny nose dabs face powder on it, and the shine is gone. What did the powder do to the light?

The thin film of oil was a smooth surface, a tiny mirror. It sent the lamp’s light off in one direction, and from that direction you saw a bright highlight. Powder is rough. Light hitting it goes off in every direction, evenly, so no direction gets a highlight. Nothing changed about the light arriving; only what the nose did with it.

Back to section 10.1

10.2

A torch beam looks bright on a wall 1 m away and much fainter on a wall 10 m away. A friend says the light “runs out of push” on the way, the way a rolling ball slows to a stop. What is really happening?

Nothing slows the light. It arrives at full speed either way, and in empty space it would carry on for ever with nothing pushing it, just as the ball on Galileo’s frictionless ramp would. What changes is that the beam spreads out as it travels, because its rays fan out in straight lines from the torch. The same light is shared across a bigger patch of wall, so each bit of wall gets less. The light is spread thinner; none of it has been used up.

Back to section 10.2

10.2

In a camera obscura the picture is upside down. A friend says “the hole flips the light over”. Give the real reason.

The hole does nothing to the light. Light from each point outside travels in a straight line through the hole. Lines from high points pass through heading downwards and land low; lines from low points land high. Because all the lines cross at one small opening, the picture is turned over, top to bottom and also left to right.

Back to section 10.2

10.3

Your friend stands 1.5 m in front of a flat mirror. How far from her is her image? She steps back another 0.5 m. How far is it now?

The image is as far behind the mirror as she is in front: 1.5 m behind, so 3.0 m from her. After stepping back she is 2.0 m from the mirror, her image is 2.0 m behind it, and the distance between them is 4.0 m. The image moved back by the same amount she did.

Back to section 10.3

10.4

Does a ray bend towards the normal or away from it when it goes (a) from air into water, (b) from water into glass, (c) from glass into air?

Towards the normal whenever the light slows down, away whenever it speeds up. Air (1.00) to water (1.333): slower, so towards. Water (1.333) to glass (1.52): slower again, so towards. Glass (1.52) to air (1.00): faster, so away from the normal.

Back to section 10.4

10.5

Why is everything blurry when you open your eyes underwater, and why does a swimming mask fix it?

Most of your eye’s focusing happens where light passes from air (index 1.00) into the cornea (1.38). In water (1.33) the change in index at the cornea falls from 0.38 to 0.05, so the cornea hardly bends the light, and the lens alone cannot bring the picture to a point on the retina. A mask holds a layer of air against your face, so light again enters the cornea from air and the cornea gets its two-thirds back.

Back to section 10.5

10.6

Sunlight takes 8.3 minutes to reach your skin, and you feel its warmth. Does anything from the Sun’s surface travel to you along with the light?

No material does. The Sun’s hot gas stays at the Sun, just as the water of a wave stays in the sea while the wave crosses it. What arrives is energy, carried by the light wave, and you feel that energy as warmth. Light is the clearest case yet of Chapter 9’s rule: a wave carries energy without carrying stuff, and this one does it across 150 million kilometres of empty space.

Back to section 10.6

10.6

Lightning flashes, and you count six seconds before the thunder. How far away did it strike? Does the time the light took matter in your sum?

Sound at about 340 m/s covers about 2,000 m in six seconds, so the strike was about 2 km away. The light from the flash covered that 2 km in about seven millionths of a second, far less than the time it took you to blink, so for this sum you can treat the flash as arriving the instant it happened. Compared with sound, light is as good as instant. Compared with Fizeau’s wheel, it is not.

Back to section 10.6

Chapter 11. Colour, and what light really is

11.1

Why can you only ever see a rainbow with the Sun behind you?

The light that makes a rainbow enters a raindrop, is bent, reflects off the inside of the back of the drop, and is bent again on the way out. After that bounce it is travelling back towards the Sun’s side of the sky. So the only drops that can send colour to your eye are the ones on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun, which puts the Sun behind you.

Back to section 11.1

11.2

A friend says your eyes “see colour” the way a torch shines: the eye sends out something that colours what it looks at. Where is the colour of a ripe mango actually decided?

Nothing leaves the eye, as the sealed dark room showed. The mango’s colour is decided by two things: which wavelengths of the arriving light the mango’s skin sends back and which it absorbs, and how the three kinds of colour-sensing cell in your eye respond to the mix that reaches them. Change the light that arrives and the mango’s colour changes, as this section shows.

Back to section 11.2

11.2

A spot of red light and a spot of green light overlap on a white wall. What colour is the overlap, and why is it not the muddy brown you get from mixing red and green paint?

Yellow. Both lights reach your eye, so your “red” and “green” cones fire together, which is exactly what yellow light makes them do. Paints subtract: red paint removes green and blue, green paint removes red and blue, and together they remove nearly everything, so the mixture is dark and dull. Light adds; paint takes away.

Back to section 11.2

11.3

A friend says the air is blue the way tinted glass is blue, so you see blue when you look through it. What is wrong with that picture?

Look through tinted blue glass at the Sun and the Sun looks blue. Look through the air at the Sun and it looks yellow-white at noon and orange at sunset: the air removes blue from the light that passes straight through it. The blue you see is in the rest of the sky, away from the Sun, where the removed blue has been re-sent towards you. That is scattering, and it is the opposite of tinting.

Back to section 11.3

11.4

Chapter 9’s sound waves were pushes passed along the direction of travel. Could a sound wave in air be polarised the way light can?

No. Polarisation is the direction of a wave’s sideways shaking, and sound in air has none: the air moves back and forth along the direction the sound travels, with no sideways motion to point one way or another. Light does shake sideways, which is why it can be polarised, and why a polarising filter can tell glare from the light of the water beneath it.

Back to section 11.4

11.4

Looking at the glare on a pond through polarised sunglasses, you turn your head sideways through 90°, and the glare gets much brighter. Why?

The glare is light reflected off the water, and it shakes mostly side to side, parallel to the surface. Upright, the glasses pass only up-and-down shaking, so they block most of the glare. Turned through 90°, they pass side-to-side shaking instead, which is exactly the glare’s direction, so now it comes through.

Back to section 11.4

11.5

Your shadow in sunlight has fuzzy edges. Is that light diffracting round you?

Mostly not. The Sun is a disc, not a point, so each point on it casts a slightly shifted shadow of you, and the fuzzy band at the edge is where some of the Sun is hidden and some is not (Section 10.2). Diffraction round something as big as a person does happen, but the spreading is a tiny fraction of a millimetre, far too small to see at that scale. Diffraction shows itself at edges less than a millimetre across.

Back to section 11.5

11.6

Put these in order of wavelength, longest first: X-rays, radio waves, visible light, infrared.

Radio waves (metres and more), infrared (longer than red light), visible light (about 400 to 700 nm), X-rays (far shorter than violet). All four travel at the same speed in empty space; only the wavelength, and with it the number of waves per second, is different.

Back to section 11.6

Chapter 12. Charge and circuits

12.1

The comb pulls the stream of water sideways. In Chapter 3 every push had a partner. Does the water pull on the comb?

Yes, with exactly the same size of force, the other way. You do not notice because you are holding the comb, and the pull is tiny next to your grip. Hang the comb from a thread and bring something charged near it, and it swings. Attraction is never one-sided.

Back to section 12.1

12.1

A rubbed balloon ends up with a charge of −3 units, where one unit is a very large number of electrons. It was rubbed on a woollen scarf. What charge does the scarf have, and how do you know without measuring it?

+3 units. Both started neutral and electrons only moved between the two, so every electron the balloon gained is one the scarf lost. The scarf is short of exactly three units of negative charge, which leaves it positive by three, and the pair’s total is still zero.

Back to section 12.1

12.2

Two coulombs of charge pass a point in a wire every ten seconds. What is the current there, and what is the current at a point on the other side of the same loop?

0.2 A at the first point: two coulombs divided by ten seconds. And 0.2 A at the other point too. Round a single loop, whatever passes one point must pass every other, or charge would be piling up somewhere, and piled-up charge pushes back until the flow evens out.

Back to section 12.2

12.3

The bill says “units consumed”. In Chapter 7 energy was never used up. Reconcile the two.

A “unit” is a kilowatt-hour of energy, and what you buy is its delivery into the flat, where it ends up as light, motion, sound and, finally, warmth spread into the air. None is destroyed; it is spread out and no longer useful. The charge is not consumed either. It stays in the wires, going back and forth fifty times a second.

Back to section 12.3

12.3

In the loop with the resistor and one red LED, where is the current largest: as it leaves the battery’s + terminal, as it passes through the LED, or as it returns to the − terminal?

Nowhere: it is the same at all three points. If it were larger leaving than returning, charge would pile up somewhere in the loop every second, and the pile would push back until the flow evened out. What differs between the three places is the energy each coulomb has left to deliver: most as it leaves, less after the resistor, least after the LED.

Back to section 12.3

12.4

A friend’s torch is dim with old cells. A meter across each old cell, with the torch off, reads 1.5 V, the same as a new cell. “So the cells are fine,” says the friend, “the bulb must be going.” What is wrong with that reasoning?

A meter draws almost no current, so it reads the push with nothing asked of the cell. The bulb draws a real current, and an old cell’s internal resistance takes a large share of the push inside the cell, leaving the bulb less. Swap in new cells: if the torch is bright again, the bulb was fine all along.

Back to section 12.4

12.5

Three identical resistors, each of resistance R, are connected in parallel. Without any arithmetic, what is their combined resistance? And how would you connect the three to get the largest possible total?

R/3. Each branch passes the same current it would alone, so three branches pass three times the current for the same push, which is what a resistor of one third the value would do. For the largest total, connect them in series: 3R, since the charge has to pass through all three in turn.

Back to section 12.5

12.6

Why must a fuse be connected in series with the circuit it protects, and not in parallel with it?

In series, all of the circuit’s current passes through the fuse, so when it grows dangerously large the fuse melts and breaks the only path. In parallel, the fuse would carry only part of the current, and melting it would leave the circuit’s own path intact. A guard has to stand in the doorway, not beside it.

Back to section 12.6

Chapter 13. Magnetism and electromagnetism

13.1

In Chapter 12 a rubbed comb lifted scraps of paper. Will the fridge magnet lift the same scraps? And will the comb lift the ₹1 coin?

Neither. These are two different forces. The comb’s charge pulls feebly on anything at all by separating the charges inside it, enough for paper scraps but never for a coin. The magnet pulls strongly, but only on the few ferromagnetic materials. A charge sitting still has no magnetic effect whatever, as Section 13.3 shows with a compass.

Back to section 13.1

13.1

A plain iron nail, which has never been a magnet, is picked up just as readily by the north end of a bar magnet as by its south end. Why is it never pushed away?

Whichever pole approaches, it magnetises the nail with the opposite pole nearest: a north end makes the near end of the nail a south pole, a south end makes it a north pole. Either way the nearest poles are unlike, and unlike attract. Repulsion needs two things that are already magnets, which is why two fridge magnets can push each other apart and a magnet and a nail never do.

Back to section 13.1

13.2

A compass in Mumbai points north. Does the Earth’s magnetic field at Mumbai point north?

Mostly it points down. The field at Mumbai dips 28° below the horizontal, so a needle free to swing in any direction would tilt its north end into the ground. An ordinary compass is held level and shows only the horizontal part, which does point north. Gilbert saw the dip on his little Earth four centuries ago.

Back to section 13.2

13.3

Your wire over the compass carries 1 A and swings the needle 27°. What two separate changes would each make the swing bigger, and roughly how?

Double the current: the wire’s field doubles to 40 μT at the same distance, and the needle swings to about 46°, since 40 against 38 is nearly an even match. Or halve the distance: at half a centimetre the field is also doubled. The field grows in proportion to the current and in inverse proportion to the distance.

Back to section 13.3

13.4

A small motor’s coil has 50 turns. The maker rewinds it with 100 turns of the same wire carrying the same current. What happens to its turning effect, and why?

It doubles. Each turn is a loop pushed by the same sideways force, so a hundred loops are pushed round twice as hard as fifty. The turning effect grows in proportion to the number of turns, and to the current and the field.

Back to section 13.4

13.5

A coil connected to a meter gives a small kick when a magnet is pushed in. Without changing the magnet or the speed, name two ways to make the kick larger, and say what would happen if you pushed the magnet in and left it there.

Wind more turns onto the coil (double the turns, double the push), or move the magnet faster so that the field through the coil changes more quickly. Pushing the magnet in and leaving it gives one kick as it enters, then nothing: with the field no longer changing, the induced voltage is zero until something moves.

Back to section 13.5

13.6

In Chapter 10 most people drew arrows leaving the eye to touch what it sees. Now that you know what light is, describe what actually happens when you see a lamp across the room.

Charges in the lamp’s hot filament or glowing LED shake back and forth, and the shaking sends ripples of electric and magnetic field in every direction at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Some cross the room and enter your eye, where they are absorbed. Nothing leaves your eye. With the lamp off, no ripples are made and you see nothing, however hard you look.

Back to section 13.6

13.6

In an electromagnetic wave travelling east, the electric field wiggles up and down. In which direction does the magnetic field wiggle, and in which direction does neither of them point?

North and south: the magnetic field is at right angles to the electric field and to the direction of travel. Neither field ever points east, along the wave’s motion. Both wiggle sideways to it, which is what “transverse” meant in Maxwell’s sentence.

Back to section 13.6

Chapter 14. Earth, Moon and Sun

14.1

Astronomers accepted that the Earth turns long before Foucault. What is wrong with saying “we know the Earth turns because we see the Sun and stars go round us every day”?

Seeing the Sun and stars go round is exactly what you would see whether the sky turned or the Earth did; Aryabhata’s boat shows why. The observation cannot choose between the two models. Foucault’s pendulum can, because a swinging pendulum keeps its plane, so when the line of its swing turns relative to the floor, the floor must be turning.

Back to section 14.1

14.2

Work out how high the noon Sun stands in Mumbai (19.08° N) on 21 December, when the Sun is overhead at 23.44° S. Then say in one sentence why that number, and the length of the day, matter more to the seasons than the 5 million km the Earth moves closer to the Sun that month.

The Sun is overhead 23.44° south of the equator, and Mumbai is 19.08° north of it, so they are 23.44 + 19.08 = 42.52° apart; the Sun’s height is 90 − 42.52 = 47.48°, about 47.5°. A Sun at 47.5° spreads the same light over about 35% more ground than a Sun at 85.6°, and shines for about two hours less each day; the extra 7% of sunlight from being closer is smaller than either effect, and it arrives in the coolest month.

Back to section 14.2

14.3

“We see the Moon because it shines.” Chapter 10 found that we see a thing when light from it enters our eyes. Where does the Moon’s light come from, and why does that explain the phases?

The Moon makes no light; sunlight falls on it and some bounces off towards us, so we see the Moon the way we see a white wall in daylight. Because the light comes from the Sun, exactly half the Moon is lit at any time, the half facing the Sun. The phases are the changing fraction of that lit half we happen to be looking at as the Moon goes round us. A Moon that glowed by itself would look full every night.

Back to section 14.3

14.3

Tonight the Moon is full. At roughly what time will it be highest in the sky, and where is the Sun at that moment?

Around midnight. A full Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, so it rises as the Sun sets, is highest when the Sun is lowest, at midnight, and sets at sunrise.

Back to section 14.3

14.4

During a total lunar eclipse the Moon does not go black. It glows a dim copper red. Where is that light coming from?

From the Sun, by way of the Earth’s air. Sunlight grazing past the edge of the Earth is bent slightly inward by the atmosphere, into the shadow, and on the way through the air the blue light is scattered away while the red gets through, as at sunset (Chapter 11). What reaches the eclipsed Moon is the red light of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at that moment, and we see it bounced back.

Back to section 14.4

14.5

“The Moon is in space, and there’s no gravity in space.” Chapter 5 had an answer about the Moon falling round the Earth. What do the tides add to it?

Gravity does not stop at the top of the air. The Earth’s pull reaches 384,000 km to the Moon and keeps it falling round us (Chapter 5), and the Moon’s pull reaches 384,000 km back and moves the whole ocean twice a day. If there were no gravity in space there would be no orbit and no tides, and the causeway at Haji Ali would stay dry.

Back to section 14.5

14.5

Are spring tides something that happens in spring?

No. They happen twice every month, at new Moon and at full Moon, in every season, when the Sun’s and the Moon’s tidal bulges line up and add. The name means the water “springs up”. Neap tides, the smallest, come at the two quarter Moons in between.

Back to section 14.5

Chapter 15. Atoms, stars and the universe

15.1

“Light is a wave, full stop.” Chapter 11 showed you Young’s fringes and Arago’s spot. Does the photoelectric effect mean Chapter 11 was wrong?

No. The fringes are real and only a wave makes them. The threshold in the photoelectric effect is real too, and only packets make it: a dim violet lamp frees electrons at once while a bright red one never does. Light travels like a wave and delivers its energy in packets of hf. Chapter 11 told you half of what light does; this section tells you the other half.

Back to section 15.1

15.1

A made-up metal needs 2.3 eV to free an electron. Red light, 1.63 eV per photon, is shone on it ten times more brightly than before. Does anything come out? What about dim violet light at 3.26 eV per photon?

Nothing comes out under the red light, however bright: each photon carries 1.63 eV, less than the 2.3 eV needed, and photons do not pool their energy. Dim violet light frees electrons at once, each leaving with up to 3.26 − 2.3 = 0.96 eV.

Back to section 15.1

15.2

A packet of chilli powder has been irradiated with gamma rays to kill insects. Is the chilli radioactive?

No. Gamma rays are photons, and photons do not change nuclei; they pass through, kill the insects by ionising the atoms in their cells, and leave nothing behind. The chilli would become radioactive only if radioactive dust had got into it, or if it had been hit with neutrons, which no food plant uses.

Back to section 15.2

15.3

“Energy is never created. So where does the Sun’s energy come from?” Chapter 7 kept a ledger with stores and transfers. What has to go in the ledger to make the Sun’s accounts balance?

Mass. Four million tonnes of the Sun’s mass disappear each second and the same amount of energy appears, at the rate E = mc². Once mass is counted as a store of energy, the Sun’s books balance exactly: nothing is created, and the total of mass-energy stays the same. Chapter 7’s rule survives; it just has a larger ledger than you knew.

Back to section 15.3

15.3

The Sun loses 4 million tonnes of mass every second. Is it in danger of running out soon? Use its mass, 2 × 10³⁰ kg, and its age.

No. Four million tonnes is 4 × 10⁹ kg a second. In 4.5 billion years, about 1.4 × 10¹⁷ seconds, that comes to about 6 × 10²⁶ kg, which is 0.03% of 2 × 10³⁰ kg. Most of the Sun’s hydrogen has not fused yet.

Back to section 15.3

15.4

Why did astronomers expect the Sun to be made of the same stuff as the Earth’s crust, and what did they get wrong?

Many of the Sun’s dark lines matched elements known on Earth, and it seemed natural that a star should be made of the familiar stuff. The mistake was to read the strength of a line as the amount of the element. Line strength depends on temperature too, because only atoms with their electrons in the right places can make a given line. Once Saha’s equation allowed for that, the Sun came out as mostly hydrogen and helium.

Back to section 15.4

15.5

Leavitt’s brighter-looking Cepheids pulsed more slowly. Why could she trust that “brighter-looking” meant “truly brighter”?

Because all her Cepheids were in the Small Magellanic Cloud, at very nearly the same distance from us. When distance is the same for every star, the ones that look brighter are the ones that really are brighter. That is what let the pulse, which anyone can time, stand in for the true brightness, which nobody can see directly.

Back to section 15.5

15.6

Will the Sun become a white dwarf?

Yes. The Sun’s mass is 1 solar mass, below the Chandrasekhar limit of about 1.4, so when its fuel is spent its core can be held up by its electrons. Only a core above the limit must collapse further.

Back to section 15.6

15.7

As the raisin bread rises, do the raisins grow? Do galaxies grow as the universe stretches?

No, and no. The dough between the raisins expands, and the raisins ride apart on it. Gravity holds each galaxy together against the stretching of space, so galaxies keep their size while the gaps between them grow. Only on the largest scales, between galaxies, does the stretching show.

Back to section 15.7

Words worth knowing

Absorption lines
Dark lines in a spectrum where atoms in a cooler gas have swallowed particular colours. Each element has its own set, but how strong the lines are depends on temperature as much as on how much of the element there is. 15.4
Acceleration
The change in velocity divided by the time taken for the change, in m/s². It is a vector: it points in the direction the velocity is changing, which is not always the direction the object is moving. 1.3
Acceleration of free fall (g)
How fast a freely falling object speeds up: about 9.8 m/s² near the ground, which means its speed grows by 9.8 m/s every second. It points towards Earth’s centre, and that direction is what we call “down”. 4.1
Accommodation
The eye changing the shape of its lens to keep the picture sharp: fatter for near things, flatter for far ones. A ring of muscle round the lens does the work. 10.5
Additive and subtractive mixing
Mixing light adds: red + green + blue light gives white, and red + green gives yellow. Mixing paint subtracts: each paint removes some colours from the light, so cyan + yellow paint gives green, and mixing all the paints gives something near black. 11.2
Amplitude
The largest displacement from the resting position: for a water wave, the height of a crest above the still level. 9.3
Archimedes’ principle
The buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces (pushes aside). 6.5
Atmospheric pressure
The pressure of the air around us, caused by the weight of all the air above. At sea level it is about 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, roughly 10 N on every square centimetre. It falls as you climb. 6.2
