Axial tilt
The lean of the Earth’s axis away from upright on its orbit: 23.44°. The axis points the same way in space all year, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for half the year and away for the other half. 14.2
Axis (of rotation)
The line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth turns, once in about 24 hours. It leans 23.44° from upright on the Earth’s orbit, which matters in the next section. 14.1
Barometer
An instrument that measures atmospheric pressure. In Torricelli’s, the height of a mercury column shows how hard the air is pressing on the mercury in the dish. 6.2
Big Bang
The name for the beginning of the universe’s stretching, about 13.8 billion years ago, when everything we can see was far closer together. It happened everywhere; there is no place in space where it was. 15.7
Brewster’s angle
The angle of incidence at which light reflected from a surface is completely polarised. For water it is 53.1° from the normal, and the reflected and refracted rays are then at right angles. It depends on the refractive index: tan θ = n. 11.4
Buoyant force
The net upward push a fluid gives to any object in it, because the fluid’s pressure on the object’s underside is greater than on its top. Some school books call it upthrust. 6.5
Camera obscura
A dark room or box with a small hole in one side. Light from outside passes straight through the hole and forms an upside-down picture on the opposite wall. A pinhole camera is a small one. 10.2
Centripetal force
The inward force, towards the centre, that keeps an object moving in a circle by continually changing its direction. It is always some ordinary force doing the job: tension, friction, gravity, the push of a wall. 4.5
Cepheid
A large, pulsing star whose brightness rises and falls over days or weeks. The slower the pulse, the brighter the star really is, so its pulse gives its distance. 15.5
Chandrasekhar limit
The greatest mass a star can end its life with and still become a white dwarf: about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, about 2.8 × 10³⁰ kg. Heavier cores collapse further. 15.6
Colour constancy
The brain’s habit of judging an object’s colour against its surroundings, so that a white shirt looks white under lamps of different colours. It fails under light of a single colour. 11.2
Compression
A region where the material a sound passes through is momentarily squeezed closer together. Between compressions come rarefactions, where it is stretched apart. 9.4
Conduction
The transfer of energy through a material, or between two touching materials, by particles colliding with their neighbours. No material moves; only the energy is passed on. 8.3
Conductor and insulator
A conductor (a metal, salty water, you) lets charge move through it easily. An insulator (plastic, rubber, glass, dry air) does not. There is no perfect example of either. 12.1
Conservation of energy
The total energy of everything involved in any process stays constant. Energy moves between stores and changes form; it is never created or destroyed. 7.1
Contamination
Radioactive material where it should not be: on skin, hair or clothing, or inside the body. It keeps emitting until it is removed. Being exposed to a beam is not contamination. 15.2
Convection
The transfer of energy by the movement of a fluid. Warmer fluid is less dense and is pushed up by the denser fluid around it, so the fluid circulates in loops. 8.6
Decibel
A unit for how loud a sound is. Every 10 dB more means ten times the sound energy arriving per second; 20 dB more means a hundred times. 9.5
Density
Mass divided by volume: ρ = m/V, in kg/m³. Water is 1,000 kg/m³, sea water about 1,025, steel about 7,800, ice 920. An object floats in a fluid if its average density is less than the fluid’s. 6.5
Diffraction
Waves spreading round an edge or through a small gap. The effect is large when the gap is about the size of the wavelength, and tiny when the gap is much bigger, which is why light usually seems to go straight. 11.5
Diffuse reflection
Light bouncing off a rough surface goes off in all directions. That is how you see a page or a wall from any angle, and it is why nothing is visible in a sealed dark room: there is no light to bounce. 10.1
Dispersion
The spreading of white light into its colours, because a material slows each wavelength by a slightly different amount. Violet is slowed and bent most, red least. 11.1
Distance and displacement
Distance is the length of the path travelled, a scalar. Displacement is the change in position, from start to finish, with its direction: a vector. 1.1
Domain
A small region inside a ferromagnetic metal in which the atoms’ tiny magnets all point the same way. A magnet nearby makes the domains that point along it grow, and the piece becomes a magnet. 13.1
Doppler effect
The change in the frequency of a wave heard or seen when the source and the observer are moving towards or away from each other. Approaching: higher. Receding: lower. 9.7
Drag (air resistance)
The force a fluid, such as air or water, puts on an object moving through it, pointing against the motion. It grows with speed and with the area facing the motion. Unlike the weight, it is zero when the object is still. 4.2
Efficiency
The fraction of the energy put into a device that comes out in the useful form: useful energy output ÷ total energy input, often given as a percentage. 7.4
Electric charge
The property of matter that makes objects attract or repel each other electrically. It comes in two kinds, positive (protons) and negative (electrons). Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. Measured in coulombs (C); one coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons’ worth. 12.1
Electric current
The rate at which charge flows past a point: coulombs per second, measured in amperes (A). 1 A = 1 C/s. Current is the same all the way round a simple loop. 12.2
Electric motor
A coil carrying a current in a magnetic field. The sideways force on the current turns the coil; a commutator and brushes reverse the current every half-turn so that it keeps turning. It converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. 13.4
Electromagnet
A coil of wire carrying a current, usually around an iron core, which acts as a magnet while the current flows and stops when it stops. Its field has the same shape as a bar magnet’s. 13.3
Electromagnetic induction
A changing magnetic field through a loop of wire produces a voltage round the loop, and a current if the loop is closed. No change, no current. The induced current always opposes the change that made it. 13.5
Electromagnetic wave
A travelling wave of electric and magnetic fields. Light is one; so are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All travel at the speed of light in empty space, and differ only in wavelength. 11.6
Electronvolt (eV)
A unit of energy for atoms and light: the energy an electron gains when pushed through one volt, about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Visible photons carry 1.63 to 3.26 eV. 15.1
Ellipse and focus
An ellipse is the closed curve you get when a loop of string is kept taut round two pins: from any point on it, the distances to the two pins add up to the same total. The pins are its two foci. A circle is an ellipse with its two foci in the same place. 5.3
Energy
A number we can calculate for every store that takes part in an event: motion, height, stretch, warmth, fuel, light and others, each with its own formula. Add them up and the total never changes. 7.1
Evaporation
Particles leaving the surface of a liquid as vapour, at any temperature below boiling. The fastest particles leave, so the liquid left behind cools. 8.6
Far side (of the Moon)
The half of the Moon that always faces away from Earth, because the Moon turns once on its axis for each orbit. It gets sunlight for half of every month, so “dark side” is the wrong name. 14.3
Ferromagnetic
Strongly attracted by a magnet, and able to be made into one: iron, nickel, cobalt, gadolinium, and alloys such as ordinary steel. Most metals (copper, aluminium, brass, gold) are not. 13.1
Fission
A heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter ones. The pieces have a little less mass than the original, and the difference comes out as energy. 15.3
Fluid
A substance that flows because it cannot resist a sideways (shearing) push: liquids and gases. A fluid at rest pushes on every surface it touches, at right angles to it. 6.1
Focal point
The point where a converging lens brings parallel rays together. The distance from the lens to it is the focal length. A fatter, more curved lens has a shorter focal length. 10.5
Force
A push or a pull on an object, with a size and a direction. It is always exerted by some other object. Measured in newtons (N), a unit you meet in Chapter 3. 2.1
Free fall
Motion under gravity alone, with nothing pushing, holding or throwing, and air resistance small enough to ignore. A tossed ball is in free fall from the moment it leaves the hand, going up as well as coming down. 1.5
Frequency
How many repeats happen each second, in hertz (Hz). Frequency = 1 ÷ period. 9.1
Friction
The part of the contact force between two touching surfaces that acts along the surfaces and opposes their sliding over each other. It is a real force, with a size you can measure and a direction you can predict. 2.5
Fundamental
The lowest frequency at which a string, pipe or drumhead can vibrate. It sets the note you hear. 9.6
Fusion
Light nuclei joining to make a heavier one. In the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus and 0.71% of their mass becomes energy. It needs a temperature above about 12 million degrees. 15.3
g, the acceleration of free fall
About 9.8 m/s², downwards, everywhere near the Earth’s surface (9.78 to 9.83 depending on where you are). Every object in free fall changes its velocity by 9.8 m/s every second. 1.5
Gauge pressure
Pressure measured relative to the atmosphere’s: positive above it, negative below it. The absolute pressure is the gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure, and it cannot go below zero. 6.3
Generator
A coil turned in a magnetic field, or a magnet turned past a coil. The changing field through the coil induces an alternating voltage. The work done to turn it is what becomes electrical energy; nothing is created. 13.5
Gravitational constant (G)
The number in Newton’s law that sets how strong gravity is: about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N for two 1 kg masses 1 m apart. It is thought to be the same everywhere in the universe. Do not confuse it with g, the acceleration of free fall, which is different on every world. 5.4
Gravitational potential energy
The energy stored by lifting a mass m through a height h against gravity: PE = mgh. It belongs to the object and the Earth together, and only changes in it matter, so you may call any convenient level “zero”. 7.3
Gravity (Newton’s law of gravitation)
Every mass pulls every other mass. The pull is bigger for bigger masses, and it weakens with the square of the distance between their centres. It never switches off; it only gets weaker with distance. 5.1
Harmonic
An overtone that is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental: 2×, 3×, 4× and so on. Strings and open pipes have only harmonics; most drums do not. 9.6
Heat
Energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder one because of the temperature difference between them. Heat is energy moving; an object does not contain heat. 8.1
Hubble’s law
A galaxy’s speed away from us is proportional to its distance: v = H × d, with H about 22 km/s for each million light-years. 15.7
Impetus
A medieval idea: a kind of force that a mover puts into a moving object, which the object carries along and uses up. A forerunner of momentum, but a force is exactly what a moving object does not carry. 2.2
Impulse
A force multiplied by the time it acts. It equals the change in momentum it produces. The same change can come from a big force for a short time or a small force for a long time. 3.5
Inertia
The tendency of an object to stay at rest, or to keep moving in a straight line at constant speed. It is a property, measured by mass. It is not a force. 2.4
Instantaneous speed
The speed at one instant, found by taking the average speed over a smaller and smaller time around that instant. It is what a speedometer shows. 1.2
Interference
What happens when two waves meet. In step, crest on crest, they add and the wave is bigger; out of step, crest on trough, they cancel. The pattern of bright and dark stripes it makes in light is the proof that light is a wave. 11.5
Internal energy
The energy of the particles within an object: their jiggling, spinning and vibrating, and their interactions with one another. Also called thermal energy here. Heating or doing work can increase it. 8.1
Inverse-square rule
A pull that weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter as strong; ten times as far, a hundredth. Gravity follows it, and the same arithmetic will come back later in the book. 5.1
Joule (J)
The unit of energy and of work. One joule is the work done by a force of one newton moving something one metre along its direction: 1 J = 1 N·m. 7.2
Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
The energy transferred by 1 kW in one hour: 3.6 × 10⁶ J. The “unit” on an electricity bill. 7.5
Kinetic energy
The energy of a moving object: KE = ½mv², with m in kilograms and v in metres per second, giving joules. Double the speed and the kinetic energy becomes four times as large. 7.2
Latent heat
The energy needed to change the state of one kilogram of a substance (solid to liquid, or liquid to gas) with no change in temperature. For water: 334 kJ/kg to melt, 2256 kJ/kg to boil at 100 °C. 8.5
Latitude
How many degrees you are north or south of the equator. Mumbai is at 19.08° N; the equator is 0°; the poles are 90°. 14.1
Law
A short statement of a pattern that has held in every case tested, often a single equation. 0.1
Longitudinal wave
A wave in which the material moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels, like a push running down a line of people. Sound is longitudinal. 9.3
Magnetic field
What a magnet (or a current) sets up in the space around it: at every point, a direction (the way a compass’s north end points there) and a strength. Measured in tesla (T); the Earth’s is about 40 to 50 millionths of a tesla. 13.2
Mass
How much matter an object contains, and so how much inertia it has. Measured in kilograms (kg). The same everywhere in the universe, unlike weight (Chapter 3). 2.4
Model
A picture or description of how something works, built from observations, used to explain them and to predict new ones. Models are always simpler than the real thing and usually right only within limits. 0.1
Momentum
How much motion an object has: its mass multiplied by its velocity, in kg·m/s. It points the way the object is moving. Hard to stop means a lot of momentum. 3.5
Natural frequency
The frequency at which something oscillates when it is set going and left alone, with nothing driving it. 9.2
Net force
The total of all the forces acting on an object, after opposing forces have cancelled. Your school syllabus calls it the resultant force. If it is zero, the object’s velocity does not change. 3.1
New Moon, waxing and waning
New Moon: the Moon lies in the Sun’s direction and shows us its night side. Waxing: the lit part grows, from new through first quarter to full. Waning: it shrinks, from full through third quarter back to new. The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days. 14.3
Newton (N)
The unit of force. One newton is the net force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². On Earth, a 100 g mass weighs about 1 N. 3.2
Newton’s first law
A body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion keeps the same speed in the same straight line, unless a force acting on it changes that state. Also called the law of inertia. 2.4
Normal
A line drawn at right angles to a surface at the point where light hits it. Angles in optics are measured from the normal, never from the surface. 10.3
Normal force
The push of a surface on anything resting on it, directed straight out of the surface (at right angles to it). It takes whatever size is needed to stop the object passing into the surface. It equals the weight only for an object at rest on a level surface with nothing else pushing on it. 3.3
Nucleus
The tiny, heavy centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons held by the strong nuclear force. About 10⁻¹⁵ m across, 100,000 times smaller than the atom. 15.2
Observation
Something seen or measured that another careful person could check. Observations are where every investigation starts. 0.1
Orbit
The path of something falling freely under gravity but moving sideways fast enough never to land. A satellite in orbit is not held up; it is falling and missing. 5.2
Order of magnitude
The power of ten of a quantity when it is written as a number times a power of ten. Two things of the same order of magnitude are within about a factor of ten of each other. 0.3
Overtone
Any of the higher frequencies at which something can vibrate, above its fundamental. 9.6
Parallax
The apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when you look from two places. The farther the object, the smaller the shift. For a star, the two places are the Earth six months apart. 15.5
Parsec and light-year
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m. A parsec is the distance at which a star’s parallax is one arcsecond: 3.26 light-years. Both are distances, never times. 15.5
Pascal (Pa)
The unit of pressure. 1 Pa = 1 N/m². 1 kPa = 1,000 Pa. 6.1
Pascal’s principle
A change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is passed on undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of its container. 6.4
Period
The time for one complete repeat of a motion that repeats, such as one full swing out and back. Symbol T, in seconds. 9.1
Perturbation
A small change in an orbit caused by the pull of bodies other than the main one, such as Jupiter’s tug on a comet or Neptune’s on Uranus. The word means “disturbance”. 5.5
Phase (of the Moon)
The shape the Moon shows us, set by how much of its sunlit half faces the Earth. Half the Moon is always lit; the phase is our view of that half from a changing angle. 14.3
Photoelectric effect
Electrons being knocked out of a material by light falling on it. Each electron is freed by one packet of light; the packet must carry at least the energy that binds the electron. 15.1
Photon
A packet of light. Its energy is E = hf: Planck’s constant times the frequency. Brighter light means more photons per second, never bigger ones. 15.1
Pitch
How high or low a sound seems. It is the ear’s reading of the frequency of the sound wave. 9.5
Plasma
A gas so hot that its atoms have lost electrons, leaving charged nuclei and free electrons mixed together. Stars are made of it. 15.4
Polarisation
The direction of a light wave’s sideways shaking. Sunlight shakes in every direction at once. Reflection off water sorts it: the glare off a surface shakes mostly parallel to the surface. 11.4
Position
Where something is, measured from a chosen point in a chosen frame: “3 m from the back of the carriage”, “200 m north of the station”. 1.1
Power
How fast energy is transferred: power = energy ÷ time, in watts. 7.5
Power of ten
The small raised number in 10⁶ or 10⁻³. It counts how many times ten has been multiplied (or, when negative, divided). 10⁶ is a million; 10⁻³ is a thousandth. 0.3
Pressure
Force divided by the area it is spread over: p = F/A. The same force gives a small pressure on a big area and a huge pressure on a tiny one. 6.1
Projectile
Anything thrown or launched that then moves under the pull of the Earth alone. Its sideways speed stays constant and it falls at g, and the two motions are independent, so its path is a curve. 4.4
Radiation
Anything that streams outward from a source: light of every colour, radio waves, X-rays, and the particles and gamma rays that some nuclei throw out. Most radiation is harmless; the harmful kinds carry enough energy per packet to knock electrons off atoms. 15.2
Radioactive
A nucleus is radioactive if it changes by itself, throwing out an alpha particle, a beta particle or a gamma ray as it does so. Most nuclei never do. 15.2
Raman effect
When light of one colour is scattered by a material, a small fraction of it comes out as light of a different colour, and the shift depends on the material. Discovered by C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan in Calcutta in February 1928. 11.6
Ray
A straight line, with an arrowhead, that shows which way light travels. It is a drawing tool. Rays work when light meets things much bigger than its wavelength, which is nearly everything. 10.2
Redshift
A stretching of light waves, so that every line in a spectrum appears at a longer wavelength than in the laboratory. It shows a source moving away, or, for distant galaxies, space stretching while the light travels. 15.7
Reference frame
The thing you choose to measure positions from, with a set of directions: the ground, a train, a boat. All steadily moving frames are equally good; motion only means something relative to a stated frame. 1.1
Refraction
The change in a light ray’s direction when it passes from one material into another, because its speed changes. Slowing down bends the ray towards the normal; speeding up bends it away. 10.4
Refractive index (n)
How much a material slows light: the speed of light in empty space divided by its speed in the material. Water is 1.333, glass about 1.52. A bigger index bends light more. 10.4
Relative humidity
How much water vapour the air has, compared with the most that can be present at that temperature, as a percentage. At 100% there is no net evaporation. 8.6
Resistance
How strongly a component opposes current: R = V/I, in ohms (Ω). A component of 1 Ω passes 1 A for each volt across it. For metals at a steady temperature R is roughly constant (Ohm’s law). For an LED it is not. 12.4
Resonance
What happens when something is driven at or near its natural frequency: each small push arrives in time with the motion and adds to it, so the motion grows large. 9.2
Retina
The layer of light-sensitive cells at the back of the eye. The cornea and lens form a small upside-down image on it, and nerves carry the pattern to the brain. 10.5
Scattering
Light that is re-sent in all directions by the small things it passes: here, the molecules of air. Short wavelengths are scattered much more than long ones, so air scatters blue far more than red. 11.3
Short circuit
An unintended path of very low resistance across a supply. It carries a very large current and heats up dangerously. A fuse or circuit breaker in series opens the circuit when the current is too high. 12.6
Solar and lunar eclipse
Solar eclipse: the Moon’s shadow falls on part of the Earth, at new Moon. Lunar eclipse: the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon, at full Moon. Neither is a phase; both are shadows. 14.4
Solstice and equinox
The two solstices (around 21 June and 21 December) are the days the noon Sun is highest or lowest for the year; the Sun is then overhead at one of the tropics. At the two equinoxes, in March and September, the Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are about 12 hours long everywhere. 14.2
Specific heat capacity
The energy needed to warm one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius, in J/(kg·°C). Water: 4186. Aluminium: 900. Steel: about 450. Wood: about 1700. Sand: about 800. 8.2
Spectrum
The band of colours that white light spreads into, red to violet. It is continuous: the colours shade into each other with no lines between them. Naming seven of them is a habit; the light itself has no lines in it. 11.1
Speed
How fast something covers distance: distance travelled divided by the time taken, in metres per second (m/s). A scalar. 1.2
Speed of light (c)
299,792,458 m/s in empty space, exactly, by definition since 1983. About 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In water light travels at three-quarters of this. 10.6
Spring and neap tides
Spring tides: the largest tides, at new and full Moon, when the Sun’s and Moon’s bulges line up. Neap tides: the smallest, at the quarter Moons, when they partly cancel. “Spring” here means springing up, and happens all year. 14.5
Temperature
A measure of how fast, on average, the particles of an object are moving. It is what a thermometer reads. Energy flows from higher temperature to lower, whatever the sizes of the objects. 8.2
Terminal speed
The steady speed a falling object reaches when the drag on it has grown to equal its weight, so the net force is zero. Both forces are still there; they cancel. 4.2
Theory
A well-tested explanation, checked many times by many people. To a scientist, “it’s only a theory” makes no sense: a theory is as good as explanations get. 0.1
Thermal conductivity
How quickly a material passes energy along by conduction, in W/(m·K). Metals score in the tens and hundreds; wood, wool and air score well below one. 8.3
Thermal energy
The energy of the random jiggling of the molecules inside stuff. Friction and squashing turn ordered motion into it. School calls this the internal (thermal) store. 7.4
Thought experiment
An experiment reasoned through in the head because it cannot be done for real, built on a trend that has been measured as far as it can be. Galileo’s flat ramp is the classic one. 2.3
Tidal bulges
The two broad heaps of ocean water, one towards the Moon and one away from it, raised by the difference in the Moon’s pull across the Earth. Water flows along the surface into them; it is not lifted up. 14.5
Timbre
The quality that makes two instruments playing the same note sound different: the particular mix of overtones each one produces. 9.6
Transformer
Two coils on one iron core. A changing current in one induces a voltage in the other, in proportion to the turns. It works only with a changing (alternating) current. 13.5
Transverse wave
A wave in which the material moves across the direction the wave travels, like ripples on water or a flicked rope. 9.3
Umbra and penumbra
The umbra is the cone of full shadow behind a body, where the Sun is completely hidden. The penumbra is the lighter region round it, where the Sun is only partly covered. 14.4
Uncertainty
The range within which a measurement’s true value probably lies. Every measurement has one. As a percentage: uncertainty ÷ value × 100. 0.2
Unit
An agreed amount of something, such as one metre or one second, that everyone measures against. A measurement is a number of units: 20 metres, 3.5 seconds. 0.2
Vector and scalar
A vector has a size and a direction (displacement, velocity, force). A scalar has a size only (distance, speed, mass, time). 1.1
Velocity
Displacement divided by the time taken: speed together with a direction. A vector. A round trip has an average velocity of zero whatever its average speed. 1.2
Virtual image
A picture formed where light rays seem to come from, when traced back in straight lines, although no light actually passes through that place. The image in a flat mirror is virtual. 10.3
Voltage
The energy transferred by each coulomb of charge as it passes between two points, in joules per coulomb, which are volts (V). A 9 V battery gives each coulomb 9 J. Across a component, the voltage is the energy each coulomb delivers there. Also called potential difference. 12.3
Watt (W)
One joule per second. A kilowatt (kW) is 1,000 W. 7.5
Wave
A disturbance that travels away from where it was made, carrying energy. The material it travels through moves back and forth, or round in small loops, and ends up where it started. 9.3
Wavelength
The distance from one crest to the next (or trough to trough). Symbol λ, in metres. 9.3
Weight
The force with which the Earth (or whatever planet you are on) pulls an object down. It equals the mass times the local strength of gravity: on Earth about 9.8 newtons for every kilogram. 3.2
Weight, and feeling weightless
Weight is the pull of gravity on an object: a force, in newtons. You feel your weight only through whatever pushes back on you, like the floor. Fall freely, and nothing pushes back, so you feel weightless although your weight is unchanged. Astronauts in orbit are in this state all the time. 5.2
Wet-bulb temperature
The lowest temperature that evaporation alone can bring a wet surface to, in air of a given temperature and humidity. Damp air gives a floor only a little below the air temperature; dry air gives a floor far below it. 8.6
White dwarf
What is left of a Sun-like star when its fuel is gone: a core held up by the pressure of electrons that cannot be squeezed closer together. This degeneracy pressure is a quantum effect, far stronger than electric repulsion. 15.6
Work
Energy transferred by a force pushing or pulling something along its own direction: work = force × distance. A force that moves nothing does no work, however hard it pushes. 7.3

About the models and numbers in this book

Where the numbers come from

Most numbers in this book are real measurements: the speed of sound and of light, the strength of gravity, the size of the Earth and the distance to the Moon, the heat it takes to warm water, the voltage of a cell. They come from MIT OpenCourseWare and OpenStax (listed in Where this book comes from), checked against standard references such as NIST, NASA, ISRO and the India Meteorological Department, and every calculation was redone by computer. They are rounded to make them easy to read, so another book may give slightly different last digits.

A few numbers are made up on purpose to make an example easy to follow, like the mass of an imaginary trolley. Whenever a number is invented, the text says so.

The models, and where they break

Points and blocks. Drawing a cricket ball, a car or the Moon as a single dot is perfect for working out how it moves as a whole. It says nothing about spin, squashing or what is inside.

No friction, no air. Many examples switch friction and air off, the way Galileo did, to show the simple rule underneath. Real things do have friction and air, and the book always comes back to say how much difference they make.

Rays of light. A ray is a pencil line showing which way light travels. It is excellent for mirrors, shadows and lenses. It cannot explain colours in a soap bubble or the bright spot in a shadow; for those, light behaves as a wave.

Field lines. The lines drawn around a magnet show which way a compass would point and where the pull is strongest. They are a drawing, not strings in space.

The circuit as a loop of rope. Thinking of the charges in a wire as a loop of rope that the battery keeps moving is a good model for why the current is the same everywhere in a simple loop. Like every analogy, it stops working if you push it too far, and the text says where.

The Sky explorer and diagrams of the Solar System. Drawn to scale, the Sun, Earth and Moon would be dots too small to see across a screen-wide gap. So the sizes are enlarged, and the explorer says when it does this. The tidal bulges are drawn hugely exaggerated: in the open ocean the real ones are around a metre high, on a planet 12,700 kilometres across.

Diagrams in general. Every picture has been chosen to show one thing clearly. When you meet a new one, ask the question this whole book is about: what does this show truthfully, and how do we know?

Further adventures

When you have finished this book, the adventure does not stop. Here are some places to go next, all free.

MIT OpenCourseWare. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology puts many of its courses online for anyone. Much of this book was built on them.

  • Physics Demonstration Videos: short films of the experiments MIT shows its students, from spinning wheels to glowing tubes. For watching: the real versions need a lab.
  • When you are older: Classical Mechanics (8.01SC), Electricity and Magnetism (8.02), Vibrations and Waves (8.03SC) and Introduction to Astronomy (8.282J).

OpenStax. Free textbooks written by teachers: Physics for school, and Astronomy 2e for the sky.

PhET simulations. The University of Colorado’s free physics simulations: build circuits, launch projectiles, float blocks, send waves down a string.

phyphox. A free phone app from RWTH Aachen University that turns your phone’s sensors into a laboratory: acceleration, sound, magnetic field, light. Several Try it at home boxes use it.

The Feynman Lectures on Physics. The lectures Richard Feynman gave to first-year students at Caltech in the 1960s are free to read online. They are hard, and wonderful. Try Chapter 1 of Volume I when you are fourteen or fifteen.

In Mumbai. The Nehru Planetarium in Worli has been showing people the sky since 1977. On National Science Day, 28 February, the anniversary of the Raman effect, many labs and universities in India open their doors.

In the kitchen. Every Try it at home box is a real experiment. Keep a notebook: what you predicted, what happened, what surprised you. That notebook is exactly what Galileo, Faraday and Raman kept.

This book is free to read, share and adapt under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 licence: give credit, don’t sell it, and share what you make from it the same way. It adapts material from MIT OpenCourseWare and OpenStax, both under the same licence; neither endorses this book. The typefaces, software and map data inside it keep their own licences.

ETHW, IEEE Milestone: First Millimeter-wave Communication Experiments by J.C. Bose, 1894-96

  • Story: Invisible waves in Calcutta1895 demonstration at Presidency College: 60 GHz over 23 m through two walls, rang a bell and detonated gunpowder; wavelengths 2.5 cm to 5 mm, chosen partly for the small laboratory; spark transmitter, coherer, dielectric lens, polariser, horn antenna, cylindrical diffraction grating; IEEE Milestone plaque dedicated 15 Sept 2012 (fetched 2026-10-28)

Encyclopedia.com, Meghnad Saha

  • Story: What the stars are made ofSaha: Presidency College 1911; lecturer at University College of Science 1916; left India September 1919; 'On Ionization in the Solar Chromosphere', Philosophical Magazine 1920; Fowler and Milne in London (fetched 2026-10-28)

MacTutor, Chandrasekhar and Eddington

  • Story: The limit worked out at seafirst limit 0.91 MSun (mean molecular weight 2.5), revised to 1.44; RAS meeting January 1935; Eddington's 'I think there should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way!'; not allowed to reply; wrote to Rosenfeld; rebuttal with Møller; 'has always operated with preconceived ideas' (fetched 2026-10-28)

MacTutor, Georg Simon Ohm

  • Story: What goes roundOhm at the Cologne Jesuit Gymnasium (well-equipped lab; experiments after Ørsted 1820); 1826 papers modelled on Fourier; leave on half pay in Berlin from August 1826; Die galvanische Kette 1827 'received with little enthusiasm', older German physicists unconvinced by the mathematical approach, Caneva on its lack of clarity; resigned Cologne March 1828; Nuremberg 1833 (title of professor, not a chair); Copley Medal 1841; Munich chair 1852; died 6 July 1854 (fetched 2026-10-28)

MacTutor, Huygens biography (derived the law of centrifugal force for uniform circular motion; Horologium Oscillatorium 1673) and Wikipedia, History of centrifugal and centripetal forces (De vi centrifuga 1659 coined 'centrifugal'; Newton coined 'centripetal' in the 1684 manuscript sent to Halley); both checked 2026-10-28, neither in research/history.md

  • Story: Why there is no force flinging you outthe opening scene; Huygens being in Paris in 1673 is UNSOURCED in the corpus
